### 2.7 Routes and GPX Import

**Routes** are defined on the road graph (4.4): an ordered list of edges with direction, start/finish markers, lap count and optional segments (sprints, KOMs). Routes are stored as TOML/JSON in the world package. A route editor in `world-builder` lets authors click edges together and set laps and segments.

**GPX import:** the user imports a GPX file (e.g. a real ride or a planned route) and rides it as a route.

1. **Parse** the GPX track (`gpx` crate); accept tracks and routes, and join multiple segments.
2. **Region check:** compute the bounding box. If no installed world package covers it, offer to download the matching package(s).
3. **Map matching:** snap the GPS points onto the road graph using an HMM-based matcher (the standard Viterbi approach used by OSRM / Valhalla), implemented in `ocw-world`. The result is the ordinary route format (edge list).
4. **Elevation from our DEM, not from the GPX:** GPS elevation is noisy, so the route uses the already smoothed road profile (4.3). The GPX elevation is only shown for comparison.
5. **Problems are reported, not hidden:** sections more than ~30 m from any road, or on roads missing from the package, are highlighted. The user can accept a detour or cancel.
6. **Result:** a personal route stored locally. It can optionally be shared with friends or used for a group ride; the server receives only the edge list, not the GPX.

GPX upload is also available in the web companion, where map matching runs on the server with the same `ocw-world` code (2.10).

**Implementation (decided):**

- **Route format:** `GraphRoute` = name, loop flag, steps: `edge <stable ID> <from m> <to m>` (metres from the edge's first vertex, `from > to` = against it) or `turn` (an explicit U-turn, required for out-and-back routes, 2.2.2). The first step may start and the last end part-way along an edge. Stored in the package as the tagged section `ROUT` (4.7), or as a standalone text file `ocw-graph-route 1` that names its package and graph fingerprint (`package NAME HASH`). Lap count, start/finish markers and segments (sprints, KOMs) come later as more lines / fields. Binary in the package and plain text outside instead of TOML/JSON: no new dependencies in `ocw-world`, and the file stays readable.
- **Resolving** a stored route against a graph checks every stable ID and the continuity of the steps (each starts where the previous one ends; a U-turn reverses the same edge) and reports the first break.
- **GPX parsing:** a small hand-written scanner in `ocw-world` (`gpx.rs`) instead of the `gpx` crate, so `ocw-world` stays dependency-free and wasm-safe. GPX 1.0 / 1.1, tracks (segments joined) and routes, namespace prefixes, comments, CDATA, entities.
- **Map matching** (`matching.rs`): points thinned to ≥ 10 m; up to 6 edges within 50 m per point as states, in each direction a one-way road allows; emission Gaussian (σ 10 m); transition `exp(−|road distance − straight distance| / 25 m)` with the road distance from a bounded Dijkstra (3 × straight distance + 300 m) over riding directions, no turning back at vertices; a U-turn on an edge costs 60 m extra; backwards jitter of up to 8 m on one edge costs 3 × its length. Points without a road within 50 m, or not connected to the previous point, are skipped and reported; more than 1.5 km of skipped track is an error ("the roads of this package do not connect the track near point N"). A track ending within 50 m of its start on the same edge becomes a loop starting at that edge's vertex. The report lists stretches more than 30 m from the matched road and skipped points.
- **Tools:** `world-builder gpx --world PKG --gpx FILE [--name N] [--route-file F] [--dry-run]` matches and stores a route in the package; `world-builder route --world PKG --from LAT,LON --to LAT,LON --name N` stores the shortest main-road route; `world-builder routes --world PKG [--from OLD] [--remove N] [--export-gpx]` lists and checks the routes (and carries them over from an older build, 4.4). The desktop app rides one with `--world PKG --route NAME` (or `--route FILE` for an `ocw-graph-route` file) or matches a GPX file at the start with `--route-gpx FILE`; the headless server takes `--world PKG --route NAME`.
- **Elevation** comes from the package's smoothed road profiles (step 4); GPX elevation is read but not used yet.

### 2.8 Training, Export and Strava

- **Structured workouts:** our own open workout format (TOML/JSON: intervals, targets as % FTP, cadence hints). Import of the open formats `.erg` / `.mrc` and FIT workout files. Workouts use ERG mode (5.3).
  - **Implementation (decided, Phase 2 basics):** module `ocw_sim::workout` (pure, wasm-safe, so the web companion can show and later edit workouts; `serde` + `toml` are its only new dependencies). A workout is a flat list of segments (steady or ramp target in watts or as a fraction of FTP, or *free*: no target), with optional cadence hint and text, plus timed text cues; intervals are expanded when parsing. Targets are resolved with the rider's FTP only when riding.
  - **Format** (`.toml`): `name`, `description`, `units = "ftp" | "watts"` (how bare numbers are read; `"250W"` / `"88%"` strings override it), `[[steps]]` with `type = "steady" | "ramp" | "intervals" | "free"`, `duration` (seconds, `"M:SS"`, `"H:MM:SS"`, `"90s"`, `"5min"`), `power` or `from`/`to`, optional `cadence`, `text`; intervals take `repeat`, `on`, `off` (each with its own duration and target); `[[cues]]` with `at`, `text`, optional `duration` (default 10 s). Unknown keys are errors (typos), messages name the step. Examples in `crates/ocw-sim/test-data/workouts/`.
  - **Import:** `.erg` (minutes + watts, absolute) and `.mrc` (minutes + % FTP): the `[COURSE HEADER]` / `[COURSE DATA]` / `[COURSE TEXT]` text format. Consecutive data points form a ramp or steady segment, a repeated minute is a step; the `MINUTES WATTS|PERCENT` header line decides the unit (else the extension). Lenient (any case, CRLF, comments, blank lines, extra columns), errors with line numbers; distance-based courses are refused. FIT workout import is still open.
  - **Workout clock:** pedalling time, not wall-clock time. It waits at 0:00 until the rider first pedals, runs while power > 0 and through up to 3 s without power, then pauses until power returns; `workout pause` / `resume` by hand. The ride itself never pauses (3.2); the ERG target stays set while the clock pauses.
  - **Client-side only:** a workout is target control between the client and its trainer; the server only receives the rider's power, as in any ride (6.1), so the protocol is unchanged. Shared workouts in group rides or events (everyone on the same step) need the server and come later.
  - **Desktop client:** `--workout FILE` (loaded and started); console `workout load FILE`, `workout start [FILE | --example NAME]`, `workout stop|skip|pause|resume|status|list`.
  - **FTP (decided):** one function (`workout::ftp_w`): `--ftp` on the command line wins (an explicit choice for this session), else the riding profile's `ftp_w` from `riders.toml` (3.2.1), else 200 W.
  - **Menu (decided, Ride → Workouts):** lists the user's workout files in `<user data dir>/ocw/workouts/` (`.toml`, `.erg`, `.mrc`, by file name; files that do not parse are left out), then the four examples of `crates/ocw-sim/test-data/workouts/`, which are **built into the app** (`include_str!`, ~2 KB) so that installed builds without the source tree (kiosk) offer them too. Choosing one loads and starts it and closes the menu, so the workout panel shows; while one runs the page also shows its step, *Skip step* (the menu stays) and *Stop workout* (closes). No confirmation: starting a workout ends nothing (the trainer mode returns when it stops). The profile preview of 3.2.1 is still open. HUD panel: target, step and time left, next step, cue text, and the workout's profile coloured by training zone with the progress; its content is computed in `ocw_sim::workout::WorkoutPanel`.
- **Export:** every ride is saved as a **FIT** activity file (power, cadence, heart rate, speed, distance, elevation, virtual GPS track). Ridden routes can also be exported as **GPX**. A FIT writer is needed; existing Rust crates mainly read FIT.
  - **Implementation (v1.6):** our own dependency-free, wasm-safe writer crate `ocw-fit` (file_id, device_info, timer events, 1 Hz records, laps, session, activity; sport cycling, sub-sport virtual activity).
  - **Checked on Strava (2026-11-17, the user):** a ride recorded with S (`2026-11-16_15-47-50.fit`, 7.9 min on Tenerife) uploads as a **Virtual Ride** with its GPS track, map and elevation, like other virtual-ride apps' activities; the map shows once a map style is chosen in Strava. **Kept as is: sport cycling, sub-sport virtual activity** (a test with sub-sport generic also showed the track, but would count the ride like an outdoor one); no change to `ocw-fit` needed.
  - **Laps (decided):** the activity carries lap marks (elapsed seconds); each mark starts a new `lap` message with its own totals (time, distance, work, averages and maxima), neighbouring laps share the boundary record so their times and distances add up to the session's, and `session.num_laps` counts them. The desktop client marks a lap at each workout start, step change (also by skip), end and stop, and at an event's start (GO), each event lap of a multi-lap race or time trial (from the own progress and the lap length) and the own finish (or the event's end). Joining an event (the countdown) is no lap of its own. Marks within half a second of the ride's first or last record are dropped. The desktop client records the local rider once per second and saves the ride on exit (rides under one minute are dropped) or with `ride.save` to `<user data dir>/ocw/rides/<UTC start>.fit`, with a `.toml` sidecar (title, description). The virtual GPS track is the road position unprojected with the route's geographic origin (`ocw_world::geo`); procedural test routes have none.
- **Strava upload for finished rides:**
  - **Account linking via our backend:** Strava's OAuth flow requires a client secret, which must not ship in the desktop app. The backend handles the OAuth exchange and stores the refresh tokens encrypted. Tokens never reach the desktop app or the browser.
  - **Upload flow:** when a ride ends, the client writes the FIT file and sends it to our API. The API uploads it via the Strava `uploads` endpoint as `VirtualRide`, polls Strava for the upload status and reports the result to the client.
  - **Options:** automatic upload after each ride, or a manual "Upload" button in the training history. Title and description can be edited; a default title is generated (route name, world).
  - **Offline:** uploads are queued and sent later.
  - **Constraints:** Strava API terms and rate limits apply. Beyond a small number of athletes, Strava requires an app review – apply early. The virtual GPS track uses real coordinates of the route; this is common practice for virtual rides, but it must be labelled as virtual.
  - Other services (intervals.icu, TrainingPeaks) may follow later.
  - **Simple upload in the browser (v4.76, the default for every rider):** no API application – Strava's own web upload page takes our FIT files (they arrive as Virtual Rides with the GPS track, checked by the user 2026-11-17). See 2.8.1 *Simple upload*.
  - **Interim desktop upload (v1.6, until the backend's Strava integration in Phase 5; since v4.76 the *advanced* way):** a user may register their *own* Strava API application and give the desktop app its client id and secret (`OCW_STRAVA_CLIENT_ID` / `OCW_STRAVA_CLIENT_SECRET` or `<user config dir>/ocw/strava.toml`). No credentials ship with the app; without them the feature is off. The client then runs the OAuth authorization-code flow itself (browser, redirect to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/strava/callback`), stores the tokens in `<user config dir>/ocw/strava-token.toml` (mode 0600) and refreshes them. A background thread uploads every **Strava recording (S … S)** not yet on Strava – never a whole saved ride (Q6, v5.07) – (`VirtualRide`, trainer), automatically while the setting `strava.auto_upload` is on (else when the rider asks), polls the upload status and keeps a sync state (`rides/strava-sync.toml`: uploaded / processing / failed with exponential backoff / rejected). Console: `strava.connect`, `strava.sync`, `strava.status`, `strava.disconnect`. Once the backend handles Strava, this path is replaced by the upload to our API described above.


#### 2.8.1 Strava recording with S and ride photos (planning, 2026-11-16, v4.11)

- **Recording without Strava set up, uploaded later: decided (2026-11-18, the user):** "allow strava recording even if strava not set up. just save the recording locally and do the upload when credentials provided." S always records, set up or not (true since v4.76); the recording is saved locally (its folder in `~/Activities/OCW`, below) and kept as **waiting for upload**. When Strava credentials become available – at the next start, **or while the app runs** (the API credentials appear in the config / secrets file or the environment, or `strava.connect` completes) – every waiting recording is uploaded automatically, oldest first, through the existing API sync (2.8.1 *Interim desktop upload*), except the ones marked as uploaded by hand (*Simple upload*). The ride page shows the recording's state (*waiting for Strava set-up* / *uploading* / *on Strava* / *failed – retry*), and a notice says when the waiting recordings went up ("3 recordings uploaded to Strava"). *Proposal, built as proposed (v4.86):* the catch-up upload asks once before uploading more than three waiting recordings ("Upload 12 waiting recordings to Strava? Yes / Pick / No"; *Pick* opens the training history's waiting rides, *No* leaves them waiting; console `strava.waiting yes|pick|no`, `strava.sync --waiting`); the browser app has no API upload yet, so there the simple upload stays the way (its ride page says *upload in your browser*). Whole rides never go to Strava (Q6, v5.07); with the setting `strava.auto_upload` off the waiting recordings are not uploaded when the credentials come – they wait for the rider's upload (the ride page's *waiting – upload now*, `strava.sync --waiting`). **Built (v4.86):** the waiting state in `strava-sync.toml`; the desktop watches `strava.toml` every 3 s while the credentials are missing (the environment is read at the start only) and starts the Strava thread when they come; the ride page's *Strava upload* row and the notices as above.
- **Where an S recording is written: decided (2026-11-18, the user):** "the activity and photos for a Strava (S … S) recording should always be written to the user's home dir – do we have a dir there already? then put it there in a subfolder (ISO date and location)." The user's folder OCW already has in the home directory is the photos folder **`~/Pictures/OCW`** (the platform's Pictures directory + `OCW`, setting `photos.folder`, 2.11 Q3, v4.74), so **every S recording gets its own subfolder there, named by its ISO date and its location**, holding **the recording's FIT file and its photos**: e.g. `~/Pictures/OCW/2026-11-18 Puerto de la Cruz/OCW 2026-11-18 10-05 Puerto de la Cruz.fit` and `… photo 1.jpg`. Written **always** – whether the ride is later uploaded by the browser, by the API or not at all; the ride history and the API sync find the files there (the internal copy in `<data dir>/ocw/rides/` may stay as the history's own record). *Details not decided (proposals):* the folder name is `YYYY-MM-DD <place>` with the place the recording **started** in – the nearest town or village from the package's places (`PLCE`, v4.77), else the route's name, else the world's name – and a second recording at the same place on the same day gets ` 2`, ` 3`, …; the time goes into the file names, not the folder; characters every system accepts. The simple upload's step text then points to this folder (the separate `rides/strava-upload/` copy goes away), and 2.8.1 Q7 (a copy in Downloads) is superseded by it. *Browser:* the same subfolder inside the folder chosen with *Photos folder: choose* (File System Access API); without it, downloads named `OCW <date> <place> …`. Built (v4.85, see below). **Changed the same day (the user): "instead of `~/Pictures/OCW` put it to `~/Activities/OCW`. Make it user configurable in config file and UI Menu → Settings."** – the recordings' folder is **`~/Activities/OCW`** (the home directory + `Activities/OCW`, on every platform), a setting of its own: `activities.folder` in the settings file (the local config file, 3.2.4; `~` allowed; empty = the default) and a row in **Menu → Settings** (General or Captures: shows the folder, *Change* opens a folder picker on the desktop / types a path, *Default* resets it; the browser's row is the File System Access folder choice). Each S recording's subfolder (ISO date and location, as above) is created there; screenshots and photos taken outside an S recording stay in the photos folder (`photos.folder`, `~/Pictures/OCW`). *(The folder `~/Pictures/OCW` above is replaced by `~/Activities/OCW` for recordings.)* **Changed again the same day (the user): "Remove the photo folder and just use the activities folder and put everything there."** – there is **one folder for everything OCW saves for the user: `~/Activities/OCW`** (setting `activities.folder`, Menu → Settings); the separate photos folder and its setting `photos.folder` (2.11 Q3, v4.74) go away. S recordings get their subfolder there as above; screenshots and photos taken outside an S recording go into the same folder too. *Proposal for the details (not decided):* those loose photos and screenshots go into a per-day subfolder `YYYY-MM-DD` (or straight into `~/Activities/OCW`), and an existing `photos.folder` value or files in `~/Pictures/OCW` are left where they are (no moving of the user's files) with a one-time notice. **Built (v4.85), the proposals as proposed:** *Naming* (`ocw_client::activities`, shared by both apps): a recording's folder `YYYY-MM-DD <place>` – the place where it **started**: the nearest place of the package's places (`PLCE`) of rank ≤ village (`PLACE_MAX_RANK` = 2: cities, towns, villages; hamlets and localities never) within 5 km (`PLACE_RADIUS_M`), else the route's name, else the world's name, else "Ride"; the date in the world's local date (the place's time zone, `WorldPlace`); a folder already there gets ` 2`, ` 3`, …; the files `OCW YYYY-MM-DD HH-MM <place>.fit` and `OCW YYYY-MM-DD HH-MM <place> photo N.jpg`; only characters every system accepts (the simple upload's `safe_file_part`, at most 60 for the place). Screenshots and photos outside a recording go into the day's folder `YYYY-MM-DD/` (the machine's local date) under their names as before (`OCW-<time>.jpg`, `OCW-<ride>-photo-N.jpg`). *Desktop* (`apps/desktop/src/activities.rs`): setting `activities.folder` (default `~/Activities/OCW`, `~/…` or a path; `OCW_ACTIVITIES_DIR` sets the default in test runs, the unit tests never use the home folder), console `activities.folder [PATH|default|choose]`, menu *Settings → Account → Folders* (the Settings page is full): *Activities folder: change* (the system's folder picker on a thread – `zenity` or `kdialog` on Linux, PowerShell's folder dialog on Windows, `osascript` on macOS; without one, and in test runs, the console opens with `set activities.folder ` to type the path) and *Activities folder: default*. The photos folder (`~/Pictures/OCW`, `photos.folder`, its console command and `OCW_PHOTOS_DIR`) is removed; the files saved there stay and are found through their sidecars' `path` (the history, `history.photos`, the Strava recordings); an old `photos.folder` line in `settings.toml` is kept and reported as an unknown setting when the settings are read (the notice). S makes the recording's folder; while it runs the ride photographer's photos go **only** there (their sidecars in `rides/<ride>/photos/` keep the `path`, so the history, `history.photos` and the API sync find them); its stop – S, `ride.save`, a ride switch, quitting – writes the FIT file there; the internal record in `rides/strava/` stays (the history's and the API sync's) and its sidecar keeps the folder FIT's path (`RideMeta::folder`); a too-short recording leaves no empty folder. The stop notice says "Strava recording saved to Activities/OCW/2026-11-18 Puerto de la Cruz: 12:34, 5.2 km" and the photo preview "Saved to Activities/OCW/2026-11-18 Puerto de la Cruz" (a screenshot: "Saved to Activities/OCW/2026-11-18"). The simple upload opens **the recording's folder** with the FIT file selected and names it in its steps ("… (its folder Activities/OCW/2026-11-18 Puerto de la Cruz is open) …"); the copy into `rides/strava-upload/` is kept only as the fallback for recordings from before v4.85 without such a folder *(and, until v5.07, for the whole ride – whole rides are never uploaded since Q6)*. *Browser* (`apps/web/src/strava.rs`): S records in the browser too now (S, the pad button, *Ride → Strava recording* – no longer dimmed –, `strava.record`); Captures → *Activities folder: choose* (`activities.folder choose|forget|status`; replaces *Photos folder: choose* and `photos.folder`): the File System Access API's picker, an `OCW` folder made in the chosen one, the handle kept in IndexedDB – the recording's FIT file and photos are written to `<date> <place>/` there, screenshots and other photos to `<date>/` (subfolders made); without it they are downloads named by the file (`OCW YYYY-MM-DD HH-MM <place>.fit`, `… photo N.jpg`, `OCW-<time>.jpg`); the ` 2` counts the recordings of the page (a page cannot list the folder). *Tests:* the naming (places, route, world, ` 2`, safe characters, the local date), the day folder, the folder made at S, the FIT and photos written there on S's stop and at the ride's end, each photo once, the sidecars and history finding them (and an older photo in `~/Pictures/OCW`), the internal record keeping the path, the simple upload opening the folder (and the fallback for the whole ride and old recordings), the folder setting and pickers, the browser's recording into a folder and as downloads and its photos by day, the menu rows; the test runs set `OCW_ACTIVITIES_DIR`. Screenshots and a listing of a test run's folder: `test-output/activities-folder/`.

**Asked by the user (2026-11-16):** "use hotkey S to start and stop strava recording. take a photo of the rider in the landscape showing nice views, choose camera angle accordingly. save those photos for later strava upload. no more than 5 photos per ride and max one photo every 20 minutes. for now, get strava account details from a config toml file."

- **Key S – start / stop the Strava recording** (free in a ride: the unicorn's WASD flying is off, `WASD_FLIES`; rebindable, M9; a pad button and a menu entry *Ride → Strava recording* for parity, B6). While it runs the HUD shows a small **● Strava** badge with the recorded time; start and stop each show a short notice and set a lap mark.
  - *What is recorded:* the ride's FIT recording (2.8 *Export*) goes on as now for the training history; the Strava recording is the part between S and S, written as its own FIT activity (`<data dir>/ocw/rides/strava/`) and queued for upload with the existing upload path (below). Leaving the ride or quitting while it runs stops it and saves it.
  - *Several S … S in one ride:* see Q1.
- **Strava account details from a TOML file (for now):** the interim path of v1.6 stays – the user's own Strava API application, `client_id` and `client_secret` in `<user config dir>/ocw/strava.toml` (or the environment), the browser authorization once, tokens stored locally; nothing is built into the app. The backend's Strava integration (9.1, Phase 5) replaces it later. Without the file the S key says "Strava is not set up (strava.toml)" and records nothing. *(Changed in v4.76: without the file S records the same and its stop points to the simple upload in the browser, see* Simple upload *below.)*
- **Ride photos – a virtual photographer:**
  - *When:* only while the Strava recording runs; **at most 5 photos per recording and at least 20 minutes between two** (the user's limits). Within each 20-minute window the photographer keeps the **best** candidate it saw and takes that one (proposal: so a photo is a good view, not the first acceptable one); a recording shorter than 20 minutes gets its single best view at the end, if any view scored high enough (Q3).
  - *What makes a nice view (a score, computed from the world, no AI):* an **open view** (how far the terrain lets the eye reach: horizon rays over `Terrain::height` in the camera's direction; a pass, a summit, a ridge, a lake or the sea in view score high; forest canopy, tunnels, narrow streets and fog low), **water** in view (the package's water areas), **landmarks** (peaks with a name, viewpoints and `tourism=viewpoint` from OSM where the package keeps them), **the light** (low sun, golden hour from `ocw-sky`; night and heavy rain low unless the sky is clear – moon, stars postponed), and variety (a photo differs in place and kind from the ones already taken).
  - *The camera angle, chosen for the view:* candidate poses around the rider – behind and above (the road ahead into the landscape), from the side with the valley behind, from ahead and low (the rider coming up a climb), a wide shot from 20–60 m with the rider small in the landscape – each tested for occlusion (terrain, buildings and tree crowns between camera and rider) and scored for the view behind the rider and the rider's framing (rule of thirds, the rider not cut by the edge). The best pose wins. The photo is rendered **off-screen** from that pose (the player's own view is not disturbed), at 2560 × 1440, **without the HUD and without name tags** (Q4 for the time stamp).
  - *Saved for later upload:* `<data dir>/ocw/rides/strava/<recording>/photo-N.jpg` with a small sidecar (`photo-N.toml`: time, position lat / lon / height, heading, the score and its parts, the camera pose) and EXIF time and GPS; the training history shows them with the ride.
- **Uploading the photos – research first (flag):** Strava's **public API has no endpoint to add photos to an activity** (as far as known on 2026-11-16: the `uploads` endpoint takes FIT / TCX / GPX only, photos are added in Strava's own apps). So the photos are **saved for later**, as asked; how they reach Strava is Q2. To be re-checked against Strava's current API documentation before building ST3.

**Stages (all questions decided, ready to build):** **ST1** – S starts / stops the Strava recording (badge, notices, lap marks, the segment as its own FIT, queued with the existing upload, `strava.toml` check); **ST2** – the photographer (view score, camera candidates with occlusion tests, off-screen render, the 5 / 20-minute rules, saving with sidecar and EXIF, history view); **ST3** – the photo upload, once Q2 is answered.

**Tests:** the start / stop state machine (S, leaving the ride, quit), the segment's FIT (start, end, laps, the totals of the part only); the photo limits as a pure function (never more than 5, never two within 20 minutes, the best of each window, a short recording); the view score on fixed scenes (a Tenerife ridge with the sea scores higher than a Black Forest track in the trees; a tunnel scores zero); the camera choice (an occluded pose is never chosen; the rider is in frame); the photo file and its sidecar (EXIF time and position); a headless photo run on marge archived in `test-output/`.

**Open questions (for the user):**
- **Q1 – Several recordings in one ride: decided (2026-11-16, the user): each S … S is its own Strava activity** (own FIT, own upload, own photos).
- **Q2 – How the photos reach Strava: decided (2026-11-16, the user): kept local and shown in the history, with a folder link** to add them in Strava's app or site by hand (Strava's public API cannot add photos). ST3 is this history view and link; an automatic upload only if Strava's API allows it later.

- **Q6 – The whole ride and the S … S part both on Strava: decided (2026-11-19, the user):** Only S … S creates a Strava activity; it is uploaded automatically (a setting for that) or by hand – "Only S..S creates a strava ride which then can be uploaded automatically (create a settings option for that) or manually." Whole rides are never uploaded to Strava. **Built (v5.07):** (1) *The API sync* (`apps/desktop/src/strava/sync.rs`: `sync_files`) lists the Strava recordings (`rides/strava/<name>.fit`) only – a saved ride is never queued, counted or sent, by any scope; whole rides uploaded before keep their state in `strava-sync.toml` and their ride page still says *on Strava*. (2) *The setting* **`strava.auto_upload`** (on / off, default on; the settings registry, kept as the one `[strava] auto_upload` of `ocw.toml` (3.2.4) – not a second key in `[settings]`; *Navi → Strava → Automatic upload*, the Strava page keeping six rows: *Upload in your browser*, *Automatic upload*, *Status*, *Link account*, *Upload now* – `strava.sync --retry`, it takes the place of *Retry failed uploads* –, *Unlink*; the console `set strava.auto_upload off` or `strava.auto_upload on|off`; desktop only – the browser has no API upload) replaces `auto_upload` in `strava.toml`: the config migration of 3.2.4 moves an old `auto_upload = …` there into `ocw.toml [strava]` once (the file kept as `.bak`), and a value found in the Strava files while the setting has none is taken once (saved, with a console line). **On:** a new recording goes up when it is saved, the waiting ones once the account is linked (the waiting and the question of v4.86 unchanged). **Off:** nothing goes up by itself – not at the start, not on `strava.connect`, not on save; the ride page's state row says *not uploaded – upload now* (`strava.sync --ride N`: that ride's recordings not on Strava yet) or *waiting – upload now* (`strava.sync --waiting --ride N`), *Navi → Strava → Upload now* / `strava.sync` uploads all; switched on, what waits goes up at once. (3) *The simple upload* (both apps) sends a ride's S recordings only (`strava.upload-manual N`, `--whole` removed); a ride without one has no upload row and no mark, only the line **Strava upload: no Strava recording – press S while riding** (`ocw_client::strava::NO_RECORDING`), and `strava.upload-manual` says so; the browser keeps the FIT files of the page's recordings (`WebStrava::kept`) and finds a ride's by time (`ocw_client::strava::within_ride`, the same rule as the desktop's). (4) *Texts:* the S stop notice says "… It goes to Strava automatically." (API, on), "… Automatic upload is off: upload it from Navi > Training history > the ride." (API, off), and without the API "It will be uploaded once Strava is set up" only with the setting on; the end of a ride no longer points to an upload ("Ride saved. Upload it …" is gone); `strava.status` starts with the rule ("Only Strava recordings (S … S) go to Strava, never whole rides; automatic upload: on|off …") and counts "Strava recordings: N uploaded, N not uploaded yet, …"; the Strava page's note and the Navi → Rides list ("not for Strava" for a whole ride). *Tests:* whole rides never queued or uploaded (the sync, the worker, the app with the stand-in Strava), the recordings uploaded with the setting on, kept waiting with it off and sent by the ride page's upload, switched on later; the old `strava.toml` key read once into the setting; the setting stored as `ocw.toml [strava] auto_upload` and read from there; the stop notices per case; the ride page's rows with and without S recordings, with the API on and off, an older whole ride on Strava; the Strava page's six rows and the setting row; the browser's row, download (the recording, not the ride) and the ride without S. Screenshots (X11, Wayland, browser): `test-output/strava-q6/`. *Was asked:* with the automatic upload (the rider's own Strava API app in `strava.toml`, `auto_upload` on) every saved ride is uploaded. A ride in which the rider pressed S also has its S … S part saved as a separate recording, which is uploaded too – so one ride reaches Strava twice, e.g. the whole 1 h 30 ride and the 45 min S … S part inside it. The two overlap in time: Strava may flag the second as a duplicate, or the rider gets two activities for one ride. Today both are uploaded. Options: (A) a ride with S recordings uploads only its S … S parts, a ride without S uploads whole (the browser's simple upload already works like this); (B) only the whole ride, S just marks a part; (C) only S recordings, rides without S are never uploaded; (D) both, as now. Proposal: A.

Configured = the interim path's `strava.toml` / environment; `--strava-dry-run` (hidden, test runs) records without it and uploads nothing.

The app reads the photos from their sidecars and the Strava recordings' times from their FIT files (`recording::rides_photos`).

**Simple upload (no API app) – built (v4.76, asked by the user 2026-11-18: "can you implement the simple strava upload for users without subscription?"):** uploads are free for every Strava account, but the API way needs each rider's own API application in `strava.toml` – too complicated for most riders. The simple way uses Strava's own web upload page, **https://www.strava.com/upload/select** (`ocw_client::strava::UPLOAD_PAGE`), which takes our FIT files as they are.

With the API set up (the advanced way) the upload row is the line *Strava upload: automatic (your API app)* (or "skipped (marked as uploaded)"); the toggle stays. The desktop's *Navi → Strava* page starts with *Upload in your browser – no API app needed* (opens the ride list). Console in both apps: `strava.upload-manual [N]` (N as in `history`, 1 = the newest; `--whole` removed in v5.07) and `strava.mark-uploaded N [on|off|toggle]`.

Photos: add them on the activity page (they are in the same folder)." – and "If you uploaded it, mark it as uploaded (below)." until it is marked. `--strava-dry-run` (test runs) opens neither program.
- **Browser app** (`apps/web/src/ui.rs`): the ride's Strava recordings (their FIT files kept for the recordings of this page, since v5.07; before, the ride's own FIT file) are downloaded under their names and the upload page opens in a new tab (`window.open`; the menu key counts as the user's gesture, a blocked tab is said with the URL); the same steps ("Strava opens in a new tab … (just downloaded) …").
- **File names** (`ocw_client::strava::upload_name`): `OCW <local date> <HH-MM> <world> – <route>[ (Strava recording)].fit` – the world and route as the history shows them, only characters every system takes (letters of any script, digits, spaces and `-_.,()'&+–`; `/ \ : * ? " < > |` and control characters become `-`; at most 80 for the place), a number when two files share the minute.
- **The mark:** the app cannot know whether the rider uploaded the file. The rider marks the ride; the mark is kept in the training history (`strava_marked`, added only when set, kept when a ride is added again) and on the desktop also in `rides/strava-manual.toml` (the ride's FIT file and its Strava recordings), which the API sync reads and skips – so setting up the API later uploads no duplicate (`strava::sync::sync_files`; `strava.status` counts without them).

Upload it to Strava in your browser: Navi > Training history > the ride" (12 s, `UPLOAD_NOTICE_S`), the end of a ride (a ride switch, `ride.save`) "Ride saved. Upload it …" (removed in v5.07: whole rides never go to Strava); `strava.connect` / `sync` / `status` explain the simple way first and the API app as the advanced option. The browser's S notice and its *Ride → Strava recording* page point to the training history.

### 2.9 In-Game Console

A developer and power-user console inside the running desktop app.

- **UI:** toggled with `` ` `` (backtick) or `F12`. Rendered with egui (`bevy_egui`) as an overlay. Includes command history (↑ / ↓), Tab completion, scrollback and log output (connected to `tracing`); Esc closes it.
- **Tab completion (v3.43):** Tab completes the word before the cursor (the words after it stay): command names; subcommands, long flags and `PossibleValue`s from the command's clap definition; values known only at run time from a **value provider** the command registers per argument (`ConsoleAppExt::console_values(command path, argument, provider)`, e.g. `set` / `get` keys and values from the settings registry, `world switch` world ids and the test routes, `ride.switch --route` / `--world`, `weather` presets / subcommands / `FIELD=` words / data sources / days, `time` presets and speeds, `camera.path load` saved paths, `help COMMAND`), so the console hard-codes no values. Only commands the session may run are offered (no `dev` commands on a remote server). **One rule:** one candidate is inserted with a space after it (none after a `field=`); several insert their longest common prefix and are listed under the input line – every further Tab inserts the next candidate in turn and marks it in the list, Shift+Tab the previous one; typing (any other change of the line) ends the cycle. Words with spaces are inserted in double quotes; a word started with a quote is completed inside it. The logic is pure and Bevy-free (`ocw_render::completion`); `console input TEXT` and `console tab` drive it from scripts and tests. Same in the desktop and the browser app.
- **Command registry:** each crate/plugin registers commands with a name, argument definition (parsed with `clap`), help text and a **permission level**. The existing `bevy_console` crate follows this pattern; evaluate it or build a small equivalent.
- **Permission levels:**

| Level | Available | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `user` | Always | `help`, `fps`, `time 18:30` (the server checks who may change the time, 14 Phase 9, 9I), `net.stats`, `devices.list`, `trainer.difficulty 50`, `camera.mode chase`, `screenshot` |
| `dev` | Single-player / local server, or debug builds | `sim.power 250` (virtual power without a trainer – useful for testing), `teleport km 12.3`, `weather rain`, `world.reload_tile`, `render.wireframe`, `render.lod_bias` |
| `admin` | Remote server, authenticated organizers / staff only; executed **on the server** | `event.start`, `event.pause`, `rider.kick <id>`, `rider.flag <id>` |

- **Multiplayer safety:** `dev` commands that affect the simulation are rejected when connected to a remote server. The server is authoritative (6.1), so a manipulated client cannot cheat with them anyway.
- **Scripts:** an `autoexec.cfg` file runs commands at startup. `exec <file>` runs command files, e.g. for automated performance tests (`tools/performance-test`).
- **Implemented (v1.9):** the commands listed in the README (rider, camera, trainer and devices, rides and Strava, `teleport`, `screenshot`, …). Scripted test rides use `--cmd COMMAND` (startup), `--exec FILE` and `--at SECONDS=COMMAND` (run once the ride has lasted that long, e.g. `--at "4=rider.lean 15"`).
- **Settings:** settings are also reachable as variables (`set render.shadows high`), so the settings UI and the console share one source of truth.

### 2.10 Web Companion

A browser app for everything **except riding**. It runs in any modern browser, including iOS / iPadOS. It uses no Bluetooth and no 3D rendering.

| Area | Features | Phase |
|---|---|---|
| Account | Sign-up / sign-in (same OIDC provider as the desktop app), profile, weight / FTP / height, privacy settings, data export and account deletion (12) | 5 |
| Training history | List of rides, ride detail (power, heart rate, cadence, speed, elevation charts; power-duration curve), personal bests, FIT / GPX download | 5 |
| Strava | Link / unlink account, auto-upload setting, re-upload of single rides (2.8) | 5 |
| Devices | Read-only list of the user's known trainers and sensors (pairing stays in the desktop app) | 5 |
| Social | Friends, groups, invitations | 5 |
| Events | Calendar, event pages, sign-up, start lists, results and live leaderboards | 7 |
| Routes | Browse routes per world package with map + elevation profile; GPX upload with server-side map matching (2.7); simple route planner (click junctions on the map) | 7 |
| World packages | List of available regions, sizes and versions; mark regions for download on the desktop app | 7 |

Technology: see 3.6.

### 2.11 The ride photographer (planned and built 2026-11-16, v4.21)

**Asked by the user (2026-11-16), verbatim:**
1. "take a photo of the rider in the landscape showing nice views, choose camera angle accordingly. save those photos for later strava upload. no more than 5 photos per ride and max one photo every 20 minutes." (with the Strava recording, 2.8.1; its decisions Q1–Q4 apply)
2. "whenever there is a photo taken for strava, make an real photographer person appear in the game, looking the exact angle as he would in reality. when the photo is taken, make a flash: visual and audible"
3. "photographer add-on, if it's in a position where a human can not stand, e.g. above ground, over water, rocky terrain etc. make the photographer stand somewhere near (visible for the rider) but make him (or her) control a drone. make the drone visible and audible and it flys around before taking the photo (between 30s and 2 minutes). before it should be visible and audible to the rider. at the time of the photo, the drone should be at the exact position from where the photo is taken."
4. "dont make the photographer part of strava, keep it as separate entitiy."

**Design (as built):**
- **Its own feature**, not under Strava: setting `photographer.enabled` (default on; Settings → Display → Graphics → *Ride photographer*; both apps since v4.74, Q3), console `photographer [on|off|status|now|drone]` (`now` plans the next photo at once, without the 20 minutes and the minimum score; `drone` the next by the drone – tests). It runs in every ride unless switched off in Settings (Q1, decided), not in scripted screenshot / capture runs (like the ride recording), not while the rider flies (unicorn mode). The photos of a ride go to the photos folder `~/Pictures/OCW` (Q3, v4.74; before: `<data dir>/ocw/rides/<ride>/photos/`, where the sidecars stay; `<ride>`: the ride's FIT stem); a Strava recording (2.8.1) uses those taken within it.
- **The limits** (`ocw_client::photographer::Limits`, `select`): at most 5 photos per ride, at least 20 minutes apart, the best view of each 20-minute window, only at or above the minimum score `MIN_SCORE` = 0.35 (2.8.1 Q3; a flat meadow at noon stays under it, relief or water lift a view over it). While riding the photographer plans on the predicted path: every 5 s it scores spots ahead on the known track (the route, or the free-ride path as far as it is known) within the window and the rider's reach and keeps the best as the plan (a better one replaces it until the photographer shows); a spot near an earlier photo (1 km) or of the same pose kind as the last scores lower (variety). **Viewpoints along the road are photo spots** (v5.03, Q4): besides the spots on its steps (every 40 m or more) the planner scores the road point nearest to every viewpoint that lies within 60 m of the road ahead (`viewpoint_spots`), so a viewpoint is never stepped over.
- **The view score** (`ocw_world::photo`, pure, wasm-safe; the world through the `PhotoScene` trait – the app's `ocw_ui::photographer::WorldScene` over the drawn ground, the camera's solid obstacles (buildings, walls), the package's land use and forest cover): 0.4 × *open view* (7 horizon rays across the photo's field of view over the ground with the tree crowns on it and the earth's curvature; a sample counts when it rises above the nearer ones; how far the eye reaches, log-scaled to 12 km) + 0.3 × *relief* (the height span seen beyond 250 m, or how far the view looks down) + 0.2 × *water* (rays that see a lake, river or the sea) + 0.1 × *landmark* (from the package's peaks and viewpoints, section `LMRK` of 4.7, built v5.03 with Q4: 1 when a named peak within 15 km is in the frame and in sight – the line to 5 m above its summit clears the ground, the tree crowns and the buildings –, or when the camera stands at a viewpoint (within 120 m) looking its way – its OSM `direction` with 30° more on each side, any way without one –; 0.6 when a viewpoint within 3 km is in the frame and in sight; passes do not count), times *the light* (`ocw-sky`: golden hour 1.0, high sun down to 0.8, the blue hour 0.6, night 0.05 – moon and stars postponed –, ×0.85 looking straight into a low sun), times *the weather* (rain and snow up to −60 %, fog under 300 m ×0.4, the visibility caps the rays) and the framing. A covered road (the ground ≥ 2.5 m above it: a tunnel) scores zero.
- **The camera poses** (`candidates`, `choose`): around the rider at the spot – ahead and low (crouching, the rider coming up), the side (the valley behind the rider), behind (the road ahead), wide (25–40 m out at eye height), and in the air: behind and above (9 m), aerial wide (40–50 m out, 20–28 m up). Each is aimed with the rider on a third of the frame (the side with the more open view) and a little low, never cut by the edge (framing factor by the rider's size in the frame), tested for occlusion (the lines to the rider's head and body against the ground, buildings and tree crowns) and scored; the best wins (a drone's ×0.92: a person's photo when nearly as good).
- **Who takes it** (the user's requests 2 and 3): **a person** where a person can stand (`standable`): on the ground, not water, rock, scree, ice or wetland, not inside a building, tree trunk or obstacle, not steeper than 0.7, off the road and ≥ 0.5 m beyond its edge, ≥ 1.5 m from the riding line, 4–40 m from the rider; the eye 1.6 m above the feet standing, 0.9 m crouching. **Otherwise a drone** at the pose (≥ 1 m above what is under it, up to 60 m from the rider), flown by the pilot standing near (`pilot_spot`: beside the road near the spot, standable, seen by the rider on the approach, with a clear line to the drone).
- **The person** (`ocw-render::photographer`): the rider model on foot (the avatar's parts and pose system: `ocw_assets::pose::photographer`, standing or crouching, both hands at a camera held to the eye, the head and camera pitched along the view; or a drone's remote at the chest, the head up at the drone), plain clothes varied per photo (a long-sleeved top and long trousers in everyday colours, no helmet, a varied character: height, build, skin, hair, glasses – nobody's likeness or name). It is placed so its camera's lens is exactly at the pose's eye. Timeline (`person_phase`): it appears ~12 s before the rider reaches the spot when out of the rider's view (at the latest 6 s before, even in view), facing the approach, out of the rider's way; takes the photo when the rider reaches the spot; vanishes once the rider is ≥ 15 m past and it is out of view (after 25 s in any case).
- **The drone** (`ocw_world::photo_drone::DroneFlight`, pure, stepped by the frames): a small quadcopter of simple shapes (body, arms, four rotors spinning, a camera gimbal, a blinking red light; ~0.45 m across; own work, no brand look). It takes off from the pilot's hands 30 s – 2 min before the photo (the duration per shot within that, no longer than the rider's time to the spot – a drone shot needs ≥ 32 s ahead), climbs 6 m, flies to the rider and follows it ~14 m ahead and ~6 m up, sweeping from side to side across the rider's view (≤ 18 m/s), visible and audible the whole time, then approaches the pose over an arc during the last 8 s of the rider's approach and is **exactly at the pose (position and view) when the rider reaches the spot**; afterwards it flies back above the pilot and lands; both vanish once the rider has passed and they are out of view. On the way it keeps 2 m above the ground, tree crowns and buildings under it and 3.5 m from the rider.
- **Leaving the planned path** (a junction taken elsewhere, a U-turn, a jump back): the visit is aborted – the drone flies back, no photo, the window stays open.
- **The flash** (`flash`): at the photo a 0.12 s burst – a point light of 4 Mlm at the camera, and a white veil (28 %) over the rider's view while the flash is in it; the **sound** (`ocw-audio`, synthesised): `Cue::Shutter` (the flash's pop, the shutter's two clicks, the recharge whine) placed at the camera, and the drone's rotor buzz (`ocw_audio::drone`: four detuned blade tones and air noise) placed at the drone with distance, direction, air absorption and Doppler (`spatial::place`), on the effects bus (`MixerMsg::PlacedCue`, `MixerMsg::Drone`).
- **The photo** (`ocw-render::photographer::take_photos`): an off-screen camera at the pose renders 2560 × 1440 with the world camera's fog, exposure, atmosphere and MSAA, without the HUD, name tags and the corner stamp (UI draws only on the window's camera; 2.8.1 Q4); the figure is behind the lens (behind the near plane), never in the photo; the player's view is not disturbed. Saved by the desktop (`apps/desktop/src/photos.rs`) off the main thread as `photo-N.jpg` (JPEG 92, EXIF time with its UTC offset and GPS latitude / longitude / altitude / UTC date: `ocw_render::media::exif_tiff_gps`) with `photo-N.toml` (time, ride seconds, ride, world, route, lat / lon / height, heading and pitch, the score and its parts, the pose: kind, person standing / crouching or drone, eye, view, feet).
- **Multiplayer (Q2, built v4.38):** the other riders see the photographer, the drone and the flash and hear the shutter and the drone – "it's happening in the world and other riders are in the photo as well". The photographed rider's client shares the visit as a `SharedShot` (`ocw_world::photo_share`; protocol `PhotoShot`) from the moment the photographer shows (the person appears, the drone's pilot 3 s before the take-off) and on every change (the drone's new timings, the photo, the end, an abort); the server checks it (`ShotLog`: ≤ 5 photos per ride, ≥ 20 min apart – servers with dev commands leave the gap out, test runs shorten it with `ocw-server --photo-time-scale` like the app's –, ≤ 40 shots announced, the camera within 400 m + 25 m/s × the time until it is due of the rider, due within 5 min, the place and the flight's past fixed, updates ≥ 0.25 s apart, never while flying as the unicorn), sets the rider and relays it to every client; a client joining gets the open shots. The times are game time, the server's tick / 50: the photographed rider runs its photographer on it, the others draw the shots at the time they draw the other riders at (0.12 s behind; `ClientCore::photo_time_s`), so the flash comes when they see the rider at the spot; news that comes after the photo's time flashes at once. **The drone's flight is a pure function of game time and its `FlightPlan`** (`ocw_world::photo_drone`: the pose, the pilot, the take-off, the rider's road from the take-off to the spot, the timings: from time *t* the rider was *d* m from the spot and is due at *T*): a changed speed is a new timing (at most one a second, when the photo's time moved > 0.25 s, never in its last 0.5 s), blended in over 1.5 s (at most half the time to the photo, so the drone is exactly at the pose for it); every client with the plan draws the same flight whatever its frame rate. Its clearance rises early before what is near (a cone over a 5 m grid, 25 m around) instead of jumping up at a tree stand's edge. Each client draws the shots whose camera is within 3 km of its rider (`RemoteShots::scenes`; the server has no interest management yet – snapshots go to everyone, too), several at once (`RideView::photographers`); the shutter is placed at the camera, the loudest drone is heard (the mixer has one drone voice). Only the photographed rider's client saves the photo. The photographed rider's photographer runs on that game time from the first snapshot on (`ClientCore::server_time_s` is `None` before it: the welcome comes first, and a 0 there started the photographer's ride at the session's start – a photo right after joining a server that had run for minutes; fixed with a regression test). The setting `photographer.enabled` (and flying) stops only the own photographer – the others see it go –, never the others'; those a rider hides with `photographer.others` (Q5, v4.99: off = not drawn, not heard, for this rider only). Both apps (`ocw_ui::photographer`); the browser takes its own photos too since v4.74 (Q3) and draws and hears the others'. Screenshots: `scripts/test-photographer-shared.sh [OUT] [SECONDS] [x11|wayland]` (two desktop apps on one `ocw-server` on marge, Tenerife: Ada Rider photographed by a drone, Bea Climber's views with it, the flash; `test-output/photographer-shared/`).
- **Dev cameras for videos (v4.50):** the dev console's `camera.drone pov|follow|off` (`ocw_render::drone_camera`, both apps, Permission Dev) puts the window's camera on the drone while one is out (the own, else another rider's): **pov** from just in front of its lens along its view with the photo's field of view (the flash's veil shows, as for a flash in view), **follow** 3 m behind, 1.2 m to the right and 0.6 m above its camera's heading, looking past it at what it films (smoothed; above the ground and buildings). With `photographer drone` and `--capture` it records a drone's flight from take-off to the photo and back (the art project's Day 6 videos); the app logs each phase change of the own drone (`photographer's drone phase=…`). `photographer drone` keeps the next shot a drone's until that visit ends (the replans before the take-off look only for a better drone's shot).
- **Tests:** `ocw-world` `photo` (a Tenerife-like ridge with the sea scores higher than a Black Forest track in the trees; a tunnel scores zero; night, fog and rain lower the score, golden hour not; standable ground classified – verge yes; road, riding line, water, building, rock, steep no – and the ground poses over water are drones; chosen poses held by a person on standable ground at eye height or by a drone with its pilot standable and in sight; an occluded pose is never chosen; the rider framed on a third and never cut; landmarks in view), `photo_drone` (30 s – 2 min, launched at its ETA, flying around clear of the ground, the trees, a house and the rider, exactly at the pose (< 2 cm, < 0.5°) at the photo, landed again; an abort brings it back without a photo), `ocw-client` `photographer` (never more than 5, never two within 20 minutes, the best of each window, a short ride, the minimum score; the flash's timing; the person's appear / shoot / vanish timeline; a ride on the test loop at 10× time gets its photos within the limits with the shutter at the camera and the photographer in the scene before; leaving the path aborts without a photo; the sidecar reads back), `ocw-audio` (the shutter placed left, the drone's buzz on and off), `ocw-assets` (the photographer's pose: feet planted, hands at the camera before the face, the lens along the pitch, crouching lowers it; the remote at the chest), `ocw-render` (EXIF GPS, the figure's facing, varied looks without helmet), desktop (`photo-N.jpg` with EXIF and its sidecar). **Headless photo run on marge** (`scripts/test-photographer.sh [OUT] [SECONDS] [drone]`: Tenerife, Buenavista – Masca – Santiago del Teide at golden hour, the virtual trainer at 350 W, the photographer's time 10× faster, a Strava recording from the start, `--strava-dry-run`, a throwaway data folder; `drone`: `photographer drone` after 25 s and 170 s): 480 s gave 4 photos (side, behind, ahead low, side; scores 0.54–0.74, the sea and the cliffs in view) with their sidecars, 12 views of the rider with the photographer in them and the Strava recording's FIT; the drone run gave drone photos (behind, above) 111 s and 117 s after the plan, exactly from the drone's pose, and views with the pilot and the drone. Archived in `test-output/photographer-st/` and `test-output/photographer-drone/` (photos, chase views, the Strava FIT, the log).
- **Open questions (for the user):**
  - **Q1 – Every ride, or only while a Strava recording runs? Decided (2026-11-16, the user): "photographer: in every ride, unless disabled in settings."** – it runs in every ride while `photographer.enabled` is on (default on; off in Settings disables it); a Strava recording only picks the photos taken within its S … S span (as built).
  - **Q2 – Do other riders see the photographer and the drone: decided (2026-11-16, = 2.8.1 Q5): yes** – other riders are in the photo, so they see the photographer, the drone and the flash too. **Built (v4.33)**, see *Multiplayer*.
  - **Q3 – The browser app: decided (2026-11-17, dashboard): "save the photos in the user's home photos directory in a subfolder OCW"** – the photos go to the user's photos folder, subfolder `OCW` (Linux: the XDG Pictures directory, e.g. `~/Pictures/OCW`; Windows: `Pictures\OCW`; macOS: `~/Pictures/OCW`). *Browser (proposal for how):* a web page cannot write to a folder silently – on Chromium browsers the File System Access API asks once for the folder (the picker starts in Pictures, `startIn: 'pictures'`; the rider picks or creates `OCW`, the handle is kept in IndexedDB and permission asked again when needed); where that API is missing (Firefox, Safari) each photo is a download with an `OCW-` file name prefix, since downloads cannot choose a subfolder. *Desktop (proposal):* the same folder for the photographer's photos and the screenshots, the ride keeping a reference to its photos for the Strava upload (instead of copies in `rides/<ride>/photos/`). **Built (v4.74; replaced in v4.85 by the one activities folder `~/Activities/OCW`, photos and screenshots in a folder per day there – 2.8.1 *Where an S recording is written*):** *desktop* – the photos folder is the platform's Pictures folder + `OCW` (`dirs::picture_dir()`, else `~/Pictures`; setting `photos.folder`: `default`, a path or `~/…`; console `photos.folder`), created when the first photo comes; a ride photo is `OCW-<ride>-photo-N.jpg` there, a screenshot `OCW-<time>.jpg` (`screenshot PATH` still writes PATH; a name taken gets `-2`, `-3`); the ride keeps its reference – the sidecar `rides/<ride>/photos/photo-N.toml` with the photo's `path` – so the training history, the Strava recordings' count and `history.photos` (opens the photos folder) find them; rides before v4.74 (`photo-N.jpg` beside the sidecar, no `path`) keep working (`ocw-desktop` `photos`). *Browser* – Captures → *Photos folder: choose* (`photos.folder choose|forget|status`) opens the File System Access API's picker (`startIn: 'pictures'`; an `OCW` folder is made in the chosen one unless it is one), the handle is kept in IndexedDB and after a reload the permission is asked again with the next key press or click; screenshots and the photographer's photos are written there, else (no folder, no API: Firefox, Safari) downloaded as `OCW-…`; the browser's photographer now takes its own photos too (setting *Ride photographer* offered there), encoded on the page's thread with EXIF time and GPS; the browser's training history does not list them yet. The HUD previews each photo for 3 s with where it went (3.2 *Photo preview*). Tests: the folder per platform and setting, photos in the folder with the ride's reference, the Strava recordings finding them, old rides, free names, the browser's captions.
  - **Q5 – May a rider hide the other riders' photographers: decided (2026-11-19, the user): yes** – a rider may hide the other riders' photographers, drones and flashes (a setting of their own, next to *Ride photographer*; proposal: `photographer.others on|off`, default on = shown; the own photographer is unaffected). **Built (v4.99):** setting `photographer.others` (default on = shown; Settings → Display → Graphics → *Ride photographer*, a page of its own with *My photographer* and *Other riders' photographers* – Graphics had six rows), console `photographer others on|off` (`photographer` prints it too); off, the others' person, drone and flash are not drawn and their shutter and drone are not heard; their shots still arrive and are drawn again at once when switched on (a shutter long past is not played late). Purely local: the own photographer runs and is shared as before, the server and the other riders see nothing change. Both apps (`ocw_ui::photographer`). Tests: `ocw-client` (the setting and its default in both apps, the menu page and its row's value), `ocw-ui` (another rider's shot drawn, flashing and heard by default; hidden and silent when off, back when on; the own photographer drawn and shared with the others hidden). Screenshots: `OCW_B_HIDE=FROM-TO scripts/test-photographer-shared.sh` – Bea hides Ada's photographer for that span and saves her view (`b/hidden-NNN.jpg`). Was open (v4.38): the setting *Ride photographer* only stops the own photos (decided with Q2); whether a rider may also hide the others' photographers, drones and flashes (e.g. a busy group ride, or flashes as a comfort option like the camera shake) is not decided – nothing built, they are always drawn.
  - **Q4 – Named peaks and viewpoints: decided (2026-11-19, the user): yes** – the world builder adds them for the landmark part of the photographer's view score. **Built (v5.03):** section `LMRK` (4.7 *Landmarks section*) with the named peaks, the mountain passes and the viewpoints; the view score's landmark part counts a peak or a viewpoint in the frame and in sight and the camera at a viewpoint looking its way, the planner scores the road beside each viewpoint (see *The view score* and *The limits*); the app's scene takes them from the loaded packages whenever the world set changes (`ocw_world::photo::Landmark::of_set`, home metres, the elevation from `ele` or the terrain). Was: they need a package section (OSM `natural=peak` with a name, `tourism=viewpoint`); not in the packages yet – a world-builder change.
- **Open (no user decision needed):** objects close in front of the lens that are not camera solids (a start arch's post, a lamp post) can fill an edge of the photo – a near-clutter test in the framing; the drone's flight time is planned from the rider's speed then, so a rider still speeding up at the start of a ride can make it a little shorter than 30 s; the obstacles of section `OBST` (posts, tree cells) are not yet part of the app's scene (`blocked`); the photographer ignores other riders (a group may stand between the camera and the rider); thumbnails of the photos in the menu; the others' drone uses the camera solids loaded around *their* camera, so a building another client has not loaded can lift the drone a little differently there; one drone voice in the mixer (two drones at once: the louder is heard); the server relays to everyone (interest management by distance is for later, with the snapshots).

---

## 3. Overall Technical Stack

### 3.1 Programming Language and Engine

- **Primary programming language:** Rust
- **3D engine:** Bevy
- **Graphics backend:** wgpu

Bevy handles 3D scenes, rendering, cameras, lighting, shadows, materials, animations, the Entity Component System, asset management, game states and the user interface.

wgpu provides the cross-platform GPU abstraction with the backends Vulkan, Direct3D 12 and Metal.

**Bevy versioning:** Bevy has breaking changes in every release until 1.0. An exact Bevy version is pinned in the workspace and upgraded in dedicated milestones, typically one release behind current, once the ecosystem crates we use have caught up. Only `ocw-render`, `ocw-client` and the apps depend on Bevy (10), so upgrades stay local.

#### 3.1.1 Engine Evaluation

**Requirements:** Rust; native on Linux, Windows and macOS; Vulkan, D3D12 and Metal (no single-API dependency); large streamed outdoor worlds; many instanced objects; skeletal animation; modifiable and open licence.

| Option | Language / Licence | Graphics APIs | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Bevy** (latest: 0.20, Oct 2026) | Rust, MIT/Apache-2.0 | wgpu → Vulkan, Metal, D3D12 | Pure Rust; ECS fits our modular crates; PBR, cascaded shadows, procedural atmosphere, GPU-driven rendering, glTF, skeletal animation; experimental path tracing (Solari); very active community | Breaking changes in every release until 1.0 (no date); no built-in large-terrain / streaming system; editor still in progress; UI still maturing |
| **B. Fyrox** (1.0, Mar 2026) | Rust, MIT | **OpenGL only** (fyrox-graphics-gl); modern backends planned | Stable 1.0 API; full scene editor; built-in terrain | OpenGL is deprecated on macOS (no Metal) → violates the "no single GPU API" goal; smaller ecosystem; no global illumination yet |
| **C. Own renderer on wgpu** (+ ECS such as `hecs`, plus `winit`) | Rust, MIT/Apache-2.0 | Vulkan, Metal, D3D12 | Full control, tailored to terrain + roads; stable API under our control | Very high effort: shadows, PBR, animation, asset handling and UI built ourselves; delays all phases |
| **D. Godot 4 + godot-rust (gdext)** | C++ engine (MIT) + Rust game logic | Vulkan, Metal, D3D12 | Mature editor and tooling; terrain plugins (e.g. Terrain3D); stable releases; good UI system | Not Rust-native: engine in C++, logic through bindings; two build systems; ECS approach does not match; ties us to Godot's scene model |
| **E. Unreal Engine 5** | C++, proprietary (royalty above revenue threshold) | Vulkan, Metal, D3D12 | Best visuals; World Partition; landscape tools | Not open source; no practical Rust integration; licence costs; very large toolchain |
| **F. Unity** | C#, proprietary | all | Mature; large asset store | Proprietary, licence uncertainty in recent years, not Rust |
| *Other Rust renderers* (`rend3`, `kajiya`, `three-d`) | Rust | wgpu / Vulkan | – | `rend3` and `kajiya` are no longer maintained; `three-d` is too limited for large worlds |

**Decision:** **Bevy (A)**, with **Godot + gdext (D)** as the documented fallback.

- E and F contradict the core goals (Rust, open, modular) and are excluded.
- Fyrox has the stable API Bevy lacks, but the OpenGL-only renderer blocks macOS and the "no single GPU API" goal. Revisit if a modern backend ships.
- An own renderer would consume a large part of the project's capacity before any cycling feature exists.
- Bevy's missing terrain/streaming system is acceptable: we need a custom solution anyway (road-conformed terrain 4.3, tiles 4.5, splat materials 4.6). It becomes our own Bevy plugin.

**Technical spike in Phase 1** (about 2–3 weeks) to confirm the decision:

1. Render a 10 km × 10 km area: streamed 1 km tiles, terrain with splat materials, road meshes, a floating origin.
2. 100,000+ instanced trees/bushes with LOD, plus 100 animated rider avatars.
3. Run on Linux (Vulkan) on minimum-spec hardware (15). Following the rollout order (11.1), repeat the spike on Windows (D3D12) and macOS (Metal) at the start of each port.
4. Measure FPS, frame-time spikes during tile loading, RAM/VRAM and load times.

**Go criterion:** stable 60 FPS on the reference hardware with no visible hitches during streaming. If Bevy clearly fails and cannot be fixed in reasonable time, run the same spike on Godot.

**Supporting crates to evaluate:** `bevy_egui` (console, editor panels), `big_space` (floating origin), KTX2/Basis texture support (built into Bevy), `bevy_mod_billboard` or impostors for distant trees.

**Spike results, Linux (November 2026).** Implementation: `apps/spike` (`ocw-spike`), run with `drive.sh spike` / `spike-video`.

- **Setup:** generated 10 × 10 km world (noise terrain standing in for the DEM, a 27.8 km winding road loop, road-conformed terrain), 1 km tiles in a 5 × 5 ring with three terrain LODs (10/25/50 m grids), built on background threads with one tile upload per frame, floating origin (rebasing per 1 km), about 140,000 trees in view, 100 riders, splat terrain material (four texture layers), cascaded shadows, fog.
- **Machine:** AMD Radeon RX Vega 56/64 (8 GB, RADV / Vulkan), 12-core EPYC, Debian 13, 1920 × 1080, vsync off, headless Wayland compositor. This GPU is clearly above the minimum spec of 15.

| Variant (40 km/h unless noted) | Mean FPS | p99 frame | Max frame | Frames > 16.7 ms | Frames > 33 ms |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| One entity per tree (`VisibilityRange` LOD), 10 km | 220 | 8.9 ms | 43 ms | 225 of 198k | 4 |
| **Trees merged per tile (per-tile LOD), 10 km** | **447** | **5.5 ms** | **11.4 ms** | **0** | **0** |
| One entity per tree, 150 km/h | 203 | 10.5 ms | 45 ms | 160 | 5 |
| **Trees merged per tile, 150 km/h** | **298** | **7.1 ms** | **15.6 ms** | **0** | **0** |
| Merged + splat material, 2 km | 387 | 6.6 ms | 11.7 ms | 0 | 0 |

Tile builds take up to 23 ms on worker threads; uploads cost at most 4.6 ms on the main thread; initial load of the 25 tiles 0.3–0.4 s; process RAM 330–470 MB; VRAM about +360 MB. Single runs vary by ±30 % (the GPU is shared with a desktop session), so only differences larger than that count.

**Decisions from the spike:**

- **Go for Bevy on Linux:** the go criterion (stable 60 FPS, no visible hitches while streaming) is met with headroom.
- **Vegetation is merged per tile and LOD**, not spawned as one entity per tree: spawning ~8,000 tree entities with a tile causes 40–45 ms hitches. Per-tile merged meshes (full trees near, impostors far) have no frame above 16.7 ms even at 150 km/h.
- **Splat terrain material** (spec 4.6) as a Bevy `ExtendedMaterial` with a WESL shader: no measurable cost.
- **Floating origin** with per-tile rebasing works; `big_space` is not needed for this world size.
- Tiles are built off the main thread and uploaded with a per-frame budget; this pattern carries over to the world streaming of Phase 3.

**Still open:** a run on minimum-spec hardware (15, GTX 1050 / RX 560 class); skeletal animation (needs a rigged rider model, Phase 4); Windows (D3D12) and macOS (Metal) at the start of each port (11.1); textures from real CC0 sources instead of procedural ones.

### 3.2 User Interface

- **Bevy UI** for the in-ride HUD (including the junction overlay, 2.2.1) and the main menus. The user interface is connected as directly as possible to the engine state.
- **egui** (`bevy_egui`) for the editor parameter panels, the in-game console (2.9) and development/diagnostic interfaces, to keep development fast. The editors are reviewed after Phase 4.

**Input devices (v1.9):** keyboard and gamepads (Bevy's gamepad support, gilrs: Xbox, PlayStation, Switch Pro and generic pads, hot-plugged). Keyboard: ↑ adds power (25 W per press, more while held, on top of any device), ↓ stops (power 0 and brake), ← / → steer (5.2.1), A autodrive, W wild mode, U U-turn, Delete / Page Down (or Q / E) the exit to the left / right (2.2.1, 3.2.5; Page Up / Page Down ±10 W until v5.17), F11 next screen, C camera reset, R restart (v2.0), V video (v2.0). Gamepad: left stick left / right steers (sets the lean directly, centred = upright); ↑ = D-pad up, left stick up or right trigger, ↓ = left stick down or left trigger (triggers and stick read as analog values, v2.0; D-pad down until v5.06, now the navigation map's zoom, 3.2 Q6); South = autodrive, West = wild, D-pad left / right = exits, East = U-turn (v2.0). Several pads: the largest stick deflection steers. **Whole UI (decided 2026-11-13, v2.54):** every screen and menu is also controllable with mouse, gamepad and – where the device has one – a touchscreen; the input model, touch in a ride and the platform facts are in 3.2.2.

**Restart and video (v2.0):** R (console `reset`) starts the whole app again as at program start, with the same command line: the app exits normally (ride saved, devices shut down) and replaces its process with a fresh one (Unix `exec`, same process id for the kiosk). V (console `video`) records the window: a screenshot is requested on every 1/25 s tick (several in flight, since the GPU readback takes a few frames), each image is placed at the video frame of its request time, and the frames are streamed as raw pixels into `ffmpeg` (H.264 MP4, CRF 18 with the `veryfast` preset since v2.30 – before `ultrafast` CRF 20 –, at most 2560 px wide, in the user's video directory, with the game sound since v2.30, 3.3); a tick without an image repeats the previous one to keep real time, the game never waits for the encoder (an image it cannot take is dropped and counted), a screenshot requested by the user or a script in the same frame takes precedence, and a running recording is finished on exit. V again stops it (the key is ignored while the console is open). While recording, the HUD shows a small blinking red dot with "REC m:ss" (recording length) at the top right; after stopping, "Video saved: <file>" (or the error) for 4 s.

**FPS counter (decided 2026-11-12):** console `fps on|off`, setting `display.fps` (*Settings → Display*): a small green badge at the top right, below the REC indicator, e.g. `58 fps  max 21 ms` – the frames drawn in the last second and the longest of them, renewed twice a second. It measures the **real render rate on the wall clock** (`ocw-render::frame_rate`, one `Instant::now()` per frame), not Bevy's `Time<Real>`, which frame capture (`--capture`) steps by a fixed 1/25 s per frame and would always show 25. `--log-fps S` logs the same rate every S seconds (`render rate fps=… worst_ms=…`, mean and longest frame over the period). Options considered: on by default for everyone (a number riders do not need, and the HUD is busy enough), only in debug builds (the release kiosk and the test videos need it too), **off by default for riders and on in every test picture and video (chosen):** `drive.sh` (screenshots, `--capture` videos, scene harness) passes `--cmd "fps on" --log-fps 5` unless `OCW_FPS=0`, and the multiplayer test turns it on for the kiosk and the camera client (11.4.1). Before, the counter was one more line at the end of the small HUD text, off by default and never on in tests – the user could not find it in the multiplayer video. For benchmarks `--no-vsync` draws without waiting for the display's refresh and `--max-fps N` caps the rate by sleeping at the end of a frame.

**Heart rate: a beating heart (built v6.82, asked by the user 2026-11-27: "make the heart of the HR pounding in pink when HR increases"):** with a heart rate the big line shows a small **heart icon** in the place of the letters "HR" ("♥ 142", the icon drawn in code – no emoji font, plain RGBA8 images, the same in both apps on WebGPU and WebGL 2; `ocw_render::heart_hud`), laid out inline in the line's text so it wraps with it and the line keeps its width and height; without a heart rate there is no heart and no "HR", as before. The heart **beats at the measured heart rate**: a short pulse in the first 35 % of each beat (sin², up to 1.15 × its size), its phase running on smoothly when the rate changes. **While the heart rate rises** it turns **hot pink** (#ff4fa3, from its normal soft red over 0.4 s; the dark outline and the panel's backing keep it readable on light and dark scenes) and **pounds**: up to 1.3 × with a slight pink glow; steady or falling, it goes back to the soft red and the soft beat. *Rising* (`ocw_render::heart::HrTrend`, pure and unit-tested): an exponential average of the heart rate (time constant 4 s) compared with the same average 10 s before – rising from +2 bpm per 10 s, steady again below +0.5 bpm per 10 s or as soon as the last 5 s rose less than that (so a peak or a drop ends it within a few seconds; falling the same way down), each state held at least 2 s, no trend before 6 s of readings; a missing heart rate or a gap of more than 5 s starts over (a strap's jitter of ± 1.5 bpm never makes it flicker). Reduced motion (`display.reduced_motion`): only the colour changes, no beat; `hud off` hides it with the panel; god mode's flight panel has none. The VR bike computer shows the heart rate in the same pink while it rises. For scenes and tests the Dev command `hr.test BPM | FROM TO SECONDS [--hold S] [--noise BPM] | off` (`ocw_ui::hr_test`, both apps) feeds a made-up heart rate, one reading per second, into the ride client.

**HUD top panel on narrow windows (fixed v4.57):** at 1280 × 720 the browser's "Virtual trainer …" line ran below the bike computer panel's bottom edge: Bevy wrapped lines longer than the panel by itself and the panel did not grow with them. The HUD now breaks every line itself for the panel's real width (`fit_top_panel` keeps it in `TopPanelWidth`; the main line between its fields, the small lines at " | ", then ", ", then between words – `ocw_render::hud::top_panel_text`), so each line fits and the panel grows with them, in both apps. Test (like the menu's fit test): every 16:9 size from 1280 × 720 to 3840 × 2160 and 4:3, the HUD at 100 – 150 %, both apps' key lines, the long weather line and device status – every line inside the panel, nothing lost, the panel on screen (in the upper half at 100 %). Scenes `fix-hud-*`.

**Phone layout (built v5.17, `ocw_render::hud_fit`):** the HUD's pixel sizes (the 26 / 15 px fonts of the bike computer, the 300 × 56 px profile, the map's 240 px, the 14 px timestamp) were chosen for windows of 1280 × 720 and more; a phone (an iPhone 15: 393 × 852 CSS px at pixel ratio 3, 852 × 393 turned) got them unchanged, so the top panel's numbers stood one per line over half the screen and the bottom boxes ran into each other. The device pixel ratio was not the cause – Bevy's logical px are the page's CSS px, and the pixel-ratio cap of the quality presets (10C) is off in WebKit anyway. Built, in both apps (they share the HUD):
- *The HUD's size follows the screen's CSS size:* `UiScale` = the HUD size setting (`display.ui_scale`, `HudSize`) × the screen's fit, `clamp(short side / 540, 0.75, 1)`, where the short side is that of the UI area (the window inside the safe area, logical px). Every window with a short side of 540 px or more – desktops, kiosks, the VR mirror, tablets – keeps its HUD exactly as before; a phone gets 0.75 (an iPhone 15: 393 / 540 is below it). The menu is sized by the window's height and stays.
- *Compact* below a short side of 500 px (a phone): the big line holds only the ride's numbers – power, speed, cadence, gradient with the 100 m average, heart rate; the weather, the wind (its arrow and speed, "↙ 6 km/h") and the clock of the place move, shortened, into the first small line; the place line carries the short status (the steering and the brake – the browser leaves the devices and the trainer to its Devices panel, `RideView::status_compact`); the elevation profile narrows to at most 40 % of the width and half the height and flattens to 44 px, off the road in the middle; the first-ride touch tip starts at 40 % of the height instead of 28 %, below the top panel. *Narrow* (compact and under 700 UI px wide: portrait): the top panel takes the whole width and the top-right column (timestamp, REC, the app message, FPS) moves below it, on the right. On the iPhone that is 2 big lines and 3 small ones in portrait, 2 + 2 in landscape (left of the timestamp's column).
- *The key lines are left out while the touch hints show* (any size): they describe keys a touch rider does not have; a key press hides the hints and brings them back.
- *The browser's Devices panel* starts collapsed to its "Devices" button on a touch-first device without Web Bluetooth (iOS: Safari and every browser there), where nothing can connect; its note then names the touch power buttons instead of the keys.
- *Measured for the tests:* `ocw_render::hud::HudBoxes` (the top panel, the top-right column and the profile in window px, the top panel's lines), in the browser `window.ocw.hudLayout()`.
