- **Q1 – Andorra's roads beyond the border: decided (2026-11-26, the user): as proposed – not now; the package ends at Geofabrik's border, neighbouring packages may come later** – the Andorra package ends where Geofabrik's Andorra extract ends, about 1 km beyond the border: the CG-2 stops just past Pas de la Casa (the climb to the Port d'Envalira from L'Hospitalet-près-l'Andorre in France, 1,436 m, and the Port de Puymorens are not in it) and the CG-1 just past the customs at La Farga de Moles (La Seu d'Urgell, 690 m, and the Spanish side of the Coll de la Gallina are not in it); the slopes beyond the border are terrain without roads (the other worlds do the same: Liechtenstein ends at the Swiss and Austrian borders). Options: (a) leave it: Andorra alone, all four climbs are inside; (b) widen the package by a margin of about 10 km into France and Spain (the roads from the Geofabrik extracts of Midi-Pyrénées and Catalonia, cut with `--bbox`), so the Envalira can be ridden from L'Hospitalet (1,000 m of climbing more) and Andorra from La Seu d'Urgell – the package grows by about half; (c) separate neighbour packages later (Cerdanya / Ariège, Alt Urgell), joined at the border like the Black Forest's parts. Proposal: a now, c when a Pyrenees region is wanted.

Packages are **signed, versioned and updatable**:

- **Ed25519** signatures. An offline root key signs rotating online signing keys. The client ships the root public key.
- Each package manifest lists SHA-256 hashes of all files.
- **TUF** (The Update Framework) is evaluated for package and app updates.
- Target size: 200–500 MB for a mid-sized region.
- The format allows streaming over HTTP in tile-sized chunks (3.5).

**Build profile (decided 2026-11-13, v2.59).** `world-builder package` prints a stage table at the end of every build: wall time, share, CPU time, the cores in use (CPU / wall) and their share of the machine, peak and final resident set per stage (`ocw_worldgen::stages`; Linux reads `/proc/self`, a sampler thread follows the resident set every 10 ms; elsewhere only times), and writes it as JSON with `--profile FILE`. `scripts/world-profile.sh` builds Liechtenstein, a Black Forest part and Tenerife into a scratch directory with the arguments of the build scripts and compares each package byte for byte with a reference build. The profile showed the build mostly single-threaded (1.3 of 12 cores in the Black Forest): five sequential PBF passes, the road profiles (twice for a part: its own graph and the context graph; most of it the gradient limit across junctions), bridge detection and the settle pass. Accelerated, with byte-identical packages:

- PBF passes decode their blobs on all cores (`osm::par_elements`, results in file order);
- `ocw_worldgen::par::map`, a parallel map with dynamic scheduling (each thread takes the next item, results in item order), replaces one contiguous chunk per thread for the DTM files (outside files cost only their header), the terrain heights of the tiles, and runs the profile DEM sampling, the bridge detection and the settle pass's constraint collection per edge or tile;
- the settle pass relaxes over vertex indices instead of a hash-map lookup per use (the same arithmetic in the same order);
- the class gradient across junctions (`limit_grades_across_junctions`, up to 2,000 Gauss-Seidel sweeps over every profile sample) skips an edge while neither its own last sweep nor a neighbour changed anything at its ends – exactly the operations that would have changed something, in the same order (2 × 23 s → 2 × 0.5 s for the Black Forest).

Measured on marge (12 threads; wall time, cores in use = CPU / wall, peak resident set; the old code on the same input for comparison):

| World | old code | new code | Hot stages (old → new) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Liechtenstein | 5.7 s, 2.8 cores, 0.81 GB | 3.1 s (−46 %), 5.6 cores, 0.83 GB | profiles 1.0 → 0.3 s, settle 1.3 → 0.25 s, bridge detection 0.5 → 0.1 s |
| Black Forest north | 164 s (load 3–10; 180–243 s at load 17–27), 1.3 cores, 6.26 GB | 57–61 s (−63 to −65 %, load 7–11), 3.5–3.7 cores, 6.5 GB | profiles 2 × 28 → 2 × 4.5 s (grades across junctions 2 × 23 → 2 × 0.5 s), PBF passes 43 → 16 s, bridge detection 2 × 7.5 → 2 × 1.3 s, settle 19.4 → 3.7 s, DTM files 2.9 → 1.7 s |
| Tenerife | 81 s (90–129 s at load 17–27), 1.5 cores, 2.23 GB | 36 s (−55 %), 3.5 cores, 2.41 GB | profiles 2 × 16 → 2 × 6.6 s, PBF passes 8.4 → 4 s, bridge detection 2 × 4.3 → 2 × 0.7 s, settle 14.8 → 2.7 s |

The machine was shared with other builds throughout; on a saturated machine the parallel passes help less (an intermediate version without the junction-grade change took 153–178 s for the Black Forest at load 17–27). The new code takes about 0.2 GB more peak memory (per-thread buffers of the parallel passes).

**Equivalence:** every package of the new code is byte-identical to the old code's on the same input (`scripts/world-profile.sh --ref`, Liechtenstein, Black Forest north and Tenerife, five rounds; the old binary built from the unchanged tree, run with `--no-profile`). One Tenerife comparison differed only because the SRTM tiles in `data/tenerife` were downloaded again between the two builds (SRTM fallback 0 → 2 tiles); old and new code on the new data are identical again, and repeated runs of the new code are identical.

**What remains (open):** the area extract (`read OSM areas` 21 s for the Black Forest: the PBF passes 12 s, `retain near` 6 s, single-threaded hash-set work), the through-road filter (2 × 3 s), land-use cleaning and water levels; the region graph's profiles are computed and then replaced by the context graph's (`transfer_profiles` takes all of them), which would save another 8 s but changes the bridge spans derived from them, so it needs its own equivalence check.

**Manifest, signatures and cache (implemented, Phase 3):**

- **Manifest** (`ocw_world::manifest`, pure and wasm-safe; ed25519-dalek + sha2): a JSON file next to the package (`<file>.ocwpkg.manifest.json`; `manifest.json` in published and cached directories). The signed part holds the format (1), the **package id** (lower-case path segments, e.g. `europe/liechtenstein`), region name, **version** (build number), creation time, generator (`world-builder 0.1.0`), package format (`OCWPKG02`), the **attributions** (© OpenStreetMap contributors with the ODbL Derivative Database notice for the road graph, the DEM source, 13) and every file with size and SHA-256 **plus each chunk** (header, every tile, every section) with offset, size and SHA-256, so single tiles fetched with range requests can be verified on their own.
- **Signature format:** the signed part is kept as raw JSON bytes (`"signed": {…}`) and signatures cover exactly those bytes behind a per-kind context string (`OCW world package manifest v1\0`, `OCW signing key v1\0`). No canonical JSON is needed, and fields added later do not break old signatures; unknown fields are ignored.
- **Key hierarchy:** the **root key** (Ed25519) is generated once (`world-builder keys init-root`) and kept offline; it only certifies **signing keys** (`keys new-signing`, default validity 365 days): a certificate with the signing key's public key, name, root key id and validity period. Each manifest carries its signing key certificate, so the client needs only the root public keys. Key id = the first 8 bytes of SHA-256 of the public key. Secret key files (`*.key`, mode 0600, never overwritten) live outside the repository (`~/.config/ocw/keys`, `$OCW_KEY_DIR`); `.gitignore` also ignores `*.key`.
- **Verification chain:** certificate signed by a trusted root → neither key revoked (a revocation list compiled into the client) → manifest signature by the signing key → manifest created within the signing key's validity period and not more than a day in the future → each file's size and SHA-256. Validity is checked against the creation time, not today, so a cached package keeps working offline after its signing key expires, while an expired or stolen-and-revoked key cannot sign new packages.
- **Trusted roots:** production roots are compiled into the client (none yet; they come with the distribution infrastructure). Development roots (`crates/ocw-worldstore/keys/dev-roots.json`, public keys only, marked development) are trusted by debug builds and with `--trust-dev-root`. More roots: `--trust-root FILE` and `~/.config/ocw/trusted-roots/*.pub.json` (private servers, own builds).
- **User keys (v3.71; 14 Phase 16, 16C *Signing and trust*, Q2):** a user's own key signs the worlds they edit and share. `world-builder keys init-user --name NAME` makes a root of their own (`user-root.key`, `user-root.pub.json`) and a signing key (`user.key`, 10 years) that carries the root's public key; every manifest it signs embeds the root (`signature.root`, ignored by older readers). A client checks such a chain with the embedded root – only if it is the root that certified the signing key – so it can tell an intact package (**`UntrustedKey`**: the user is asked) from a damaged one (a bad signature or a file that does not match the manifest: refused, never asked about). The key's **fingerprint** is the SHA-256 of its 32 raw bytes as 16 groups of four upper-case hex digits (`3F2A 9C11 …`; the key id is its first four groups); the name in the key is only **claimed** and always shown so ("signed by 'Ada Rider' (unverified name)"). `world-builder keys fingerprint FILE` prints it for a key file, a package or a manifest.
  - **Trusted user keys** (`ocw_worldstore::userkeys`): name, public key, key id, fingerprint, date added, note; per user in `<data dir>/ocw/trusted-keys.json` (`$OCW_TRUSTED_KEYS`; written atomically) on the desktop and the server, in `localStorage` (`ocw-trusted-keys`) in the browser. A corrupt store trusts none, says so (*Trusted world keys*, `world trust list`) and is not overwritten until the list changes. The keys are appended to the trust store after every built-in root (production, development, preview, `--trust-root`, `trusted-roots/`) and marked as user keys; a built-in root can neither be added to the list nor overridden by it. Packages they sign are **unofficial** (World menu: *unofficial, 'name'*; untrusted: *unknown key, 'name'*).
  - **The decision** (`userkeys::decide`): a built-in root → load (official); a trusted user key → load (unofficial); an unknown user key → the **trust dialog**; trusted, then removed → the dialog again; a bad signature or a revoked key → refused; unsigned or an unknown root without its key → the policy below, as before. `UntrustedKey` is refused by both policies (also with `--allow-unsigned`): nothing loads a user-signed world without the user's (or the server operator's) consent.
  - **The trust dialog** (both apps, the shared menu model's `ConfirmTrust` page and `ocw_ui::trust`; keys, gamepad, mouse and touch; ten-foot sizes): the title *Trust this world's key?*, "Signed by 'Ada Rider' (unverified name):", the full fingerprint large (two lines of eight groups, monospaced), the warning "This world was not made by Open Cycling World. Only trust keys whose fingerprint you checked with their owner, for example in person or over a channel you trust.", the world (name, id, version, build date; in a shared ride "Cancel leaves the shared ride"), and the data sources with their licences. *Trust this key* (remembered, then loaded), *Load once* (accepted until the app quits, not remembered: to look at a friend's world without keeping their key; the key protects the same either way, so loading once is no weaker than trusting), *Cancel* – focused, so Enter right away cancels; Back, Esc, B and closing the menu decline too. Shown when a world is chosen in the World menu or with `world switch` / `ride.switch`, for `--world` at the start (the app starts on the built-in loop and switches once trusted) and in the browser for the page's `?world=` (the stream waits after the manifest; the loading screen steps aside).
  - **Managing them:** *Settings → Account → Trusted world keys* lists the keys (name as claimed, the fingerprint's first groups) and a key's page (name, date, note, the full fingerprint) removes it after "Remove this key?" (Cancel focused); the console: `world trust list | add PUBKEY|FILE [--name] [--note] | remove FINGERPRINT | show | accept | once | decline` (a fingerprint prefix of 8+ digits will do).
  - **Shared rides:** the server checks its own trust and is **configured, never told**: `ocw-server --trust-key KEY|FILE` and the `trusted-keys.json` of the account it runs as (*Load once* is a rider's answer, never the server's); a host's `WorldRequest` for a world whose key the server does not trust is answered "this server does not trust the user key that signed it … `--trust-key`". When the server switched (`WorldChange`), each client checks its own copy (`ocw_client::world_trust::follow`): trusted → load and join again; unknown → the dialog, with "Cancel leaves the shared ride"; declined or refused (damaged, another version) → the client leaves the shared ride with a message and rides on alone on the built-in loop – it never rides a world it did not accept.
- **Policy for packages not signed by a trusted root:** integrity failures (hash or size mismatch, bad signature, revoked key, malformed manifest) are **always refused**. Packages that are intact but unsigned, signed by an unknown root or outside the key's validity are a trust failure: from the **cache** (by id) they are **refused** unless `--allow-unsigned`; from a **path** (local builds, power users, 4.2) they load **with a warning** unless `--require-signed`. A package without a manifest counts as unsigned (id `local/<name>`, version 0). Multiplayer sessions (Phase 5) will require trusted packages.
- **Identity:** id, version and the SHA-256 of the package file (`Manifest::identity()`, `PackageIdentity`) tell client and server whether they ride the same world (and the same stable edge IDs). Builds are deterministic, so the same input gives the same content hash on every build machine.
- **Cache:** `$OCW_WORLD_CACHE` or `~/.local/share/ocw/worlds/<id>/<version>/{manifest.json, <files>}`; downloads collect in `.partial/<id>@<version>/` and are moved into place only when every file is verified. Packages are verified again on every load. `--world` takes a path or a cache id (`ID` = newest version, `ID@VERSION`); `--list-worlds` and the console commands `worlds.list` / `worlds.verify` show and check the cache.
- **Download:** `ocw-desktop --fetch-world URL` fetches the manifest first and checks its signature before any large download, then the files next to it (the layout `world-builder publish` writes: `<base>/<id>/<version>/manifest.json`), resuming interrupted downloads with HTTP range requests (`Range: bytes=N-`; a server answering 200 restarts the file). Local directories and `file://` URLs install the same way. Downloads happen before the ride, never during it (4.2). `world-builder publish` also writes `<base>/<id>/latest` (the newest version number) for clients that name a world by id. TUF remains under evaluation for app updates and key rotation metadata.
- **Streaming (v2.99, 14 Phase 10 B2):** the browser app streams a package by chunk instead (`ocw_worldstore::stream`, pure and wasm-safe; the manifest check `accept_manifest` is shared with `--fetch-world`): manifest and signature chain first, then the base (`header`, `sections`, every `section …`) and the `tile X,Z` chunks around the rider with merged `Range: bytes=a-b` requests; each chunk is checked against its SHA-256 in the manifest before use or caching, a mismatch is fetched once more on its own and then refused with an error naming the chunk. Verified chunks are cached per id / version / chunk (the browser's OPFS) with least-recently-used eviction by a size budget. `ocw_world::package::StreamedPackage` decodes the base once and the tiles one by one; the result equals the whole file's decode with those tiles.
- **Rebuilds:** `world-builder diff OLD NEW` (`ocw_worldgen::diff::GraphDiff`) lists the edges whose stable ID survived (unchanged or moved), was removed or added; routes over surviving edges re-match directly, the others are flagged.
- **World patches (v5.99, 14 Phase 16 16C, 16H Q9):** a package built with world patches (`package --patch`) has them as files next to it (`<file>.ocwpatch`, a stack as `<file>.2.ocwpatch`, …) and its manifest records each one's `path`, `size` and `sha256` in the optional signed list `patches` (not in `files`: clients do not download or verify it; older readers ignore it). `publish` and `scripts/prepare-world-release.sh` ship the patches whose SHA-256 matches; a missing or changed one is a warning in the report and left out, never a failure. Later steps keep the record, steps with `--out` copy the patches along.
- **Rewrites (v2.24):** commands that change a built package in place (`route --world`, `gpx`, `routes --from / --remove`) write its manifest again (same id, name and attribution, next version), because the old one lists the old SHA-256 and every client refused the package as damaged. A signed manifest becomes unsigned (the key is not at hand); the command says to sign it again.

### 4.8 World Cleaning (decided 2026-11-13, v2.39)

OSM and the DEM are not physically consistent: roads step and kink, ends stop a metre short of the road they join, rivers on SRTM step up and down, culverts were drawn as open water, and the terrain grid cannot follow two roads at different heights a few metres apart. The world builder therefore **cleans the world while building it**. It may deviate a little from the source data to get a physically believable world, within the limits below; what riders ride stays the same road network.

**Never changed:** the topology of the road graph (vertices, edges, junctions, one-ways), the stable edge IDs and therefore the routes (2.7, 4.4); the road classes, names and widths; the OSM land classes (only slivers are merged). `world-builder package --no-clean` (and `route --no-clean`) builds without the cleaning, for comparisons.

#### 4.8.1 Lint: measuring what looks wrong

`world-builder lint --world PKG [--pbf EXTRACT]` (`ocw_worldgen::lint`, pure) counts every finding with its extent and the worst cases (local metres, latitude / longitude, OSM way):

| Check | Finding |
|---|---|
| `road.vertical.grade_over_limit` / `.step` / `.kink` | a 5 m interval steeper than its class limit + 1 %; a step (> 1 m and > limit + 5 %); a gradient change > 8 points between two intervals (**kinks by cause**, v5.36, J3: `kink.crease` – within one interval of where a side road leaves a main road's edge at its own grade, 4.8.8 Q6 (d); `kink.junction` – within 30 m beyond a junction surface's reach; `kink.other`). **Grade by cause** (`grade_over_limit.CAUSE`, v5.19, 4.8.8 J2b; `ocw_worldgen::junctions::steep_intervals`): `source_steep` – the road's own fixed heights round the interval (its two junction heights, bridge decks) lie farther apart than the limit + 1 % allows (the source data is steeper); `junction_room` – the source heights would allow it, but not with the junction surfaces level with their main roads (a side road's mouth on the main road's surface and the next fixed height – another junction surface, a bridge deck – too close: J3's clusters, 4.8.8 Q6); `junction` – within 30 m beyond a junction surface's reach and could hold the limit (the re-limiting's target: 0); `other` – elsewhere |
| `road.horizontal.duplicate_node` / `.spike` / `.self_crossing` | points < 0.25 m apart; an out-and-back point (turn > 150°, a leg < 15 m); a centreline crossing itself |
| `road.near_miss_end` | a dead end within 3 m of another road it does not join |
| `junction.height_mismatch` / `junction.seam` / `junction.overlap` / `junction.no_surface.REASON` | profile ends at a junction differing by > 5 cm; at a junction with a surface (patch or mitre, 4.8.8) the drawn carriageways – the patch's triangles and the shaped strips' rows, as the renderer draws them – sampled every 0.2 m from above over the patch and its mouths (at least the widest half width + 2.5 m): a jump of the top carriageway between two roads above 2 cm less the slope (`seam`), carriageways of two roads within 1 cm over more than 0.5 m² (`overlap`, z-fighting); where two or more roads meet on the ground without a surface, its reason (J3's work); `junction.measured` counts the junctions measured (v5.14, 4.8.8 J2; replaces `junction.surface_step`: a strip lying on another road's strip with > 0.25 m height difference, which J1's trimmed strips no longer draw); `junction.mouth.above_main` (v5.56, 4.8.8 Q7): at a junction with a through road, sampled every 0.2 m over its carriageway (on the patch and along its arms' strips), a side road's surface more than 2 cm above the main road's drawn surface – `.mesh` the junction surface lifted above the main road's own surface by a side road's corner, `.strip` a side road's strip over the main road – one finding per junction; `side.gap` / `side.step` / `side.kink` / `side.corner` (v5.56, 4.8.8 Rule): the sides of every junction surface as drawn – a mouth corner of the outline that no row of its arm's strip starts at, a jump of the side's height (more than 2 cm between outline and strip at a mouth corner, more than 5 cm plus a quarter of the distance between outline points less than 0.6 m apart), a change of grade above 8 points along a corner's outline over stretches of at least 1 m, a bend in plan above 25° along a corner or where it turns into its arm's edge – one finding per junction and kind; **since v5.61 (J5, the Rule built)** measured against the drawn surface's slope: a side that turns on a sloping surface changes its grade by the turn alone (on a plane at 20 % round a 1.5 m corner by 13 points per metre), so `kink` is the change of grade between stretches of at least 1 m less what the turn explains on the surface's slope there (its gradient times the change of direction), also where the outline meets its arm's strip edge (the outline's last metre against the strip edge's first); `step` a jump between outline points less than 0.6 m apart that the surface's slope does not explain (more than 5 cm), as before 2 cm between outline and strip at a mouth corner; `corner` the bend between pieces of at least 0.3 m (a curve cut finely is measured over 0.3 m: radii under about 0.7 m count) |
| `road.crossing_step_untagged` | strips of two roads without a shared junction overlapping at different heights, neither tagged as bridge or tunnel |
| `road.float.{untagged,bridge}.BAND`, `road.buried.*` | sampled every 2 m at the centre and both edges: terrain more than 0.8 m below the road surface (bands 0.8–1.5, 1.5–3, 3–6, > 6 m), or above it; floating untagged roads get a cause: `water` (a water vertex under the road), `lower_road_nearby` (the cut zone of a lower road within 15 m), `other` |
| `road.over_water_untagged` | road length over water cells without a bridge (a missing bridge) |
| `water.river_uphill` / `.river_step` / `.lake_not_level` / `.level_step` | along each river with a water surface (in OSM flow direction, every 10 m) the level rising > 0.3 m above the lowest so far, or jumping > 0.5 m; a lake whose levels span > 0.25 m; neighbouring water vertices > 0.5 m apart |
| `building.floating` / `.half_buried` / `.on_steep_slope` | wall foot above the ground; ground above half the wall height; > 3 m of slope under the footprint |
| `landuse.sliver` / `.gap` | patches of ≤ 2 cells (≤ 50 m²) of one class; unclassified holes of ≤ 6 cells enclosed by one class |
| `bridge.SOURCE.STRUCTURE` | the bridges built (4.8.6), by source and structure |

#### 4.8.2 Roads: horizontal

- **Duplicate nodes** (< 0.25 m) are removed; **spikes** (turn > 150° with a leg < 15 m, the point at most 15 m off its neighbours' chord) are removed, repeatedly. Graph vertices never move here.
- **Near-miss joins:** a dead end (one road, not at the region border, not a bridge or tunnel) within **3 m** of another road is moved onto that road's centreline (the largest horizontal deviation the builder allows), and after the profiles its end takes that road's height there; its road is re-limited to its class gradient. No junction is added (that would change topology and stable IDs).

#### 4.8.3 Roads: vertical

On top of 4.3 (sampling, median and Gaussian filters, class gradient limits along through-roads and across junctions):

- **Gradient limits per class** stay those of 4.3: 15 % trunk / primary / secondary, 20 % tertiary / unclassified / residential / cycleway, 25 % service / track / path; bridges and tunnels are straight between their ends.
- **Vertical curvature:** inside each road (not at its junction ends) the gradient may change by at most **0.5 % per metre** on trunk / primary / secondary and **1 % per metre** on all others; kinks are rounded into vertical curves (a sample moves towards its neighbours' chord, so no interval gets steeper).
- **Junction mouths:** a wider road is drawn flat across, so a side road leaving it must not climb or fall within the wider road's half width: its first 5 m interval is limited to a **0.15 m** step at the wider road's edge (never so far that its far end leaves the class gradient), the rest re-limited from there. **Since J2 (v5.14) only where the junction has no surface:** at a patched junction the side road's blend onto the main road (4.8.8) replaces it. **Since J2b (v5.19)** the class gradient and vertical-curvature limits above are applied again after that blend, with the junction surfaces as fixed heights (4.8.8 *Built (J2b)*): a side road's missed height is spread over as long a stretch as it needs. **Since J3 (v5.36, 4.8.8 Q6 (d))** a side road's own surface starts at the main road's edge, at its own grade, its blend and the re-limiting from there; the corner between the two roads slopes.
- **Terrain under roads:** after the road-conformed terrain (4.3) and the water (4.8.4) the terrain grid is **settled**: every road strip and bridge deck is sampled every metre along and 0.5 m across, and wherever a terrain triangle (split as in the client mesh) rises closer than **5 cm** to the surface, its three vertices are lowered by the least amount (a Gauss–Seidel projection over the violated samples; lowering never breaks a satisfied one). Vertices shared by neighbouring tiles change in every copy. The result: no terrain shows through any road.
- **Terrain smoothing off the roads (v5.56, 4.8.8 Q7 (d)):** after the settling, every terrain vertex moves towards a local quadratic surface fitted (Gaussian-weighted least squares, a Savitzky–Golay filter) to its neighbours within **10 m** (`terrain_smooth::RADIUS_M`; at the packages' 10 m grid the 3 × 3 vertices, 20 m across): bumps smaller than the window go, slopes and the curvature of hills, ridges and valleys stay; no vertex moves more than **0.5 m**. Vertices under a road on the ground (its half width plus a grid spacing), a junction surface or blend, water or a building site keep their heights, and the change fades in over the window beside them; the terrain is settled under the roads again. `world-builder package` does it while cleaning (before the building sites), `world-builder smooth-terrain --world PKG [--out NEW] [--radius M] [--max-change M]` for a built package.
- **Terrain conforming per road (the cause of floating roads):** before v2.39 every segment within a road's cut zone (half width + 15 m) cut the terrain to its height at its nearest point – for the segment behind the one under a point that is the node between them, up to 15 m back and on a 10 % climb 1.5 m lower, and the blend could take that height as well. One third of Liechtenstein's and 28 % of the Black Forest's road length stood 0.8 m or more above the ground (`road.float_cause.other`). Now each road shapes the terrain through its **nearest point only**, the cut is its half width + 0.5 m, and the settle pass does the rest.
- **Where the grid cannot follow** (the upper leg of a hairpin 10–15 m above the lower one, a road beside a lower road): the road's edge face reaches down to 0.3 m below the terrain at its edge (at least 2 m, at most 40 m), so it stands on a **retaining wall** instead of floating as a slab; on bridge decks the strip has no edge face (the deck has its own sides).
- **Road edge into the terrain (v2.60, Phase 8 T5):** the drawn surface lies `ROAD_SURFACE_LIFT_M` (2 cm) above the profile and the settled terrain at least 5 cm below it, so on flat ground the old vertical edge face (light grey, 2 m deep) stood above the terrain as a slab edge (Las Cañadas). Now the edge has a 3 cm lip, then a **shoulder** (verge, the gravel layer beside paved roads, the road's own material beside unpaved ones) sloping 1 : 1.5 down to 4 cm under the terrain surface, 0.4 m wide plus 1.5 × the drop (at most 2.65 m), with a 0.3 m skirt below its outer edge; in junction zones it stays 0.4 m wide (the crossing road's surface covers the lip). Where the ground lies more than 1.5 m below the edge the retaining wall of the previous rule remains (now in the kerb concrete). No edge geometry on bridge decks. The riding surface and the wheel contact (v2.47) are unchanged; riders never touch the shoulder (road edge rule 5.2.1).

#### 4.8.4 Water

- **Rivers** (OSM `waterway` lines with a drawn surface, ≥ 8 m wide; their direction is the flow direction) are joined across way splits into chains (same name or width, one way continuing at the shared node). The natural DEM along each chain every 10 m is fitted by the best **non-increasing** profile (least squares, pool adjacent violators): rivers never flow uphill and never step up. Main rivers are levelled first; a tributary ends at least at the main river's level, a branch starts at most at it.
- **Lakes** (water areas that are not river surfaces: not `water=river|stream|canal|…`, not `waterway=riverbank`) get one level: the median of the DEM under them.
- Every water vertex takes its lake's level, else the nearest river chain's within its half width plus three grid cells; the terrain under water is carved 1 m below the new level.
- **No water under roads:** vertices within a road's half width plus one grid cell (roads on the ground; bridges excepted) are never carved and get their road-conformed height back – before, carving lowered the terrain under roads beside rivers and lakes by a metre and more, and left them floating.
- **Culverts:** `tunnel=*` and `location=underground` on waterways are now read (they were dropped when reading the areas), so culverts under roads are no longer water bands.

#### 4.8.5 Buildings and land use

- **Building sites:** the terrain vertices inside a footprint (and within 1 m of it) move to the footprint's mean ground, by at most **1.5 m** (steeper sites keep their slope: a house set into the hillside), never under roads or water; the building is then placed as in 4.6 (walls from 0.5 m below the lowest ground).
- **Land use:** patches of at most 2 cells of one class (not water) take the most common class around them; unclassified holes of at most 6 cells enclosed by one class take that class. Patches at a tile edge are kept.

#### 4.8.6 Bridges

**Which stretches are bridges:**

1. OSM `bridge=*` (not `no`) ways – the whole edge (as before).
2. Untagged roads inside a `man_made=bridge` outline.
3. **Detected:** an untagged road crossing water – a water area or a waterway line ≥ **3 m** wide (narrower streams pass in a culvert) – with water on both sides of the road (a road along a shore is not a bridge; water stretches > 250 m along a road are mapping overlaps); or a road more than **5 m** above the natural ground (at least 10 m somewhere) for **8–150 m** (a gap the elevation filter bridged; longer is an embankment). Each detected span reaches 3 m beyond the obstacle (the abutments), merges with spans less than 8 m apart, and is left out where a tagged bridge already starts at that end. The build log counts them; their deck is planned **straight between the abutments**, and the terrain is cut under them but not pulled up to the deck, as under tagged bridges.

**The structure** (`ocw_world::bridges`, section `BRDG`, additive; older clients skip it and draw plain road strips):

- **Structure type:** `bridge=covered` → covered; `bridge:structure` arch / humpback → arch, truss → truss, suspension / simple-suspension / cable-stayed → suspension, anything else → beam; untagged → beam, except **stone** (`bridge:material` stone / masonry / brick) bridges up to 40 m, which are **arches**.
- **Material:** `bridge:material`, else by structure (covered → wood, truss / suspension → steel, arch → stone), paths up to 25 m → wood, other paths and cycleways → steel, roads → concrete. **Railing:** stone and concrete road bridges have solid **parapets** (0.9 m high, 0.35 m thick), steel, wood and path bridges **rails** (posts every 2 m, rails at 0.55 and 1.1 m).
- **Deck:** the road strip on top (the deck surface 1 cm under it), 0.6 m kerbs beyond the carriageway on each side; thickness by structure and span between supports: beam span / 18 (0.45–2.5 m; wood span / 25, 0.3–0.8 m), arch 0.45 m, truss 0.6 m, suspension 0.8 m, covered 0.5 m. Road strip points on a deck get no edge faces into the terrain (the deck has its own sides).
- **Supports:** abutments at both real ends (a block from the deck bottom to 0.6 m below the ground just outside the end; none where the bridge continues on the next bridge edge); **piers** where the bridge is longer than the structure's maximum span – concrete 35 m, steel 45 m, wood 12 m, stone beam 15 m, stone arch 18 m, other arches 50 m, truss 60 m, covered 30 m, suspension none – evenly spaced, each a wall pier from the deck bottom to 0.6 m into the ground (or river bed), only where the deck is more than 1 m above it.
- **Arches:** between consecutive supports, springing from the lower ground at the two supports (at most half the span below the crown), crown 0.35 m under the deck bottom; spandrel walls on both faces and the arch underside. Too low for 0.8 m of rise → a slab.
- **Above the deck:** truss sides (height length / 8, 2.5–7 m; chords, verticals, alternating diagonals), suspension towers and main cables with hangers, covered bridges with posts every 3 m, board walls to 1.2 m and a gable roof.
- **Rendering:** `ocw-render::bridges` builds the meshes per tile (a bridge belongs to the tile of its middle) with plain colours per material and part (`bridge_colour`, the hook for the material library of Phase 8). The terrain and water continue under the deck.

Reference photos (Commons links only): `docs/reference/bridges.md`.

#### 4.8.7 Results (2026-11-13)

`scripts/world-clean-compare.sh li|bf` builds each package with `--no-clean` and with the cleaning and lints both; the high-resolution DEMs of v2.35 (swissALTI3D, DGM1) are used. Share of the road length (untagged roads):

| Check | Liechtenstein before | after | Black Forest south before | after |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| floating > 0.8 m | 32.2 % | 7.2 % | 26.2 % | 5.3 % |
| floating > 3 m | 5.2 % | 0.7 % | 3.2 % | 0.6 % |
| buried | 2 m | 2 m | 326 m | 6 m |
| vertical kinks (> 8 points) | 774 | 6 | 11,678 | 40 |
| junction surface steps | 1,045 | 792 | 11,957 | 8,880 |
| near-miss ends / duplicate nodes / spikes | 3 / 6 / 1 | 0 / 0 / 0 | 30 / 40 / 10 | 6 / 4 / 0 |
| rivers uphill (length) | 6.5 km | 0 | 31.5 km | 70 m |
| tilted lakes | 41 | 0 | 286 | 4 |
| land-use slivers / gaps | 3,301 / 1,588 | 16 / 5 | 177,971 / 24,957 | 1,083 / 264 |
| bridges built (`BRDG`) | – | 274 (2 over water, 6 over gaps, 15 in outlines detected) | – | 2,826 (47 over water, 82 over gaps, 453 in outlines detected; 9 covered) |

With SRTM (before v2.35) the same passes took Liechtenstein from 33.9 % to 3.9 % and the Black Forest from 28.0 % to 4.1 % floating road length. The rest is mostly where the 10 m grid cannot follow (`lower_road_nearby` 2.9 %, hairpins and steep river banks with the sharp DTM): there the road's edge face now reaches the ground as a retaining wall. Build time of the Black Forest package: 228 s, settling 26 s.

**Open:** no structure of the two packages is an arch yet (OSM rarely tags `bridge:material=stone`); junction steps between a wide road drawn flat across and a steep side road remain (measured and planned in 4.8.8); `water.river_step` counts natural drops of steep mountain rivers; the grade limits of 4.3 are exceeded by 76 short stretches already before the cleaning (with the DTM).

#### 4.8.8 Smooth junctions (investigation 2026-11-15; J1 built 2026-11-16, J2 built 2026-11-19, J3 built 2026-11-22, J4 (Q7) and J5 (the Rule) built 2026-11-23)

- **Rule: the sides of a road are as smooth as the road** (the user, 2026-11-23: "can you make a rule in world building that smoothens the sides, too?"). Everything beside a carriageway – verges, sidewalks, kerb bands, cycle-lane bands, the side bands of a junction's corners and the terrain right next to them – follows the road it belongs to: in plan the same rounded corner as the carriageway (no sharp polygonal bends, enough segments for the radius), in height the same smoothed profile as the road (its vertical curves, never a step, crease or kink of its own), and it meets the neighbouring road's side band and the junction surface without a gap, hole or lip. The world builder and the renderer apply it for every package; the lint reports violations (`side.gap`, `side.step`, `side.kink`, `side.corner`) and must stay at 0. First part built with J4 (v5.56, *Built (J4 / Q7)*: the corner verges meet the arms' verges; the lint `side.*` in place). **Built with J5 (v5.61, *Built (J5 / the Rule)*)**: the outlines along the real edge lines with rounded corners, the mouth rows leaning with the main road or the blended plane, the sides smoothed along the outline, the corner verges as wide as the ground asks; `side.corner` halved (515 – 6,995 per package), `side.kink` 7 – 10 % fewer, `side.step` 15 – 74, `side.gap` 0 – 1 – **not at 0**: corners squeezed by short arms, chains that cannot be drawn star-shaped and kinks of steep junctions remain (the causes listed there). **Built with J6 (v5.65, *Built (J6 / the Rule)*)**: the verges' outer edges run on smoothly (no V at Letzanaweg), a side road never stands above the main road (`junction.mouth.above_main` 0 in all five packages), outlines need only be simple polygons and each corner takes the chain that bends least; `side.corner` −17 to −22 %, `side.kink` −2 to −4 % – still not at 0: clusters with paths along both roads, corners squeezed by short arms, forks and steep junctions (counts and pictures there). **Built with J7 (v5.67, *Built (J7 / the Rule)*)**: paths along a road (OSM sidewalk and cycle-track ways) are drawn as a band of its side – one band round the junction's corner, no mouth of their own, still routable and rideable on the band –, a corner its arms cut short turns round again (the Black Forest path view's round nose), clusters get rounded corners between arms of different members; `side.corner` −21 to −32 %, `side.kink` −2 to −8 %, seams and overlaps fewer – still not at 0: corners squeezed by short arms, clusters without paths, forks and steep junctions (counts there). **Built with J8 (v5.78, *Built (J8 / the Rule)*)**: a junction's arm runs on past a plain way split that squeezed it, the mouths lie out for their corners along the real edge lines (on arms at most 6 % steep), both only where the junction's sides bend no more; `side.corner` −5 to −9 %, no junction loses its surface – still not at 0: short arms between two junctions, steep junctions, clusters, island tips and roundabout entries (counts there). **Built with J9 (v5.91, *Built (J9 / the Rule)*)**: two junctions whose patches meet on a short edge but fit no star-shaped outline share one patch with a simple outline, and an arm whose edge's far end has no junction surface (a bridge, a dead end, a mitred way split) takes the room that end leaves – both only on arms at most 6 % steep and where the sides bend less; `side.corner` −4 to −13 %, `side.kink` up to −3 %, road kinks within +1 %, no junction loses its surface, a painted crossing stays where OSM has it – still not at 0: steep junctions (a strip's cross slope turned flat in a short edge), dual carriageways side by side, short arms between two junctions, island noses and roundabout entries (analysis there).

The user reported this bug on 2026-11-15: "junctions of roads are sometimes not cleanly going into one another but have bumps and quirks – the road segments just seem to be slammed together". This section has the measurements and the plan. **Stage J1 is built** (v4.29, on the current packages: see *Built (J1)* below), **J2 is built** (v5.14, the world builder: see *Built (J2)*), with the grade limits applied again after the blend (v5.19, *Built (J2b)*), **J3 is built** with Q6 (d) (v5.36, *Built (J3)*), **J4** with Q7 (d) and the terrain smoothing (v5.56, *Built (J4 / Q7)*).

**How a junction is drawn today (v3.65):**

- **No junction geometry.** Every graph edge becomes road strips (`ocw_worldgen::package::road_strips`), with a point every 5 m at the edge's profile height. Each strip runs **to the graph vertex** and **ends square there**, in the middle of the other road. `ocw-render::road_mesh` draws each strip **flat across**: there is no crossfall, and both edge vertices of a row sit at the centreline height. All strips lie at the same `ROAD_SURFACE_LIFT_M` with no depth offset between them, so the strips of all roads at a junction simply **overlap**.
- **Heights.**
  - The profiles of all roads end exactly at the shared vertex height (4.3 pass 2, `limit_grades_across_junctions`), so they agree **at the vertex point only**.
  - A metre away, each strip follows its own grade. Inside the main road, the side road's strip rises or falls with the side road's grade (g_side × distance). Across the main road, the flat side strip cannot follow the main road's grade (g_main × the side road's half width).
  - Junction mouths (4.8.3, `clean::ease_junction_mouths`) only ease the first 5 m interval of a **narrower** side road, to 0.15 m at the wider road's edge. Roads of equal width (most residential T junctions) and the main road's own grade are not handled.
- **Verges, kerbs, walls.**
  - Each strip keeps all its edge parts up to its end: the 3 cm lip, the shoulder (0.4 m wide in the junction zone), the skirt and, in towns, the kerb and sidewalk. Kerbs and sidewalks taper over 3 m into the junction zone (`RoadDress::junction_m`).
  - Where one strip lies higher, its lip and shoulder (or kerb) lie on the other road's carriageway.
  - Only sidewalk corners are rounded (`road_corners`, v3.15), and only when two roads **of the same tile** meet 20°–160° apart, both with sidewalks on the facing sides. The carriageway has **no corner radius**, and junctions cut by a tile border get no corner at all.
- **Markings.** Each strip's longitudinal lines run to its end. A marked side road's lines therefore reach the main road's centre, and the main road's edge line runs across the side road's mouth. Both z-fight with the other strip's asphalt where the heights agree.
- **Riders** follow the path heights: the edge profiles, blended over the rounded path corner (5.2 `RidePath::blend_corner_heights`). They do not follow the strip drawn on top. `wheel_contact` already reports residuals "up to 0.2 m where strips overlap at junctions" (v2.47).

**Measurements.** The analysis test `crates/ocw-render/tests/junction_seams.rs` meshes the strips of every junction exactly as the renderer does. It samples the junction disc (widest half width + 2.5 m) every 0.2 m from above and reports:

- *visible step*: the jump of the top surface between neighbouring samples where the top carriageway changes from one road to another;
- *z-fight*: carriageways of two roads overlapping within 1 cm;
- *gap*: area inside a road's outline but under no carriageway;
- *verge on road*: a shoulder, kerb or sidewalk of one road more than 1 cm above another road's carriageway.

The data are the packages of 2026-11-15 on marge: every vertex on the ground, away from the region border. The test is the basis for this plan's regression test.

| T / Y junctions (degree 3) | 3,247 | 39,598 | 30,752 |
| … visible step: median / p90 / max | 0.14 / 0.48 / 1.84 m | 0.11 / 0.47 / 1.83 m | 0.25 / 0.57 / 2.28 m |
| … step > 10 cm / > 25 cm / > 50 cm | 56 % / 31 % / 9 % | 52 % / 28 % / 9 % | 85 % / 50 % / 15 % |

| crossings (degree 4): step median / max; z-fight | 0.07 / 0.94 m; 91 % (6.7 m²) | 0.11 / 1.70 m; 84 % (5.4 m²) | 0.31 / 1.74 m; 91 % (2.2 m²) |

**Causes, in order of how visible they are:**

1. **Steps.** The strips are drawn flat across, each at its own grade, and overlap inside the junction. The step grows with the grade: 2–3 cm at flat junctions, half a metre where a road climbs at 15 % or more, so hilly Tenerife is worst. Two suspected causes were ruled out: there is no height mismatch at the shared vertex (0 by construction), and no difference in camber (no road has camber).
2. **Z-fighting.** Where the overlapping strips happen to agree (flat junctions, near the vertex), their asphalt and markings flicker against each other.
3. **Verges and kerbs on the road.** The higher strip's lip, shoulder, kerb and sidewalk lie on the lower road.
4. **Wedge gaps.**
   - Two square strip ends at an angle leave a wedge on the outside of every bend: at way splits and on roundabout rings (the Adlerkreisel in Vaduz: 66 m²).
   - Where the width changes, the wide road ends in a square shoulder (Avenida de La Galga, Tenerife: 19 m meets 5 m, 93 m²).
5. **Sharp corners.** The carriageway has no corner radius; sidewalk corners are rounded only within one tile.
6. **Kinks of a through road at a junction.** The vertical-curvature rule (4.8.3) holds only *inside* a road, so a through road may change its grade at a junction (Valünastrasse, Liechtenstein: −3 % on one side, 25 % on the other).
7. **Markings across the junction.** Only 0.5–2 % of junctions have a marked minor road ending in them, because most side roads are unmarked. But every marked main road's edge line crosses the mouths of its side roads.

The scenes `junction-*` in `scripts/scenes.toml` are the before / after pictures. Each junction has a `-rider` scene near rider height and a `-drone` scene from a low drone angle. The first set is in `test-output/junctions-investigation/` (X11 on marge). What the pictures show:

- Bergstrasse: Sennwisstrasse's strip lies on the main road as a tilted slab, with its gravel verge and wall face across the asphalt and its square end at the main road's centre line.
- Adlerkreisel: jagged square strip ends and wedges around the ring, plus shoulder and kerb pieces inside it.
- Planknerstrasse: the track's strip and verge rise above the road edge as a ramp.

**Design: a junction surface (planned).**

At every junction the strips stop at a **mouth line** a few metres out on each arm. **One surface** fills the junction between the mouths, bounded by the roads' edge lines and rounded corners. Its height field meets every arm's surface with the same height and slope. Nothing overlaps any more, so nothing can step, z-fight or poke through.

- **Junction patch** (`ocw_world::junction`, pure, wasm). It is computed from the road graph, so the server, the client's prediction and the renderer all get the same result. There is one patch for every vertex of degree ≥ 3, and for a degree-2 vertex that bends more than 10° or changes the width.
  - **Arms:** the incident edges sorted by angle, each with its direction, half width, class and profile.
  - **Outline:**
    - Between neighbouring arms, the edge lines (offset centrelines) meet in a **corner arc** tangent to both.
    - The kerb radius depends on the smaller road's class (proposal, Q4): 8 m for primary / secondary / trunk, 6 m for tertiary / unclassified / residential, 3 m for service / track, 1.5 m for cycleway / path. It gets smaller where the arms are short or nearly parallel, as `road_corners` limits its arcs today.
    - An arm's **mouth** lies at the farther tangent point of its two corners: at least the widest other arm's half width, at most 25 m and half the edge's length.
    - Longer junctions, such as 10° forks, fall back to overlapping strips and use only the other parts of this plan.
  - **Height field:**
    - Each arm's surface is extended linearly past its mouth, with its height and grade at the mouth, flat across like the strip.
    - Inside the patch, the extensions are blended by inverse-square distance to the mouth lines (Shepard weights with linear nodal functions). At a mouth the weight of that arm is 1 and its derivatives vanish, so the patch meets each arm **with the same height and slope** (C1): no crease, no step.
    - Where there is a clear **through road**, the proposal (Q1) is that the **main road keeps its own surface** across the junction: its plane, along its grade. A clear through road means two arms of the highest rank less than 30° from straight; most T junctions and roundabout entries have one.
    - The side arms meet the main road: from its mouth outwards, a side arm's heights are blended onto the main road's plane over `L = clamp(|Δh| / 0.01 per m, 5 m, 30 m)`, where 0.01 per m is the class's grade-change limit. Real side roads adapt to the main road, not the other way round.
    - Equal crossings, Y forks and multi-way junctions use the Shepard blend.
  - **Mesh:**
    - The patch polygon (corner arcs every 10°, as in `road_corners`) is triangulated with an interior grid of 1 m for the height field.
    - It is `Kind::Surface` in the main road's surface layer (`RSRF`) and colour.
    - Its uv runs across / along the main road's axis, so asphalt textures continue.
    - Its lines code is 0 (markings: see below).
- **Strips trimmed.**
  - Every strip ends at its arm's mouth: the carriageway, lip, shoulder, skirt, kerb and sidewalk.
  - Between the mouth and the end of a side arm's blend, the strip's point heights come from the patch module (re-heighted at load).
  - Strips are matched to their edge by geometry. The analysis test matched every strip of the three packages (0 unmatched).
  - A junction near a tile border is drawn **whole** in the tile of its vertex. The strips of the neighbouring tile are trimmed by the same pure function, so there is no seam at the border.
- **Way splits (degree 2).** **Mitred** strip ends (the last row of each strip lies on the bisector of the two directions) remove the wedge gaps and overlaps of small bends without a patch. Bends over 30° and width changes get a patch, and the width tapers over the patch.
- **Verges, kerbs, walls.**
  - The patch outline is just another edge polyline, so it gets the same lip, shoulder, skirt and retaining-wall rules as a strip edge (`road_mesh::shoulder`). Its shoulder continues the arms' shoulders at the mouths.
  - Where an arm has a sidewalk, the corner arc gets the kerb and the sidewalk as an annular sector. This is today's `road_corners`, now on the carriageway outline and across tile borders.
  - Kerbs no longer taper into the junction zone; they follow the arc.
- **Markings.**
  - The patch carries no longitudinal lines.
  - The main road's edge lines end at the corner tangent points, so the side road's mouth is open.
  - The main road's centre line continues across the patch, as in Swiss and German practice for a priority road (Q2).
  - The side roads' lines end at the mouth.
  - Stop and give-way lines stay those of OSM (`highway=stop|give_way`, today's overlays), now at the mouth line. Default give-way lines without OSM tags: Q3.
- **Terrain.** The corner arcs reach beyond the strips' footprint, where the terrain was not settled (4.8.3). At load, the renderer lowers the terrain mesh under each patch to 5 cm below the surface, as `tunnel_cut` does for tunnels. Later the world builder settles it in the package (J2), and the load-time step goes away.
- **Roundabouts.**
  - The ring is the through road at each entry: `junction=roundabout` is one-way, and each entry is a T with the ring as main road. Each entry gets a patch, and the mitred splits close the ring's wedge gaps.
  - Small roundabouts (outer diameter < 30 m) whose entry patches overlap merge into one patch; the central island stays a hole.
  - `highway=mini_roundabout` nodes get a painted disc later.
- **Complex junctions.** Vertices inside one another's patch are clustered into one patch with all their arms: dual carriageways, slip roads, offset T junctions a few metres apart. The short edges between them lie inside the patch.
- **Performance.**
  - Patches at degree ≥ 3: about 3,700 in Liechtenstein, 45,000 in the Black Forest north and 35,000 on Tenerife.
  - A patch has about 100–300 triangles, roughly what the overlapping strip ends had, so the triangle count stays about the same.
  - Patches are built per tile at load, with the strips. The budget is < 3 ms per tile, measured in J1, so the tile streaming of 4.5 does not stutter.

**Riders and physics.**

- The junction module also gives the **ridden height**. `RidePath` takes its heights inside a patch, and along a side arm's blend, from the same function. The server's 1D physics (5.2: grade, gravity), the client's prediction and the other riders' copies then agree.
- The rounded path corner gets the patch's surface instead of `blend_corner_heights`, which stays for corners outside patches.
- Inside the patch the surface is not flat across, so the rider's height is evaluated at the rider's real position (centreline point + lateral offset), not at the path centre.
- The physics grade stays the grade along the path centreline. The difference is the patch's cross slope times the offset change per metre, which is negligible.
- The drawn surface and the ridden height then come from one function, within the 2 mm wheel-contact rule (v2.47), at junctions too.

**Profile reconciliation in the world builder (J2, a package rebuild).** The same patch surfaces are baked into the package:

- the side arms' profiles follow the patch, so the package's road-graph heights are the drawn heights and the load-time re-heighting goes away;
- the blend replaces `ease_junction_mouths`;
- the vertical-curvature limit applies across junctions for the through pair, so there are no kinks like Valünastrasse's;
- the terrain is settled under the patch polygons.

Two optional, additive sections, which older clients skip: `JNCT` (precomputed patch outlines, saves the load time) and `RDGE` (the edge index of every strip, replaces the geometry matching). The format of existing sections does not change.

**Cheaper path first.** J1 changes only the renderer and `ocw-world`, and works with the existing packages without a rebuild: the patches, trims, mitres and ridden heights are pure functions of the package's road graph and strips. J2 only moves work into the builder and fixes the remaining kinks.

**Tests:**

- **`ocw_world::junction` unit tests** on synthetic junctions: a T (main road at 8 %, side road at 20 %), an equal crossing, a 20° Y, a roundabout entry, a hairpin split, a width change. They check that:
  - the outline is closed and simple;
  - every mouth matches its arm within 1 mm in height and 0.5 % in slope;
  - the patch and the trimmed strips do not overlap (area < 0.01 m²);
  - heights stay between the arms' extremes;
  - the result is the same for any edge order.
- **`ocw-render` tests:** trimmed strips and patch meshes in the road vertex format; the patch outline's shoulder meets the arms' shoulders.
- **`junction_seams`** (this analysis) becomes the regression test over the test packages (`OCW_JUNCTION_WORLD`). Today 56 % of Liechtenstein's T junctions have steps above 10 cm. The test requires, at every junction:
  - no visible step above 2 cm;
  - no z-fighting overlap;
  - no gap over 0.05 m²;
  - no verge on a carriageway.

  A synthetic package of junction types runs without the real packages (CI).
- **`wheel_contact`:** riders go straight on, turn left and turn right through junctions of the synthetic package and of Liechtenstein (the worst cases above). The tyres stay within 2 mm of the drawn patch, and `RidePath` heights equal the patch heights at every sample.
- **`world-builder lint`:** `junction.seam` replaces `junction.surface_step` and measures the drawn surfaces, as the test does. J2's packages report 0.
- **Scenes** `junction-*` before / after, on X11 and Wayland.

**Milestones:**

- **J1a – mitred way splits** (renderer only): closes the wedge gaps of degree-2 vertices below 30°.
- **J1b – junction patches** (`ocw_world::junction`, renderer): outline, height field, mesh, strip trimming and re-heighting, tile borders; `junction_seams` asserts.
- **J1c – ridden heights:** `RidePath`, the server and the prediction take heights from the patches; `wheel_contact` at junctions.
- **J1d – outline dress:** shoulders, kerbs and sidewalks on the outline (replacing `road_corners`), markings at the mouths, terrain lowered under the patches at load.
- **J2 – world builder (built v5.14):** profiles reconciled, terrain settled, no kinks across junctions, `JNCT` / `RDGE`, lint; rebuild and deploy all packages (Q5).
- **J3 – roundabouts and complex junctions (built v5.36, with Q6 (d)):** merged patches, clusters, mini-roundabout discs.

**Built (J1, 2026-11-16; J1a–J1d in the renderer on the current packages, 4.8.8 Q5).**

- **`ocw_world::junction`** (pure, wasm; `JunctionSet`, made per vertex on first use and kept, the same in the renderer, the server and the client's prediction): a **patch** at every vertex of degree ≥ 3 on the ground and at a way split that bends more than 30° or changes the width; a **mitre** at the other way splits (bends of 0.5°–30°: the last rows of both strips on the bisector, their corner heights continue both grades).
  - Outline: the arms by angle; between neighbours the edge lines meet in a corner arc tangent to both, radius by the smaller road's class (the Q4 fallback: 8 / 6 / 3 / 1.5 m), smaller where the arms are short; convex sides through the edge lines' crossing; a width change keeps the wider road's width up to the vertex and tapers beyond it. Mouth = the farther tangent point, at least the widest other arm's half width, at most 25 m and 45 % of the edge. Forks below 15°, acute corners beyond those limits and outlines that are not star-shaped from the vertex keep the overlapping strips.
  - Height field: the inverse-square (Shepard) blend of the arms' linear extensions by distance to the mouth lines, C1 at every mouth. A clear through road (the only pair of arms of the highest class less than 30° from straight) keeps its own surface (Q1): only its two arms take part; its side arms lie on the main road's surface at their mouths and blend into their own profile over `L = clamp(|Δh| / 0.01, 5 m, 30 m)` (at most half the edge) by a cubic Hermite blend (C1 at both ends), rows 1 m apart.
  - Mesh: the outline (corner arcs every 10°, mouths every 1 m on the straight mouth line, edge lines every 1.5 m) and rings scaled towards the vertex about 2.5 m apart (100–600 triangles). `Patch::height_at` interpolates on exactly these triangles and `JunctionSet::drawn_height` on the blended rows as the strips draw them, so ridden = drawn.
  - `shape_strip`: matched to its edge by geometry, a strip is trimmed at the mouths (its rows there are the patch's mouth rows), its points along a side arm's blend are replaced by the blended rows, mitred at way splits; strips stored against their edge's direction are turned and shaped alike. `fixtures`: synthetic junctions for the tests.
- **Renderer** (`ocw-render::junction_mesh`; `road_mesh` draws a strip along explicit rows, the side dress is shared): per tile the strips are shaped (also where a neighbouring tile's junction reaches in), the tile draws the patches of its vertices whole. The patch is a carriageway in the main arm's layer, colour and strip frame (u across, v along, so dashes and textures run on). **Markings (Q2 fallback):** a through road's centre line continues across the patch, its edge line breaks on the sides where other roads leave and continues on the other side; side roads' lines end at their mouths; no lines across other junctions. **Q3:** stop and give-way lines stay those OSM tags; one that now lies in the patch moves to the mouth. The outline gets lip, shoulder, skirt or retaining wall like a strip edge, and kerb and sidewalk where the arms have them (tapering along the arc where only one has, Q4 fallback; `road_corners` stays for junctions without a patch). The terrain is lowered at load under a patch (5 cm under its surface) and beside a side road the blend lowered (by as much, faded out over one grid spacing): the builder settled the ground to the old profile. `OCW_JUNCTIONS=off` draws the strips as before (A/B).
- **Ridden heights (J1c):** `RoadNetwork` owns the `JunctionSet`; `RidePath` takes the drawn heights inside patches and along blends (path points 0.5 m apart there; `blend_corner_heights` only at corners without a patch), `Track::surface_height(d, lateral)` gives the drawn surface beside the centre line, and the wheels stand on it (`riders::contact_height`, also corrected for the path's curvature beside the centre line).
- **Tests:** `ocw_world::junction` (T at 8 % / 20 %, equal crossing, 40° and 10° forks, 12° split, hairpin, width change, edge order, reversed strips; outline closed and simple, mouths within 1 mm and 0.5 % slope, no overlap with the trimmed strips, drawn = mesh heights), `ocw-render::junction_mesh` (no seam, overlap, verge on a road or gap on the synthetic junctions; the outline dress meets the arms' dress; markings; give-way line at the mouth; terrain lowered), `wheel_contact::tyres_touch_the_junction_surfaces` (straight on, left, right through the T, the crossing and the hairpin: path = drawn surface within 3 mm, tyres on the centre line within 2 mm (worst 2.0 mm at the hairpin), beside the centre within 5 mm at the T and the crossing (4.1 mm); at the hairpin's 3 m corner 44 mm beside the centre – the rider placement by path distance, not the surface), `junction_seams` (before / after, the patched-only shares and why the others have no patch, the tile build time; `junction_in_detail` for one junction).

**Measured (`junction_seams`, before → after, the same packages of 2026-11-15):**

**Open after J1:**
- **J2** (world builder) – **built (v5.14)**, see *Built (J2)* below: profiles reconciled with the patches (the side-road blend can steepen a side road near the junction: a 20 % road that left the vertex at the main road's height now starts flat and climbs the missed height over its blend), the terrain settled in the package (the load-time lowering is coarse: a 10 m grid), kinks of through roads across junctions (Valünastrasse: −3 % / −25 % remain), `JNCT` / `RDGE`, `junction.seam` lint; rebuild and deploy (Q5).
- **J3:** roundabouts (the Adlerkreisel: its entries get patches, but the ring's split vertices and the merged small-roundabout patch are open), clusters of vertices a few metres apart (dual carriageways, the Landstrasse / Gagoz split in Balzers: short edges of 4 m with mitres only), forks below 15°, mini-roundabout discs. The junctions without a patch (table above) keep the strips of before: about a quarter to a third of the T junctions, mostly outlines that are not star-shaped from the vertex (arms that curve within the junction, very different widths) and acute corners whose arc would lie beyond the mouth limits; they are J3's first work. The gap measure stays at 11–18 % even at patched T junctions (round road ends and arms that curve between the corner and the mouth, where the outline follows the straight arm) – to be examined with J3.
- **4.8.9** tables per region (lines through junctions, kerbs and radii from real images): none yet; J1 uses the Q2 / Q4 fallbacks.
- The `junction_seams` asserts of the plan (no step > 2 cm, no z-fight, no gap, no verge on a road at every junction of the test packages) hold on the synthetic junctions (`junction_mesh` tests) but not yet on the real packages, until J2 / J3 close the junctions without a patch.
- In joined world sets the border vertices of two packages may get a patch the per-package renderer does not draw (ridden heights there follow the patch); rare.

**Built (J2, 2026-11-19; the world builder, 4.8.8 Q5).** `ocw_worldgen::junctions` (pure) bakes the junction surfaces of `ocw_world::junction` into the package; `world-builder package` runs it while cleaning (in the prepared graph after the planned bridge decks and before a world patch's height points, which keep the final say; the terrain is conformed to the reconciled profiles), `world-builder junctions --world PKG [--out NEW]` does the same for a built package (every other section as it was, the strips' points moved with their profiles, the manifest renewed):

- **No kinks across junctions** (`smooth_through_kinks`): the vertical-curvature limit of 4.8.3 (0.5 % per metre on trunk / primary / secondary, 1 % on the others; of two classes the more permissive) applies to the joined profile of each through pair – a patch's through road (its two arms, Q1) and the two edges of every way split on the ground – within 40 m of the vertex; a kink is rounded as inside a road (a sample moves towards its neighbours' chord, never steeper), the vertex sample moves too and every other road at the vertex takes its height (the side roads are blended onto the main road next). Not at junctions without a clear through road (equal crossings, forks), on bridges, in tunnels, at the region border.
- **Profiles reconciled** (`reconcile_profiles`): every profile sample within a junction's reach takes the drawn height on its centre line – inside the patch its mesh, along a side road's blend the blended rows – so the road graph's heights are the drawn heights and the strips (made from them) are drawn as they are. A side road whose blend the edge's length cut short (J1 blends over at most half the edge: a steep side road a few metres to the next junction climbed its missed height at once) gets the blend it needs in its profile: `L = clamp(|Δh| / 0.01, 5 m, 30 m)` from the main road's surface at the mouth (height and slope) into its own profile, up to one sample before the other end's junction. Kept as they are, so that the patches made again from the new profiles are the same (a fixed point): the two samples round each main arm's mouth (their height and grade there shape the patch) and round the end of each side road's blend; the arms' vertex samples change only all together (one height at the vertex); the planned bridge decks. Four rounds (patches made again on the reconciled profiles); afterwards 1 – 36 samples per package (of 6,600 – 130,700) lie more than 1 cm off the drawn surface. The blend replaces the mouth easing of 4.8.3 at the patched vertices (`ease_junction_mouths_except`); the grade limits were not re-applied after it in v5.14 (45 – 1,589 intervals per package near a junction steeper than their class limit + 1 %: the side roads' missed height); since v5.19 they are (*Built (J2b)* below).
- **Terrain settled in the package:** the settle pass of 4.8.3 also takes the drawn junction surfaces (`surface_samples`: each patch every 0.5 m and its outline, every side road's blend every metre along and 0.5 m across – its rows are not flat across), 5 cm under them. The renderer no longer lowers the terrain at load for such a package (`JNCT` flag; packages without it keep J1's lowering).
- **Sections `JNCT` and `RDGE`** (4.7 *Junction sections*): the junction rules and patch outlines (a stored patch is the computed one to the bit; the renderer takes them, the server and the prediction may compute them – the same) and the edge of every strip (no geometric matching in the renderer). A streaming client (the browser) leaves `JNCT` out of its base (1 – 26 MB) and computes the junctions.
- **Lint** (4.8.1): `junction.seam` (by cause `.short_side_road`, `.mitre`, `.patch`), `junction.overlap`, `junction.no_surface.REASON`, `junction.measured` replace `junction.surface_step`; they measure the drawn carriageways over the patch and its mouths as the renderer draws them (the strips shaped by `shape_strip`, the patch's triangles).

What remains (not J2's): most seams lie where a side road ends a few metres on at the next junction (two vertices inside one another's reach – J3's clusters; the blend has no room) and at the mouths where a short blend meets the strip's 5 m points with a kink (the measure takes the step less the slope between 0.2 m samples, so a change of slope of 10 % counts as 2 cm); the overlaps are at patches whose arms curve back over the neighbouring strip; the junctions without a surface are unchanged (J3). **Built (J2b, 2026-11-19; follow-up of J2 in the world builder):** the class grade and vertical-curvature limits of 4.8.3 are applied again after the junction blend, with the junction surfaces as fixed heights, so a junction stays level with its main road and a side road's missed height is spread over as long a stretch as it needs (`ocw_worldgen::junctions::relimit_grades`, inside `reconcile_profiles`, so both `world-builder package` and `world-builder junctions` do it):

- **Fixed** (`fixed_samples`): both vertex samples, at a junction surface the samples up to its mouth (for a side arm at the drawn height, the patch's mesh – J2 could leave a sample pinned round the end of a short blend inside the patch off it), a side arm's mouth itself on the main road's surface (a point between the samples), a main arm's sample past its mouth (it shapes the patch), the planned bridge decks.
- **Grade:** between two fixed heights every free sample is clamped to its neighbour's cone of the class grade, forward and back until it holds – a stretch too steep beside a junction is pulled towards the junction's height and climbs at the limit until it meets the road's own profile. Where the fixed heights themselves lie farther apart than the limit allows, the stretch between them climbs at the least grade possible.
- **Vertical curvature:** from a fixed stretch (a junction's mouth) the profile stays between the highest and lowest a road can climb or fall from there, starting at the junction surface's grade and changing it by at most 0.5 % / 1 % per metre up to the class grade (it bends into the climb), the same from the far side; the remaining kinks are rounded as inside a road, within the grade limit (where both cannot hold, the grade wins: a road already at its limit right after a level junction keeps a kink).
- Then the profiles are reconciled with the junction surfaces again (the patches made again on the new profiles; at most three cycles of re-limiting and reconciling, the fixed point of J2 kept: 1 – 30 samples per package more than 1 cm off the drawn surface afterwards).
- **Lint by cause** (4.8.1, `steep_intervals`): `road.vertical.grade_over_limit.{source_steep, junction_room, junction, other}`; the build log counts the same.

Tests (11.4): a step beside a fixed stretch spread at the limit, the fixed samples kept, the road far away unchanged, the mouth's kink rounded (`relimiting_keeps_the_junction_and_lengthens_the_blend`); fixed heights too far apart spread at the least grade and counted `source_steep` (`relimiting_spreads_what_the_source_makes_too_steep`); a T junction with an 18 % side road: steep after the blend alone, within the limit afterwards, the junction level with the main road, the main road unchanged, still the drawn surface, lint 0 (`side_roads_keep_their_class_grade_after_the_blend`); a 25 m road between two level main roads counted `junction_room` (`short_roads_between_junctions_have_too_little_room`); the J2 tests with the side road at its class limit spread over its whole length.

What the numbers say: wherever the limit can hold it now holds – `other` (the profile stage's leftovers, e.g. Liechtenstein's 76 path intervals at 26 %) goes to 0, `junction` from 2,776 to 280 in the Black Forest north, kinks and steps near junctions fall by a third to a half. The target "0 except where the source is steeper" is **not** reached: (1) **`junction_room`** dominates – J2's rule that a side road's mouth lies on the main road's surface across (Q1) puts the mouth up to 3 – 4 m above or below the side road's own height where it leaves a steep main road at a narrow angle (mouths 10 – 14 m from the vertex), and when the next fixed height (another junction surface – often the same road's other end 20 – 35 m on –, a bridge deck) is close, no profile can hold the limit (Black Forest north: a 33 m track whose mouths lie 3.6 m above and 3.7 m below its own heights falls at 88 % between them; a track whose deck starts 14 m past the mouth, 6.4 m lower, at 98 %). It grows from J2 to J2b (BF north 1,832 → 3,158), not fully examined: re-limiting also rounds the through roads' kinks beyond their pinned samples, which moves the main road's surface at far side-arm mouths. This needs a change of the junction surfaces themselves (Q6, J3). (2) **`junction`** keeps 8 – 496: a side road leaving with the main road's slope in the opposite direction (the blend's Hermite curve starts at the main road's grade along the arm – +21 % – and the road beyond falls at its limit, 25 %): the blend, drawn by the renderer from the patch, cannot stay within the limit without changing its rule (Q6). (3) `source_steep` grows a little (Tenerife 506 → 585) because the least-grade stretch between fixed heights now spreads to both of them.

**Seams (item 2 of the J2 follow-up):** no change of the seam itself was cheap: the worst `patch` seams examined (Liechtenstein vertices 5276, 5152, 3304: 0.12 – 0.26 m) lie at arms of 10 – 13 m (the next junction inside the blend) and at blended patches, both J3's; the re-limited profiles move the seams only a little – `junction.seam` J2 → J2b: Liechtenstein 201 → 200, Tenerife 3,283 → 3,164, Black Forest north 2,833 → 2,809 (the `mitre` cause grows by 6 – 33 where re-limited profiles meet at a mitre's corner).
