- **Tested over the network:** `make test-multiplayer` runs the server and the kiosk's client on one build machine and headless `ocw-bot` riders on the others (Linux, macOS, Windows) and checks joins, snapshots, mutual visibility, progress, prediction error and tick timing (11.4.1).

**TLS in development mode (decided; until the backend exists).** TLS 1.3 only, via rustls with the ***ring*** crypto provider (licence Apache-2.0 AND ISC; already in the tree through `ureq`; chosen over the default aws-lc-rs to avoid its CMake/C toolchain on all three platforms). The server uses a self-signed certificate from `rcgen`, new at every start or kept in `--tls-dir DIR` (`cert.der`, `key.der` with mode 0600), and prints its SHA-256 fingerprint. The client must say how to trust it – there is no default: `--server-cert SHA256` pins exactly that certificate (any address), `--insecure-dev` accepts any certificate but is refused for non-loopback addresses (checked when the options are parsed and again when the TLS configuration is built). Both verify the handshake signature, so the server must hold the key. Not yet: certificates from a public CA (WebPKI roots or the platform verifier), OIDC sign-in and per-session tokens (6.4, 12); until then a reachable server accepts anyone who has its fingerprint. New dependency licences: quinn, quinn-proto, quinn-udp, rcgen MIT OR Apache-2.0; rustls Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT; ring Apache-2.0 AND ISC. They are used only by `ocw-server` (and the desktop through it), never by the wasm crates (3.5).

**WebTransport endpoint for browsers (decided, v3.02, 14 Phase 10 B3).** `ocw-server --listen … --webtransport [ADDR]` opens a second QUIC endpoint (HTTP/3, ALPN `h3`, **UDP 47801** by default) feeding the same `GameServer` session through the same `NetServer` (one event channel, one peer table, one broadcast): desktop, `ocw-bot` and browser riders share one session.

- **Library: `web-transport-quinn` 0.13** (MIT OR Apache-2.0; with its `ring` feature, no aws-lc-rs): it does HTTP/3's SETTINGS and the extended CONNECT on a `quinn::Connection` of *our* endpoint, so our quinn 0.11, rustls config, *ring* provider and transport settings (keep-alive 4 s, idle 15 s) stay; its streams are tokio `AsyncRead` / `AsyncWrite`, so the native framing (`net::framing`) is reused unchanged, and it has a client (`NetClient::connect_web`, used by the loopback tests and `ocw-bot --server https://…`). Considered: `wtransport` 0.7 (MIT OR Apache-2.0, complete, but its own endpoint and configuration types around quinn, so a second TLS / transport setup to keep in step) and `h3` + `h3-webtransport` (still experimental, much more glue). New transitive licences: `web-transport-proto`, `web-transport-trait`, `kio`, `rustls-platform-verifier`, `fastbloom`, `sfv` MIT OR Apache-2.0; `webpki-root-certs` CDLA-Permissive-2.0 (data, as `webpki-roots` already in the voice build). All native only.
- **Same channels:** the browser opens one bidirectional stream with the length-prefixed frames of every reliable message; snapshots and samples go as WebTransport datagrams (QUIC datagrams with the session id in front; `max_datagram_size` minus that header), with the same fallback to the stream. The wire rules without I/O moved to the wasm-safe `ocw_server::wire` (frames, the incremental `FrameDecoder`, which messages are unreliable, `LinkStatus`) together with the client's connection state machine `ClientLink` (queued until connected, Hello and early samples on the stream until the server answers, datagrams only when the peer takes them and they fit, a broken frame closes the link, the first close reason stays, RTT from the transport or Hello → Welcome). The session path is `/ocw/1` (or `/`); other paths get 404.
- **Certificates (development):** browsers take a self-signed certificate by its SHA-256 (`serverCertificateHashes`) only if it is ECDSA (P-256) and valid for at most 14 days. `net::tls::WebIdentity` makes one valid for 13 days (from an hour back), kept in `--tls-dir` (`web-cert.der`, `web-key.der` mode 0600, `web-cert.validity`) and reused while more than two days are left; the running server checks every minute and **rotates** it two days before the end (`Endpoint::set_server_config`: new sessions get the new certificate, open ones go on), logs and prints the new hash and rewrites `--web-info-file` (JSON: URL, hash, expiry, page options). Pages then need the new hash (`cert-hash=OLD,NEW` takes two). It is a separate certificate from the native one (whose fingerprint desktop clients pin for good). Production: certificates from a CA with hosting (B8), then without `cert-hash`.
- **Counters:** `NetServer::counters(Transport)` (connections, messages, datagrams per endpoint), in the log at the end and in `--stats-file` (`web_sessions`, `web_messages_in`, `web_datagrams_in`).

### 6.3 Synchronization

The simulation accounts for differing frame rates, differing network latencies, packet loss, connection drops, reconnection, server-side timestamps, interpolation of other riders and client-side prediction.

| Topic | Target |
|---|---|
| Riders per session (v1) | 100 |
| Design target | 1,000 per event through **interest management**: full-rate updates for riders within ±500 m, reduced rate beyond, aggregated (count / gap) for the rest |
| Server physics tick | 50 Hz |
| State broadcast | 10 Hz (enough for cycling with interpolation) |
| Interpolation delay | ~100–150 ms |
| Playable latency | up to 250 ms RTT |
| Downstream bandwidth | < 64 kbit/s per client in a 100-rider session |
| Reconnect | Session state kept on the server for 2 min; the rider resumes at the server-side position |

- **Fixed (v5.40): the riders jumped at 25 frames a second – in every `--capture` video and on slow machines** (reported by the user 2026-11-22 from the test videos: "the rider does not move smooth anymore, its laggy/jumpy"). *Not a recent regression:* a probe of the client loop as the desktop app runs it (`ocw-client` test `motion_probe_numbers`: 60 s with six bots, the server's messages in `PreUpdate`, the 50 Hz prediction in `FixedUpdate`, the view at the overstep) gives bit for bit the same numbers on 2827ee2 (2026-11-19) and on 103ca25 – the predicted bumps (5.22), the lazy road geometry (5.23), the wet leaves (5.34) and the road feel (5.35) changed nothing there; the recordings themselves are exact (`--capture` steps the game by 1/25 s a frame; ffprobe: 25 fps, every frame 40 ms, no dropped or doubled frames). *Cause:* the client reads the server's messages once per frame and took every snapshot as fresh. At 25 fps a frame holds two physics ticks and a snapshot (every fifth tick) is read either on time or a tick late, alternating at 10 Hz; at 60 Hz or 30 Hz the phase stays the same and nothing shows. Each late snapshot pulled the own prediction back by a tick's ride (16 cm at 30 km/h; 597 of 600 snapshots a minute corrected, 91 mm off on average), and the others' interpolation, timed by arrival, ran 80 / 120 ms between snapshots 100 ms apart – their speed jumping ±20 % at 10 Hz: a bunch surging against the own rider, a close-up of another rider's face shaking (the lips video). *Fix:* `ocw_client::arrival::ArrivalClock` counts the prediction steps against each snapshot's server tick; the freshest snapshot of the last 2 s is on time, any other is late by the ticks it lags (lateness over 25 ticks starts again: a new session or world). The prediction extrapolates a snapshot by its lateness plus the network's age, and the snapshot is timed for the others' interpolation, the event clock and the effects at when it would have come on time. *Numbers* (change of the drawn velocity per frame, RMS; before → after): 25 fps capture: own rider 0.017, corrections a minute 597 → 10, mean error 91 → 3.6 mm, others 1.43 → 0.11 m/s; 14 fps: own 0.42 → 0.025 m/s, others 1.94 → 0.45 m/s; 60 / 144 fps unchanged. Remote rides gain the same (network jitter is lateness too); the browser app shares the client. Regression test `riders_move_smoothly_when_snapshots_are_read_late` (fails on the old client); the probe stays as an ignored test for comparisons. Videos `test-output/motion/` (before / after, the Loop with 12 bots, `--capture`, time and weather fixed): the own rider's jersey on screen changes its velocity by 5.5 px a frame RMS before (up to 25 px) and 1.5 px after (up to 5 px).

The multiplayer logic is developed independently of the graphics engine.

### 6.4 Data Integrity and Anti-Cheat

Goal: **detection and flagging of implausible data**. Power comes from user hardware and cannot be fully verified.

1. **Transport integrity:** authenticated QUIC (TLS 1.3), per-session tokens, sequence numbers and server timestamps (prevents replay and injection).
2. **Plausibility checks (server):**
   - Power-duration curve compared with the rider's history and with absolute W/kg limits.
   - Unrealistic spikes and slopes (power changes faster than physically possible).
   - Power without cadence, or perfectly constant power over long periods.
   - Heart rate not responding to load changes (when heart rate is present).
3. **Device trust levels:** smart trainer only < trainer + independent power meter ("dual recording") < verified setup. Organized races can require a minimum trust level.
4. **Weight:** the biggest real-world manipulation vector. Weight changes are logged; races may lock weight some time before the start.
5. **Consequences:** flagging, results marked "unverified", and manual review. No automatic bans in v1.
6. **Hearts (v2.53, 14 Phase 4, 4E):** hearts are credited only by the server – the game server that saw the power stream, or the backend from an uploaded ride after these checks; never for virtual power, god mode, bots or captures; flagged rides hold their hearts until reviewed; a daily cap. Purchases are server-side transactions against the server's catalogue price. Since hearts have no money value (no purchase, no cash-out) and races can ignore parts (*Profile* / *Equal* modes), a cheated balance gains little.

### 6.5 Steering in Multiplayer

- The client sends a reliable `TurnIntent { junction_id, exit_edge_id }` as soon as the choice changes (2.2.1).
- With neighbouring packages (2.2.2) junction ids are vertex indices of the joined graph, `WorldPackageId.name` is the joined name (`Home + Neighbour`) and `graph_hash` the joined graph's fingerprint, so client and server must have the same packages installed; a missing neighbour on one side shows as a graph mismatch. (v1.6: plus a sequence number and the exit's riding direction; no `exit_edge_id` = no choice, the default; `junction_id` is the vertex index in the world package's graph – client and server use the same package.)
- A manual U-turn is a reliable `UTurn { distance, speed }`: where the client turned, so the server builds the same loop when it is close to its own state.
- **Same package on both sides (decided):** because junctions are vertex indices, the client sends `Hello.world = WorldPackageId { name, graph_hash }` and the server sends its own in `Welcome.world`. `graph_hash` is the FNV-1a 64 fingerprint of the road graph's package encoding (the `GRPH` payload), so any rebuild that changes the graph changes it. The server rejects a Hello with another hash ("world package mismatch … install the same package version"); a client refuses a Welcome with another hash (for servers that do not check). Sessions without a road graph (route files, test routes) skip the check. Package signing and manifests (4.7) are separate.
- **Rider weight (v2.7):** `Hello.rider_weight_kg` carries the rider profile's weight; the server clamps it to 30–200 kg and uses its curated physics profile otherwise (`Hello.profile` is deprecated, 3.2.1).
- **Voice (Phase 6):** `ClientMessage.voice` (9, `VoiceTokenRequest`) asks for a LiveKit token, `ServerMessage.voice` (7, `VoiceGrant`) answers it; `Welcome.voice` (9) says the server offers voice, `Snapshot.human_riders` (3) counts the riders of connected clients (2.4, 7). Voice itself never uses this connection.
- **Bike and look (Phase 4):** `Hello.bike_profile` (field 6) names the curated physics profile by id (unknown → default), `Hello.look` (field 7, `RiderLook`) the cosmetic look; `RiderUpdate.bike_profile` (11) and `RiderUpdate.look` (12) pass both to the other clients (2.5).
- **Workshop and hearts (Phase 4, W1 / W2, v3.00):** `ClientMessage.bike_change` (16, `BikeChange`: garage bike id, frame profile id, look, part ids; reliable) is sent when the rider leaves the workshop; the server applies profile (its own table, the rider's weight) and look at once outside events, refuses it for an entrant of an unfinished event ("from the next start") and answers with a `DevCommandResult`; part ids are cosmetic until W3. `SensorSample.virtual_power` (7) flags keyboard / virtual-trainer power; `RiderUpdate.hearts` (18) is the server's running total of the rider's credited hearts in the session (1 per 10 kJ of accepted work + 1 per 20 m climbed; none for virtual power, god mode, while down, for bots or the Echo rider).
- **Build physics (Phase 4, W3, v3.03):** the parts of `BikeChange` now count: the server computes the build from its own catalogue copy (14 Phase 4, 4G) and applies it at once outside events; for an entrant of an event that is not over it waits and applies when the event ends (from the next start) – the answer says which. `Hello.parts` (8) is the build the rider joins with. `ServerMessage.rider_build` (10, `RiderBuild`: rider, `build_hash`, profile, the fitted part ids in slot order, the server's effect against the stock bike – flat and 6 % climb in 1e-4, bike mass in g, capped) goes reliably to everyone once per change (and to a joining client for every rider with parts); the snapshots carry only `RiderUpdate.build_hash` (19, fixed32, 6 bytes; 0 = stock), and a client draws a rider's parts only while the hash matches the last `RiderBuild`. `EventStart.physics` (7) / `EventState.physics` (14) carry the race mode (`PhysicsMode`: unspecified = by the kind; an older server's state = open). `DevCommand.bot_bike` (4, `BotBike`: a bot's profile, parts, steady power, fixed lane, name; local servers only) compares builds side by side.
- **Character and kit (Phase 4, W4, v3.07):** `RiderLook` gains the character (spec 14 Phase 4, 4C) as optional fields – `height_cm` (5), `body_build` (6), `skin` (7), `face` (8), `hair` (9), `hair_rgb` (10, fixed32), `glasses` (11); absent = the default, out-of-range values the default's, the height clamped to 150–205 cm. They travel in `Hello.look` and `BikeChange.look` and from the server once per change in `RiderBuild.look` (9; also sent when only the character changed, and to a joining client for every rider with parts or a non-default character); the snapshots' `RiderUpdate.look` keeps only the colours and the pattern. The worn kit is catalogue ids among the parts (`Hello.parts`, `BikeChange.parts`, `RiderBuild.parts`; kit counts in the build and its hash).
- Route rides: `Welcome.graph_route` names the route; leaving it is an ordinary `TurnIntent`, rejoining a reliable `RouteRejoin { distance, speed }` (2.2.1).
- The server sends each rider's path as reliable `PathUpdate`s (the steps from an index on, or a new path after joining or a teleport); clients use them for the other riders and to correct their own prediction.
- The **server decides** at the lock point and broadcasts the chosen edge.
- The client predicts with its own choice and is corrected only in the rare case of disagreement (e.g. the intent arrived too late → the server default applies).
- In group rides with "follow leader", the server applies the leader's choice to all followers.

---

## 7. Voice Chat

Infrastructure: **LiveKit** (WebRTC SFU).

Features: voice rooms, participant management, audio transmission, dynamic subscription to audio tracks, group communication. Always on with automatic join and open microphone; microphone mute and speaker mute toggles with keyboard and gamepad hotkeys (2.4); no push-to-talk.

- The client uses the official **LiveKit Rust SDK**. It wraps libwebrtc, but LiveKit provides prebuilt binaries for all target platforms.
- It is isolated in the `ocw-voice` crate behind a trait, with a cargo feature `voice`, so the app also builds and runs without it (CI, minimal builds).
- **Platform plan (decided 2026-11-12): LiveKit on every platform.** One self-hosted LiveKit server for all clients; the game server issues the tokens and decides the rooms, so rooms, tokens, spatial selection and mute logic are shared. Each platform plugs its own LiveKit client in behind the `ocw-voice` trait:

  | Client | LiveKit client | Notes |
  |---|---|---|
  | Desktop (Linux, Windows, macOS) | LiveKit Rust SDK (libwebrtc) | Building it on Linux needs clang ≥ 21 (`make deps-llvm-debian`, apt.llvm.org; Debian 13 ships 19) |
  | Browser (the browser app, 14 Phase 10; built in B5, v3.21) | `livekit-client` (JS) behind the page's shim `ocw-voice.js`, driven by `ocw_voice::web::WebVoiceBackend` | Uses the browser's own WebRTC; no native build; the same controller, rooms and tokens |
  | iOS / Android (future apps) | Native LiveKit Swift / Android SDK, or the Rust SDK if the app is Rust | Prebuilt WebRTC from the SDKs |

  The trait therefore must not assume threads, a file system or a native audio device in its API (the browser backend is asynchronous JS); the pure logic (mute state, hotkeys, auto-join, spatial attenuation, nearest-N) stays in platform-independent code that also builds for wasm.
  Options considered: (1) LiveKit everywhere – chosen; (2) another WebRTC SFU (mediasoup, Janus, Jitsi, own on Pion / webrtc-rs) – no gain, the browser and mobile still use WebRTC and we would rewrite LiveKit's signalling and room logic per client; (3) own Opus over QUIC / WebTransport without WebRTC – possible in browsers (WebTransport + WebCodecs) and on mobile (OS echo cancellation), but needs own jitter buffer, loss concealment, NAT traversal and scaling, and the desktop still needs a C/C++ echo canceller; much more work for likely worse quality. Uncertainty: Rust SDK support for iOS / Android not verified yet.
- The **LiveKit server is self-hosted** (Apache 2.0) as a separate service. Our API issues short-lived LiveKit access tokens (JWT) per room. *Built for the headless server and the kiosk (v4.25, 7.1.8):* the game server starts it as a child process; a separately run LiveKit stays possible with `--livekit-url`. *Ride → Host a ride* starts it the same way (v4.31, 7.1.9); shipping it in the app packages follows (7.1.6 V6).
- Voice is **not** transmitted over the QUIC game-state connection. Voice and game server are separate services with separate scaling.
- **Spatial audio** on the client:
  - Subscribe only to the nearest **N riders (e.g. 8–12)** plus explicitly chosen group members.
  - Attenuate volume by distance along the route (optionally pan by lateral offset).
  - Mix on the client.
- Echo cancellation and noise suppression come from the WebRTC audio processing module included in libwebrtc.
- Voice is **never recorded or stored** on our side.

**Implementation (Phase 6, first increment; decided 2026-11-12):**

- **Crate layout.** `crates/ocw-voice` holds the logic, all pure and unit-tested: `mute` (the two switches), `join` (auto join / leave, retry back-off), `spatial` (attenuation, pan, nearest-N), `device` (device choice with fallback), `mix` (the mixer, resampler, confirmation sounds) and `controller` (`VoiceController`: drives a `VoiceBackend` trait with commands only when something changed). The LiveKit backend (`ocw-voice::livekit`) is behind the crate feature `livekit`; the desktop's cargo feature **`voice`** turns it on and is **off by default**, so CI, minimal builds and the other platforms build without libwebrtc. Without it the same controller runs on a null backend: switches, settings, menu and console work, the status says "not built in". `apps/desktop/src/voice/` is the Bevy glue (plugin, hotkeys, console commands, Settings → Voice pages); `ocw-render::voice` draws the HUD indicator.
- **Game server: rooms and tokens.** The client sends `VoiceTokenRequest { channel, group }` (reliable, on the game connection); the server answers `VoiceGrant { url, token, room, identity, expires_unix_s, channel, error }`. The server decides the room: the session room `ocw-<instance>` (default), the event room `…-event-<id>` (only for entrants of the running event), or a group room `…-group-<name>` (names of 1–32 characters a–z, 0–9, `-`); `<instance>` is a per-start id so servers sharing one LiveKit never share rooms. The token is a LiveKit JWT (HS256, signed with `sha2`-based HMAC in `ocw-server::voice`, no new dependency) valid for **10 minutes** (LiveKit checks it at join and refreshes it for connected clients; the client asks again before every reconnect), allowing join, subscribe and publishing the **microphone only** (no data, video or admin rights). One token per connection per 2 s. URL, API key and secret come from `OCW_LIVEKIT_URL`, `OCW_LIVEKIT_API_KEY`, `OCW_LIVEKIT_API_SECRET` (`--livekit-url`, `--livekit-api-key` override the first two; the secret is never a command-line option, it would show in `ps`) and never enter the repository. **Dev-mode assumption until accounts exist (Phase 5):** the identity is `rider-<rider id>` of the connection and the token name its display name; anyone in the session who knows a group's name can join it. With OIDC the identity becomes the account and groups get invitations; the token issuing moves to the API (12) unchanged in shape.
- **Platform independence (platform plan: LiveKit everywhere).** Everything in `ocw-voice` outside the `livekit` module – mute state, hotkey mapping (`hotkeys`: M / Shift+M, Select / R3 as library-free inputs), auto join / leave, spatial attenuation, nearest-N, device fallback, mixer, controller – uses no threads, clock, file system or audio device (times are passed in) and is part of the wasm check (`make test-wasm`, CI). The `VoiceBackend` trait only queues commands (`send`) and returns events already received (`poll`), and device lists are what the backend last learnt, so a browser backend (livekit-client JS called from Rust/wasm, asynchronous) or a mobile one (native LiveKit SDKs or the Rust SDK) fits behind it without changing the controller.
- **Client audio path.** Options were (a) the SDK's platform audio (WebRTC's own device module: capture, playout, echo cancellation, device selection built in) or (b) own audio I/O. (a) mixes all remote voices inside libwebrtc with no per-participant volume, which spatial audio needs, so **(b) is chosen**: cpal (already in the tree through Bevy's audio) captures the microphone and plays a stereo mix; every subscribed voice comes from a `NativeAudioStream` (48 kHz mono) into the `Mixer` with its own gain (spatial × voice volume) and constant-power pan; WebRTC's audio processing module (from libwebrtc) does echo cancellation, noise suppression, gain control and a high-pass filter on the microphone, fed with the played mix as the echo reference; the processed 10 ms frames go to a `NativeAudioSource` published as the microphone track. Devices are opened only while in a call; devices without 48 kHz are resampled (linear). Uncertainty: the echo canceller's delay estimate with cpal's buffering is untuned (headphones avoid the issue); if it proves poor, option (a) with nearest-N only (no attenuation) is the fallback.
- **Mute.** Microphone mute mutes the published track (others see it muted, unmuting is instant) and stops sending samples; the speaker mute silences the mix but keeps the voices subscribed.
- **Spatial audio and nearest-N.** *Changed (v4.51, 7.1.11, 7.1.7 Q6 / Q10): no floor – the gain fades to zero at 300 m; at most 24 voices, talking riders first; the game server decides who may hear whom. Changed again (v4.66, Q20): full to 5 m, zero at 10 m, selected riders at any distance.* Gain 1 up to 10 m, then 10 m / distance, floored at 0.15 inside 300 m, nothing beyond; pan up to ±0.5 by the lateral offset, only for riders beside the listener. The client subscribes to the nearest `voice.max_voices` (default 10) riders in range; a voice already heard counts 15 m nearer when ranking, so riders at almost the same distance do not swap. Distance: on a route the gap along it (the shorter way round on a loop); in free ride, where riders ride their own paths, the straight-line distance (an approximation of the road distance; good enough for "near" vs. "far"). Participants that are not riders, or riders not yet placed, are heard at the floor gain while there is room. In a group room everyone is heard at full voice volume (chosen partners), as with `voice.spatial off`.
- **Platform status (2026-11-12).** The SDK used is `livekit` 0.10.1 (libwebrtc downloaded prebuilt by its build script). **Linux:** from `webrtc-sys` 0.3.43 the prebuilt libwebrtc is built against Chromium's hermetic libc++, and the C++ bindings must be compiled with **clang ≥ 21** (`CXX=clang++-21`; GCC would silently break the ABI, the build refuses it). Debian 13 ships clang 19, so **Linux voice builds need clang >= 21: `make deps-llvm-debian` (apt.llvm.org)** – `clang-21`, `lld-21`, `libclang-21-dev`; `make deps-linux-debian` runs it and installs `libglib2.0-dev`. Considered: pinning `livekit` 0.8.3 / `webrtc-sys` 0.3.42 (builds with GCC, needs only the glib headers, but an older SDK), clang 21 from trixie-backports, or waiting for Debian's clang 21; the user chose apt.llvm.org's clang with the current SDK. Checked on marge (Debian 13, clang 21.1.8 from apt.llvm.org, `CC=clang-21 CXX=clang++-21`): the workspace with the `voice` feature builds, is clippy-clean and passes its tests; `make build` / `make release` and `scripts/deploy-test.sh` enable the feature by themselves when `clang++-21` is installed (`VOICE=0` / `VOICE=1` force it), so the kiosk build has voice. **macOS:** builds with Apple's toolchain (checked on the M1 build machine; its Command Line Tools lack the C++ headers on the default include path, worked around with `CXXFLAGS=-isystem …/MacOSX15.2.sdk/usr/include/c++/v1` – a broken install, reinstalling the Command Line Tools fixes it). **Windows:** `ocw-voice` with the `livekit` feature compiles on the Windows build machine (MSVC); the desktop with `voice` and a run with audio devices are not checked yet.
- **Integration test.** `crates/ocw-voice/tests/livekit_two_participants.rs` (feature `livekit`, `make test-voice-livekit`) connects two headless participants (no sound card: microphone samples pushed in, the mix read out) with tokens minted like the game server's; both must see each other, each sends a tone and must hear the other's, then one mutes and leaves and the other sees both; a second test does the same through two desktop `VoiceController`s (token request, grant, join, spatial subscription, hearing; v4.30). It starts a `livekit-server` of its own on free loopback ports when it finds the binary (`OCW_LIVEKIT_SERVER`, `~/.local/bin/livekit-server`, `PATH`), uses the server of `OCW_LIVEKIT_URL` / `_API_KEY` / `_API_SECRET` when they are set, and passes without doing anything otherwise; the feature (and so the test) is off in the plain `cargo test --workspace`, which stays network-free. The tests' event wait (`tests/support::wait_for`) keeps every polled event (`tests/backend_events.rs`, v4.30). CI with a LiveKit service container is still open.
- **Echo bot (the echo test; asked for by the user 2026-11-14, v2.96).** To test voice alone, an **Echo** rider stands on the road and plays the rider's own microphone back to them, delayed, from its place.
  - *Server.* `EchoRequest { on, here }` (reliable, answered with a `DevCommandResult`) puts the session's one Echo rider on the road – 20 m ahead of the asker on their track (in free ride on a copy of their path), 1.5 m right of the centre (less on narrow roads) – or takes it away; asked again it stays where it is, `here` moves it. It is a rider of its own kind in `ocw-sim` (`Control::Echo`): it stands still, is out of the physics and drafting, takes no start-formation slot, is not a bot, in no event, entrant list or standings and earns nothing; snapshots mark it (`RiderUpdate.echo`), its name tag is "Echo", it is not counted in `human_riders`. Allowed on the local servers (`ServerConfig.allow_echo_bot`, `Welcome.echo_bot`); `ocw-server --echo-bot` allows it on a shared server and puts one at the start of every session (logging its id and voice identity). The client asks for it once per session while the echo test is on (again after a ride switch), and takes it away when it is turned off.
  - *Near.* The controller (`ocw-voice::echo`, `VoiceController::set_echo`) sees the Echo rider like any rider (the gap on the route, the straight-line distance in free ride): the microphone is recorded in full up to **30 m**, linearly less up to **60 m**, nothing beyond (what was recorded still plays out, quieter, as the rider rides on, so passing it is heard as approach, echo, fade); the playback is placed like a voice (7: gain 1 to 10 m, then 10 m / distance, pan by the lateral offset beside it; × the voice volume; without spatial voice at the volume). The microphone is opened for it only within the voice range (300 m).
  - *Delay.* **300 ms by default** – clearly an echo, apart from the own voice (a few ms would only colour it like a comb filter), short enough to answer oneself; 20 ms – 3 s (`voice.echo delay MS`, setting `audio.echo_delay_ms`, 100 ms steps in the menu). A `DelayLine` (fixed ring buffer, one allocation) delays sample-exactly at 48 kHz: every block gives as many samples out as went in, so nothing drifts or piles up (unit-tested over 5 minutes of odd block sizes; the whole loop over 3 minutes with the mixer's buffer never above one 10 ms frame). The record gain ramps across each 10 ms block (no clicks).
  - *The path.* **Solo rides (local loopback, the default; no infrastructure, works on the kiosk):** the LiveKit backend opens the microphone and speaker even without a call while the echo test is active; the microphone frames go through WebRTC's audio processing (noise suppression, gain control, high-pass, echo cancellation – fed with the played mix, so the echo is not echoed again through speakers), then through the `EchoLoop` into the mixer as the voice `echo`, played with its gain and pan, the speaker mute and the voice volume like any received voice. Not in this path: Opus and the SFU (libwebrtc encodes inside the published track, which needs a room). In a call the same frames feed both the published track and the loop. Mute switches: microphone muted → silence goes into the delay line (nothing said while muted is ever echoed; what was said before still plays out within the delay); speaker muted → the echo is silent like all voices. **With a LiveKit server:** `cargo run -p ocw-voice --features livekit --example echo_participant -- ROOM RIDER_ID [DELAY_MS]` joins the room *as the Echo rider* (`rider-<id>`, token minted like the game server's), hears everyone and publishes it delayed; clients in the call see that participant and switch their loopback off (status "via server"), so the echo crosses Opus and the SFU twice and is placed by the normal nearest-N logic. Without the `voice` feature the echo test says "unavailable" (no audio devices in the null backend).
  - *UI.* Console `voice.echo [on|off|here|delay MS|status]` (on / off and the delay are remembered as `audio.echo_bot` and `audio.echo_delay_ms`, scope live), `--echo-bot` (on for the run), **Settings → Audio → Voice** (asked for by the user): the Audio page would exceed the ten-foot limit of seven items (3.2.1) with two more rows, so its Voice row now opens a sub-page with the voice volume (Enter plays the test tone), "Echo test" (on / off, with its state: speak now, N m away …) and "Echo delay (ms)" (20 ms – 3 s in 100 ms steps). HUD: while it is on, a line under the voice indicator – "ECHO TEST - speak now (300 ms echo)" when near, else where the Echo rider is – with two level meters (microphone, echo as played; −60 … 0 dBFS).
  - *Tests.* Delay exactness and bounded buffers, clamping, the record gain by distance, the loop and the microphone mute (`echo.rs`); end to end with the loopback backend (`tests/echo_loopback.rs`: a tone in → the same tone exactly 14 400 samples later, at the Echo rider's gain and pan; fading with distance, silent far away; mute switches; 3 minutes without drift; delay change); the headless LiveKit backend's local loopback (feature `livekit`); the server's request, marking and refusal; the sim's standing, slots, events and free-ride copy; the client's request; the app's console, menu rows, HUD and request-once logic; the protocol round trip. `OCW_ECHO_DEMO=FILE.wav cargo test -p ocw-voice --test echo_loopback` writes a 24 s demo: a synthetic voice riding past the Echo rider at 6 m/s (silent far away, the echo fading in, loud and right-panned beside it, fading out). *Uncertain:* not heard on real audio yet (the build machine marge has no sound card; the kiosk's microphone is untested), the echo canceller may partly cancel the echo picked up by the microphone through speakers – intended (no feedback loop), but it can make the echo sound thinner without headphones; the echo participant is build-checked only (no LiveKit server on the build machines).
- **Not yet:** voice for event and group rooms from the menu (console only), push-to-talk (dropped, 2.4), the participants' speaking marker on the minimap, hot-plug of audio devices during a call (a changed device reopens the streams), a Windows run of the `voice` feature, private rooms with invitations (Phase 5).

### 7.1 Voice built in and always on: the voice server comes with the app; Voice room *Everybody* or *Selected riders* (planning, asked by the user 2026-11-16, v4.01)

The user (2026-11-16): "i want all required binaries and libraries to be part of ocw-desktop (or the browser version) or if that's not possible that the voice server gets launched from the ocw-desktop app. Similar for the browser. Make it always on, so you can talk to everybody freely in the world per default = Voice Room: everybody. Make it possible to change that to selected users, so that you only can listen to them."

**What exists today (checked 2026-11-16).**

- *Client side is already built in.* Release builds (0.2.x) are made with `--features ocw-desktop/voice` on Linux, Windows and macOS, so `ocw-desktop` links the `livekit` crate 0.10.1 with LiveKit's prebuilt libwebrtc (echo cancellation, noise suppression, Opus); nothing has to be installed to *join* a call. The browser app bundles LiveKit's JS SDK (`livekit-client` 2.23.0, pinned and hash-checked by `scripts/fetch-livekit-client.sh`, served next to the page with its Apache-2.0 licence) behind `apps/web/web/ocw-voice.js` / `ocw_voice::web`; `make web-preview` (the public preview) leaves it out.
- *The voice server is not.* Voice needs a **separately run LiveKit server** (`livekit-server`, Go) and a game server started with `OCW_LIVEKIT_URL`, `OCW_LIVEKIT_API_KEY`, `OCW_LIVEKIT_API_SECRET` (or `--livekit-url`, `--livekit-api-key`); otherwise `ocw-server` logs "voice chat off" and clients show "no voice on this server". The in-app servers never offer voice: the local server and *Ride → Host a ride* (`LocalServer::spawn_hosting`, v3.73) run with `voice: None`; the kiosk's game server (`ocw-kiosk.sh`, v3.72) is started without LiveKit. Only tests use a real one: `livekit-server` v1.13.10 in `~/.local/bin` on marge for `make test-web-livekit` and the env-gated `livekit_two_participants` test.
- *Rooms today:* one session room per game server (`ocw-<instance>`), plus event and group rooms; the client subscribes only to the nearest `voice.max_voices` (10) riders within 300 m (`auto_subscribe = false`, `set_subscribed` per publication in both backends); auto join needs ≥ 2 human riders; open microphone by default (2.4, decided 2026-11-12).

#### 7.1.1 Everything inside the app, or the app starts the voice server

An SFU (selective forwarding unit) is needed in the middle; the question is where it comes from. LiveKit's server is Go (Apache-2.0) and cannot be linked into a Rust binary (a cgo `c-archive` of a whole Go server with its own runtime and goroutine scheduler is possible in theory but unsupported upstream and not worth it). Options:

| | (a) Bundle `livekit-server`, started by the app / server as a child process | (b) Own audio SFU in Rust inside `ocw-server` (`str0m` or webrtc-rs) | (c) Peer-to-peer mesh, no SFU |
|---|---|---|---|
| What it is | The unchanged LiveKit binary shipped next to `ocw-desktop` / `ocw-server` in every package; whoever hosts the game server starts it with a generated config and stops it on exit | A minimal forwarding SFU for Opus audio only (no video, no simulcast, no transcoding) in the game server process; `str0m` is a pure-Rust, sans-IO WebRTC library (MIT / Apache-2.0) suited to SFUs | Every client opens a WebRTC connection to every other one; the game server only relays the offers / answers |
| One binary | No: a second executable (~57 MB unpacked, see below) | **Yes** | Yes (no server part) |
| Client changes | **None** – the Rust SDK and the JS SDK stay | Large: our own signalling; desktop needs a WebRTC client without the LiveKit SDK (str0m client side + an audio processing module for echo cancellation), browser uses `RTCPeerConnection` directly instead of `livekit-client` | Medium: raw peer connections on both clients (the `livekit` crate re-exports libwebrtc's peer connection API; the browser has it natively) |
| Scales to "everybody in the world" | Yes (LiveKit: hundreds per room) | Yes for audio (forwarding RTP, cheap) | **No**: n − 1 uploads per rider; fine for ≤ 6–8 riders, not for a kiosk session or an event |
| NAT / riders behind CGNAT | Clients only connect out to the host's public ports; ICE/TCP fallback; LiveKit's embedded TURN if needed | The same, done by us | Worst: two clients behind CGNAT / symmetric NAT cannot reach each other without a TURN relay |
| Browsers on https pages | Signalling is a WebSocket: needs **`wss://` with a CA-trusted certificate** (a home host has none) – see *Network* | Signalling can go over a WebTransport session to the game server, which already works with `serverCertificateHashes`; WebRTC media need no CA certificate (DTLS fingerprints in the SDP) | Signalling through the game server; media direct |
| Selective listening, permissions | Built in (subscription per track, track subscription permissions, token grants) | Ours: the game server knows positions and lists, so it can forward exactly what each rider may hear (server-side nearest-N) | Trivial (connect only to the chosen) |
| Build needs | Ships a prebuilt binary; no Go in our build (macOS: see below) | Could later drop libwebrtc and the clang ≥ 21 requirement from the desktop build, if an echo canceller is found elsewhere | As today |
| Effort | **Small** (about a week: launcher, config, ports, packaging, tests) | Large (SFU core 1–2 weeks, both clients' voice backends rewritten, interop and NAT testing: several weeks) | Medium, and a dead end for large sessions |

**Proposal: (a) now, (b) as a later option** (7.1.7 Q1). (a) gives "voice works without setting anything up" with no change to the clients and the existing tests; (b) is the way to one binary and to browser voice on home-hosted rides without a domain, and the `VoiceBackend` trait (7) keeps it possible without touching the controller, the rooms logic or the UI. (c) is not proposed.

**(a) in detail – the voice launcher (`ocw_server::voice::launcher`, native only):**

- *Who starts it:* whoever hosts the game server hosts voice, automatically:
  - *Ride → Host a ride* (the in-app server, `spawn_hosting`) – the desktop app starts `livekit-server` beside its `NetServer`;
  - the kiosk's game server (`ocw-kiosk.sh` → `ocw-server`) and every headless `ocw-server --listen …` – the server starts it itself;
  - not the plain local server of a solo ride (nobody to talk to; the echo test keeps its local loopback, 7 *Echo bot*).
  - `--livekit-url` / `OCW_LIVEKIT_URL` still win: a server configured with an external LiveKit (a hosted deployment, B8) does not start its own. `--voice off` (setting `host.voice` in Host a ride, default on) turns it off; `--voice-server PATH` names the binary (default: next to the executable, then `PATH`).
- *Config, generated per start:* a fresh API key and secret (random, 32 bytes; held in memory, given to the child in the environment `LIVEKIT_KEYS="KEY: SECRET"` – never on the command line, never in the repository); the config as YAML in the environment (`LIVEKIT_CONFIG`) or a 0600 file under `<data dir>/ocw/voice/` (*to be verified* which `livekit-server` 1.13 accepts): `port` (signalling, TCP, default **7880**), `rtc.tcp_port` (ICE over TCP, **7881**), `rtc.udp_port` (all media on **one UDP port, 7882**, LiveKit's UDP mux – one forwarding rule instead of a 10 000-port range), `rtc.use_external_ip` (on for an internet host, off on a LAN; LiveKit then asks a STUN server for the public address – *proposal*: our own or none, 7.1.7 Q5), `turn.enabled: false` by default, `room.empty_timeout`, logging to `<state dir>/voice.log`. The game server then uses the same key pair to mint tokens (7 *rooms and tokens*, unchanged).
- *Lifecycle:* started before the game server opens its port, ready when its HTTP port answers (`/` returns "OK"; at most 10 s, else the session runs without voice and the HUD says why); stopped with the game server (*Stop hosting*, quit, the kiosk's restart). A crash of the app must not leave it running: Linux `PR_SET_PDEATHSIG`, Windows a job object with *kill on close*, macOS a pid file checked and cleaned at the next start. A crashed child is restarted with back-off (2, 4 … 60 s); clients reconnect by themselves (7 retry).
- *Packaging (11.3):* the binary ships in every package next to `ocw-desktop` / `ocw-server`: AppImage (`usr/bin/livekit-server`), the Linux tar.xz, the Windows zip (`livekit-server.exe`), the macOS app bundle (`Contents/MacOS/livekit-server`, signed with the app; with notarisation later it needs the hardened runtime too). Fetched pinned and hash-checked by a new `scripts/fetch-livekit-server.sh` (like `fetch-livekit-client.sh`). **Sizes (measured 2026-11-16, release v1.13.10):** `livekit_1.13.10_linux_amd64.tar.gz` 19.4 MB, `linux_arm64` 17.5 MB, `windows_amd64.zip` 19.6 MB; unpacked the Linux binary is **57.0 MB** (marge). So each package grows by about 19–20 MB compressed (the AppImage is squashfs-compressed, similar). **macOS:** the GitHub release has **no darwin binary** (LiveKit ships macOS through Homebrew); we build it from the pinned source tag on the Mac build machine with Go (`GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64`, `-ldflags "-s -w"`, which may also shrink the others – to be measured), or take Homebrew's bottle (7.1.7 Q2). Licence: Apache-2.0 – `livekit-server.LICENSE.txt` and its NOTICE, plus the licences of its Go dependencies (pion and others, mostly MIT / BSD; generated with `go-licenses`) go into each package and the release notes' licence list (13).
- *Size budget:* + ~20 MB per download, + ~57 MB on disk; the world packages (88–500 MB) stay the larger part. Alternative if this is too much: download the binary at the first *Host a ride* (pinned, hash-checked) – the user asked for it bundled, so not proposed.

**Joining needs nothing extra:** the game server's `Welcome.voice` already tells clients that voice is offered, and each `VoiceGrant` carries the URL and token, so no rider configures anything. New: the URL in the grant is the one *the rider can reach*: the server knows the address the client connected to (its local address of that connection) and puts it in (`ws://THAT_ADDRESS:7880`), instead of one fixed URL – riders on the LAN get the LAN address, riders over the internet the public one (from the join link's host, `host.public_name`).

**The browser:**

- It cannot run a server (no listening sockets), so it never hosts voice; it joins the voice of whoever hosts, with the bundled `livekit-client` (already there). Hosting from the browser stays "Hosting needs the desktop app" (v3.73); a ride on our hosted servers (Phase 10 B8) gets a LiveKit behind TLS on the domain there.
- **The certificate problem:** a page served over `https://` (every browser app outside `localhost`; WebTransport and the microphone need a secure context anyway) may open only `wss://` WebSockets with a **CA-trusted** certificate. A desktop or kiosk host on a home line has none (its WebTransport works only through `serverCertificateHashes`, which WebSockets do not have). Ways:
  1. **A signalling bridge (proposal, 7.1.7 Q3):** the browser opens a *second* WebTransport session to the game server's UDP port (path `/voice`, the same certificate hash as the game connection), the game server forwards it byte for byte to its child's `127.0.0.1:7880`, and `ocw-voice.js` gives `livekit-client` a `WebSocket` look-alike over that stream for this URL only. Only signalling crosses it (a few kB); the **audio still goes over WebRTC directly** to the voice server's UDP port (DTLS-SRTP, no CA needed). It is a separate session, not the game connection, but it bends the rule "voice never over the QUIC game connection" – the rule would read "voice *media* never …" (7.1.7 Q3). Uncertain: whether `livekit-client` 2.23 keeps working with a substituted WebSocket class (it constructs `new WebSocket(url)`; to be tested in `make test-web-livekit`).
  2. A host with a domain: `ocw-server --tls-cert/--tls-key` (or ACME later) serves `wss://` itself and proxies to the child (LiveKit has no TLS of its own; a reverse proxy like Caddy also works). For the headless server on a rented machine.
  3. Pages on `localhost` may use `ws://` (development, the kiosk machine itself).
  Without 1 or 2 a browser rider on a home-hosted ride rides without voice and the HUD says "voice needs the desktop app on this server".

**Network (what the user opens, what the app does):**

- *Ports of a host:* UDP **47800** (the game, QUIC; 47801 WebTransport), TCP **7880** (voice signalling), TCP **7881** (voice over TCP, for riders whose networks block UDP), UDP **7882** (voice media). The Host a ride summary and the join-link page list them, with the firewall / port-forwarding hint they already show (README *Riding on a server on the internet* gets the three voice ports). Windows asks once to allow `livekit-server.exe` through its firewall.
- *Automatic port mapping:* **proposal: UPnP-IGD / NAT-PMP / PCP from the app when hosting** (the `igd-next` crate: map 47800/udp, 7880–7881/tcp, 7882/udp for the hosting's lifetime, remove them after; a switch *Open the router's ports automatically*, default on for Host a ride, off for the headless server) – 7.1.7 Q4. Many routers have UPnP off; the hint stays. *Built (v4.31, 7.1.9):* UPnP-IGD as proposed; NAT-PMP / PCP open (7.1.7 Q13).
- *CGNAT:* a host behind CGNAT cannot accept anything (the game neither) – unchanged advice: IPv6 or a rented server. *Riders* behind CGNAT need no TURN: they connect out to the host's public ports (ICE, then the TCP fallback). LiveKit's embedded TURN (UDP 3478; TURN/TLS 5349 needs a certificate) stays **off** and can be turned on for the headless server (`--voice-turn`).

#### 7.1.2 Always on, default *Voice room: Everybody*

- **Join:** as soon as a rider is in a shared ride – any game server with at least one other human rider (2.4: `Welcome.voice` and `Snapshot.human_riders`), joined through *Ride → Join*, a join link, `--server`, the kiosk, or hosting – the client joins the session room automatically, as today. Since every host now offers voice, voice is on in every shared ride without setup. Solo rides stay without a call.
- **Everybody hears everybody.** *Voice room: Everybody* (the default) means the whole session: today's 300 m range and nearest-10 limit no longer silence anyone. **Proposal (7.1.7 Q6): spatial volume, never silent** – full volume up to 10 m, then 10 m / distance, floored at **0.3** (today 0.15, and nothing beyond 300 m); panning beside the rider stays; `voice.spatial off` gives everybody equal volume. The subscription cap rises from 10 to **24 voices** (`voice.max_voices`, Opus at ~32 kbit/s: < 1 Mbit/s down); above that the riders who are *speaking* (LiveKit's active speakers) are preferred over silent near ones, then the nearest, so a large session still lets every speaker through.
- **Microphone default:** today's decision is an open microphone on joining (2.4, 2026-11-12). With voice on for everybody on every shared ride, strangers too, **proposal: keep the open microphone, but the very first call shows a notice** ("Your microphone is on – everybody in this ride hears you. M mutes.") for 8 s, and the HUD indicator stays visible; alternatives are muted-but-listening on the first ride, or always joining muted (7.1.7 Q7). Push-to-talk stays dropped.
- **Status signs** (changed by Q7 and Q11 below): a muted microphone in a call shows an **X over the mouth** to everybody; **headphones** show per viewer on a rider who cannot hear the viewer (2.6 *Rider status signs*; the reasons are Q12).

#### 7.1.3 *Selected riders*: listen only to chosen riders

- **Settings → Voice → *Voice room*: Everybody / Selected riders** (shared page in `ocw_client::menu`, both apps; setting `voice.room = everybody | selected`, default `everybody`, scope live). With *Selected riders* a row *Choose riders* opens a list of the riders in the session (name, distance, a speaking marker; bots and the Echo rider not listed), each with a check mark; a rider not in the session but selected before is shown greyed under *Not here now*. The HUD voice indicator shows "ROOM: everybody" or "ROOM: 3 selected (2 here)".
- **Remembered across sessions** in `voice.selected = [...]` (settings file / `localStorage`), keyed by the rider's **account id** when signed in (9.1, `acct:<id>`; stable, the name may change) and by the **rider name** when not (`name:Ada Rider`; rider names are unique, 14 Phase 4 4N). Today's voice identity `rider-<rider id>` changes every session, so the grant / snapshot must carry the stable key: `RiderUpdate.account_key` (new field: the public account id, empty when not signed in).
- **"Only listen to them":** with *Selected riders* the client subscribes only to the selected riders' microphone tracks (the existing selective subscription, `set_subscribed` / `setSubscribed`, with the selection as the filter instead of nearest-N; spatial volume as in Everybody, no range limit). It stays in the session room, so switching back is instant and no new token is needed.
- **Who hears me:** the user's words fix only what one hears. **Proposal: a separate setting *Who hears me*: Everybody (default) / Same as my selection** (`voice.heard_by = everybody | selected`, 7.1.7 Q8). With *Same as my selection* the client sets LiveKit's **track subscription permissions** on its microphone track (allowed identities = the selected riders; `LocalParticipant::set_track_subscription_permissions` in the Rust SDK 0.10.1, `setTrackSubscriptionPermissions` in `livekit-client`) – enforced by the SFU, so others cannot hear the rider even with a modified client. Everybody else sees the rider as "private" in their list (no headphones sign: the microphone is not muted, only not shared with them).
- **Block and per-rider volume (proposal):** in the participants' list (Settings → Voice → Participants, today "mute one rider for yourself") each rider gets *Mute for me* (this session, as today), **Block** (remembered in `voice.blocked = [...]` with the same keys: never subscribed, and denied my track through the permissions, in every room mode) and a **volume** (0–200 %, 10 % steps, `voice.rider_volume = { key = percent }`, applied in the mixer's per-voice gain; the browser in its gain node). Riders who blocked you are not told.
- **Selection is a listening filter, not a private room:** private rooms with invitations stay the group rooms (7, Phase 5). *Selected riders* works in the session and event rooms; in a group room everybody in it is heard (the group already is the selection).

#### 7.1.4 Protocol, server and settings (fields only added)

- `VoiceGrant.url` per connection (the address the client reached); `Welcome.voice_info { ports, bridge_path }` (the signalling bridge for browsers, 7.1.7 Q3); `RiderUpdate.account_key` (stable key for selections and blocks); no new messages for the selection itself (it is client-side plus LiveKit permissions).
- Token grants unchanged (join, subscribe, publish microphone only); setting the own track's subscription permissions needs no extra grant.
- `ocw-server`: `--voice auto|off` (default auto: start the bundled server unless `--livekit-url`), `--voice-server PATH`, `--voice-ports 7880,7881,7882`, `--voice-turn`, `--voice-public-host NAME`; the kiosk passes nothing new (auto). Startup log: "voice chat on (bundled LiveKit 1.13.x, ports …)".
- Desktop: Host a ride gets *Voice* (on / off) and *Open router ports* in its options step; `host status` lists the voice state. *Built:* *Open the router's ports* (v4.31), *Voice* (v5.20, Q15).
- Settings keys (since v5.26, 7.1.12: `voice.my_voice` = `everybody` | `selected` and `voice.i_hear` = `everybody` | `selected` | `nobody` instead of `voice.heard_by` / `voice.room` / `voice.enabled`, which are migrated): `voice.room` (`everybody` | `selected`), `voice.selected` (list), `voice.heard_by` (`everybody` | `selected`), `voice.blocked` (list), `voice.rider_volume` (table), `voice.max_voices` default 24; `host.voice`, `host.upnp`.
- HUD: the voice indicator gets the room line; the talking riders' names and the green marker above talking avatars stay (2.4); selected riders who talk are listed first; a rider heard as "private" is not marked.

#### 7.1.5 Tests (11.4)

- *Unit, no network:* the selection filter (everybody / selected / blocked, by account key and by name, riders leaving and coming back, keys changing from name to account at sign-in), the subscription planner with the new cap, active-speaker priority and floor gain, the permission list built for *Who hears me*, the per-rider volume in the mixer, settings round trips; the launcher's config generation (ports, keys never in argv or the log, external IP on/off) and its lifecycle against a fake child (ready probe, timeout, crash and back-off, stop on exit); `VoiceGrant.url` per connection address; Host a ride's options and the menu pages (page-fit test, both apps).
- *Integration on marge with the real `livekit-server`* (v1.13.10, `~/.local/bin`, later the bundled copy): `ocw-server --listen` starts it by itself, two headless participants (`livekit_two_participants` extended) join without any `OCW_LIVEKIT_*` variable; *Selected riders* – A selects B only and hears B, not C; *Who hears me* – C cannot subscribe to A's track; stop kills the child (no process left). `make test-voice-bundled`.
- *Browser:* `make test-web-livekit` extended: two headless Chromium riders and a desktop bot on a self-hosted `ocw-server` with the bundled LiveKit, through the signalling bridge (if 7.1.7 Q3 is yes), selection and permissions as above.
- *Packaging:* a release check that every package contains the voice server, its licence files and that `--version` of it matches the pin; the AppImage smoke run hosts a ride and sees "voice chat on".

#### 7.1.6 Milestones (proposal)

V1 launcher + headless server + kiosk (Linux, then Windows, macOS binary) – **built (v4.25, 7.1.8)**; V2 Host a ride with voice, per-connection URL, ports page, UPnP (7.1.7 Q4) – **built (v4.31, 7.1.9)**; V3 *Everybody* (no range limit, floor, cap 24, active speakers, first-call notice) – **built (v4.51, 7.1.11)** as decided later: spatial to zero at 300 m with the server sending voice only to riders who can hear it (Q6, Q10), joined muted (Q7), cap 24 with talking riders first, the notice adapted; V4 *Selected riders*, *Who hears me*, block, per-rider volume (both apps) – **built (block and volume v4.48, 7.1.10; the rest v4.51, 7.1.11)**, *Who hears me* as decided (Q8: No one / All nearby / Selected riders; since v5.26 the rows *My voice* and *I hear*, Q16, 7.1.12); V5 browser signalling bridge (if 7.1.7 Q3); V6 packaging of all four release packages, licences, README and release notes. Later: (b) the Rust SFU, if chosen.

#### 7.1.7 Open questions (for the user)

- **Q1 – How the voice server comes with the app: decided (2026-11-16, the user): (a) bundle LiveKit's `livekit-server` now** – the user: "(a) bundle now". A second executable shipped in every package and started by whoever hosts (7.1.1 (a)); an own Rust audio SFU inside `ocw-server` (b) stays a later option.
- **Q2 – The macOS voice server: decided (2026-11-16, the user): built from LiveKit's pinned source tag on the Mac build machine**, like the other release binaries (not Homebrew).
- **Q3 – Browser riders on home-hosted rides: decided (2026-11-16, the user): the signalling bridge** – a second WebTransport session to the game server carries LiveKit's signalling; the audio stays WebRTC (the rule becomes "voice *media* never over the game connection").
- **Q4 – Router ports: decided (2026-11-16, the user): UPnP / NAT-PMP / PCP from the app while hosting** – on by default for *Host a ride*, off for the headless server; switchable.
- **Q5 – Finding the public address for voice: decided (2026-11-16, the user): as proposed** – the join link's host; a STUN server only when none is given.
- **Q6 – Volume in *Everybody*: decided (2026-11-16, the user): spatial, fading to silence with distance; the server sends voice only to riders who can hear it** – the user: "spatial, but riders get quieter the further away until the are not audible at all. server: save resources by sending voice data only to riders that can be heard." Volume falls with distance down to **zero** (no floor); the game server knows every position and grants each rider subscriptions only to the riders within hearing range (server-side, through LiveKit's subscription permissions / the grant), so voice data never travels to riders who could not hear it. The range is Q10.
- **Q7 – Microphone when joining: decided (2026-11-16, the user): always join muted; muted riders show an X mouth** – the user: "join always muted, show as ingame status by giving muted riders an X mouth". Every rider joins every shared ride with the microphone **muted** (M unmutes; nothing remembered across rides); a muted rider's avatar shows an **X over the mouth** to everybody (a status sign, 2.6). Whether the headphones of 2.6 stay for a muted microphone is Q11.
- **Q8 – With *Selected riders*, who hears me: decided (2026-11-16, the user): a setting *Who hears me*, default *No one*** – the user: "default: no one, other options all nearby, selected riders (names...)". *Who hears me*: **No one** (default) / **All nearby** (everybody within hearing range, Q6) / **Selected riders** (chosen by name in a list, remembered as in 7.1.3). Enforced by the server's grants (Q6) and LiveKit's track subscription permissions.
- **Q9 – Block and per-rider volume: decided (2026-11-17, dashboard): add both** – the participants' list gets *Block* (remembered across sessions, both directions: neither rider hears the other) and a volume per rider, beside today's *Mute for me*. **Built (v4.48, 7.1.10):** both apps; Block enforced through the game server (`VoiceBlocks` → `VoiceApart` to both riders) and the voice server (track subscription permissions); the volume 0 – 200 % in 10 % steps on top of the spatial gain; remembered by account, else by name per server; the status signs unchanged then – since v5.33 a block and 0 % show headphones (Q18).
- **Q10 – Hearing range (follow-up of Q6): decided (2026-11-16, the user): full volume up to 10 m, then fading to zero** *(range changed by Q20, 2026-11-17: fading from 5 m, silent beyond 10 m; selected riders always audible – built v4.66, 7.1.11)* – the user: "full volume up to 10 m, then fading to zero". The fade ends at **300 m** (the proposal's range, today's voice range; the user gave the curve, not a new distance), smoothly; the server's grants follow the same range with a small margin so nobody pops in or out.
- **Q11 – Muted: X mouth and headphones (follow-up of Q7, 2.6): decided (2026-11-16, the user): two different signs** – the user: "headphones means: cant hear you. the X means microphone muted." **X mouth** = this rider's **microphone is muted** (seen by everybody). **Headphones** = this rider **cannot hear you** – a sign seen per viewer: each rider sees headphones on the riders who do not receive the viewer's voice. This replaces 2.6's "headphones for a muted microphone" (v4.07). Which reasons count is Q12. Built v4.25 (2.6 *Built*).
- **Q12 – When the headphones show "cannot hear you" (follow-up of Q11): decided (2026-11-18, dashboard): as proposed** – only when the other rider **chose not to hear you** (their sound / voice is off, they listen to *Selected riders* without you, they muted or blocked you, Q9), **not** because of distance (beyond the hearing range of Q10 nobody hears anybody). As built in v4.34.

- **Q13 – NAT-PMP / PCP besides UPnP: decided (2026-11-21, the user): (a) only when riders report routers without UPnP, then as a second try after UPnP finds no router – not built until then** – Was asked: when a rider hosts a ride at home (*Host a ride*), riders on the internet can reach that computer only if the home router forwards the game's ports to it. The app asks the router to do so automatically with UPnP, the most common way (built in V2). Some routers – Apple AirPort, some OpenWrt set-ups – do not speak UPnP but NAT-PMP or its successor PCP. Supporting them takes another library (`crab_nat`, MIT) plus one more to find the router's address, and a background runtime. Options: (a) add it only when riders report routers without UPnP, then as a second try after UPnP finds no router; (b) add it now. Proposal: a.
- **Q14 – Browsers joining a desktop host (UDP 47801): decided (2026-11-17, dashboard): as proposed** – *Host a ride* opens WebTransport on PORT+1 (UDP 47801) together with the browser signalling bridge (V5, Q3), and lists and maps that port then; until V5 browser riders cannot join a ride hosted in the desktop app (only the headless server's `--webtransport`).
- **Q15 – A Voice switch in Host a ride: decided (2026-11-21, the user): (b) a Voice row on the Options page of Host a ride (`host.voice`, on by default)** – **Built (v5.20):** the row *Voice* (on / off) on the Options page (*Time and weather* moved to the Weather page for it), `host.plan voice on|off`, `host start --voice on|off`; saved in `ocw.toml` (3.2.4). Off: no voice server, no voice ports on the router, the hosted server offers no voice (as `--voice off`), so the riders see "no voice on this server" and no voice signs (no X mouth, no headphones: nobody is in a call); the summary and `host status` say "no voice". Was asked: the planning (v4.01) gave *Host a ride* two options, *Voice* and *Open router ports*. Only the router switch was built (V2): voice chat is always on in a hosted ride and is off only when the voice server program is missing or does not start. So a host who does not want voice chat at all cannot turn it off in the app (the headless server can, with `--voice off`). Options: (a) no switch, as built; (b) a *Voice* row on the Options page of *Host a ride* (`host.voice`, on by default). Proposal: a.
- **Q16 – Voice turned off entirely, X mouth too?: decided (2026-11-18, dashboard): two separate settings** – the user: "muting voice (who can hear me) is a complete separate setting to muting audio of other player (who do i choose to hear)." There is no single "voice off" that does both: **my microphone / who can hear me** and **whom I hear** are independent settings. The signs follow them: microphone off (nobody hears me) → the **X mouth**; not hearing others → the **headphones** ("cannot hear you", Q12). **Layout decided (2026-11-22, the user: "build proposal"):** the Voice page shows the two as separate rows (*My voice: on / off · Everybody / Selected* and *I hear: everybody / selected / nobody*), and the old combined `voice.off` becomes both rows off. **Built (v5.26, 7.1.12).**
- **Q17 – Who has muted whom, per viewer from the server?: decided (2026-11-21, the user): (b) the server works out per viewer whether each rider cannot hear that viewer and sends one yes / no per rider, never the mute lists** – **Built (v5.20):** the clients send their reasons to the server as before (`RiderStatus.hears_nobody`, `not_hearing`); the server works out per viewer the riders who cannot hear that viewer (`ocw_server::headphones`) and sends only that viewer a `NotHearingYou` (a new message, field 14: the riders with "yes"; on every change); the snapshots no longer carry `not_hearing` (deprecated there, number kept), so the lists never leave the server; old clients do not crash – they see headphones only for *hears nobody*. Reasons unchanged (Q12): mutes and *Voice room: Selected riders* count, *Who hears me*, distance and blocks did not (Q18; since v5.33 blocks and 0 % volume count too). Was asked: a rider sees headphones on another rider when that rider cannot hear them, e.g. because they muted them (status signs, v4.34). To draw this, the server today sends every client every rider's list of whom they muted (up to 64 riders), although each client only needs its own case. A modified app could read those lists and learn who muted whom – private information. Options: (a) as now, every list to everybody; (b) the server works out for each viewer whether each rider cannot hear *that viewer* and sends only one yes / no per rider. Asked 2026-11-16. Proposal: b.
- **Q19 – One list of Selected riders or two (follow-up of Q8): decided (2026-11-21, the user): (a) one list – the riders I can hear can hear me, too (as built v4.51)** – Was asked: voice has two settings that use a hand-picked list of riders: *Voice room: Selected riders* (I hear only these riders) and *Who hears me: Selected riders* (only these riders hear me). Built (v4.51): **one shared list** – the riders picked in *Choose riders* are both the ones I hear and the ones who hear me. So someone who wants to listen to a friend without being heard by them, or the other way round, cannot do so. Options: (a) one list, as built; (b) two lists – whom I hear, who hears me – each with its own *Choose riders*. Asked 2026-11-17. Proposal: a, the simpler one, with b only if riders ask for it – a suggestion, the spec makes none.
- **Q20 – Selected riders far away (follow-up of Q6 / Q10 with 7.1.3): decided (2026-11-17, dashboard): selected riders are always audible; everyone else only close by – fading from 5 m, silent beyond 10 m** – the user: "selected riders are always audible. other riders only around 5m (start fading) and not audible >10m." This changes Q10's range (full to 10 m, fading to 300 m, v4.51): riders not selected are at full volume up to 5 m, fade to zero at 10 m, and the server sends their voice only within that range; riders one has selected (Voice room *Selected riders*) are heard at any distance and are always sent. **Built (v4.66, 7.1.11 *Hearing range*):** full volume to 5 m, the same smooth fade to zero at 10 m; the server grants within 10.5 m and keeps to 12 m; a rider listening to *Voice room: Selected riders* hears the selected riders at full volume at any distance (the speaker's *Who hears me* and blocks still apply); the Echo rider keeps its 300 m curve. ~~Open (asked 2026-11-17, v4.51). The planning of 7.1.3 said a selected rider is heard "with spatial volume as in Everybody, no range limit"; Q6 / Q10 then made the volume fade to zero at 300 m and the server send voice only within hearing range. Built: **the range holds for selected riders too** (beyond 300 m a selected rider is not heard and gets nothing). Alternative: selected riders are heard at any distance (at a fixed low volume or full), and the server sends their voice whatever the distance.~~
- **Q21 – voice.spatial off with the hearing range: decided (2026-11-22, the user): (a) as built – with spatial off everybody within the 10 m range is heard at the same volume, selected riders at any distance; the server keeps sending voice only where it is heard** – Was asked: voice is normally spatial: other riders get quieter with distance – full volume up to 5 m, silent beyond 10 m (Q20), riders one has selected at any distance. The setting `voice.spatial off` was meant as "everybody at the same volume, no range". Built: with spatial off every rider **within** the 10 m range is heard at the same volume, and selected riders at any distance; riders further away are still not heard, because the server sends their voice only within the range. Options: (a) as built; (b) spatial off removes the range too – the server would then have to know the setting and send everybody's voice to that rider. Asked 2026-11-17. Proposal: a, which keeps the server's saving of sending voice only where it is heard – a suggestion, the spec makes none.
- **Q22 – Unmuting while nobody hears you: decided (2026-11-22, the user): (b) when M turns the voice on while nobody can hear it, the HUD shows "nobody hears you – Settings > Voice" for a few seconds (since v5.26 the case is *My voice: on · Selected* with no rider selected, or every hearer blocked)** – **Built (v5.33, 7.1.12 *HUD and notice*):** both apps (the shared `VoiceDriver`); on every turn-on of My voice (M, the menu, the console) in the call, "Voice: nobody hears you - Settings > Voice" for 5 s on the voice notice line when no other rider in the call can be a hearer – with *Selected* none selected (or every selected one blocked, apart or out of the call), with *Everybody* every rider in the call blocked or apart (and other riders in the session; alone there is nothing to change); distance is no reason; muting again ends it. Was asked: with the chosen defaults a rider joins every ride muted and with *Who hears me: No one*. Pressing M unmutes the microphone, but still nobody hears them until *Who hears me* is changed in the settings – easy to miss. Built: the first call's notice says so once ("you join muted – M unmutes. Who hears you: no one (Settings > Voice > Voice room)"), the HUD's voice line always shows "heard by: no one", and M itself says nothing more. Options: (a) as built; (b) when M unmutes while *Who hears me* is No one, the HUD shows "nobody hears you – Settings > Voice > Voice room" for a few seconds. Asked 2026-11-17. Proposal: b.
- **Q18 – Block, a rider's volume and the headphones (follow-up of Q9, with Q12 / Q17): decided (2026-11-22, the user): a rider shows headphones to another rider who they muted for themselves, blocked, or set to 0 % volume – all three count as "cannot hear you"** – **Built (v5.33):** *Mute for me* was already sent (`RiderStatus.not_hearing`); the client now sends the riders it set to 0 % in `RiderStatus.silenced` (field 7, added; client → server only, sorted, at most 64, never relayed – a server older than v5.33 drops the unknown field); the server adds its blocks (`voice_block::blocked`, one way: the blocker shows headphones to the rider it blocked, the blocked rider shows none to the blocker unless it blocked back) to `headphones::cannot_hear`, so each viewer still gets only its yes / no per rider (`NotHearingYou`). This overrides 7.1.10's "the blocked rider is not told" for the sign. Old clients: they send no `silenced`, and see the new headphones through `NotHearingYou` like any other. Was asked: headphones on a rider's avatar mean "this rider cannot hear you" (Q11). A *Block* keeps two riders apart both ways, so each cannot hear the other; a rider's volume can also be set to 0 %, which silences them while their voice still arrives. Built (v4.48): **neither shows headphones**, so a blocked rider does not learn of the block from a sign. Options: (a) as built – no headphones for a block or for 0 %; (b) headphones on both riders of a block, each seen by the other – the blocked rider then sees the same as after a *Mute for me* and may guess, and with Q17's per-viewer flag nobody else would see it; (c) only the blocker sees headphones on the blocked rider, the blocked rider sees nothing. Separately: should 0 % count like *Mute for me* and show headphones? Asked 2026-11-17. Proposal: a, which keeps a block private, and 0 % not counted – a suggestion, the spec makes none.

#### 7.1.8 Built (V1): the voice launcher (v4.22)

- **What.** `ocw_server::voice::launcher` (native only) and its use in the `ocw-server` binary. A server that others join (`--listen`) without an external LiveKit starts `livekit-server` **before it opens its port**: the binary from `--voice-server PATH`, else next to the executable, else on `PATH` (`launcher::find_binary`). Per start a fresh API key (`OCW` + 16 hex digits) and secret (32 bytes from the OS, 64 hex digits; `getrandom`), held in memory; the child gets them only in its environment (`LIVEKIT_KEYS="KEY: SECRET"`) and its generated config in `LIVEKIT_CONFIG` (`launcher::config_yaml`; checked: `livekit-server` 1.13.10 accepts the config body from the environment and refuses unknown fields) – its command line is the bare binary. Inherited `LIVEKIT_*`, `NODE_IP`, `UDP_PORT`, `REDIS_*` and `OCW_LIVEKIT_API_SECRET` are removed from its environment. Config: `port` 7880, `rtc.tcp_port` 7881, `rtc.udp_port` 7882 (`--voice-ports SIGNAL,TCP,UDP`), `turn.enabled: false`, `room.empty_timeout: 300`; the media address (Q5): `--voice-public-host HOST` resolved → `rtc.node_ip` with `advertise_internal_ip` (LAN riders keep their direct path), none → `use_external_ip` (STUN; on marge LiveKit then needs about 6 s, its external-IP check times out behind NAT), a loopback `--listen` → signalling bound to 127.0.0.1 (`bind_addresses`) and media on this machine's interface addresses without STUN (a `node_ip` of 127.0.0.1 does not work: WebRTC clients bind their sockets to the interface addresses). Its log is `<data dir>/ocw/voice/livekit-PORT.log`.
- **Ready check.** Before the start the three ports must be free (else "port … is in use"); then ready when `GET /rtc/validate?access_token=…` with a token signed by *this* start's keys answers 200 – so another LiveKit on the same port is never taken for ours. At most 10 s (`READY_TIMEOUT`); an exit or a timeout stops the child and the session runs without voice: the log says `voice chat off: …` with the reason and the last lines of the voice server's log (the HUD's reason comes with V3: clients see "no voice on this server").
- **Lifecycle.** Stopped with the game server (`Drop`: kill and wait; Ctrl-C, `--seconds`). A child that ends by itself is restarted with the same keys and ports after 2, 4 … 60 s (`VoiceServer::poll`, once a second from the game loop, without blocking it); a child that ran 60 s starts the back-off again. **No orphan:** Linux starts it through util-linux's `setpriv --pdeathsig KILL` (`PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` without unsafe code, which the workspace forbids; `setpriv` execs, so the pid is LiveKit's; without `setpriv` a warning); Windows assigns it to a job object with *kill on job close* (`win32job`); every Unix writes `livekit-PORT.pid` and the next start ends a leftover process that is still a `livekit-server` (ps name check; the macOS mechanism). The parent-death signal follows the *thread* that started the child: the binary starts it from its main thread.
- **Overrides.** `--livekit-url` / `OCW_LIVEKIT_URL` (with key and secret) win: no own voice server. `--voice off`: no voice at all. Without `--listen` none is started (nobody to talk to).
- **The URL in the grant (Q5).** The bundled config carries `VoiceConfig.reach` (port, public host). The QUIC / WebTransport transport tells the game server each connection's addresses (`GameServer::set_connection_addresses`: the local address the client's packets arrived at, quinn's `local_ip`, and the client's); `voice::reach_url` puts `ws://ADDRESS:7880` into the grant – the reached address for riders on this machine or the LAN (loopback, private, link-local, ULA, CGNAT), the public host for riders from the internet, else the reached address; unknown → `ws://FALLBACK:7880` (public host, else the listen address, else the first LAN address). An external LiveKit keeps its fixed URL.
- **Ready for per-rider grants (V3 / V4).** Token grants go through `voice::TokenGrants` (`access_token_with`); `VoiceServer::api_url` and `keys` give the LiveKit server API (room service) the server-side "who hears whom" of Q6 / Q8 / Q10 will use.
- **Fetching the binary.** `scripts/fetch-livekit-server.sh [PLATFORM] [OUT]`: LiveKit 1.13.10 for linux-amd64, linux-arm64, windows-amd64 from the GitHub release, checked against pinned SHA-256s (they match the digests GitHub lists for the assets), cached in `target/voice-vendor/`, with its licence; darwin-arm64 is built from the tag's source with Go (`CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags "-s -w" ./cmd/server`, the tag checked against its commit; Q2) – not yet run on the Mac.
- **Tests.** Unit (`launcher.rs`, `voice.rs`, `lib.rs`): ports parsing, config per media-address mode (no keys in it), key generation (fresh, never in `Debug`), binary lookup order, back-off, the built command (secret and config only in the environment, never in argv – with and without `setpriv`), the removed inherited variables, busy ports; against a fake `livekit-server` (a shell script recording its argv, `/proc` command line and environment): start with the keys in the environment and nothing on the command line, pid file, stop leaves no process, a new start gets new keys; the readiness timeout (no process left); an exit at start says why (log tail); a crash restarted with the same keys; a leftover from a crashed run ended at the next start (and an unrelated process under the pid left alone); **no orphan** – the test binary runs itself as the host, is killed with SIGKILL, and the fake voice server must be gone (Linux); `reach_url` (LAN, IPv6, IPv4-mapped, public host, unknown) and the per-connection grant URL in the game server. Integration on marge, `make test-voice-bundled` (`scripts/test-voice-bundled.sh`, real `livekit-server` 1.13.10): `ocw-server --listen` without any `OCW_LIVEKIT_*` variable starts it as its child; the secret is in its environment and not on its command line or in any log; two headless riders (`crates/ocw-voice/tests/bundled_voice_server.rs`, the LiveKit Rust backend) get grants from the game server naming the voice URL and connect to the room, and LiveKit's server API (`RoomService/ListParticipants`, asked with this start's keys) lists both in the session room; then both riders must see each other and hear the other's tone; `kill -9` of `ocw-server` ends `livekit-server`; `--voice off` and `--livekit-url` start none. Result on marge (2026-11-16): all checks pass; the hearing step was skipped as KNOWN until v4.26 (see *Fixed*).
