### 11.4 Testing Strategy

**Rule: no step is done without tests.** Every development step in 14, every feature and every pipeline step comes with unit tests that are merged together with the code. CI runs them on every change; a failing test blocks the merge.

| Level | What | Where | When |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Unit tests** | Functions and modules in isolation: physics, route sampling, protocol encoding, session logic, parsers, pipeline steps | `#[cfg(test)]` modules next to the code in every crate | Every commit, all platforms in CI |
| **Integration tests** | Several crates together: client ↔ local server over the protocol, world-builder on a small OSM extract, device backend ↔ app channel | `tests/` directory of the crate | Every commit (Linux); per platform once ported |
| **End-to-end smoke test** | The real desktop app under Xvfb with software rendering (Mesa lavapipe): launch, ride on the virtual trainer, run console commands, take a screenshot, exit | `tools/` / run skill driver | Every commit on Linux |
| **Scene renders** | Reproducible scenes of the real desktop app (`scripts/scenes.toml`: arguments, timed console commands, screenshot / short video; a scene names the world package it needs, `world = true` for Liechtenstein, `world = "blackforest"` for the Black Forest) rendered headlessly on Wayland on a Linux build machine (`scripts/render-scenes.sh`, `make test-scenes`); reviewed by eye, the good ones kept in the build history | `scripts/` + run skill driver | After user-visible changes, before releases |
| **Multiplayer over the network** | Server + kiosk client on one build machine, headless `ocw-bot` riders on the others (Linux, macOS, Windows); joins, snapshots, visibility, prediction, tick timing; kiosk screenshots and video | `scripts/test-multiplayer.sh` (`make test-multiplayer`, 11.4.1) | On demand, before Phase 5 milestones |
| **Browser tests** | The browser app in headless Chromium driven over the DevTools protocol (no Python packages): load, ride, menus, worlds, multiplayer, devices, audio; the README's walkthrough (`make test-web-readme`) | `scripts/test-web*.py`, the pinned browser of `scripts/web_browser.py` | Phase 10 changes, on marge |
| **Hardware-in-the-loop** | Real trainers and sensors (FTMS, power meter, heart rate) | Manual test protocol, later a test bench | Before each release |
| **Performance tests** | Frame time, streaming hitches, memory (15) | `tools/performance-test` (console `exec` scripts, 2.9) | Nightly / before releases |

**Principles:**

- **Tests run without hardware, network or GPU.** Devices are replaced by the virtual trainer or mock backends (`DeviceBackend`, 3.4); network transports by in-process channels; rendering-free logic lives outside Bevy (10) and is tested headless.
- **Core crates are tested for wasm too:** `ocw-core`, `ocw-sim`, `ocw-protocol` and `ocw-world` must build for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` (3.5).
- **Physics tests check physical plausibility**, not only code paths: steady-state speed for given power and gradient, energy balance, no rolling backwards, stability at the 50 Hz tick.
- **Protocol compatibility tests:** encoded messages of earlier protocol versions are kept as fixtures and must still decode (6.2).
- **World-builder tests** use small, checked-in OSM / DEM fixtures with known expected results (golden files), e.g. a junction, a bridge, a dead end.
- **Test media carry their time (decided 2026-11-12, v2.30):** every picture and video the app writes has the ISO 8601 timestamp in the image (HUD, 3.2) and in the file: screenshots (console `screenshot`, `--screenshot`, `--at "T=screenshot …"`) are **JPEG, quality 90** by default with EXIF `DateTime`, `DateTimeOriginal`, `DateTimeDigitized` (`CreateDate`) in local time, `OffsetTime` / `OffsetTimeOriginal` / `OffsetTimeDigitized` (`+01:00`) and `Software` = `Open Cycling World <build id>` (`ocw-render::media`, own TIFF writer, the image crate's JPEG encoder); a path ending in `.png` gives a lossless PNG with `tEXt` chunks `Creation Time` (the registered keyword, ISO 8601 with offset) and `Software`. PNG stays where the picture is the input of another step: the `--capture` frames (lossless input of the H.264 encode, each stamped with its stepped time); `--capture` also writes `still.jpg` (last frame) and `metadata.txt` (ffmpeg metadata: `creation_time` of the first frame in UTC with `Z`, `comment` = software), which `drive.sh` maps into the MP4. MP4s the app encodes itself (V) get `creation_time` (start of the recording, UTC) and `comment`. The scripts that re-encode media keep it (`render-scenes.sh --pick` copies the EXIF / text chunks into a shrunk image and the metadata and sound into a re-encoded video). Test pictures and videos are **2560×1440** (`drive.sh` `OCW_SIZE`, default of the scene harness, the multiplayer camera client; the kiosk keeps its screen), videos H.264 CRF 18 with `-preset slow` (`OCW_X264_PRESET`), yuv420p, `+faststart`, 25 fps, AAC sound.
- **Build history:** the harness keeps every scene reproducible (fresh config and data folders, virtual trainer, fixed start, world package from `--world` / `$OCW_WORLD` / `data/pilot/` / the kiosk install); `render-scenes.sh --pick` copies the reviewed renders, kept small (images above 600 KB: PNG palette or JPEG quality ~80, metadata kept; videos ≤ 3 MB, sound and metadata kept), into `test-output/build-history/` with an index, for the zip on the GitHub release `build-history` (media are not committed to git).
- **Test pictures stand alone (decided by the user 2026-11-14, v3.25):** screenshots and frames are sent to the user and archived for the art project **one by one**, each as its own file (the original render with its timestamp, 3.2) – never joined into a grid or contact sheet. A joined image is made **only to show a comparison** (before / after, two settings, two dates or places side by side), and then in addition to the single pictures, which are sent and archived as well. See OCW-ART's `ART-PROJECT.md` 2.
- **Browser tests' browser (decided 2026-11-14, v3.40):** the browser tests run a **pinned Chromium build**, not whatever the machine has installed: `scripts/browsers.json` names open-source Chromium (BSD-3-Clause, third-party licences in about:credits) from Chromium's own snapshot builds (`chromium-browser-snapshots`, a main-branch revision just before a stable branch point: 157.0.8103.0, r1717344 for Linux x64 and macOS arm64, r1717343 for Windows x64) with the SHA-256 of each zip (computed on download; the bucket publishes only MD5). `make deps-browser` (`scripts/web_browser.py fetch`) downloads, checks and unpacks it into `~/.cache/ocw/browsers/<name>-<version>/` with the Unix modes and symlinks of the zip (members leaving the directory are refused). Every browser test takes `--chromium`, else `OCW_BROWSER`, else the pinned build, else the system's chromium with a warning, and writes the browser's path and `--version` into its JSON summary. Chrome for Testing was the alternative (proper version numbers, but Chrome's terms); a new pin is a new revision with its checksums. The flags are the tests' own (WebGPU: Dawn on Vulkan; WebGL 2: ANGLE on Vulkan; SwiftShader with `--software`).
- **The README walkthrough (v3.40):** `make test-web-readme` (`scripts/test-web-readme.py`) checks the README's "Browser app" section as a new user follows it: a fresh copy of the current commit (`git archive HEAD`, or the files git would not ignore in a `remote.sh` copy) in `target/readme-walkthrough/`; `make web-serve` there before any build must fail with the message; then the `make` lines of the section's bash blocks in their order (`deps-web`, `web`, `web-worlds`, `web-serve`) and every URL of the section (the placeholder and the example key replaced by the real key, the one-liner's output, the links `make web-serve` prints; multiplayer is left to `make test-web-multiplayer`) in the pinned browser: HTTP 200 for the page, the app ticks and the rider moves, the expected GPU build, no HTTP error in the browser's network log or the server's log; and `WEB_BIND=0.0.0.0`: the warning, the LAN URLs, the WebGL 2 build by LAN address. One screenshot per URL and a `verdict.json` in `test-output/web/readme-<time>/`. The world package is linked from the build machine's `data/pilot/` (a new user builds it with `scripts/fetch-pilot.sh` and `scripts/build-liechtenstein.sh`). The parsers are unit-tested (`scripts/test_web_scripts.py`, run by `make test-remote`).
- **Regression rule:** every fixed bug gets a test that failed before the fix.
- Commands: `cargo test --workspace` runs all unit and integration tests; `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` must pass.
- **Make targets (decided 2026-11-12):** every test is a `test-*` target: `test-unit` (`cargo test --workspace`; `make test` runs the same), `test-wasm` (the 3.5 build check), `test-kiosk` (`scripts/test-kiosk.sh` with a fake app), `test-screenshot` / `test-screenshot-wayland` / `test-smoke` (both) and `test-video` / `test-video-wayland` (headless desktop runs, run-ocw skill), `test-multiplayer` (11.4.1) and `test-multiplayer-local` (the same pieces on one machine over loopback: `ocw-server` with a bot, three `ocw-bot` riders, the verdict; in CI). `check` (= `lint test-unit test-wasm`), `lint`, `fmt`, `clippy` keep their names – they are checks, not tests – and so does `deploy-test` (a deployment). Options for the old names (`smoke`, `screenshot`, `screenshot-wayland`, `video`, `video-wayland`, `wasm`): remove them at once (clean, but breaks habits and notes), keep silent aliases forever (no reason to move), or **deprecated aliases** that print "use make test-…" and run the new target (chosen); they are left out of `make help` and can go once nobody uses them.

#### 11.4.1 Multiplayer Test over the Network (decided 2026-11-12)

**Purpose.** The loopback tests (`services/server/tests/quic_loopback.rs`) prove the QUIC transport on one host. `make test-multiplayer` (`scripts/test-multiplayer.sh`) checks the whole Phase 5 path (6.2, 14) on real machines and a real network: several operating systems as clients at once, one remote server, the GUI client among them, and a picture of the result on a screen. It is an on-demand test (it needs the build machines of `config/machines.toml`, a few minutes and the kiosk screen), not part of CI; CI runs `make test-multiplayer-local`, the server, three bot riders and the verdict on one machine over loopback.

**Topology and roles.**

| Machine (`config/machines.toml`) | Role |
|---|---|
| `marge` (Linux, the kiosk screen; `OCW_MP_SERVER`) | `ocw-server --listen 0.0.0.0:47800 --bots 0 --seconds S --stats-file …`; the kiosk's `ocw-desktop`, which joins it over `127.0.0.1` as rider "Kiosk"; if needed a headless `ocw-desktop` "Camera" (below); one bot process; the verdict |
| `macos`, `Win11Builder`, `leela` (`OCW_MP_BOTS`) | one `ocw-bot` process each with `OCW_MP_RIDERS` (default 2) riders, joining the server over the LAN |

Machines that do not answer ssh within the connect timeout are skipped and listed as such; the server machine must be reachable. Riders are named by OS (`lin-1`, `mac-2`, `win-1`), never by host name. The script first builds the release binaries on all machines in parallel (`ocw-server` + `ocw-bot` on the server machine, `ocw-bot` elsewhere; `remote.sh` queues for build slots).

**Bot client (`apps/bot`, binary `ocw-bot`).** Options considered: a headless mode of `ocw-desktop` (reuses `ClientCore` exactly, but `ClientCore` uses the renderer's view types, so every bot machine would build Bevy – about an hour on the 8 GB Windows machine – for a client that never draws); moving `ClientCore` out of the desktop crate (right eventually; a larger refactor of the view types); **a small Bevy-free crate (chosen)** that builds in minutes everywhere and reuses the pieces `ClientCore` is made of: `NetClient` (6.2), `Predictor` and the drafting rule (`ocw-sim`), the protocol helpers, the server's `physics_profile` (the prediction uses exactly the profile the server derives from the bot's Hello) and the `bot_bike` looks. Uncertainty: the bot and `ClientCore` can drift apart; the kiosk's real client in the same session covers the desktop path. A process runs `--riders N` riders, one QUIC connection each, in one 50 Hz loop: samples at 4 Hz like a trainer (power, a plausible cadence, brake), prediction every tick, reconciliation on every own snapshot with half the round trip as the snapshot's age. Pacing: its own power (`--power`, a few per cent apart per rider, ±10 % slow variation), or `--follow NAME`: keep 6, 10, 14 … m ahead of that rider (wanted speed from the gap error; the leader's power plus a speed correction; brake when much too fast), so the remote riders gather in front of the kiosk's camera; without that rider in the session a bot rides its own power. `ocw-bot verdict` evaluates a run (below). All logic is in the library and unit-tested against an in-memory `GameServer`; the binary only adds the network loop.

**Configuration and address discovery.** The server address is the server machine's `host` from `config/machines.toml`, read by the script with `scripts/remote.sh MACHINE field host` and passed only on the bots' command lines (`OCW_MP_HOST` overrides it, e.g. for another interface). It is never shown: everything the script prints or keeps goes through a filter that replaces the `host` of every machine involved, the peer addresses in the server's connection log (IPv4 or IPv6) and every other IPv4 address except loopback (ssh errors and the server's log contain them). Options considered: mDNS / broadcast discovery (no configuration, but multicast through every firewall and a new dependency, while the address is configured anyway); a rendezvous service (comes with the backend, 9). Further settings: `OCW_MP_SECONDS` (server run time, default 180 s), `OCW_MP_PORT` (47800), `OCW_MP_RIDERS`, `OCW_MP_KIOSK=0` (bots only), `OCW_MP_CAMERA=auto|1|0` (the camera client), `OCW_MP_BUILD=0` (skip the builds), `OCW_MP_T1` (app time of the kiosk's first screenshot).

**Network, port and TLS.** One UDP port (47800, 6.2), no TCP. TLS as in 6.2's development mode: the server keeps its certificate in the checkout's `target/mp/tls` (`--tls-dir`); the script reads the SHA-256 fingerprint from the server's output and passes it as `--server-cert` to every bot and to the kiosk (pinning; `--insecure-dev` is only valid for loopback and not used). **Firewalls are never changed** by the test. A blocked port shows as bots without an answer: the QUIC handshake times out ("no answer from the server" after the 15 s idle timeout; a bot gives up on a rider without a Welcome after 25 s), the bot prints a hint (is the server running, does a firewall let UDP 47800 through?), and the script reports per machine that UDP 47800 on the server machine seems blocked from there and what to open. The bot on the server machine itself separates "server down" from "port blocked from outside". A port already in use (another server) fails at the start with a message.

**World data and course.** Both sides must ride the same course (6.2 course check, 6.5). The kiosk normally rides a route file (`--route-file …/vaduz-malbun.route`, with the world package for the terrain, 4.7), i.e. a 1D `Route`. The script reads the kiosk's effective arguments on the server machine (its command line and `ocw-desktop.args`) and makes the server ride exactly that: `ocw-server --route-file` (new) with the kiosk's file, which the script copies to every bot machine (`scripts/remote.sh … put` into the checkout's git-ignored `target/mp/`); the bots load it with `ocw-bot --route-file`. Every side builds the route with the same `RouteFile::to_route`; the server records the file's SHA-256 in its statistics, every bot reports the SHA-256 it loaded, and the verdict compares them and the route ids (a bot also refuses a Welcome for another route, like the desktop). Without a route file the kiosk's test route is used (`--test-route` / `--route`); without a kiosk the test loop. Options considered: every bot machine fetching the pilot data and building the world package (slow and large, and the bots need no terrain); sending the route in the Welcome (a protocol change for a test); thin bots that send no world and do not predict (no desync check). Limitation: the bot rides no road graph (free ride and package routes need the package's graph and the path messages of 6.5); with a kiosk in free ride the run is "bots only".

**Duration and timeline.** The server runs `OCW_MP_SECONDS` (180 s) and then shuts down, which ends every client normally ("server shutting down"); the bots' own limit is 60 s longer, as a safety net. The kiosk's app rides at 200 W from its start (virtual trainer); the bots, joining a few seconds later behind it, catch up (at most 4 m/s faster) and stay 6–14 m ahead of it. A first idea – the kiosk waits at 0 W and `--at "T=sim.power 200"` starts it once the bots are there – does not work: `sim.power` is a dev command, refused on a remote server (2.9).

**Kiosk handling.** The kiosk (`ocw-kiosk.sh`, in the desktop user's session) cannot be restarted with other arguments over ssh, but it restarts the app whenever the binary changes, and the app reads `ocw-desktop.args` beside the binary first (the kiosk's own command line wins). So the script saves `ocw-desktop.args`, writes it with the saved content plus `--server 127.0.0.1:47800 --server-cert FP --name Kiosk --virtual --power 200 --record false` and `--cmd "fps on"` (the FPS counter in every picture), `--video-dir` and timed console commands (`--at`: three screenshots from app time T1 and a real-time video of `OCW_MP_VIDEO_S` (15) s from the app's own recorder, `video start` / `video stop`; a kiosk build without `--video-dir` gets the screenshots only), and replaces the binary by a copy of itself (a new inode: the kiosk restarts the app). Afterwards – also after a failure or Ctrl+C (exit trap) – it puts the saved file back and restarts the app the same way, but only if the file is still the one it wrote (a deployment in between wins). The kiosk is never left in multiplayer mode, and no FIT file is recorded for the test ride. The app (desktop user) writes its screenshots into a fresh `/var/tmp/ocw-mp/<run>/` (mode 0777) that the script owns and deletes afterwards.

**Locked kiosk screen and the camera client.** *Update 2026-11-12:* the cause is the present mode: the kiosk session is X11, and while the session is locked the screen is off; a window that waits for the display's refresh (vsync, the app's default) is then paced by the X server at one frame a second (measured: the FPS counter shows `1 fps  max 1000 ms`). With `--no-vsync` the same locked kiosk drew 312 fps at 2560×1600 on marge's GPU. So the script now gives a kiosk build that has them `--no-vsync --max-fps 60` for the test (60 fps at most, restored afterwards with the other arguments), and the kiosk takes its stills and video while locked too; the camera client starts automatically only without a kiosk or with an older kiosk build (`OCW_MP_CAMERA=1` still forces it). The rest of this paragraph describes the first runs. Found in the first runs: when the desktop session on the kiosk machine is locked (`loginctl … LockedHint=yes`), the compositor hides the app's window and lets it draw only about once a second. The app keeps riding (device samples still reach the server), but its game time – which `--at` uses and which advances at most 0.25 s per frame – crawls, so no screenshot is ever taken. The test cannot unlock the screen (it changes no system state), so it detects the lock, says so, and – with `OCW_MP_CAMERA=auto` (default: when the screen is locked or there is no kiosk), or always with `1` – starts a **camera client**: the desktop app (release build, `OCW_PROFILE=release`) under a headless weston on the server machine (`drive.sh shot-wayland`; weston's GL renderer, so the app draws on marge's GPU), joining as rider "Camera" with the same course and world package, at 200 W, taking three stills and a real-time 25 fps video of `OCW_MP_VIDEO_S` s with the app's own recorder (`video start` / `video stop`, `--video-dir`), with the FPS counter on and `--log-fps 5`. The bots then follow "Camera", so the pictures show the remote riders around it. Options considered: only reporting the missing pictures (no picture at all while the screen is locked); recording the screen of the other user's session (not possible over ssh without its credentials); `--at` on wall-clock time (changes the meaning of `--at` for scripted and captured rides). The camera client is a second real `ClientCore` in the session, so the desktop path is covered even when the kiosk cannot be watched.

**Render rate and videos (2026-11-12).** The first multiplayer videos looked choppy: 5 frames per second. Measured with the wall-clock render rate (`--log-fps 5`, FPS counter) on marge, release build, headless weston on the GPU, Vaduz–Malbun with the world package, 9 riders: single player (in-process server, 8 bots) and multiplayer (`ocw-server --listen` + 8 `ocw-bot` riders over QUIC, following the client) both draw 37–40 fps with vsync (the headless weston paces there; even a 320×180 window without riders reaches only 39.7 fps) and the debug build the same (39.5); without vsync both reach about 80–200 fps (varies with the view and with the other load on the machine – builds, the kiosk sharing the GPU – more than between the modes; no difference above that noise); the locked kiosk drew 1 fps (above). So the client has no multiplayer-specific bottleneck: snapshot handling is non-blocking (`NetClient::receive` drains a channel), the interpolation works on 9 riders at 10 Hz, avatars are moved, never respawned, and no mesh or material is added per snapshot (regression test `riders::moving_riders_keep_their_avatars_and_assets`); a rider's looks are stable per snapshot, so `sync_riders` does not rebuild them. The 5 fps came from the recording: the camera client took one screenshot per 1/5 s of game time and the script encoded them at 5 fps (the kiosk: 3 per second). Now both record with the app's own real-time recorder (console `video`, 25 fps, every tick a new image as long as the app draws ≥ 25 fps; the recorder's log line counts unique, repeated and dropped frames), the camera runs the release build, and the FPS counter is in every picture. Frame capture with a fixed game-time step per frame (`--capture`, what `make test-video` uses) cannot record a networked client: its game time must run in real time with the server's (`--server` conflicts with `--capture`).

**Checks and pass criteria** (`ocw-bot verdict`; every check is printed as PASS / FAIL with its numbers):

| Check | Passes when |
|---|---|
| Bot processes reported | every started process printed its `OCW-BOT-REPORT` line, with all its riders |
| All clients joined | every bot rider and the kiosk are in the server's `joined` list |
| No client left early | nobody disconnected before the server's end (it writes its statistics before closing the connections) |
| All riders at once | the server's peak rider count ≥ bot riders + kiosk |
| Real time, tick timing | a real-time run; mean tick work ≤ 25 % of the 20 ms budget, ≤ 0.1 % of the ticks over budget, ≤ 1 % of the ticks started a whole tick late |
| Same course | every bot's route id (and route-file SHA-256) equals the server's |
| Per rider | joined (no Reject, no course mismatch); ended normally (server shutdown or its own end; a reset or timeout counts as normal only if its last snapshot came within 5 s of the server's end – the server's closing message was lost – not earlier); ≥ 90 % of the 10 Hz snapshots over its connected time and no gap > 1 s; saw every other client by name and each of them moving (≥ 5 m); one snapshot with all riders; rode ≥ 20 m; the server applied its samples (`last_input_seq`); prediction error at reconciliation after a 3 s warm-up: mean ≤ 0.5 m, max ≤ 5 m (the snap threshold, 5.2) |

The thresholds are first guesses for a LAN (uncertain; adjust after more runs). **Suspended machines:** a bot compares the wall clock with the monotonic clock (which stops while a machine sleeps, on macOS) and reports the difference; the verdict notes it next to the rider's numbers. Found in the first runs: the Mac (on Wi-Fi) suspended for about 2 s twice a run, which showed as 2.6 s snapshot gaps, prediction errors just over 5 m and a broken link at the end; `pmset -g log` showed why: the Mac (system sleep after 1 min idle) was in dark wakes, entering "Maintenance Sleep" for 5–6 s every minute even while the bot ran. The script therefore runs the bot there under `caffeinate -i -s` (an assertion that prevents idle and system sleep while the process runs, on AC power; no setting is changed). The server's numbers come from `ocw-server --stats-file` (`ocw_server::stats`: ticks, mean / max tick work, ticks over budget, late ticks, peak riders, who joined and left, route id and SHA-256).

**Outputs.** On the terminal: machines used and skipped, the course, a note if the kiosk's screen is locked, the verdict's lines and `RESULT: PASS` / `RESULT: FAIL` (exit code 0 / 1). Kept in `test-output/multiplayer/<run>/` (git-ignored): `summary.txt`, the build, server and bot logs, `stats.json`, `verdict.txt`, the kiosk's arguments and `kiosk/` with the stills and `kiosk.mp4` (the app's recorder: 25 fps, at most 1920 px wide), and `camera/` with the camera client's stills, last screenshot, `camera.mp4` (25 fps, 1280×720) and its log `app.log`; the summary gives each video's size, frame rate and length, the camera's measured render rate (mean and lowest of the 5 s log lines) and its recorder's unique / repeated / dropped frames. Stills, video, verdict and summary are also archived like the run-ocw skill's runs (`test-output/YYYY-MM-DD/HHMMSS-<commit>-multiplayer-*` with a row in `test-output/index.md`, mode `multiplayer`).

**Limitations.** Route rides only (no road graph, see above); one server machine; no packet loss or latency injection (later: `tc netem` needs root, a userspace UDP relay would not); the videos are the app's own real-time recordings (another user's desktop session cannot be recorded over ssh): a tick the app did not draw repeats the previous frame, so they are only as smooth as the app's render rate (the FPS counter in the picture shows it); frame capture with a fixed game-time step (`--capture`) cannot be used, because a networked client's game time must run in real time with the server's; the kiosk takes pictures only while its screen is unlocked; the kiosk's trainer is the virtual one during the test; the thresholds are uncertain; the test uses the kiosk build that is deployed – if its protocol version differs from the server's, it is rejected and "all clients joined" fails (deploy first: `make deploy-test`).

### 11.5 Hosting the server on Fly.io (v6.19; deployed v6.53; status page v6.65; rider names v6.73; the default server v6.81)

The user asked for the game server and its voice server to run on Fly.io (2026-11-26). Vercel was ruled out: it runs no long-lived processes and no UDP. Files: `deploy/fly/ocw-server/` (`Dockerfile`, `Dockerfile.dockerignore`, `fly.toml`, `start.sh`). The README section *Hosting the server on Fly.io* has the commands.

- **One machine, app `ocw-server`, region `fra`** (Frankfurt, near the riders in Central Europe), size `shared-cpu-1x` with 1 GB, always on. Fly's proxy wakes a stopped machine only for TCP and HTTP, never for UDP, so auto-stop would break joining. Measured with Liechtenstein, 3 bots and the Echo rider: `ocw-server` holds 490 MB and `livekit-server` 80 MB, and the 50 Hz tick takes 0.05 – 0.06 ms of its 20 ms (one shared CPU is plenty). 512 MB would not fit.
- **The image:** two build stages, pinned `rust:1.99.1-slim-trixie` (the version of `rust-toolchain.toml`) and `debian:trixie-20261104-slim`. It builds only `ocw-server` (release, default features), on Fly's remote builder (`fly deploy --remote-only`), never on the coordinator. `livekit-server` 1.13.10 is checked against its release checksum and placed next to the binary. The server runs as the user `ocw`: `start.sh` prepares the volume as root, then drops to it with `setpriv`. The build context is an allow-list: the workspace crates, `proto`, `assets`, the logos, and the LFS models (the server's collision shapes come from `ocw-assets`; the build stops on LFS pointer files).
- **UDP on Fly:** UDP needs the app's **dedicated IPv4**, and a machine receives it only on the address `fly-global-services`, from which the replies must leave too. `start.sh` binds QUIC (UDP 47800) and WebTransport (UDP 47801) to that address. LiveKit's UDP mux binds each interface address on its own, `fly-global-services` among them (checked on the smoke machine), so its media port 7882 works without a change to the launcher. The public address (`--voice-public-host`, LiveKit's `node_ip`, the join link) is the IPv4 of `ocw-server.fly.dev`, which is the dedicated IPv4 once it is allocated (or `OCW_PUBLIC_HOST`). UDP works only over IPv4, so riders use the address for the game, not the name. **No UDP segmentation offload (v6.53):** Fly's UDP path drops the batched packets QUIC sends with GSO, so most handshakes got no answer (the server saw the clients' Initial packets and logged `WebTransport handshake failed … timed out`; HTTP/3 handshakes to 47801 were answered 0 – 50 % of the time, full QUIC handshakes to 47800 2 of 15, Chromium failed with `QUIC_NETWORK_IDLE_TIMEOUT`), and replies on the reliable stream, such as voice grants, were lost the same way ("no answer from the game server"). `ocw-server --no-gso` (quinn's `enable_segmentation_offload(false)`) sends every packet on its own. **No path MTU discovery (v6.53):** with discovery the server raised its packet size, and larger packets to the riders were lost on Fly's path. The datagrams (snapshots, smaller) kept arriving, but the reliable stream stalled after its first frames: the server logged "voice token issued" for both riders, yet neither client got a grant (the browser's `frames_in` stayed at 7). The same outside test against `ocw-server` on marge got its grants. `ocw-server --no-mtu-discovery` (quinn's `mtu_discovery_config(None)`) keeps every packet at QUIC's 1200 bytes. `start.sh` passes both options; other hosts keep the defaults.
- **Ports:** UDP 47800 (game, QUIC), UDP 47801 (game, WebTransport), TCP 7880 (LiveKit signalling, through Fly's proxy as plain TCP, with a TCP health check), TCP 443 (TLS ended by Fly's proxy, to the join endpoint on 8080 since v6.56: `https://ocw-server.fly.dev/join.json`, and the same signalling passed on: `wss://ocw-server.fly.dev`), TCP 7881 (ICE over TCP), UDP 7882 (voice media).
- **Voice stays in the same machine (decided here):** `ocw-server --listen` starts the bundled LiveKit with fresh keys, as on every host (7.1.1, 7.1.8). It has one UDP port for all riders, the TCP fallback, and the dedicated IPv4 as its node IP. Why not a second Fly app for LiveKit: it would need a second dedicated IPv4 ($2 a month more), its keys as Fly secrets (today they are new at every start and live only in the process environment), a second deploy, and its own code path apart from home hosting and *Host a ride*. Voice is still separate from the game connection (spec 7): its own process and ports. TURN stays off: ICE over TCP 7881 covers networks without UDP. A TURN/TLS server on 443 would need a certificate for a name of our own.
- **The volume `ocw_data` (1 GB, `/data`):** `worlds/` holds the packages with their manifests and routes, which are uploaded from marge's live packages (the J9 build of 2026-11-25), comparing their SHA-256 on both sides. The session rides `OCW_WORLD` (Liechtenstein); the other packages next to it can be switched to. `tls/` holds the server's own identity, the QUIC certificate (its fingerprint stays across restarts and deploys) and the WebTransport certificate (13 days, renewed by the server). `home/` is the server user's data dir (the voice server's logs), and `web-info.json` the browser page options. The packages are unsigned dev builds: loading by path accepts them (4.7). No Fly secrets are needed; nothing secret is in the repository or the image.
- **Options:** `OCW_SERVER_ARGS` in `fly.toml` (default `--bots 0 --echo-bot`: no server bots, the Echo rider for the voice echo test).
- **Costs** (Fly's prices of November 2026, Frankfurt): machine about $7.73, dedicated IPv4 $2, volume $0.15, traffic $0.02/GB. About $10 a month. **Budget (decided by the user, 2026-11-26; raised the same day): at most $16 a month for Fly.io.** About $10 is for this game server ($9.88 fixed plus traffic). About $4 is for Managed Postgres (Developer) and $0 – 2 for the accounts service with auto-stop; both come later in a step of their own and are not created yet. Nothing beyond that is created without a new decision: no second game machine or IPv4, no larger size, no extra volume.
- **Voice from pages served over `https://` (v6.53):** such pages (the GitHub Pages preview) may not open `ws://IPV4:7880` (mixed content). Fly's proxy ends TLS on 443 for `ocw-server.fly.dev` with Fly's shared `*.fly.dev` certificate (Let's Encrypt; no certificate of our own is issued for it, so it costs nothing and needs no renewal on our side) and forwards the WebSocket (`handlers = ["tls", "http"]`) to LiveKit on 7880. `ocw-server --voice-public-url wss://NAME` names that URL in the grants of riders from the internet (riders on the machine's own network keep `ws://ADDRESS:PORT`); `start.sh` sets `wss://$FLY_APP_NAME.fly.dev` (`OCW_VOICE_PUBLIC_URL=""` turns it off). The desktop app takes `wss://` too (LiveKit's Rust SDK with webpki roots). The browser's game connection stays WebTransport to `https://IPV4:47801` with the certificate hash: `web-info.json` now has `public_url` / `public_query` with the public host (`--voice-public-host`), next to the internal `url` / `query`.
- **Status (v6.53): deployed.** App `ocw-server` (personal organisation), one machine in `fra` (`shared-cpu-1x`, 1 GB, always on), the volume `ocw_data` (1 GB), the dedicated IPv4 213.188.222.85, release v4 (image `nogso-mtu`). Endpoints: `ocw://213.188.222.85?cert=0ae1fb51…&world=liechtenstein@10` (QUIC, UDP 47800; the fingerprint stays on the volume), WebTransport `https://213.188.222.85:47801` (cert-hash in `web-info.json`'s `public_query`; the certificate is renewed every 11 days), voice `wss://ocw-server.fly.dev` (TLS on 443) and `ws://213.188.222.85:7880`, media UDP 7882 / TCP 7881. The world is Liechtenstein, the J9 build of marge's live data: package `e5b3f612…fbf8`, manifest `3a6954c1…`, route `vaduz-malbun.route` `44dc3dcb…`, the same SHA-256 on marge and on the volume. **Outside tests from marge** (`scripts/test-remote-server.sh`, keyless: the clients ask the game server for their voice grants as riders do; the server's LiveKit keys are not read): the desktop app (voice build, Xvfb) joined over QUIC, rode 90 s and connected to the voice room over `wss://`; a browser rider on a page served over `https://` joined over WebTransport, got a `wss://` grant, connected to the room with the real livekit-client and saw the desktop rider there. Browsers and lost UDP flows: see *Lost UDP flows* below (v6.54). Before v6.53 (v6.19) the image was built and a smoke machine ran without a volume; the dedicated IPv4 needed the card the user then added.
- **Lost UDP flows (v6.54):** now and then a browser's WebTransport handshake to Fly got no answer (`QUIC_NETWORK_IDLE_TIMEOUT` after 4 s; on v4 3 of 4 attempts in a busy test hour, 1 of 10 later). **Cause, outside our control:** Fly's UDP path (or the path to it) loses a whole new UDP flow – a capture on the machine (`tcpdump` on `eth0`, ports 47800 / 47801 / 7882) shows that not one packet of the failed connections arrives, while the same browser's next connection (a new source port) gets through and the server answers every handshake it receives at once. The suspects of v6.53 are ruled out: Chromium's post-quantum ClientHello (two Initial packets of 1250 bytes) passes on every other flow, and test datagrams of 1200, 1252, 1300 and 1380 bytes all arrive on a fresh flow, in any size; curl's 30 of 30 handshakes from deb simply met no lost flow. Many new flows in a row make it worse: of 16 test flows 3 s apart from marge, the first 9 arrived and the next 7 not at all (every size), and new flows got through again within a minute (earlier the same day after many more flows: about 8 minutes); STUN servers of other networks answered new flows from marge 25 s after the last lost one (so the home router is unlikely, though not ruled out: a test from another network would settle it). Fly documents no such limit. **Fix in our control (v6.54): the browser app opens a new connection – a new UDP flow – when a handshake gets no answer**, up to 3 more times after 0.5, 1 and 2 s (`netconn::handshake_retry_s`; a bad URL, a stream that cannot open or a connection lost after it was up are not tried again), and the link stays *connecting* meanwhile, so the Hello is sent on the connection that comes up. In the two-browser run the second browser's first two handshakes were lost (not in the capture) and the third joined. **Result:** with the retry, 12 of 12 browser joins from a page served over `https://` on marge (8 single riders a few minutes apart, and the two riders of two voice runs) joined; 2 of them needed it (one lost two flows, one one flow), so without it 10 of 12 would have joined. Before (v6.53, no retry): 1 of 4 on v4 in a busy hour; the handshakes alone today 18 of 18 from a localhost page and 9 of 10 from the public preview's origin. Measuring tool: `scripts/test-webtransport-handshake.py` (handshakes alone, `--parallel`, `--page` for another origin such as the public preview, `--net-log`). Options if it gets worse: a TCP fallback for browsers (WebSocket over Fly's TLS proxy on 443, as voice signalling already is), the desktop's QUIC on the same retry, or another provider. The public preview (`newkit.github.io/OCW/`) had `"server": ""` in its `config.json` until v6.56 (*Join info* below); handshakes made from its origin reached the server 9 of 10 times without the app's retry.
- **Join info: the public page rides together (v6.56; decided by the user, 2026-11-26: everyone on the public page can ride and talk together on this server).** A page cannot have the WebTransport certificate's hash baked in: the certificate lives 13 days, is renewed two days before its end and is new on a new volume. So the server tells pages at runtime: `ocw-server --join-http 0.0.0.0:8080` (`start.sh`) answers `GET /join.json` with `{"webtransport": "https://213.188.222.85:47801", "cert_hashes": [current, next?], "not_after_unix_s", "voice": "wss://ocw-server.fly.dev", "world": "liechtenstein", "world_version": 10, "world_sha256": "e5b3f612…", "query": "server=…&cert-hash=…", "join": "ocw://213.188.222.85?cert=…&world=liechtenstein@10"}` (`net::join_http::JoinInfo`; a test route instead of a world gives `route`; `join`, v6.69, is the desktop's QUIC join link with the fixed `--listen` fingerprint, for the kiosks, 11.2 *Kiosks joining a remote server*, present with a public host). It holds no secret – it is what a join link says – and is served with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (no credentials; the preview's origin and local test pages alike), `Cache-Control: no-store`, `Connection: close`. Every other request on the port is passed on unchanged to LiveKit's signalling port (`--join-upstream`, default `127.0.0.1:<signal port>`, `none`: 404): WebSocket upgrades as they are, plain requests with `Connection: close`, so a proxy that keeps connections open never sends a later `/join.json` to LiveKit. Fly's proxy routes TCP 443 (`handlers = ["tls", "http"]`, Fly's `*.fly.dev` certificate) to 8080 with a TCP health check; voice keeps `wss://ocw-server.fly.dev` through it, and no new IP, machine or cost is needed. The server republishes the info when the certificate is announced or renewed and when the session switches world. **Renewal with overlap:** three days before the end the server makes the next certificate and announces it (`WebCertChange::Announced`, the second hash; kept in `--tls-dir` as `web-next-cert.der` / `web-next-key.der` / `web-next-cert.validity`, so a restart keeps it); two days before the end it takes over (`Renewed`; a restart after that time takes it from the volume too). The page passes every hash (`serverCertificateHashes` takes a list), so a page that fetched the info in the announced day still connects after the switch; open sessions go on regardless, and a reload fetches the info again. **The page:** `config.json` of the preview has `"server": "https://ocw-server.fly.dev/join.json"`, `"voice": "wss://ocw-server.fly.dev"`, `"signin": ""` (`scripts/web-preview-site.py`, `PUBLIC_SERVER`; `--no-server` leaves it out); the start page's first ride, *Ride together: Liechtenstein (public server)*, is `?together=1`: index.html fetches the join info before the module starts and replaces the address with `server=`, `cert-hash=` (both hashes) and `world=` (the server's package id; the preview must ship the same package file, else the road graphs differ and the app says so), then rides as from a join link; if the server cannot be reached the page says so with *Try again* and *Rides*. The ride is only offered when the server's world is among the preview's worlds. Ride → Join in the app takes `https://` join links on the public page too now. The preview ships LiveKit's JS SDK (pinned, hash-checked) and names it in the credits; the privacy note says what riding together shares (the name and rider for everyone on the server, power and steering to the server, its log of joins with name and IP address at Fly.io, the voice only while it is on). Without sign-in every browser rider has the default look (the workshop's looks need an account) and the name of the Riders page (default *Rider*). Test: `scripts/test-remote-web.py --together --dir SITE --https` (two browsers with different names, `--hear` each other).
- **The public server as the default – for now (v6.81; the user, 2026-11-27: "insert the url of the fly.io server as default for all apps for now").** Every app that chooses a server offers this one first. **One constant:** `ocw_client::public::PUBLIC_JOIN_INFO` = `https://ocw-server.fly.dev/join.json` (and `PUBLIC_VOICE` = `wss://ocw-server.fly.dev`); what cannot use the constant (`scripts/ocw-kiosk.sh`, `scripts/ocw-kiosk.ps1`, `scripts/kiosk.env`, `apps/web/web/index.html`, `scripts/web-preview-site.py`) carries the same text, and a test fails when one differs. **"For now":** when the server moves or a public server list comes (3.2.4 Q5, Phase 5), only that constant (and its copies) changes. **The setting `net.public_server`** (desktop; `ocw.toml [settings.net]`, live): `default` (the constant), `off` (no public server: its rows and `join public` go away) or another join info URL (`https://…`; other values are refused) – changed or cleared without a rebuild. **Per app:** *Desktop* – Ride → Join's first row *Public server (ocw-server.fly.dev)*, the start choice's first row, `join public` / `--join public`: the join info is fetched in the background (10 s, at most 64 kB, untrusted: only checked values are taken – the `join` link, else the WebTransport URL with the first certificate hash), the server's world is looked for among the installed packages as the kiosk does (11.2: a package of the server's id whose SHA-256 is the server's; without a SHA-256 the id and version), and only then is the link joined (one connection, as any join – no extra UDP flows to Fly). A missing world (or another build of the same version) is said on the page before any connection; *Download the world and join* is offered when the join info names a manifest URL (`world_manifest`, which the server does not serve yet), else the page says what to install (the package from the release zips or the preview's worlds; World → Change world; `--fetch-world`). Solo rides stay local: *Ride locally* is still the start choice's default and nothing joins without the rider's choice (or `--join public`). *Browser* – index.html (and `PageConfig::join_info`) takes the constant when `config.json` names no `server` (no key, or no file); `"server": ""` still means none; `?together=1` then joins as before, and `join public` in the console starts the page again with it. *Kiosks* – `OCW_KIOSK_REMOTE` defaults to the constant's URL on Linux and Windows (since v6.69). *`ocw-bot`* – **no default**: `--server` stays required, because its riders are test riders (the multiplayer test and the scripts start their own local servers; tests must never load Fly, whose UDP path drops bursts of new flows for minutes, *Lost UDP flows*), and the public server rides a world's road graph, which bots cannot ride. *OCW Studio* – no game server. *Voice* – nothing to default: the server's grants name its voice URL (`wss://ocw-server.fly.dev`). *Tests* (no test touches the network): the setting's values, the parser, the world match, the rows with and without the setting, `join public` reaching each app's hook, the browser's fallback and query, every copy of the address. One real join from marge (the desktop on Xvfb via the new default) checks it end to end.
- **Status page (v6.65; asked by the user, 2026-11-26: "build the statistic page for the server").** `https://ocw-server.fly.dev/` was LiveKit's plain "OK"; now the join endpoint (`--join-http`, `net::join_http`) serves a small status page there. **Routing:** a `GET` or `HEAD` of `/` without an `Upgrade` header gets the page (HTML with its style and script inline, no external scripts or fonts, `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'` with only inline style and script and requests to its own origin, light and dark from the system, phone width); `GET /stats.json` the statistics (JSON, `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, `Cache-Control: no-store`, 503 before the first second); `/_ocw/` holds the page's own files (now `/_ocw/icon.svg`, the logo; a prefix LiveKit does not use). Everything else is passed on to LiveKit as before: WebSocket upgrades (to `/` too), its signalling paths `/rtc` and `/rtc/v1`, the checks `/rtc/validate` and `/rtc/v1/validate`, its API `/twirp/…`, other methods on `/`; `/join.json` answers exactly as before (tested). **The page:** what this is (Open Cycling World's public test server; a test that may restart), the button **Ride now in your browser** (`https://newkit.github.io/OCW/?together=1`, the public page's *Ride together*; a link to the start page), **Right now** with the live counts refreshed every 10 s, **The world** (region, package version, the ride: the route, or a free ride on every road), **The server** (version, uptime and start time, tick load, Frankfurt on Fly.io), **Ride with the desktop app** (the releases page, Ride → Join, the join link with the public IPv4 and the QUIC certificate's fingerprint, a *Copy* button) and a privacy note. The page is filled in by the server (the link and the world change at a world switch), the numbers come from `/stats.json` by script. **`/stats.json`** (`public_stats::StatsReport`): `version`, `now_unix_s`, `started_unix_s`, `uptime_s`, `since_unix_s` (when the totals began), `world` (`id`, `name`, `version`, `route` when one is ridden), `riders` (`humans`, `bots`, `voice`: now; since v6.73 `online`, the riders on the road by name, and `more`, see Q1 below), `today` (`date` – the UTC day –, `peak_humans`, `peak_bots`, `rides_humans`, `rides_bots`, `km_humans`, `km_bots`), `total` (the rides and km since `since_unix_s`), `tick` (`hz` 50, `budget_ms` 20, `window_s` 60, `mean_ms`, `p95_ms`, `max_ms` of the tick's work). **Counting** (`public_stats::PublicStats`, pure): every tick the game loop hands over numbers only (`GameServer::public_observation`): riders on the road and the sum of their speeds, each capped at 30 m/s so a glitch adds no distance (a rider flying the unicorn counts with speed 0), people and bots apart; km are the speeds times the tick. **Bots** are the server's own (`--bots`), the Echo rider and test clients that say so: `Hello.bot` (field 11, set by `ocw-bot`; absent: a person). A **ride** starts with a connection's first hello (a world switch, where everyone says hello again, is no new ride). **Voice** counts the riders whose status says they are in the voice room. The tick load is over the last 60 s. **Kept:** the totals and today's numbers are written every minute and at the end to `--public-stats-file` (`/data/public-stats.json` on the volume, a few hundred bytes, written as a new file and renamed), so a restart or deploy keeps them; a new volume or a lost file starts again, and the page says since when it counts. **Privacy (decided here: counts only; since v6.73 the names riders ride under too, Q1 (b)).** The server log keeps names and IP addresses (the privacy note of the public page says so), but publishing them was never decided: the page and `/stats.json` show **counts only – no rider names, no account ids, no IP addresses, no positions or roads** – and the counting never takes them (the observation holds numbers only; a test checks that the names of joined riders appear nowhere in the JSON). Tests: the router (`/` for a browser vs. a WebSocket to `/` vs. LiveKit's paths vs. `/join.json` vs. `/stats.json` vs. `/_ocw/`; over real sockets too), the escaping of the page's values, the counting (joins and leaves, peaks, km, the cap, people vs. bots, the UTC day, a restart with the kept totals, the tick window) and that the report names nobody. No new machine, IP or cost. **Deployed 2026-11-26** (Fly release v6, image `statuspage`, the same machine, rolling with health checks): `/` the page (phone, desktop, dark checked in headless Chromium), `/stats.json` answers, `/join.json` byte for byte as before, LiveKit's `/rtc/validate` still answered by LiveKit; two browsers from the live public page (`scripts/test-remote-web.py --together --url https://newkit.github.io/OCW/`) joined, connected to the voice room over `wss://ocw-server.fly.dev` and heard each other, and `/stats.json` counted them (2 riders, 2 in voice).
- **Q1 – Rider names on the status page: decided (2026-11-27, the user): (b) – "yes, show riders name"; built (v6.73).** **Built:** the game loop hands over, for each rider on the road, the name the others see on its name tag (after the name checks of 14 Phase 4, 4N: a refused name such as `<script>…` shows as the fallback `Rider NNNN`), whether it is a bot (server bots, `ocw-bot` clients, the Echo rider) or the Echo rider, and its speed (`public_stats::RiderTick`; `GameServer::public_observation`). `PublicStats` follows each ride by a key that is never published (a client's connection, so a world switch is no new ride; a server rider's id): its start and km (speeds capped as for the totals). `/stats.json` gets `riders.online` = `[{"name", "bot", "echo", "riding_s", "km"}]` – people first, then bots, each by name, at most 50 (`ONLINE_CAP`) – and `riders.more` (the rest); a rider who leaves the road leaves the list at the next second. No IP address, account, device or position is taken or published, and no name is kept in `/data/public-stats.json`. Escaping: the page adds names only as text (`textContent`), `/stats.json` sends `<`, `>` and `&` as `\u` escapes (and `nosniff`). **The page:** *On the road (N)* under *Right now* – names as chips with the ride's time and km, bots and the Echo rider tagged, "+N more" past 50, wrapping at phone width; the eight tiles fill whole rows (4 a row, 2 on phones; before: 5 + 3 on a desktop). **Privacy notes:** the page's: "The names riders ride under are shown here while they ride (bots marked), with how long and how far they have ridden this time; no IP addresses, no accounts, no positions."; the browser app's (`credits.html#privacy`, with the next preview publish): the name one rides with is shown on the status page while one rides, never the IP address or where one rides. Tests: the named list (joins and leaves, a new ride, people before bots, the cap and `more`), a hostile name (refused by the name checks; raw text in the JSON, no markup characters in the served body, the page without `innerHTML`), no address, position, account or key fields, the even grid. **Deployed 2026-11-27** (Fly release v8, image `statuspage-names`, the same machine, the default rolling strategy with its health checks, no new resources): `/` the page with the list, `/stats.json` names the riders on the road, `/join.json` byte for byte as before, LiveKit's `/rtc/validate` still answered by LiveKit, 2 of 2 checks passing; a keyless browser rider from the live public page on marge (made-up name *Fenna Freewheel*) appeared on the page and in `/stats.json` next to the Echo rider. Before: the page showed counts only (v6.65, decided there); options were (a) counts only, (b) the names of the riders online now with a line in the app's privacy note, (c) names only of riders who turn it on, (d) the names of signed-in riders only.

## 12. Security and Privacy

Particularly important for multiplayer and voice communication:

- Encrypted network connections (QUIC / TLS 1.3, HTTPS).
- Authentication (OIDC).
- Server-side authorization.
- Detection of manipulated training data (6.4).
- Protection against replay attacks (sequence numbers, server timestamps, per-session tokens).
- Rate limiting.
- Secure token management (Strava and LiveKit tokens handled only by the backend).
- Microphone permissions.
- Visible microphone activity.
- Muting.
- Privacy-friendly telemetry.
- Signed world packages and updates (4.7): Ed25519 root key kept offline, rotating signing keys with a validity period, SHA-256 of every file and tile chunk, verification on every load. Tampered or damaged packages are always refused; unsigned or untrusted ones only load from local paths with a warning (or with `--allow-unsigned`), never silently. Secret keys never enter the repository.
- **User keys** (4.7 *User keys*, v3.71): worlds shared by users are signed with their own keys and load only after the user trusted the key in the trust dialog, having compared its fingerprint with its owner over a channel they trust; the name a key gives itself is shown as unverified. The trusted keys are per user and cannot replace the built-in roots; servers trust only keys their operator configured. Throwaway test keys are made in tests and temporary directories, never committed.

**Data separation and GDPR:**

| Data | Handling |
|---|---|
| Identity | Account schema |
| Training data | Separate schema / service module |
| Voice | Only relayed, never recorded or stored |
| Telemetry | Opt-in, pseudonymized |
| User rights | Data export (FIT + JSON), account deletion including training data |
| Hosting | EU |

Personal data, voice data and training data are handled separately.

## 13. Licensing and Open-Source Strategy

| Item | Classification | Licence / Obligation |
|---|---|---|
| Source code | Own work | **Dual MIT / Apache-2.0** |
| Own 3D assets (`assets/models/`, generated) | Own work | Like the code: **MIT / Apache-2.0** (Phase 4, 2.5); each listed in `assets/models/manifest.toml` |
| Own sounds | Own work | Decided separately; suggestion **CC BY 4.0**, or proprietary if monetized. The game sounds so far are synthesised in code (`apps/desktop/src/audio/`), so they are source code (MIT / Apache-2.0) and there are no sound files to license |
| Own artwork (logo, icons, `artwork/`) | Own work | Like the code: **MIT / Apache-2.0** |
| Third-party assets | External | Tracked in each asset's manifest (`license`, `source`, `author`); the asset validator rejects assets without a licence entry |
| Tiling materials (`assets/materials.toml`, v2.46) | External, CC0 1.0 (ambientCG, Poly Haven) | Not in git: pinned by URL + SHA-256, fetched and converted by `scripts/fetch-materials.sh`, shipped beside the binary with `CREDITS.md`; credited on the credits list (console `materials`) although CC0 needs no attribution; the validator rejects share-alike, non-commercial, no-derivatives and unknown licences (Phase 8A) |
| Road graph + attributes in world packages | **Derivative Database** (ODbL) | Published under ODbL; extracted data offered for download alongside each package |
| Meshes, textures, rendered views | **Produced Work** (ODbL) | Attribution "© OpenStreetMap contributors" |
| DEM-derived terrain | Depends on source | Each source's required attribution notice (Copernicus, regional providers) |
| Weather data (spec 14 Phase 9, S7; fetched by the game server, not stored in packages) | External, open data | Shown in the weather machine and the HUD while the weather is real ("Weather: MeteoSwiss, MET Norway, CC BY 4.0"), and on the credits list: **MeteoSwiss** CC BY 4.0, "Source: MeteoSwiss"; **DWD** CC BY 4.0, "Source: Deutscher Wetterdienst"; **MET Norway** CC BY 4.0 and NLOD 2.0, "Data from MET Norway"; **Open-Meteo** CC BY 4.0, "Weather data by Open-Meteo.com" (its free API is for non-commercial use, which fits Phase 8 Q2); **ERA5** (via Open-Meteo, or the CDS) CC BY 4.0, "Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information [year]". The recorded test answers carry their sources and licences in `crates/ocw-weather/tests/data/manifest.toml` |
| Imagery and land cover | Depends on source | Only sources permitted in 4.6; attribution per source. T3 (v2.47): Orthophoto Liechtenstein 2025 (Opendata BY, ATG / swisstopo), swisstopo SWISSIMAGE (OGD), LGL DOP20 (dl-de/by-2-0), IGN PNOA (CC BY 4.0 scne.es), Copernicus Sentinel-2 ("Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2023-2025"): stored with each package (section `PALT`), copied into its manifest's attribution, hence into `LICENSE-DATA.md` of the release zips, the credits list and *World → About this world → Data sources* |

- **Licence change considered and declined (2026-11-13):** switching to CC BY-SA (for the code, or code and assets) was discussed (CC licences suit assets, not software: no patent grant, no source obligation, narrower compatibility) and the user decided to **keep MIT / Apache-2.0** for now; rule 8A (permissive third-party licences only) stays.
- **Attribution in the app:** loading screen, about / credits screen, the in-ride minimap and the web companion map.
- **No use of `tile.openstreetmap.org`** or other public OSM services at runtime. The use of public OSM tile servers must not be confused with the free use of the raw data. Data comes from Geofabrik extracts at build time; packages and vector tiles are served from our own infrastructure.
- Geographic data and rendering software are considered separately from a licensing perspective.
- Before commercial release, the data and asset licences must be reviewed by a lawyer.
