    | Stellarium star catalogues and sky cultures | stars from Hipparcos / Tycho-2 / Gaia (NC chain); sky cultures `modern`, `modern_iau`, `modern_rey` CC BY-SA 4.0, `modern_st` CC BY-SA 2.0, `modern_sternenkarten` CC BY-ND 4.0, `modern_hlad` GPL-2.0 | no | – |
    | Celestia (CelestiaContent) | `stars.dat` CC BY-NC 3.0 IGO (© ESA), `starnames.dat` GPL-2.0-or-later | no | – |
    | d3-celestial (Olaf Frohn) | repository **BSD 3-Clause**; stars from XHIP (Hipparcos-based, so the NC chain), constellation lines own work after the IAU constellation charts | lines: yes; stars: no | 88 constellations (lines, names, boundaries) |
    | SKY2000 Master Catalog v5 (Myers et al., NASA GSFC Flight Dynamics Division 2006, VizieR V/145) | **no licence or restriction stated**; NASA product (US-government work, 17 U.S.C. 105, so public domain in the US – but some authors were contractors and NASA states no explicit PD notice) | probably yes, **to confirm** | 299 460 stars to V ≈ 8, J2000, proper motion, V, **B–V**, HD / SAO ids |
    | IAU WGSN star names (IAU-CSN, exopla.net) | names are scientific standards, "free to use … not subject to copyright"; the WGSN texts are CC BY (some CC0) | yes | ≈ 650 proper names with HIP / HR ids |
    | CDS / VizieR | no blanket licence: free access "essentially for scientific use"; the catalogue's own ReadMe licence applies; requested acknowledgement "This research has made use of the VizieR catalogue access tool, CDS, Strasbourg, France (DOI 10.26093/cds/vizier)" | depends on the catalogue | – |

    Note: positions and magnitudes are facts, and the EU database right of Hipparcos (1997) has expired, but rule 8A follows the licence the publisher states, so the NC catalogues stay out.

  - **Proposal (not decided):** (a) **stars: SKY2000 v5**, filtered by the world builder / a build script to V ≤ 6.5 (≈ 9 000 stars; RA / Dec J2000, proper motion, V, B–V), after a short confirmation request to NASA GSFC / HEASARC that it is a public-domain US-government work; fallback: our own list from **Wikidata** (CC0; RA / Dec, apparent magnitude, B–V colour index; coverage not yet measured). (b) **Names: IAU WGSN** list, plus Bayer / Flamsteed letters from the catalogue's ids. (c) **Constellation lines: d3-celestial** `constellations.lines.json` (BSD 3-Clause: keep the copyright notice and licence text in the asset manifest), snapped to our star positions. Attribution lines: *"Star data: SKY2000 Master Catalog, Version 5 (Myers et al., NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, 2006), via VizieR V/145, CDS, Strasbourg, France"* · *"Star names: IAU Working Group on Star Names (WGSN)"* · *"Constellation lines: d3-celestial, © 2015 Olaf Frohn, BSD 3-Clause, after the IAU constellation charts"*. **Avoid:** Hipparcos, Tycho, Tycho-2, Gaia (NC), HYG / AT-HYG and Stellarium sky cultures (SA / ND / GPL), Celestia data (NC / GPL), d3-celestial's star files (Hipparcos-derived), BSC5 (unclear copyright).
- **Q8 – Historic weather: decided (2026-11-14, dashboard: keep it only if the data fits our licence) – kept, the data fits.** ERA5 (ECMWF / Copernicus C3S reanalysis, hourly from 1940) is published under **CC BY 4.0** for most datasets (e.g. ERA5 hourly single levels, ERA5-Land) and otherwise under the *Licence to use Copernicus products* – both are allowed by rule 8A (attribution: "Contains modified Copernicus Climate Change Service information [year]"; the exact licence is checked per dataset on its CDS page before use). Sources: the Copernicus Climate Data Store (free account needed for downloads, on our infrastructure) or Open-Meteo's historical API (ERA5-based, CC BY 4.0 data; its free API is non-commercial, which fits the decision of no commercial release); for the regions, MeteoSwiss and DWD historic station data (open data) refine it. If a dataset turns out to have an incompatible licence, that source is dropped, not the feature.
- **Q9 – Extreme weather: decided (2026-11-12):** realistic, **no cap**. Storms, hail, heavy snow, thunderstorms with lightning, dense fog and gale-force wind are all part of the simulation, the weather machine and real weather. The only limit is the physics switch (Q4).
- **Q10 – Priority: decided (2026-11-14):** after S1 and S3 (done), the order is **S2 → S4 → S5 → S7 → S8 → S6** (S2 done, 9I-S2; S4 done, 9I-S4; S5 done, 9I-S5; S7 done, 9I-S7).
- **Q11 – Season override: decoupled from the date? Decided (2026-11-15, dashboard: "the season override jumps only to the season's representative day"):** **no decoupled override** – choosing a season on *World → Time → Season* sets the clock's **date** to that season's representative day for the place (keeping the time of day), so landscape, sun, light and day length always match. S9b is built that way: no `season_override` field, no "· autumn look" mark; the season row is a date jump like the calendar's shortcuts.
- **Q12 – Remember the season choice? Decided (2026-11-15, dashboard: "Start with the local date and time (and season) of where the world is rendered"):** every ride starts at the real local date and time of the world's place, and the season **follows that date** – the season override (S9b) is not remembered across rides, like the time machine (9A).
- **Q13 – The seasons' representative days: decided (2026-11-23, the user): (a) the nearest such day, as built (v4.28); and check per world whether its place has seasons at all – e.g. Tenerife has hardly any – and offer the season jumps only where they mean something (see below)** – Was asked: on *World → Time → Season* choosing a season moves the date to a day that stands for that season at the world's place, keeping the time of day (Q11). Built as proposed (v4.28), open for confirmation: spring = halfway from the first green to full leaf; early summer = halfway from full leaf to summer; summer = the warmest day; autumn = the peak of the autumn colours; late autumn = when most leaves have fallen; winter = the middle of the snow season at the rider's altitude, else the coldest day; places without deciduous trees go by the temperature's year. The jump goes to the nearest such day: in November "summer" is the past July and "winter" the coming January. Options for the year: (a) the nearest, as built; (b) always forward, the next one; (c) always within the current calendar year. Proposal: a – as built.
  - **Worlds with weak or no seasons (the user, 2026-11-23: "do check if the map is in a region where there are seasons, e.g. in Tenerife there are not"):** the world package's climate (the season data of `ocw_sky::season`: the yearly temperature range, the deciduous share of its forests, a snow season at the rider's altitude) decides per place how marked the seasons are; where they are weak – evergreen and subtropical places such as most of Tenerife – the *Season* page says so and offers only the jumps that change something there (e.g. *winter* where the Teide gets snow, nothing that would only recolour leaves that do not turn), and the look follows (no autumn colours or leaf fall on evergreen trees). **Built (v5.42):**
    - **Season strength** (`ocw_sky::season::SeasonStrength::at`, pure and deterministic, per place and altitude): the **yearly temperature range** (twice the climate's amplitude at the altitude: Vaduz 18.8 °C, Black Forest 18 °C, Puerto de la Cruz 6.6 °C, Las Cañadas 11 °C, the Teide's summit 14 °C), the **share of trees that drop their leaves** around the rider – the larger of the forests' (deciduous broadleaves and larches; where the package has a forest section, its measured broadleaf share within 1.5 km of the rider, counted as deciduous only where the region's broadleaves are – Tenerife's are laurel forest) and the lone trees' in the open – and the **days of lying snow** at the rider's altitude (climatological cover ≥ 50 %).
    - **Thresholds:** the leaves turn – **Marked** seasons – where at least **15 %** of the trees drop their leaves and the deciduous phenology runs a whole cycle at the altitude (some day ≥ 15 % coloured, some day ≤ 15 % in leaf); Liechtenstein and the Black Forest have 17 – 88 % up to 2 000 m and stay Marked everywhere, measured or not. Otherwise the seasons are weak: **snow only** with a snow season of at least **14 days** a year, else **weak**. A range of at least **10 °C** is a marked temperature year; it only changes the wording of the line (it brings back neither leaves nor snow).
    - **Tenerife:** evergreen at every height (at most 10 % deciduous lone trees – fruit trees, chestnuts): Puerto de la Cruz and the coast weak (6.6 °C, no snow), the pine forest and Las Cañadas weak (no lying snow in the climatology up to the roads' 2 350 m), the Teide's summit cone above about 3 500 m snow only (126 days).
    - **The page** (both apps, the shared menu): where the seasons are weak, one line under the title – e.g. *"Weak seasons here: evergreen trees, only 7 °C between the coolest and the warmest days, no lying snow. Summer and winter only."* – and only **Summer** (the warmest day: the highest sun, the longest day, dry meadows) and **Winter** (the middle of the snow season at the altitude, else the coldest day; its value shows the snow line on the peaks below 4 000 m, e.g. "14 Feb 2027 · snow above 3,390 m", as the Teide is white then seen from the coast). **Spring, Early summer, Autumn and Late autumn are hidden** there: they would only move the date between days that look the same (no green-up, colours or leaf fall). The "(now)" mark and the Season row's ← / → on World → Time keep to the offered seasons; the console's `time season PICK` still jumps to any season (a tool, conservative: nothing is refused). Where the seasons are marked nothing changes (six seasons, no line).
    - **The look:** trees already followed the phenology (Tenerife's forest trees are evergreen, measured or not: laurel, fayal-brezal, Canary pine; no autumn colours, no leaf fall – test). The **leaves on the road** (4.6.2) and the verge litter were not: the laurel wood counted as 70 % deciduous broadleaves. Now Tenerife's woods count as open land (`ocw_world::leaves::evergreen_woods`) and the season's leaf fall where the broadleaves are evergreen is that of the few deciduous lone trees (`SeasonDay::leaf_fall_share`, 10 %): at most 0.006 leaves a metre all year (Black Forest woods 0.8 in November), the road's slickness below 2 % even soaked.
- **Q14 – Calendar: does choosing a day set it or only select it?: decided (2026-11-23, the user): (a) keep both as built – a click / Enter / South on a day sets it at once and stays on the calendar; Select sets the highlighted day and goes back** – Was asked: on *World → Time* a calendar sets the world's date (v4.46). Built for now: a click, Enter or the gamepad's South button on a day sets that date at once and stays on the calendar, so the world changes while browsing; the *Select* button (9J, v4.45) sets the highlighted day and goes back. In most date pickers a click on a day only highlights it and OK confirms, so browsing never changes anything. Options: (a) keep both as built; (b) a click / Enter on a day only highlights it, only Select sets the date; (c) as b, and a double click or a second Enter on the highlighted day sets it too. Proposal: c – a suggestion, the spec makes none.

---

### Phase 10 – Browser App: riding in the browser (planning, 2026-11-13; B1 – B6 done, B5 v3.21, B6 v3.24; B7 WebGL 2 part v3.27; the local sensor bridge v5.76; open: the backend relay and B8 hosting, after Phase 5)

**Goal:** ride Open Cycling World in a web browser, with no installation: the same worlds, physics, multiplayer, voice and riders as the desktop app. It complements the **web companion** (Phase 5, account / history / routes, no riding); it does not replace the desktop app. 3.5 has kept this possible from Phase 1: the core crates build for wasm, devices sit behind `DeviceBackend`, the protocol is transport-independent and packages can be streamed.

#### 10A – Browser platform facts (as found 2026-11-13; re-check before starting)

| Capability | Needed for | Support |
|---|---|---|
| **WebGPU** | 3D rendering (Bevy / wgpu) | Chrome / Edge since 113 (desktop), Chrome Android since 121 (Android 12+); **Safari 26** (macOS, iOS, iPadOS 26; on iOS all browsers use WebKit); Firefox 141 on Windows, 145 on Apple-silicon macOS, Linux / Android in progress. Fallback: WebGL2 (wgpu supports it, fewer features: no compute, weaker shadows) |
| **WebTransport** (HTTP/3, QUIC datagrams + streams) | the game connection (6.2) | Baseline in 2026: Chrome / Edge since 2022, Firefox since 2023, Safari 26.4 |
| **Web Bluetooth** | trainer, power meter, heart rate (FTMS etc.) | **Chromium only** (Chrome / Edge / Opera on Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS, Android). **Not** Safari / iOS, not Firefox (only experimental extensions) |
| WebRTC | voice (LiveKit `livekit-client`, 7 platform plan) | all browsers |
| Web Audio, AudioWorklet | game audio (3.3) | all browsers |
| Gamepad API | gamepads (3.2.1) | all browsers |
| OPFS / IndexedDB, Storage API | world package cache (hundreds of MB) | all browsers; quota per origin, ask for persistent storage |
| Canvas capture, MediaRecorder, WebCodecs | screenshots and videos (art project rules: ISO timestamp, JPEG q90, audio) | all current browsers (WebCodecs: Safari 26 for video) |
| Wasm threads (SharedArrayBuffer) | parallel systems, decoding | needs cross-origin isolation (COOP / COEP headers) |
| Wasm memory | the loaded world | 4 GB address space (wasm32); practical limit lower, so streaming is required |

**Consequence:** full riding with a trainer works in Chromium browsers on Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS and Android. In Safari / iOS / Firefox the 3D world, multiplayer and voice work, but **no direct Bluetooth**: riding there needs one of the bridges in 10D or virtual power.

#### 10B – Architecture

- **New app `apps/web`:** the same Bevy client as the desktop, built for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` with the WebGPU backend (WebGL2 fallback), via `wasm-bindgen` / `trunk` (or `wasm-pack`) and served as static files. Platform differences sit behind the existing traits. There is **one renderer**: `ocw-render` stays shared. Desktop-only parts (btleplug, cpal native, ffmpeg, file dialogs, the kiosk) are cfg-gated and replaced by web backends.
- **Client core:** `ClientCore`, prediction, `SnapshotBuffer`, workouts and the console are already Bevy-free and wasm-safe. The local server (single player) runs **in the browser too**, as the same `GameServer` driven by the frame loop or a Web Worker instead of a thread.
- **Game connection:** a **WebTransport endpoint** on the game server next to native QUIC. The protobuf messages are identical: snapshots go as datagrams, reliable messages as streams. On the server: `web-transport-quinn` on our quinn endpoint (chosen in B3 over `wtransport` and `h3-webtransport`, 6.2). TLS needs a real certificate (no self-signed pinning in browsers), or `serverCertificateHashes` for development (≤ 14-day ECDSA certificates, rotated).
- **World data:** packages are **streamed by tile over HTTP** (range requests on the package file, or per-tile chunks: 3.5 / 4.7) from our CDN. They are verified (signatures, chunk hashes, 4.7) and cached in OPFS. Only nearby tiles are in memory, which the desktop needs anyway for larger worlds (Black Forest measurements, spec 2.27).
- **Audio:** game audio via cpal's Web Audio backend or our mixer in an AudioWorklet. Voice via `livekit-client` (JS) behind the `VoiceBackend` trait (7). *Built in B5:* our mixer, rendered in the frame loop into scheduled Web Audio buffers (10G, B5).
- **Devices:** `WebBluetoothBackend` implements `DeviceBackend` on top of the pure `ocw-devices` protocol state machine (`gatt`, `ble::protocol`). Only the `GattLink` is new (navigator.bluetooth via `web-sys`). The user grants device access per page (browser chooser).
- **Captures:** screenshots from the canvas as JPEG q90 with EXIF date and time written by our own encoder step. Videos via MediaRecorder / WebCodecs with game audio mixed in. The ISO timestamp is in the HUD top right (art project 2.1).
- **Settings and rides:** settings in browser storage, with account sync via the backend (Phase 5). FIT export as a download; Strava upload through the backend (2.8).
- **Input:** the input model of 3.2.2 as on the desktop; touch is the main input on phones and tablets (the touch overlay in a ride, touch-mode hit targets everywhere), pointer events via `bevy_picking` as on the desktop. Steering by tapping / holding the screen's left or right half, the page's gesture blocking (pull-to-refresh, pinch), safe areas, wake lock and full screen: 3.2.3 (planned, v3.78; the steering, its hints and the overscroll blocking built v4.23).
- **Hosting:** static app + package CDN + game server endpoints, behind the same domain as the web companion. Single sign-on with the account (OIDC, 9). COOP / COEP headers for wasm threads. A strict CSP.

#### 10C – Performance budget

- **Download:** initial app (wasm + assets) ≤ 30 MB compressed, cached; world tiles on demand. First ride within 30 s on a 50 Mbit/s line.
- **Frame rate:** 60 fps at 1080p on a mid-range laptop GPU in Chrome; 30 fps minimum on WebGL2 / phones (lower quality preset).
- **Memory:** ≤ 1.5 GB tab memory with a streamed world.

#### 10D – Riding without Web Bluetooth (Safari / iOS / Firefox)

1. **Virtual power:** keyboard / gamepad / on-screen power (as in the desktop's virtual trainer). Always available, also for spectators and tours.
2. **Phone or desktop as a sensor bridge:** the native app (desktop, or a future mobile app) connects to the trainer over BLE and relays the sensor samples through the backend to the browser session (both logged in to the same account). The server already takes timestamped `SensorSample`s (6.1), so the bridge is a thin relay. Trainer control (ERG / SIM) goes back the same way.
3. **Third-party iOS browsers with Bluetooth** (e.g. Bluefy): possible, but not supported officially.

##### 10D.2 Built (local bridge) – v5.76

The local bridge of v5.72 is built: the desktop app keeps the trainer and the heart-rate strap on Bluetooth (as today: `ocw-devices`, the BLE runner, or the virtual trainer) and relays power, cadence and heart rate to **one browser session on the same network**; the browser's ride sends the trainer control (SIM gradient with wind, ERG target) back. Paired with a short code, no account, no backend. The backend relay through accounts (point 2 above) still comes with Phase 5.

**The transport: WebTransport with `serverCertificateHashes`.** The page comes over HTTPS from GitHub Pages (Phase 14 Q6), so it cannot open plain `ws://` to a LAN address (mixed content, blocked everywhere) and a self-signed `wss://` certificate is rejected. WebTransport (HTTP/3 over QUIC) accepts a self-signed **ECDSA** certificate valid for **at most 14 days** by its SHA-256 – no CA, no warning, no "trust this certificate" step – and the desktop already has the WebTransport stack of B3 (quinn, `web-transport-quinn`). The other routes, and why not:

| Route | Works from an HTTPS page to a LAN address? | Why not chosen |
|---|---|---|
| `ws://` | no – mixed content, blocked by every browser | – |
| `wss://` with a self-signed certificate | only after the rider opens `https://LAN-IP:PORT` and clicks through the certificate warning, per browser and again after a restart (Safari, Quest browser) | fragile, scary, and no safe way to say "this one" on a headset |
| The desktop serves the page itself over HTTPS with a generated certificate the user trusts once | yes, after installing the certificate (iOS: a configuration profile and *Certificate Trust Settings*; the Quest has no UI for user CAs in its browser) | contradicts Q6 (the page from GitHub Pages); the 40 MB app from the desktop; the trust step on iOS is long |
| **WebTransport + `serverCertificateHashes`** | **yes**, if the page knows the hash | **chosen**: no trust step; the hash comes from the code (below) |
| WebRTC data channel | yes (all browsers, also Safari before 26.4) | needs signalling: offer / answer. Without a server it could be derived from the code (ICE-lite on the desktop, ufrag / password and the DTLS fingerprint from the secret, as libp2p's *WebRTC-direct* does) – but it needs a WebRTC stack (ICE, DTLS, SCTP) in the desktop app; kept as the fallback for Safari before 26.4 (Q11) |

**Support matrix** (checked 2026-11-24; WebTransport and its `serverCertificateHashes` option):

| Browser | WebTransport | `serverCertificateHashes` | Local network access | Bridge |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Meta Quest Browser** (Chromium-based) | from its Chromium 97 base | from Chromium 100 (released 2022; Quest Browser 32 is Chromium 122, 33 is 124) | Chromium 147+ asks "access devices on your local network" once (also for WebTransport, [Intent to Ship](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/OuQArRDHoBg)) | **yes** on Quest 2 / 3 / 3S / Pro; **Quest 1: expected** – its browser is frozen at its last update (Meta stopped Quest 1 features in March 2023, fixes on 31 Aug 2024), whose Chromium base is newer than 100 by the release history, but its exact version was not found in a source and could not be read from the headset (to check in W4: the page says "not in this browser" when `WebTransport` is missing) |
| **Safari on iOS / iPadOS 26** | **26.4** and later | **26.4** ([WebKit bug 300057](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=300057), fixed Oct 2025; [caniuse](https://caniuse.com/mdn-api_webtransport_webtransport_options_servercertificatehashes_parameter)) | iOS asks for *Local Network* per app (Safari) | **yes from iOS 26.4**; **iOS 26.0 – 26.3 and older: no route without the backend** (no WebTransport; the WebRTC fallback is Q11) – updating to 26.4 is the way |
| Chrome Android | yes | Chromium 100+ | prompt from 147 | **yes** (it also has Web Bluetooth: the bridge is for a trainer that is paired with the desktop) |
| Desktop Chrome / Edge | yes (97+) | 100+ | prompt from 147 | **yes** |
| Desktop Firefox | 114+ | **125+** ([Bugzilla 1806693](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1806693)) | Firefox's own local network access work is in progress | **yes** (the way to ride a trainer in Firefox, which has no Web Bluetooth) |
| Safari on macOS | 26.4+ | 26.4+ | – | yes from 26.4 |

Sources: [caniuse: WebTransport](https://caniuse.com/mdn-api_webtransport), [Chrome: serverCertificateHashes, Intent to Ship](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/g/blink-dev/c/m0v9XiwKA4M), [Chrome: Local Network Access](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/local-network-access), [Meta Quest Browser versions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Quest_Browser). A page served with a Content-Security-Policy would need `'unsafe-webtransport-hashes'` in `connect-src` for a connection with hashes (the preview has no CSP yet; B8).

**The pairing code carries everything** (`ocw_bridge::code`): the page cannot ask the desktop anything before it is connected, so the code holds the desktop's **IPv4 address on the local network** (192.168.x.y in 16 bits, 172.16–31.x.y in 20, 10.x.y.z in 24, others in 32), which of four UDP ports it listens on (**47810 – 47813**, the first free one), a **30-bit secret** and a **check symbol** (a typo is reported at once). Crockford base32 in groups of four, case-insensitive, O = 0, I / L = 1: **11 characters** on a 192.168 network (`7K2M-Q9XP-4DA`), 13 on 10.x. The desktop keeps the secret in `secrets.toml [bridge]`, so the code stays the same across restarts (the browser reconnects by itself) until *New code*; it changes when the computer's address changes.

**The certificate comes from the code** (`ocw_bridge::cert`): both sides derive the same certificate – an ECDSA P-256 key from SHA-256 over the secret, every field fixed, the validity the **week** (Unix time / 7 days) from a day before its start for **13 days**, the signature deterministic (RFC 6979; RustCrypto `p256`, pure Rust, so the same code runs in the browser's wasm) – so the DER bytes and their hash are equal everywhere. The browser offers the hashes of the last, this and the next week (a clock a few days off still works). The browser then proves the code in its hello (a hash of the secret, inside TLS). Security: whoever has the code can pair; the endpoint takes connections from the local network only (loopback, the private IPv4 ranges, link-local, IPv6 unique-local; others are refused before the handshake); one browser at a time. A 30-bit secret can be found by trying keys against the certificate within hours by someone already on the network who wants to – acceptable for power and heart-rate readings at home, and *New code* ends it; the backend relay (Phase 5) has accounts.

**Protocol** (`ocw_bridge::msg`, `relay`): one bidirectional stream, JSON messages in length-prefixed frames (a stream keeps the order; at 4 readings a second on a LAN datagrams would gain nothing). Browser → desktop: `hello` (version, proof, the page's session id, the browser's kind – "Quest Browser", "Safari on iPad", no versions), `control` (SIM or ERG, clamped to sane limits on the desktop), `ping` (1 Hz), `bye`. Desktop → browser: `welcome` (its name, its run, its devices), `refused` (why), `power` / `heart_rate` (numbered, stamped with the desktop's time), `device` (connected, reconnecting, failed), `applied` (a control reached the trainer), `pong`, `closed`.

- **Order and timestamps:** readings are numbered on the desktop; the browser drops duplicates and late ones (after a reconnect) and starts the count again for a new desktop run. Their times go onto the browser's clock with the offset from the ping with the shortest round trip, never into the future and never backwards; that is the device event's timestamp, so the `SensorSample`s are as from a Bluetooth trainer.
- **Pairing:** one browser at a time – another page is refused ("another browser (Quest Browser) uses this trainer – stop it there first") while the paired one was heard within 5 s; the same page reconnecting (a reload keeps its session id in `localStorage`) takes over at once; a page gone quiet is replaced.
- **Reconnect:** after a drop the browser tries again after 0.5, 1, 2, 4, then every 5 s; the ride gets no power meanwhile (as while a Bluetooth trainer reconnects); the last control is sent again with the hello. A refusal ends the attempts.
- **Control:** the browser's `TrainerControl` sends SIM / ERG to every device of its ride, the bridge included; while a browser is paired the desktop's own ride stops setting the trainer's load (the browser's ride wins), and its controls go to the desktop's devices.
- **Clean stop:** *Stop using it* in the browser sends `bye`; *Share with a browser: off* on the desktop sends `closed` and frees the port; the app's exit stops it.

**UI:** desktop – Settings → Trainer → Devices → **Share with a browser** (the page `Sensor bridge`: on / off, the pairing code, the address `https://IP:PORT`, the paired browser, *New code*; while the page is open a **QR code** of the preview link with the code, `https://newkit.github.io/OCW/?bridge=CODE`, for a phone or tablet's camera); console `bridge.share on|off|new-code`, `bridge.status`; `--share-bridge`. Browser – Settings → Trainer → Devices → **Use a trainer from another device** (*Enter the pairing code* opens the page's own prompt, so the headset's or tablet's system keyboard comes up; the code, the state, *Stop using it*); console `bridge.pair [CODE]`, `bridge.stop`, `bridge.status`; page option `?bridge=CODE`; the bridge is then the device *Desktop trainer (bridge)* in the list and the HUD, `window.ocw.devices().bridge` has its numbers. Pair on the flat page before *Enter VR*; the code is remembered, so the next visit connects by itself.

**Code:** `crates/ocw-bridge` (pure, wasm: `code`, `cert`, `msg`, `relay`; native: `host`, the endpoint on its own thread), `apps/desktop/src/bridge.rs`, `apps/web/src/bridge.rs` (the WebTransport bytes, thin), the rows in `ocw_client::menu::devices` (`BridgeInfo`, `Page::Bridge`).

**Tests (11.4):** the code (every address form, typing variants, typos caught), the certificate (equal on every derivation, validity within 14 days, the DER), the messages (frames in any split, controls clamped), the relay (one browser at a time, the same page reconnecting, order and timestamps on the browser's clock, duplicates and late readings, a new desktop run, the backoff, the control and its round trip), the menu rows; **loopback** (`crates/ocw-bridge/tests/loopback.rs`): the desktop's endpoint and a WebTransport client that trusts it only by the hashes it derives from the code, as a browser does – pairing, 20 readings in order with their timestamps, heart rate, the SIM control round trip, a second page refused, the same page taking over, a wrong certificate failing the handshake, a forged proof refused, `bye`, the clean stop; the desktop's sharing (start, the code kept across restarts, a new code, stop, the QR code). **End to end** (`make test-bridge`, `scripts/test-bridge.py`): the desktop shares its devices on a headless Wayland compositor, headless Chromium opens the browser app with `?bridge=CODE` and rides Liechtenstein; latency, control and screenshots of both sides.

**Measured (marge, 2026-11-24; `scripts/test-bridge.py`, 120 s of Liechtenstein, Vaduz – Malbun):** the desktop app on a headless Wayland compositor (debug build, about 40 fps), headless Chromium 157 (WebGPU) with the browser app from the dev server, both on marge; two runs – the code naming marge's LAN address, and naming 127.0.0.1 (the run whose pictures are kept: no real address in them):

| | |
|---|---|
| pairing | the page paired 0.6 – 2.3 s after its ride started and stayed paired 98.9 – 99.6 % of the ride (the rest: the first frames before the hello) |
| readings | 476 in 120 s in each run (3.97 a second, the desktop's 4 Hz), none dropped or out of order |
| age of a reading on arrival | p50 **10 / 14 ms**, p95 **31 / 35 ms**, max 223 / 158 ms (single readings while the world's tiles loaded) – the target was < 150 ms |
| ping round trip | p50 21 / 26 ms, p95 42 / 41 ms (the page's event loop between frames; 0.4 ms when idle) |
| trainer control round trip (browser → desktop → its devices → `applied`) | p50 **24 / 31 ms**, max 72 ms / once 1.0 s (a hitch of the debug desktop); 116 / 118 SIM controls in 120 s |

**Not yet with the KICKR's own power:** in the hardware run the desktop could not reach the Wahoo KICKR (the trainer did not advertise at all – asleep or off – and a Bluetooth scan on marge found no fitness device), so the browser's readings came from the desktop's virtual trainer (180 W) through the same relay, and the SIM controls went to the virtual trainer; with the desktop connected to the KICKR (`make test-bridge BRIDGE_DEVICES=/tmp/ocw/kickr/devices.toml` on marge, once someone wakes the trainer by turning the pedals) the same run carries its power. Also to check on devices: the Quest 1's browser (W4), Safari on iOS 26.4, Firefox, and the local-network permission prompt of Chrome 147+ from the GitHub Pages page.

##### 10D.2 Sharing screen – v5.82, built v5.83

**While the desktop shares its trainer with a browser, it shows a simple *Sharing* screen instead of its own ride** (decision of v5.82, option (c); the others were mirroring the headset's view and following the same ride). It comes up as soon as a browser pairs and goes when the browser leaves or the rider chooses *Stop sharing*; back in the ride everything is as before.

- **What it shows** (full window, the menu's panel, rows and text sizes): the paired browser by its user agent's short name ("Quest Browser", "Safari on iPhone", "Chrome on Linux"); the live power, cadence and heart rate from the desktop's trainer and strap, large ("–" when a reading is older than 3 s); the grade (SIM, with the wind from 0.5 m/s) or ERG target the browser sets; the bridge's state ("connected for 2 min 05 s, 500 readings sent", or "waiting for the browser (last heard 7 s ago)") and its round trip (QUIC's smoothed estimate, `BridgeHost::link`); the last report of the page if any – the headset's beacon (14I W4: fps, frame time = work p50) or a flat page's (`window.ocw.bridgeReport(kind, json)`: `fps`, `frame_ms_p50`); the pairing code for re-pairing; *Stop sharing*; the keys.
- **Input:** Enter / Space, the pad's Confirm (A, or B with `controls.pad_confirm east`) or a click on *Stop sharing* stop sharing (as *Share with a browser: off*); Esc opens the menu over the screen, the console works as always. No ride input meanwhile (`InputContext::Sharing`).
- **The own ride pauses** (the browser's ride is the one that counts): the samples carry no power, cadence or heart rate and the brake, flagged as virtual power (`ClientCore::set_paused`) – the rider rolls to a stop (at 3 m/s², about 25 m from 30 km/h) and stays; the server credits no distance and no hearts. The FIT recording (and the Strava recording) writes no records meanwhile and does not credit the roll to a stop when the ride goes on; a running workout pauses and resumes with it. The console says where the ride paused and went on.
- **Light:** the world's camera is off while the screen shows (no 3D frame is drawn); a UI camera of its own draws the screen and the HUD is off. The simulation and the app's other systems still run, so on marge the frame costs the same as riding (CPU-bound; p50 6.8 ms vs 6.9 – 7.1 ms in a release build without vsync) – the GPU's world work is what goes, which helps a browser on the same computer.

**Code:** `crates/ocw-render/src/sharing.rs` (`SharingView`, `SharingPlugin`: cameras, HUD, drawing, the click), `crates/ocw-client/src/menu/sharing.rs` (`SharingInfo` → the view, `SetLoad`, `Report`), `apps/desktop/src/bridge.rs` (`sharing_screen`: pause, resume, input, the view), `ocw_bridge::host::BridgeHost::link`.

**Tests (11.4):** the content (browser, numbers, stale readings, grade and ERG, the bridge's states, the round trip, the headset's and the page's reports, the code, the pads' Confirm); the screen in the app: up on pairing with the reading, the own ride paused, gone on *Stop sharing* by a click and by Enter and when the browser leaves, the ride going on, the console lines; the drawing (the world's camera off, a UI camera of its own, the HUD off, everything back as it was, a camera or HUD that was off before stays off); the pause against an in-memory server (the rider stops within 25 m, no distance and no hearts for 60 s of 400 W, riding and earning again after); the recording (nothing recorded while paused, the roll to a stop not credited); the bridge's link (round trip, heard, paired) in the loopback test. **End to end:** `make test-bridge` checks that the desktop's log shows the screen coming and going, the ride pausing and going on (under 30 m rolled), takes a desktop screenshot every 15 s and has the page send its frame rate as a report; `--desktop-arg=--no-vsync` with `OCW_PROFILE=release` measures the frame cost (`--log-fps`).

**Measured (marge, 2026-11-25, 127.0.0.1 in the code):** the screen came up when Chrome on Linux paired and closed when it left; the own rider stopped 26 – 27 m after the pause (debug / release) and stood for 132 – 150 s; release desktop without vsync, frame p50: 7.7 – 8.0 ms with the screen up while Chromium rode on the same machine, 6.8 ms once the browser's ride had ended, 6.9 – 7.1 ms riding after; the browser's readings and control as in v5.76.

#### 10E – Milestones (proposal)

- **B1 – Wasm build:** `apps/web` compiles. Bevy runs on WebGPU with a test route and the local server in the browser; virtual power. CI builds it.
- **B2 – Worlds over HTTP:** tile streaming, verification, OPFS cache, loading screen, memory budget.
- **B3 – Multiplayer:** WebTransport endpoint on the server, browser client joins the same sessions as desktop riders.
- **B4 – Devices:** `WebBluetoothBackend` (FTMS, Cycling Power, CSC, Heart Rate, Wahoo), ERG / SIM control.
- **B5 – Audio and voice:** Web Audio game audio, LiveKit voice, mute hotkeys. **Done (v3.21, 10G).** *Planned (v4.01, 7.1):* the browser joins the voice server that every host now starts; on home hosts without a domain certificate through a signalling bridge over WebTransport (7.1.1, 7.1.7 Q3); *Voice room* Everybody / Selected riders on the shared Voice page.
- **B6 – UI parity:** menus, settings, HUD, console permissions, gamepad, captures with timestamps, FIT download. **Done (v3.24, 10G).**
- **B7 – Sensor bridge** (10D.2) and WebGL2 fallback quality presets. **WebGL 2 fallback and quality presets done (v3.27, 10G); the sensor bridge is open until Phase 5 (accounts and the backend).** **The local bridge is built (v5.76, 10D.2 *Built (local bridge)*):** the desktop shares its trainer with one browser on the same network, paired by a code.
- **B8 – Hosting and release:** domain, CDN, certificates, CSP / COOP / COEP, account sign-on, browser test matrix. Voice there: a LiveKit (bundled or separate) behind TLS on the domain (`wss://`, 7.1.1); the browser itself never hosts voice.
- **B8a – Public preview on GitHub Pages (decided by the user 2026-11-15, v3.36; stage 1 of B8):** a solo preview of the browser app – the built-in test routes and the Liechtenstein world, virtual power or a trainer over Web Bluetooth in Chromium – served by **GitHub Pages** (HTTPS, static, deployed by a GitHub Actions workflow; site ≤ 1 GB, soft 100 GB / month). Needs: a size-optimised release wasm (no debug info, `wasm-opt`), a **preview signing root** built into the preview build (the worlds signed with it when publishing; its private key never in the repository or CI logs – no dev keys, no unsigned worlds on a public page), the page configuration (worlds / server / voice URLs) instead of localhost assumptions, an attribution and licence page (OSM ODbL, elevation sources, Copernicus, materials) and a short privacy note; the README links the preview right after its headline. **Stage 2 (later):** an own small server in the EU (Caddy: HTTPS, precompressed wasm, range requests for all worlds) for multiplayer (WebTransport), voice (LiveKit) and sign-in (9.1) – it needs a domain. **Multiplayer and voice on the preview (v6.56):** the page rides together on the Fly.io server (11.5 *Join info*): `config.json` names its join info and `wss://` voice; sign-in stays off.

**Unit tests:**

- WebTransport framing and server endpoint loopback tests (native, like the QUIC tests);
- tile range-request planner and cache eviction;
- package verification on streamed chunks;
- the Web Bluetooth `GattLink` against the existing protocol mocks;
- bridge relay ordering and timestamps;
- EXIF / JPEG writer;
- MediaRecorder / audio mix glue kept thin, with pure logic tested natively.

**Browser tests:** headless Chromium (`wasm-bindgen-test`, Playwright) for start-up, a ride on the test route and a screenshot. A smoke matrix of Chrome / Edge / Firefox / Safari on the build machines (the Mac for Safari, Windows for Edge).

#### 10F – Open questions (for the user)

- **Q1 – Target browsers: decided (2026-11-14, dashboard: "that's fine"):** Chromium-based browsers (desktop + Android) for riding with a trainer (Web Bluetooth); Safari / iOS / Firefox ride with virtual power and the sensor bridge.
- **Q2 – Sensor bridge: decided (2026-11-14, dashboard):** **yes, build it** (10D.2) – the way to ride with a trainer on iPad / iPhone (and in browsers without Web Bluetooth) before a native iOS app exists.
- **Q3 – Priority vs. other phases: decided (2026-11-14, dashboard):** **start now** – the browser app is built in parallel with Phases 8 / 9, beginning with B1 (wasm build on WebGPU with the test route, the local server in the browser and virtual power).
- **Q4 – Hosting: decided (2026-11-14, dashboard):** **own servers for now** (no CDN provider); world packages are served from our machines with HTTP caching and range requests, a CDN can come later if traffic needs it.
- **Q5 – Anonymous access: decided (2026-11-14, dashboard):** **anonymous riding is allowed**, but with a plain default ("boring") bike and character and **no customization**: the workshop and the character editor are locked (shown with a "log in to customize" hint), no hearts are earned or spent, nothing is saved across visits. Only logged-in users customize their bike and character (and keep hearts, parts and kit, 14 Phase 4).
- **Q6 – Same app or a lighter "web edition"? Decided (2026-11-14, dashboard): full parity** – the browser app is the same app with the same worlds and features as the desktop (quality presets and streaming adapt to the device, not a reduced edition).
- **Q7 – Black Forest in the public preview: decided (2026-11-15, dashboard: "mark as fixed"):** closed for now – the preview keeps Liechtenstein and Tenerife (the user: "only Tenerife for now"); the Black Forest comes with B8 stage 2's own server or when the user reopens it. The background: GitHub Pages holds at most 1 GB per site, and release files cannot be fetched by the browser (no CORS headers; checked 2026-11-15). The preview carries Liechtenstein (88 MB) and Tenerife (500 MB) since v3.51 (the user: "only Tenerife for now"); a Black Forest package is 436–578 MB. Options: **(a)** a smaller web cut of the Black Forest (for example Freiburg – Schauinsland – Feldberg, about 250 MB) – **proposal**; **(b)** web copies of the packages with lighter orthophotos so that more fit; **(c)** an external host with CORS (a Cloudflare R2 bucket: 10 GB free, no egress fees; or B8 stage 2's own server), which needs an account and a domain from the user.
- **Q8 – Render distance: dynamic by default? Decided (2026-11-15, the user: "make dynamic mode default: on"):** *Adjust to the frame rate* is **on by default everywhere** – desktop, browser, phones and VR; the slider's default (the preset's distance) is its upper limit.
- **Q9 – Target frame rate: decided (2026-11-15, the user: "target the display refresh rate; 60 on browser and phone via browser"):** the desktop targets **the display's refresh rate**; the browser app – on computers and phones alike – targets **60 fps**; VR the headset's refresh. The rider can still choose another target.
- **Q10 – Build the browser app with WebAssembly SIMD?: decided (2026-11-24, the user): (a) as proposed; built (v5.80, 10G *The module's size*: both builds with `+simd128`, the page's SIMD test and the too-old message)** – Before the first frame a phone compiles the browser app's whole code module and keeps about four times its code in memory (10G *The module's size*). Built with WebAssembly SIMD (`+simd128`, vector instructions) the module is 2.5 MB smaller (the preview's WebGL 2 module, the one iPhones load: 43.4 → 40.8 MB; egui's text rasteriser then drops its large scalar fallback, and some loops run faster). The catch: a browser without WebAssembly SIMD cannot load the module at all – Safari before 16.4 (iPhones and iPads that stay on iOS 15 or iOS 16.0 – 16.3), Chrome before 91, Firefox before 89; today the module already needs Safari 15. Options: (a) SIMD in both builds, and the start page says "this browser is too old" when a tiny SIMD test module does not validate; (b) SIMD only in the WebGPU build (every WebGPU browser has SIMD) – no gain for iPhones, which load the WebGL 2 build; (c) a third build, WebGL 2 with SIMD, chosen by the page when the test module validates (one more build of about 5 minutes per release, 43 MB more on the server); (d) no SIMD. Proposal: (a) – the phones that cannot update past iOS 16.3 (iPhone 7 and older, 2 – 3 GB of memory) cannot hold a ride within iOS's tab limit anyway.
- **Q11 – Riding with the desktop's trainer on iPhones and iPads before iOS 26.4: decided (2026-11-26, the user): (a) for now – the page asks to update to iOS 26.4 and says why; (b) or (c) may follow later** – **Why the bridge matters on Apple devices:** Safari on iPhone and iPad has **no Web Bluetooth**, so the browser app there cannot talk to a smart trainer or a heart-rate strap at all. The sensor bridge (10D.2) is the only way an iPad or iPhone rides with real power: the trainer stays connected to the desktop app (on a Mac, PC or Linux machine in the same home network), the rider types the desktop's 11-character code into the browser app, and power, cadence and heart rate come over the home network. **Why iOS 26.4:** the bridge uses WebTransport with a certificate both sides derive from the code (`serverCertificateHashes`), and Safari has both only from **iOS / iPadOS 26.4** (released 2026; support matrix above). On iOS 26.0 – 26.3 and older, the Devices page says "not in this browser" and the ride uses virtual power. **Who is affected:** every device that runs iOS 26 can take the free update to 26.4 in a few minutes; the ones really left out are devices that are not updated, and devices too old for iOS 26 at all (they stay on iOS 18 and never get WebTransport in Safari). The same WebTransport is also how the browser app joins a **group ride** (B3), so those devices can ride only solo anyway – a second transport for the bridge alone would not bring them into group rides. **Example:** a rider with an iPad on iPadOS 26.2 opens the game, picks *Devices*, and reads "not in this browser – update to iPadOS 26.4"; after the update the same page offers *Use the desktop's trainer*. Options: (a) **nothing more:** the page asks to update to iOS 26.4 and says why; (b) **a second way for older Safari,** a WebRTC data channel from the desktop app to the page – it works in every Safari since iOS 11, but the desktop app needs a WebRTC stack (ICE, DTLS, SCTP; a Rust crate such as str0m), the bridge gets two transports to test, and it is about a day of work – for devices that still could not join group rides; (c) **wait for the backend relay** of Phase 5 (accounts), which reaches every browser over the internet, also away from home. Proposal: (a) – iOS 26.4 is a free update for every device that runs iOS 26, older devices would gain only solo rides from (b), and the backend relay comes later anyway.


#### 10G – Status: B1, B2, B3, B4, B5, B6 and B7's WebGL 2 part built (2026-11-14); the render distance built (2026-11-16); B3's network worker built (2026-11-25)

**B1 – Wasm build: done.** `apps/web` (crate `ocw-web`, a `cdylib`) is the same client as the desktop app, built for `wasm32-unknown-unknown` and run by the browser on **WebGPU** (Bevy's `webgpu` + `web` features, only for the wasm target):

- **One client, shared crates (Q6: full parity).** The desktop's Bevy-free client logic moved into the new crate **`ocw-client`**: `ClientCore` (prediction, reconciliation, interpolation, the ride view), events and ghosts, god-mode state, the pure key logic (`input`: power ramps, `KeyThrottle`, lean and line steering, junction keys), the GPS position and the sky (`sky`: the zone of the place, the HUD clock, `sky_view`). `apps/desktop` uses it unchanged in behaviour; the renderer `ocw-render` is shared as before. Desktop-only parts stay in `apps/desktop` for now and move into shared crates behind web backends milestone by milestone (devices B4, audio and voice B5, menus / settings / captures B6), until both apps are thin entry points over the same plugins.
- **Local server in the browser.** The same `GameServer`, driven by the frame loop: `ocw_server::local::FrameServer::advance(frame time)` runs the 50 Hz ticks that fit (counted in whole µs, no drift) and drops a backlog beyond 0.25 s like the server thread (`MAX_BACKLOG_S`, e.g. a tab in the background). Unit tests: tick counts over uneven frames, tick-for-tick equality with `SteppedServer`, the backlog rule, the same snapshot rate as the threaded `LocalServer` over the same wall time.
- **Virtual power.** `ocw_devices::FrameVirtualTrainer`: the virtual trainer's logic (`virtual_power`, shared with the threaded `VirtualTrainer`) reporting at 4 Hz from the frame time; 200 W at the start, the desktop's keys (↑ adds power, ↓ stops, Page Up / Down ±10 W, A autodrive, W wild, ← / → line or lean) and the console (`sim.power`, `teleport`, `net.stats`, every `ocw-render` command).
- **The test route** (Hills, or `?route=loop`), 5 bots, the sky and lights from the server's world clock (`ocw-sky`, Vaduz time), the chase camera, the HUD with the ISO timestamp, the console. Page options in the query string (`route`, `bots`, `power`, `start`, `name`).
- **wasm-safety fixes:** `std::time::SystemTime` panics on wasm32-unknown-unknown, so the server's clock, the voice clock and the HUD timestamp use `web-time` there, and chrono's `wasmbind` gives the local UTC offset; `ocw-devices` builds without btleplug / tokio on wasm32; the server's `net`, `worlds` and `LocalServer` thread are native only. No getrandom backend was needed.
- **Tooling:** `make deps-web` (wasm-bindgen-cli of exactly the `wasm-bindgen` version in `Cargo.lock`, 0.2.130, via `cargo install --locked`, no sudo), `make web` (`scripts/build-web.sh`: the `web` profile = release, `opt-level = "s"`, thin LTO; wasm-bindgen `--target web` without the name section; `wasm-opt` when installed; output and `sizes.txt` in `target/web/`), `make web-serve` (`scripts/web-serve.py`: COOP / COEP headers, wasm MIME type), `make test-web` (`scripts/test-web.py`: headless Chromium on WebGPU over the DevTools protocol, console log, timings, a screenshot in `test-output/web/`). `make check` builds `ocw-web` for wasm32 (`test-web-build`); `test-wasm` also checks `ocw-devices` and the `ocw-server` lib; CI has a `web` job that runs `make web` and keeps `target/web/` as an artifact.

| | |
|---|---|
| `ocw_web_bg.wasm` | 63.8 MiB raw, 14.3 MiB gzip -9, 9.1 MiB brotli -q 11 (budget 10C: ≤ 30 MB compressed); the name section (another ~87 MB) is stripped; no wasm-opt yet. Code ~53 MB, data ~13 MB (embedded models, fonts, styles) |
| `ocw_web.js` | 180 KiB (wasm-bindgen glue) |

**Not yet / notes for later milestones:** WebGL2 fallback (Bevy selects WebGPU or WebGL2 at compile time: a second build, B7); multiplayer (B3), Web Bluetooth (B4), audio (B5; Bevy's audio plugin is off), menus, settings, gamepad parity and captures with EXIF (B6; the test screenshot comes from the DevTools protocol, without EXIF); the material library (flat land-use colours, as on the desktop without it); `wasm-opt` and a CDN with brotli (B8). The canvas fills the page; the arrows ride instead of scrolling it.

**B2 – Worlds over HTTP: done (v2.99).** `?world=liechtenstein&route=vaduz-malbun` streams a world package from our own server (Q4) into the browser app; the ride starts when the first tiles are there, more come while riding.

- **Shared, pure and tested natively:** `ocw_worldstore::stream` builds for wasm32 (the crate's file system, keys and `ureq` parts are native only; `test-wasm` checks it). `accept_manifest` (size, parse, signature chain under the unsigned policy) is the same check `--fetch-world` now uses; the desktop's download is otherwise unchanged. `plan`: the base chunks (`header`, `sections`, every `section …`), the `tile X,Z` chunks around a position (nearest first), merged into `Range` requests (gap ≤ 64 kB, ≤ 4 MB each). `load::load_chunks`: cache first, then the ranges; every chunk is checked against its SHA-256 in the manifest before use; a mismatch is fetched once more on its own, then the load fails with "chunk … does not match its SHA-256 … the copy on the server is damaged" (nothing damaged is cached). `cache::ChunkCache` over a `ChunkStore` (async trait: OPFS in the browser, `MemoryStore` in the tests): files `<id>@<version>@<chunk>`, an index with sizes and last use, LRU eviction by a size budget (default 1 GiB), re-verification on read (a damaged cached file is removed and refetched), store errors (quota, no OPFS) never stop the ride. `resident::ResidentTiles`: tiles within the fetch radius (3) are fetched, beyond the keep radius (5) dropped, over the memory budget (96 MB of decoded tiles) the farthest beyond the fetch radius first. `driver::StreamDriver`: the sequence as async steps (`latest` → manifest → base → tile batches) sharing `StreamShared` (progress, base, requests, arrived tiles) with the app. `progress::LoadProgress`: the loading screen as text.
- **Signatures in the browser:** ed25519 and SHA-256 (`ocw_world::manifest`) build for wasm, so the full signature chain is checked as on the desktop. The page trusts the production roots (none yet); on development pages only (localhost) also `trust=dev`, `trust-root=HEX` and `allow-unsigned=1` (chunks still verified). `make web-worlds` (`scripts/publish-web-worlds.sh`) signs a copy of the pilot package with a development root kept in the git-ignored `target/web-keys/` and publishes it to `target/web/worlds/` (`world-builder publish`, which now also writes `<id>/latest`); `make web-serve` serves it with single byte ranges (206, Content-Range, 416) and prints the links.
- **The app (`apps/web`):** `world.rs` (Bevy glue, tested natively with the driver stepped over an in-memory server: load, ride the package route, teleport → tiles come and go, second load from the cache); `browser.rs` (wasm only, thin): `fetch()` with `Range`, `OpfsStore` (`navigator.storage.getDirectory()`, folder `ocw-worlds`, `persist()` asked), the storage estimate, the driver in a `spawn_local` loop, the loading screen in the page's `#ocw-status`. The session waits for the base and first tiles (`WebSession::ride` on `Course::RouteRide` / `FreeRide` over the package's road graph); `WorldSet::update_tiles` hands changed tiles to the renderer without re-meshing the near tiles (`tiles_version` rebuilds the far terrain). Page options: `world` (id, `ID@VERSION`, manifest URL), `route` (package route, by name or slug), `free=1`, `tiles`, `keep`, `memory-mb`, `cache-mb`, `cache=0`; console `world.info` and `time …` (the time machine, as on the desktop); `window.ocw.console(line)` and `window.ocw.wasmMemory()` for tests. Fix on the way: after a jump the renderer waited for the urgent tiles' tasks with `block_on`, which never returns on wasm (one thread): there they are built in place.
- **Test (`make test-web-world`, `scripts/test-web.py --world`):** headless Chromium on marge streams Liechtenstein (signed by the dev root) from the dev server, rides Vaduz – Malbun at noon (`time noon`), teleports to km 6, screenshots (loading screen, ride, after the teleport), then loads the page again in the same profile: from OPFS, no package bytes over the network, faster.

**Measured (marge, 2026-11-14, Chromium on WebGPU, localhost):**

| | first load (network) | second load (OPFS cache) |
|---|---|---|
| world ready after navigation | 2.74 s (2.49 s in an earlier run) | 2.16 s (1.60 s) |
| in the app (stream start → ride) | 1.88 s: manifest 0.01 s, base 1.1 s (11.2 MB in 15 chunks: mostly decoding), 49 first tiles | 1.50 s |
| package bytes over HTTP | 14.2 MB in 34 requests (manifest and merged ranges) before the start; 15.9 MB served with the teleport (45 % of the 35.2 MB package) | 0 (only `latest` and the manifest, 105 kB) |
| from the cache | 0 | 14.2 MB in 64 chunks; OPFS holds 15.7 MB in 94 files (quota 10.7 GB, not persisted in headless) |
| resident tiles | 49 of 510 at the start (3.1 MB decoded), peak 4.2 MB; 7 dropped after the teleport | 49 (3.1 MB) |
| wasm memory | peak 652–759 MB (it only grows; the renderer's meshes and assets, not the tiles); JS heap 28 MB | 700 MB |
| `ocw_web_bg.wasm` | 71.7 MiB raw, 15.8 MiB gzip, 10.0 MiB brotli (B1: 63.8 / 14.3 / 9.1; collisions and Avian came in between) | |

**Update (v3.70, Phase 8 T8 *Memory*):** part of this was the tile stream starting every tile again while it waited for its upload; with that fixed and the near plants built only near the camera, a Liechtenstein world ride peaks at about 430 MB, and `scripts/test-web.py` fails world rides above 1,500 MB. **Open (B2):** the base (11 MB) is fetched whole before the ride – the seasonal tint maps (`SEAS`, 4.8 MB) and the land use could come per tile with a package format that splits them; range requests run one after another (parallel fetches would help on real networks); neighbour packages (`WorldSet` with several members) stream only the home package so far; no Service Worker for the app itself; signatures by production roots (and their distribution) come with B8.

| Liechtenstein, WebGPU | 504 → **433 MB** | 431 → 348 MB | 499 → 441 MB | 34 MB |
| Liechtenstein, WebGL 2 | 602 → **500 MB** | 522 → 426 MB | 445 → 386 MB | 33 MB |
| Tenerife, WebGPU | 2,129 → **684 MB** | 2,080 → 635 MB | 463 → 429 MB | 33 MB |

The tiles themselves were never the cost: a decoded tile (terrain, road strips) is 0.1 MB, its meshes 8 – 21 MB of GPU arrays (built in 14 – 28 MB of heap, freed after the upload – `RenderAssetUsages::RENDER_WORLD` – leaving 1 – 2 MB per tile on the CPU: plant recipes, ground-detail terrain, crowns, footprints). The memory went into copies of the package's base, by step (native, Tenerife / Black Forest north, MB):

| step | before | after | what changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| base decoded | 345 / 314 | 250 / 241 | the land use stays encoded (`ocw_world::landuse::LandUseIndex`: 75 / 20 MB of runs instead of 169 / 93 MB decoded), each tile decoded when its tiles come; the base's chunks freed as they are joined (the driver held them, a growing copy and the decode at once) |
| the ride (network, obstacles, client) | 175 / 264 | 46 / 69 | the network shares the package's graph (`RoadNetwork::new` takes an `Arc`) and builds an edge's dense geometry when it is first asked for (`OnceLock`; the nearest point is searched on the edges' own polylines first, god mode's area from them) |
| renderer's package, per set of resident tiles | 321 / 279 | 15 / 14 | `StreamedPackage::package` keeps the per-tile parts (land use, buildings, bridges, obstacles, roofs, seasonal maps, forest, vegetation) only for the resident tiles and the ring around them (`WorldPackage::cut`, `resident_cut`; the tile meshes read no farther), the road graph shared; one tile with sea stays so the far terrain still draws it |
| world set, and its copy at each change | 34 + 34 / 48 + 48 | 0 / 0 | `WorldSet` shares the graph (`Arc`) |
| versions kept alive | one per tile upload | the current one | the ground detail's chunks hold their version weakly and build from the member's current package (`DetailSource::package`) |
| junctions | made again for each version | once per graph | `junction_mesh::package_junctions` keyed by the shared graph |
| GPU index buffers | 32 bit | 16 bit below 65,536 vertices | `package::indices` (−10 – 13 % GPU mesh bytes; desktop too) |

Not done (no gain for its risk): the vertex colours as 4 bytes – the shaders read data from them (a road's half width in metres in the alpha, a building's material number), so 8-bit unorm cannot hold them and Bevy has no 16-bit float vertex values; the mesh allocator's slabs – WebGL 2 has no base vertex, so every mesh has its own vertex buffer there anyway.

**The module's size (v5.66, B7):** an iPhone compiles the whole wasm module before the first frame and keeps about four times its code in the web process, so the module was measured (`scripts/wasm-size.sh`: per build the sections, `twiggy top` / `dominators` and the code summed by crate; `scripts/wasm-size-rides.sh`, `scripts/wasm-size-preview-rides.sh`, `scripts/wasm-size-fps.sh`: sizes, the 5-minute WebKit rides and the uncapped frame rate in one go; `scripts/wasm-opt-compare.sh`: wasm-opt's pass sets on one module). What it was made of (`make web`'s WebGPU module, main at 7d15976d: 70.2 MiB of code, 16.9 MiB of data): `bevy_ecs` 22.2 MiB – generic system, query and observer code instantiated for every component and system –, `core` / `alloc` 8.4, `bevy_reflect` 3.5, `bevy_asset` 2.0, Avian 1.9, egui's CPU text rasteriser (`vello_cpu` with `fearless_simd`'s scalar fallback) 2.1, `bevy_color` 1.4, `ocw_render` 1.3 MiB; in the data 4.6 MiB of model files (221 `.glb`, `ocw-assets`' embedded library), 1.6 MiB of fonts (our Fira Mono, egui's Hack, Ubuntu Light and two emoji fonts, Bevy's ASCII subset), 1.4 MiB of type names, 0.9 MiB of shader sources, 0.7 MiB of tonemapping tables. Done:

- **Bevy's features pruned** (workspace `Cargo.toml`): instead of the `2d`, `3d` and `ui` sets the shared crates and the browser get an explicit list – the app, window, gamepad, 3D (render, core pipeline, lights, PBR, tonemapping tables with KTX2 / zstd), text and UI with UI picking. Gone from the browser: glTF loading and scenes (the models come from `ocw-assets`' own reader), animation and morph targets, gizmos, the anti-aliasing and post-processing passes (the renderer uses MSAA), the HDR and SMAA tables, mesh and sprite picking, states, UI widgets, the clipboard, custom cursors, the system-information diagnostics – and `webgl2` from the platform set, so the WebGPU build no longer carries wgpu's GL backend (it was as big as the WebGL 2 build). The desktop, OCW Studio and the spike name `2d`, `3d`, `ui` in their own `Cargo.toml` and keep every plugin; `ocw-render`'s test of the shipped models with Bevy's glTF loader takes `bevy_gltf` / `scene` as a dev-dependency. −11.3 MiB (WebGPU) / −9.1 MiB (WebGL 2) of `make web`'s modules, −7.0 / −5.2 MiB of the preview's before wasm-opt (−5.7 / −4.1 after it).
- **wasm-opt on every release build:** the build machines had no binaryen, so `make web` served its modules unoptimised (the module the WebKit tests measured was 83 MiB, the preview's 47); `scripts/build-web.sh` now takes the pinned binaryen of `scripts/fetch-binaryen.sh` for every non-dev build (passes as before: -Os, the preview -Oz). −9.7 / −10.0 MiB.

Measured and not done: **Bevy's reflection auto-registration** off saves 20 KB (kept); **panic = abort** is already what wasm32-unknown-unknown does (no unwinding); **opt-level and LTO** (WebGL 2, pruned, served / after `-Oz`): "s" with thin LTO 73.7 / 56.6 MiB, "s" with fat LTO and one codegen unit 59.8 / 49.1 (10 min per build instead of 4), "z" with fat LTO (the preview's) 51.4 / 43.4 – `make web` keeps "s" / thin for its build time, the preview keeps "z"; **wasm-opt's passes** on the preview's WebGL 2 module: `-Oz` 43.4 MiB, `-Oz --converge` 43.3 (+50 s), `-Os` 46.2, `-O3` 47.1 – `-Oz` stays; **WebAssembly SIMD** – built since v5.80 (below); **egui** (the console, both apps) and its fonts stay (parity); serde_json (0.4 MiB), clap (0.1) and regex (0.2) are used by shared code; the **model files** (4.6 MiB) stay embedded – fetching them would need an async preload in front of the synchronous, lazy `ModelLibrary` and keeps the same bytes in the heap until parsed, so it saves only the module's copy.

**WebAssembly SIMD (v5.80, Q10 (a)):** both builds are compiled with `+simd128` (the wasm32 rustflags in `.cargo/config.toml`; `scripts/build-web.sh` adds the flag to a RUSTFLAGS from the environment, which would replace them, checks every release build's cargo module with `scripts/wasm_features.py` (its `target_features` section must list `simd128`) and runs wasm-opt with `--enable-simd`; `sizes.txt` says `wasm features: +simd128`, and `scripts/web-preview-site.py` refuses a build without that line, so the Pages workflow can only publish SIMD builds – the WebXR build under `/xr/` too: `WEB_GPU=webxr` goes through the same check, and `--xr-build` is refused without the line). Before any module is fetched the page validates a 31-byte test module (a function returning a v128: `i32.const 0`, `i8x16.splat`, `i8x16.popcnt`; `ocwGpuChoice.simd` in `ocw-gpu.js`); without SIMD – Safari before 16.4, Chrome before 91, Firefox before 89 – the start page and every ride link show "This browser is too old for Open Cycling World – please update (Safari 16.4 / Chrome 91 / Firefox 89 or newer)" with the way to update an iPhone, and nothing else is loaded.
