Both builds run at the headless page's 60 Hz cap on this GPU, so the presets' saving does not show here (it is for weak GPUs and phones). In the same view the WebGL 2 Low picture differs as expected: the simple sky (plain blue instead of the atmosphere's haze), shadows only within 70 m (the near trees' shadows stay, the far ones go), no MSAA on the edges; terrain, road, trees, rider and HUD are the same. Without WebGPU, Chromium on marge still has `navigator.gpu` but gives no adapter: the page's fallback took the WebGL 2 build ("WebGPU without an adapter"). At a device pixel ratio of 2, Low drew the canvas at 1280 px for 1280 CSS px.

**Choices made here (proposals, for the user to confirm):** (1) **two builds chosen by the page** rather than one module (Bevy cannot switch at run time); the WebGL 2 module is only downloaded where WebGPU is missing. (2) **Degrade by run-time capability checks in the shared renderer**, never by cfg in the shared crates: the same code decides on a desktop GL adapter too. (3) **The presets' numbers** (table above) and **auto's rules** (WebGL 2 and phones Low, small devices Medium, desktop and WebGPU High): High is exactly the old look, so nobody's picture changes unless the device is weak. (4) **Trees: a draw distance instead of thinning or impostors** – thinning would leave invisible trees the server still collides with (14 Phase 12), and the ground's forest colour already stands in at a distance. (5) **The pixel-ratio cap only in the browser** (the desktop's window scale is the user's). (6) **The Graphics page under Display** with Quality, Sky and Fullscreen (Fullscreen moved there: the Display page had six rows). (7) **Levels of detail switch without fading on WebGL 2** (a Bevy limit; the alternative, patching Bevy's view layout, was not worth a fork).

**Open (B7):** the sensor bridge through the backend (Phase 5; the local bridge is built, v5.76); the Graphics page's Sky row shows the setting (`atmosphere`) on WebGL 2, where the simple sky is drawn (the console's `sky.mode` says so); WebGL 2 on real phones and tablets (Android Chrome with WebGPU off, Safari before 26, Firefox on Linux) and the 30 fps target there (10C) – the headless runs use a desktop GPU; the pixel-ratio cap was tested at a device pixel ratio of 2 in Chromium's emulation only; a cheaper tree mesh for Low (crowns with fewer faces) if the draw distance is not enough on phones; Bevy's 16-byte layout for the visibility ranges (an upstream fix would bring the LOD fade back to WebGL 2); the WebGL 2 module's size (only one module is downloaded; since v5.66 the WebGPU module is 1.6 – 1.9 MiB smaller, without wgpu's GL backend).


**Safari and iPhones (the user's report of 2026-11-15, v3.68).** On an iPhone 15 with iOS 26 the preview showed the loading screen and played the game sound but drew no image. Safari 26 (iOS 26, macOS 26) has WebGPU on by default, so the page loaded the WebGPU build; the app ran (sound from the frame loop) while nothing reached the canvas.

- **What was tried.** The Mac build machine has macOS 26.7.3 with Safari 26.6.2 (the same WebKit WebGPU as iOS 26), but no desktop session is logged in: Safari cannot start from ssh ("Launch failed … Domain does not support specified action"), neither can a `WKWebView` (its XPC services do not start), `safaridriver` needs `sudo safaridriver --enable`, and `screencapture` gets no display. So the WebGPU failure was **not reproduced** in Safari. WebKit itself was run through **Playwright's WebKit build** on marge (WebKit 27.2-era, no WebGPU on Linux, WebGL 2 through ANGLE): the preview's WebGL 2 build rides and draws there, on a desktop viewport and an emulated iPhone 15 (393 × 659, pixel ratio 3, touch). Known WebKit WebGPU bugs of the time fit the symptom: a regression that left views black in Safari 26.4 (WebKit bug 315186, fixed in May 2026), a device lost on `setPipeline` in Safari 26.1 / iOS 26 (Dear ImGui #9103), and a game engine falling back to WebGL on iOS 26 because WebGPU was unusable there. WebKit's own limits for Apple GPUs are not lower than what Bevy needs (11 bind groups, 44 storage buffers per stage, `rg11b10ufloat-renderable`, `float32-filterable`, `indirect-first-instance`), so a limit is not the likely cause. **The cause in our WebGPU path stays open** until it is seen in Safari (below).
- **The fix: the page's GPU choice and a watchdog** (`apps/web/web/ocw-gpu.js`, loaded by `index.html`; `window.ocwGpuChoice`): (1) `?gpu=webgl2` / `?gpu=webgpu` choose; (2) a WebGPU failure remembered in this browser (`localStorage` key `ocw.gpu.webgpu-failed`, with the user agent: a browser update tries WebGPU again; every read and write in try/catch) → WebGL 2; (3) **Safari's WebKit → WebGL 2** – found by `navigator.vendor` ("Apple Computer, Inc." in WebKit only) plus a narrow iOS check (iPhone / iPad / iPod in the user agent, or a "MacIntel" with touch points: iPadOS); every browser on iOS is WebKit; (4) a WebGPU adapter → WebGPU, else WebGL 2, else the message. With WebGPU the **watchdog** reports a failure when the device is lost or reports an uncaptured error (listeners added by wrapping `GPUAdapter.requestDevice`), `requestDevice` is refused, the module does not start, **Bevy's renderer reports an error** (the app's `RenderErrorHandler` no longer quits – Bevy's default, which left sound and a black canvas – but stops rendering and calls `window.ocwRenderFailed(kind, description)`), **no frame** is drawn after 20 s of a visible page once the module runs (frames counted by wrapping `GPUCanvasContext.getCurrentTexture`), or the canvas stays **one colour** in three samples 2 s apart once the ride shows (32 × 18 pixels read with `drawImage` in a microtask after the app's frame, before the browser presents it). Then the page remembers the failure and reloads the same ride with `gpu=webgl2&quality=low&webgpu-failed=1`; the WebGL 2 page shows a note for 12 s ("WebGPU failed in this browser (…) – using WebGL 2"). A forced `?gpu=webgpu` shows the error with a link to the WebGL 2 ride instead, and forgets a remembered failure once it draws; a WebGL 2 renderer error is shown too. The app accepts `webgpu-failed` as a page option.
- **Mobile.** The start page's *WebGL 2 with low graphics (phones, Safari, older GPUs)* box is pre-ticked where the page would take WebGL 2 anyway and on phones and tablets (unticked there, the ride link asks for `gpu=webgpu`), with a 44 px target; its browser line says "WebGPU (not used in Safari yet)". The page fills `100dvh` (mobile Safari's bars) and stays in the safe areas (no `viewport-fit=cover`). **The pixel-ratio cap does not work in WebKit:** winit sizes the canvas from `devicePixelContentBoxSize`, which WebKit lacks, so on the emulated iPhone the drawing buffer stayed at 1179 × 1977 while Low's override only shrank the HUD and menus to a third; the app now leaves the cap off where the browser has no `devicePixelContentBoxSize` (`usable_pixel_ratio_cap`), so an iPhone draws at its own 3× with a HUD of the right size (WebGL 2 Low; a real cap there needs a winit / Bevy change). Touch: menu pages take touch (3.2.2), but a ride has no touch overlay yet (M10) – there is no on-screen way to open the menu or change the power, so a phone rides with virtual power and autodrive.
- **Tests:** `make test-web-gpu` (`scripts/test-web-gpu.py`, headless Chromium with WebGPU; part of `make test-web-webgl2`): 38 checks of the rules as pure functions (Chrome, Safari on macOS, iPhone, iPad as a Mac, Chrome on iOS, Android; `?gpu=`; a remembered failure, an updated browser, a damaged entry, a storage that throws; no adapter, an adapter that throws, no WebGL 2; the fallback URL; the start page's box; the one-colour check), then the real app with **WebGPU failures injected** before the page's scripts (DevTools `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument`): an uncaptured validation error 6 s after the device exists (Bevy's renderer told the page, "Quitting the application" never logged), `requestDevice` refused, the canvas' `configure` refused (no frame) – each reloads on WebGL 2 with the note, remembers the failure, rides and draws; the remembered failure takes WebGL 2 without `gpu=`; `?gpu=webgpu` draws, passes the watchdog and forgets the failure; a healthy WebGPU ride raises no alarm; an iPhone's Safari (user agent, `navigator.vendor`, touch, pixel ratio 3) with Chromium's WebGPU adapter rides on WebGL 2 and draws. `make test-web-webkit` (`scripts/test-web-webkit.py`, Playwright's WebKit from `make deps-webkit`: a venv in `~/.cache/ocw/playwright-venv`, Playwright 1.65.2, no sudo) gives WebKit Safari 26's `navigator.gpu` with an adapter: an iPhone 15's start page (box ticked, finger-sized) and ride, Safari on macOS – WebGL 2 without asking for an adapter, rides and draws, canvas fills the viewport, no cap. Native: `render_errors_go_to_the_page`, `the_pixel_ratio_is_capped` (the WebKit case). `scripts/test-web-safari.py` drives the **real Safari** over `safaridriver` (W3C WebDriver, no packages): the page's GPU choice, the watchdog's state, a screenshot; `--gpu webgpu` forces Safari's WebGPU – the way to find the cause.
- **Fixed (v5.39): the restarts on an iPhone** (the user's report of 2026-11-22: iPhone 15, iOS 26, Safari and Firefox tabs; the ride's picture shows for a moment, then the page starts again). **Cause (found in WebKit, not seen on the phone):** iOS Safari loads a tab again when its WebContent process was killed; two ways our page got there: (a) after a **lost WebGL context** wgpu's GL backend went on rendering into nothing and never freed a frame's buffers – the wasm memory grew by ~45 MB a second (Hills: 224 MB → 3.9 GB, then a wasm trap; `test-output/web-ios/baseline/`) – and iOS loses a page's context when its GPU process is short of memory or the page goes to the background; (b) the **big worlds' memory** on a phone profile (Low, WebGL 2, 1179 × 1977 px): Liechtenstein 477 MB wasm + 355 MB GPU, Tenerife 653 + 245, Black Forest north 856 + 640 – the GPU part arrives in the seconds after the first frames, at or over what iOS gives a tab together with the compiled module. Our own reload paths did not loop: the WebGPU watchdog (and its one-colour canvas sample, which does read one colour, rgb 0 0 0, from WebKit's WebGL 2 canvas outside a frame) runs on WebGPU only, and every iOS browser (Safari, CriOS, FxiOS, EdgiOS) takes WebGL 2. **Fix:** `webglcontextlost` → `window.ocw.gpuLost()` stops the app (`AppExit`), the page loads the ride again once it is visible – at most once in ten minutes per tab, else a message with *Load the ride again* / *Rides*; the WebGPU fallback at most once and never from WebGL 2 or a fallback page (`ocwGpuChoice.mayFallBack`); a ride whose page was killed (no pagehide; `lastRideDied`, sessionStorage) rides on with `memory=saver&quality=low` and a note, and the second time the page stops with the reason instead of loading it again; phones and tablets ride in the **Phone memory mode** (`apps/web/src/memory.rs`: 3 × 3 meshed tiles through `ocw_render::package::StreamRadiusCap`, fetch 2 / keep 3 rings, 48 MB of tiles; `saver`: fetch 1 / keep 2, 32 MB; `memory=normal|phone|saver|auto`), desktops unchanged. Measured (WebKit, iPhone 15 profile, Low, 4 – 5 min rides; wasm peak + GPU meshes + textures, before → after): Hills 258 → 205 MB (and after a lost context flat at 166 MB instead of 3.9 GB), Liechtenstein 832 → 624 (GPU 355 → 156), Tenerife 898 → 767 (GPU 245 → 130), Black Forest north 1,499 → 1,165 (GPU 640 → 322); the wasm peak of the world's start (Black Forest north 843 MB while its live heap is 360 MB later) is untouched and the next cut for phones (`test-output/web-ios/baseline/`, `after/`, `live/` – the live site, also clean). **To check on the phone:** Safari's text if it shows one ("A problem repeatedly occurred …" = the tab was killed), whether the Hills test route restarts too (it needs ~260 MB: if it does, the cause is not the world's memory), and Safari's Web Inspector console through a Mac (the page logs "the WebGL context was lost" / "the page before died in the ride").
- **Fixed (v5.46): the iPhone dying in every ride, the test routes too** (the user's report of 2026-11-23: iPhone 15, iOS 26, Safari and Firefox on the live page with v5.39; the page died even on the Loop test route, and after the death v5.39's note "The page was closed in the ride (probably for memory) – riding on with less detail" showed and it died again). **Measured** in WebKit with the iPhone 15 profile, now with every WebGL allocation counted (`scripts/test-web-ios.py` hooks the context's textures, renderbuffers and buffers and adds the canvas: what iOS counts against the tab besides the wasm memory; before, only the app's own meshes and images were summed): the Loop route took 323 MB (wasm 176 + WebGL 143, a peak of 238 MB of WebGL in the first two seconds) and WebKit's web process 1.2 GB (311 MB empty, 400 MB with the start page, +210 MB for compiling the 50 MB module). Causes, each world or none: (1) the first frames rendered at Bevy's default window of 1280 × 720 at the iPhone's pixel ratio 3 – three 3840 × 2160 targets of 31.6 MB; (2) WebKit (every iOS browser) has no `devicePixelContentBoxSize`, so the Low preset's pixel-ratio cap never applied there and every screen-sized target was 1179 × 1977 (four of 8.9 MB and the canvas' 18 MB); (3) Bevy's point-light shadow cube (1024² × 6, 24 MB) is allocated although no light of ours casts a point shadow, the sun's map was 2048² (16 MB); (4) each ride photo rendered at 2560 × 1440 into five targets and a read-back buffer (85 MB of WebGL and 42 MB more wasm memory for a moment, Hills); (5) in the worlds the base's per-tile parts for the whole package (Tenerife: buildings 37 MB, vegetation 30, seasons 23, forest 12, obstacles 12, the land use 75 encoded, the ride's obstacles 33) and its decode from a joined copy of all chunks, the 3 × 3 urgent tiles built at once (14 – 28 MB each until uploaded), meshed tiles kept up to two rings beyond the wanted ones (up to 25 instead of 9), and the trees: half a forested tile's GPU memory (Black Forest: 11 of 21 MB). **Fix (phones and tablets; desktops unchanged):** the window starts at the page's CSS size (`initial_resolution`); the page tells the app a `devicePixelRatio` of 1.5 on WebKit phones (1 in the saver and minimal modes; `?pixel-ratio=` chooses; `ocwGpuChoice.pixelRatioCap`) – the canvas keeps its CSS size; the sun's shadow map 1024² (`quality::ShadowMapCap`), the point-light cube 16²; photos at 1280 × 720 (`photographer::PhotoSize`); one tile meshed at a time, none kept beyond the wanted 3 × 3 (`package::TileBuildPace::PHONE`); every second tree (`package::PlantThinning`); the base decoded chunk by chunk (`StreamedPackage::from_chunks`) and its per-tile parts kept only within the residency's rings + 1 of the course – along the route, or 8 rings around a free ride's start – cut while it is decoded (`from_chunks_kept`, `world::course_tiles`, `StreamConfig::keep`; beyond the course a free ride has no houses, trees or obstacles, the tiles' terrain and roads stay); a **memory guard** (`memory::MemoryGuard`: 450 MB phone, 400 saver, 350 minimal) at 85 % keeps only the tiles around the rider and the smallest shadow map, at 95 % no ring beyond the rider's and a third of the trees, logged and printed in the console; **each death one step further** (`ocwGpuChoice.nextMemoryStep`): the first time `memory=saver`, the second `memory=minimal` (one ring of tiles fetched and kept, 512² shadows, pixel ratio 1, a third of the trees), the third time the page stops with the reason and the links – never a loop; the start page says on phones why to start with a test route (the first phone visit loads nothing big: the start page lists the test routes first); Bevy without its unused `audio` feature (−0.85 MB of code). `window.ocw.heap()` now also gives the main world's image and mesh copies, the biggest images and a heap trace by frame and stage (`heap::mark`). **Measured after** (WebKit, iPhone 15 profile, 5-minute rides with the page hidden every minute and, in the worlds, a teleport 3 km further every minute; Every ride rode 5 minutes and drew, without a reload or a page error; the lost context (stops, loads once, then a message) and three emulated deaths (saver, minimal, then the reason) as wanted (Loop); the page draws 590 × 989 instead of 1179 × 1977 and runs at two to three times the frame rate in WebKit. Screenshots after 5 minutes: `test-output/web-ios-phone/after/` (index.md). **Open:** the test routes (Loop, Hills) stay at about 235 MB of the 200 MB target – 178 MB of wasm memory (a heap of 116 MB, 40 MB more for the first four frames, by the trace in Bevy's first extract and prepare – shader and pipeline building – and the main world's first text and UI pass; 18 MB of static data), 60 MB of WebGL (text atlases 16 MB, meshes 15 MB, screen targets and canvas 9 MB at 1.5); Tenerife and the Black Forest stay 30 – 50 MB over at the end of the ride and 80 – 130 MB at their peaks: the wasm memory keeps the start's highest mark (the base's 104 / 146 MB of chunks are all fetched before the decode, and the allocator leaves 60 – 110 MB over the heap's own peak) and a teleport holds old and new tiles on the GPU for a moment (Black Forest: 153 → 248 MB). Next: decode the base's chunks as they arrive, the start's pipelines in fewer frames, and fewer text atlas sizes. WebKit's own process (1.2 – 1.5 GB RSS on Linux, of which ~200 MB compile the module) is not measured on the phone: the 50 MB module (35.6 MB code, 13.8 MB data) is the next cut there – Bevy's features pruned workspace-wide.
- **Open (B7, Safari):** the cause in Safari's WebGPU – needs the Mac's desktop logged in and `sudo safaridriver --enable` once, then `scripts/remote.sh macos run 'scripts/test-web-safari.py --gpu webgpu'` (after the next deployment, or with `--url` on a local server); or the iPhone itself with Safari's Web Inspector through a Mac (Settings → Safari → Advanced → Web Inspector; on the Mac Safari → Develop → the iPhone), the console shows the watchdog's reason on `?route=hills&gpu=webgpu`. Then WebGPU for Safari can come back behind an adapter check like `ocw-render::webgl`'s. A working pixel-ratio cap in WebKit; a HUD laid out for a phone's width (at 393 CSS pixels its top line wraps over a third of the view and the Devices panel covers the bottom – `test-output/web/web-webkit-20261115-160056-iphone.png`); the ride's touch overlay (M10); the 30 fps target on a real iPhone (WebGL 2, 3× pixels).


**The page log (v6.67, B7 / B8a):** a rider whose phone does not run the app has no console to look at (an iPhone's Safari console needs a Mac and a cable, Android's `chrome://inspect` a computer), so the page keeps its own log and shows it on the screen.

- **Capture from the first line:** `apps/web/web/ocw-log.js` is the page's first script (before `ocw-gpu.js`, the module and the wasm). It wraps `console.log / info / warn / error / debug` (the line is recorded, then the browser's console called as before) and listens for uncaught errors (message, file:line:column, stack), failed loads of scripts and images (the capture phase of `error`), unhandled promise rejections, CSP violations and the page's life (hidden / shown, pagehide, back/forward cache, freeze, online / offline); every 15 s while the app runs it notes the wasm memory (and Chrome's JS heap) when it changed by 8 MB or more. The app's Rust lines come in through the same console: Bevy's `tracing-wasm` writes `%cINFO%c file.rs:12%cmessage` with `console.log` (the styles are dropped, the level kept: `rs file.rs:12 message`), its panic hook `console.error`. Each line is `+SECONDS LEVEL text` with the seconds since the page started (E error, W warning, I info, L log, D debug, ! uncaught / a failed load, P the page).
- **Cheap when it is off:** a ring buffer of the last 2,000 lines (lines over 4,000 characters cut); the panel is not built until it is shown. The lines are also kept in **sessionStorage** (this tab; written at most every 1.5 s, at once when the page is hidden or closed; at most 700,000 characters per load, the page's own keys keep their room; every access in try / catch): the next load moves them to *the page load before* and says whether it ended normally (pagehide) or not (the browser killed the page – iOS does that when a page uses too much memory – or it crashed). So a reload after a crash shows the log of the run that crashed.
- **Opening it:** `?log=1` in the address; **five taps within 3 s on the version stamp** (the app's build id, bottom right) or on the start page's *Build …* line – no URL editing on a phone; once open it stays open over reloads (sessionStorage) until *Hide*. Without either, a **Show log** button appears by itself when the page shows an error (the status's class `error`: too old, no WebGPU / WebGL 2, the module or the wasm did not load, a renderer failure, the ride stopped after repeated crashes, the public server unreachable) or the loading screen stays for 45 s.
- **The panel:** translucent, at the top of the screen inside the safe areas (58 % of the height, *↕* the whole height), scrollable, 12 px monospace, finger-sized buttons (40 px), touches stay in it (no steering): **Copy** (the Clipboard API; else the text in a selected box for `execCommand("copy")` or the phone's own Copy), **Share** (the Web Share API, e.g. iOS's share sheet: a `.txt` file where files can be shared, else the text; hidden where there is no Web Share), **Download** (`ocw-log-DATE-TIME.txt`), **Clear** (this load and the one before), **Hide**.
- **The environment header** (built when shown or copied and renewed every 3 s while shown; the GPU facts asked once): the page's start time; the page build (config.json `build`, channel) and the app's build id (from its start line); the address with its query – secret-looking keys (token, code, state, bridge, name, password, …) as `(hidden)`, and the same patterns scrubbed from every line (`access_token=…`, `?code=…`, `Bearer …`, the app's `name = …;` fields), and the build machine's home folder in the app's source paths shortened (`cargo:bevy_…`, `~/…`); user agent, platform (and User-Agent Client Hints), touch points, language; the screen, window, pixel ratio (and the one the page draws at), orientation, home-screen start; device memory, cores, the JS heap and the wasm memory; WebAssembly, SIMD, threads (SharedArrayBuffer and cross-origin isolation); WebGPU (the adapter's vendor / architecture / device, fallback adapter, limits; 4 s at most) and WebGL 2 (unmasked vendor and renderer, maximum texture size; its context released at once); the backend the page chose and why, a remembered GPU failure, the lost-context state; frames, riding, online, Web Bluetooth; the line counts and the levels.
- **Old browsers:** the file is plain ES2017 (no optional chaining, no `??`), so "this browser is too old" can still show its log.
- **Tests:** `make test-web-log` (`scripts/test-web-log.py`, Playwright): WebKit as an iPhone 15 and Chromium as an Android phone (412 × 915, ratio 2.625) – `?log=1` shows the panel before the wasm, the header's facts, the page's and the app's lines without styles, a `console.error`, an uncaught error with its file:line and an unhandled rejection, the panel on the screen with finger-sized buttons, Copy (Chromium: read back from the clipboard; WebKit: copied or selected), Download (the same text), Share only where the browser has it, the ring buffer at 2,600 lines, a reload with *the page load before* (closed normally), Clear, Hide (and a load without `?log=1` builds nothing); a load whose pagehide never comes (as when the browser kills the page; Playwright cannot go on after a real renderer crash): the next load's *page load before* ended without pagehide and has its last line, in both browsers; five taps on the version stamp; *Show log* with the cause on the too-old screen (no SIMD), with the wasm blocked ("Start failed") and (Android) without WebGPU and WebGL 2. **Measured (marge, 2026-11-26):** 84 of 84 checks passed (Playwright's WebKit 27.2 as the iPhone, Chromium 157 as the Android phone; `test-output/web-log/web-log-20261126-234258*`).

**Bisecting a phone's crash (v6.74, B7):** the user's iPhone (iOS 18.7, Firefox for iOS 157.1 – WebKit, Safari 18's engine; 430 × 932 at 3, 4 cores, WebAssembly SIMD, no threads) lost the page three times in a row on `?route=hills&gpu=webgl2&quality=low` – the test route, no world package, Low, pixel ratio 1, the last time with `memory=minimal` – within about 2 s of the first frames and without a pagehide; the page then said "This ride stopped 3 times". The last line the log had kept (written every 1.5 s) was Bevy's note that `see_through.wesl` has an unresolved import `bevy_pbr::render::mesh_bindings`, at +1.54 s; at +0.77 s an "uncaught Script error." without a file. So it dies while the first pipelines compile and the first frames draw (WebKit on iOS 18: WebGL through ANGLE on Metal), not of world memory. There is no iOS device or Simulator here, so the proof comes from the phone: switches in the address each turn off one suspect, the early log shows how far a load got, and the obvious suspects are fixed for every browser.

- **The switches** (`apps/web/src/bisect.rs`, `ocw_render::switches`; `=0` turns one off again, unknown values are ignored with a warning, the log names what is on: "bisect switches: …", "render switches: …"): `nosee=1` the trees' see-through shader (Bevy's standard shaders instead: no fade, sway or snow), `noarrays=1` the texture-array shaders of road, ground, houses and gear (their base colours with the standard shaders), `plain=1` every material shader of ours (water and the far terrain too), `noshadow=1` all shadow maps, `nomsaa=1` multisampling on every camera, `nosky=1` the cloud dome and the night sky (the simplest sky), `noegui=1` egui (the console's overlay; the commands still run, `window.ocw.console`), `novoice=1` voice (the page loads no LiveKit SDK, the Voice page says why), `noaudio=1` the game sound (no Web Audio), `pipelines=serial` one render pipeline started per frame (`=N` N per frame, `=all` all at once), `frames=N` the cameras stop drawing after N frames (`0`: none is drawn – the app runs without compiling the scene's pipelines), and **`ios=safe`** all of them but `frames`. The shader switches make the material extensions return Bevy's default shaders (`MaterialExtension::*_shader` read a flag set before the plugins are added), so the materials, their bind groups and every system stay the same.
- **The pipeline budget and log (`vendor/bevy_render`, a small patch of 0.20.1 through `[patch.crates-io]`; `vendor/README.md`):** `PipelineCache::compile_budget` lets at most N pipelines start compiling per frame (the oldest first; one waiting for a shader or an import does not count) and `PipelineCache::compile_log` reports every attempt (label, shader, ms, outcome, how many still wait). WebGL 2 compiles and links each program on the page's thread, all of a frame's at once before; now the WebGL 2 build starts **4 per frame** by default (`bisect::WEBGL2_BUDGET`; the desktop and WebGPU unchanged, `pipelines=` overrides). The browser logs every compile for 30 s, later only those over 50 ms and failures: "pipeline 12 ok in 85 ms: pbr_opaque_mesh_pipeline (embedded://ocw_render/road.wesl), 4 more queued".
- **The unresolved import** is not an error: Bevy loads `mesh_bindings.wesl` as an asset when its mesh plugin finishes (its shader defs depend on the device), and a pipeline tried before that answers `ShaderImportNotYetAvailable` and is tried again in a later frame – the log now shows "pipeline N waits for a shader or import", then "pipeline N ok", and the page log marks Bevy's warning as such. `nosee=1` takes the shader out altogether.
- **The early log** (`ocw-log.js`, the first 15 s): every line goes to sessionStorage at once (before, at most every 1.5 s – a kill took the last second and a half with it); the first 30 frames with their times and every frame of 250 ms or more after; the memory every 100 ms (wasm, the JS heap where the browser has `performance.memory`, the frames), logged when it moved by 1 MB or a second passed, and each sample with the last line into its own small key (`ocw.log.pulse`): the next load's title of *the page load before* says "last sign of life at +2.9 s (wasm … MB, frames …)" (`ocwLog.state().previous_pulse`).
- **"Script error."** is what a browser shows for an error of a script from another origin. Every script of the page now loads with `crossorigin="anonymous"` (the tags and the scripts loaded later; GitHub Pages sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`), so the page's own errors keep their message and stack; one without a file is marked as most likely the browser's own (Firefox and Chrome for iOS inject scripts into every page).
- **Fixed for every browser:** the pipelines paced on WebGL 2 (above); **LiveKit's SDK (~500 kB of JavaScript) is loaded only when a voice room is joined** (`ocwVoice` loads `window.ocwVoiceSdk` on its first `connect`), not with every page that has a voice server – a solo ride never fetches or parses it.
- **Tests:** `bisect::tests` (each switch alone, `ios=safe` and a later `=0`, the pipelines' pace, bad values), `switches::tests` (the default changes nothing, the names, the compile line, shadows / MSAA / frames on a scene); `make test-web-bisect` (`scripts/test-web-bisect.py`, Playwright): WebKit as the reporting iPhone (430 × 932 at 3, Firefox for iOS's user agent) and Chromium as an Android phone ride the Hills on WebGL 2 at Low with every switch – it draws, no page error, the log has the pipeline compiles, the frame times and the memory samples, the early lines are in sessionStorage at once, the switched-off shaders never compile, no LiveKit SDK is fetched, a killed load's last sign of life; the README's *Something doesn't work on my phone* lists the links to tap on the phone.
- **The finding (the user's iPhone, 2026-11-27, build ac614c0, v6.83):** `?route=hills&gpu=webgl2&quality=low&log=1` with everything on: all 24 pipelines compiled by 3.5 s (wasm 143 MB), frame 18 drawn at 3.52 s – the first full frame – then the page was gone without a pagehide, three times in a row, also on the automatic retries with `memory=saver` and `memory=minimal`. `ios=safe` rode; **`noshadow=1` alone rode** (everything else on: see-through, texture arrays, clouds, egui, pixel ratio 1.5; 300 frames, the memory flat at 143 MB); `noarrays=1` and `plain=1` (only Bevy's standard materials, shadows on) closed right after the last pipeline (`clouds.wesl`) and the first full frames (last sign of life +4.1 – 4.2 s, wasm 142 – 143 MB); `nosky=1` closed once (+3.8 s, wasm 139 MB, 37 frames, pixel ratio 1) and rode on the `memory=saver` retry (300 frames, ~30 fps, shadows on). So the **directional light's shadow pass** decides, and it looks **memory-bound** (the tab's total with the GPU's allocations, which the wasm number does not show): with shadows on only the simplest sky plus the saver mode survived. The shadow map drawn there was **1024²** (a phone's memory cap, `ShadowMapCap`; one cascade over 70 m, `Depth32Float`, 4 MB) – the quality line said 2048², the preset's number, and now names the map as drawn.
- **Why the shadow pass, the candidates (not proven; no iOS device here):** the shadow map itself is small, but on WebGL 2 Bevy's shadow prepass emulates unclipped depth in its fragment shader (`depth_clip_control` is missing), so every caster in the cascade (the cascade's box reaches far towards the sun: terrain, trees, houses) is drawn once more with a fragment shader into a `Depth32Float` target, and the main pass samples it with the 9-tap Gaussian filter (`ShadowFilteringMethod::Gaussian`, 9 comparison samples per pixel) – a big first frame for a tile-based GPU behind ANGLE on Metal, and with it the memory of the extra pass (WebKit's GPU process keeps the command buffers and the depth texture's Metal copy). A 16-bit depth format would need a patched `bevy_pbr` (`CORE_3D_SHADOW_MAP_FORMAT` is a constant) and the map already is a plain 2D texture on WebGL 2 (one layer, a `D2` view), so neither is a switch.
- **Default now (v6.83):** on iOS / iPadOS WebKit (`ocw_client::quality::is_ios_webkit`: `iPhone`, `iPad` or `iPod` in the user agent, or a `Macintosh` agent / the `MacIntel` platform with more than one touch point – iPadOS asking for desktop pages; every browser there, Safari, Firefox, Chrome, is WebKit) with the WebGL 2 build the **shadows are off** (`Bisect::platform_defaults`, the same as `noshadow=1`), logged as "shadows off on iOS WebKit with WebGL 2: the shadow pass closed the page on an iPhone (iOS 18.7); noshadow=0 or shadowmap=N turns them on"; the quality line says "shadows off (iOS WebKit with WebGL 2: …)" and Settings → Display → Graphics has a *Shadows: off on iOS (WebGL 2)* row with the reason in the page's text. iOS WebKit also starts in the **saver memory mode** (`memory::MemoryMode::resolve`: fetch 1, keep 2, 32 MB of tiles, the guard at 400 MB; pixel ratio stays 1.5 – `noshadow=1` rode at 1.5; `memory=phone` chooses the phone's). **WebGPU on iOS is not used by default** (`ocw-gpu.js` rule 3: Safari's WebGPU → WebGL 2, – WebKit with a `navigator.gpu`, as on that iPhone, whose log reports an adapter – takes WebGL 2 without asking for one), so a link without `gpu=webgl2` rides the same WebGL 2 build with the same defaults; with `gpu=webgpu` the shadows stay on (untested there). Android, desktops and Safari on a Mac are unchanged.
- **Test switches (v6.83):** `noshadow=0` turns the shadows on again (at the phone's 1024²); **`shadowmap=N`** (256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096) turns them on with a sun map of at most N² (it replaces the memory mode's cap; one cascade on WebGL 2 anyway; logged "shadow map: N² at most (shadowmap=N; 1 cascade on WebGL 2)"); **`shadowfix=`** `hw2x2` (the cameras filter with `ShadowFilteringMethod::Hardware2x2`: one hardware comparison sample) and/or `near` (one cascade over 30 m instead of 70: fewer casters drawn into the map), comma-separated – each only a test, a default only after the phone confirms.
- **The GPU memory in the page log (v6.83):** `vendor/bevy_render` counts every texture and buffer created through its `Texture` / `Buffer` wrappers while it lives (`render_resource::gpu_allocated`: bytes of all mips, layers and samples; render targets, depth and shadow maps, uniform buffers, mesh slabs and images alike – the asset sums of `gpu_memory` missed the targets and the maps); the app logs "gpu allocated 61 MB (textures 48 MB in 120, buffers 13 MB in 300; peak 70 MB)" whenever the total moved by 8 MB, `window.ocw.gpuAllocated()` gives the JSON, and the page log's memory samples add "gpu ~N MB (renderer N MB, canvas N MB)" (the canvas: about two colour buffers and a depth buffer of its size) and the pulse keeps it for *the page load before*. An estimate: the driver's padding and the browser's own share are not in it.
- **Tests (v6.83):** `quality::tests::ios_webkit_is_every_browser_on_iphone_and_ipad` (Safari, Firefox, Chrome on iPhone and iPad, iPadOS's desktop agent; a Mac, Android, Windows and Linux are not), `bisect::tests` (the iOS default, `noshadow=0`, `shadowmap=N`, `shadowfix`, bad values), `switches::tests` (`shadowfix` on the cameras and the sun), `memory::tests` (iOS starts in the saver mode), `ocw_ui::quality` (the quality line with a capped map and with the shadows off), `ocw_ui::menu` (the Graphics row), `gpu_memory::tests` (the vendored count of a texture, the log line); `make test-web-bisect` (the iPhone with Firefox for iOS's agent rides without shadows by default in the saver mode; `noshadow=0`, `shadowmap=512&noshadow=0`, `shadowmap=1024`, `shadowfix=hw2x2,near&noshadow=0` ride with shadows as asked; Android keeps its shadows; every ride logs the GPU allocations), `make test-web-webkit` (iPhone: shadows off; Safari on a Mac: on), `make test-web-log` (the GPU lines; the iOS line only on the iPhone). Measured on marge, 2026-11-27: `make test-web-bisect` 281 / 281, `make test-web-webkit` 102 / 102, `make test-web-log` 88 / 88; the renderer allocated about 63 MB at the start on Android's Chromium (textures 48 MB in 51, buffers 15 MB in 551; the canvas ~30 MB more) and about 40 MB in WebKit at the iPhone's size without shadows (textures 25 MB).
- **Measured (marge, 2026-11-27, `make test-web-bisect`: 195 / 195 checks; WebKit with the reporting iPhone's size, the Hills at Low on WebGL 2, `test-output/web-bisect/`):** the start compiles 26 pipelines (15 with `ios=safe`); each of Bevy's PBR main-pass pipelines takes 160 – 205 ms to compile and link in WebKit (ours: `see_through.wesl` 170 ms, `gear.wesl` ~110 ms; prepass, UI and egui 2 – 30 ms), 2.0 s in all – before, all of them in one frame. Every PBR pipeline of the first frame waits one round for Bevy's `mesh_bindings` (not only the trees'; Bevy warns once, for the first shader it meets), then compiles. With 4 per frame the longest frame of the start was 1.2 s, with `pipelines=serial` 0.67 s, with `ios=safe` 0.73 s; wasm memory 147 – 156 MB a few seconds in. `make test-web-log` 84 / 84, `make test-web-webkit` 99 / 99.

**B8a – Public preview on GitHub Pages: built (v3.45).** <https://newkit.github.io/OCW/> serves a solo preview of the browser app: a start page with the Hills and Loop test routes and Liechtenstein (Vaduz – Malbun, a free ride), virtual power or a trainer over Web Bluetooth in Chromium; multiplayer, voice and sign-in are off with the note "coming in the hosted version" (stage 2).

- **Size-optimised build (`make web-preview`, `scripts/build-web.sh --preview`):** both modules into `target/web-preview/` with the profile **`web-preview-release`** (the `web-release` profile with `opt-level = "z"`, fat LTO, one codegen unit) and **`wasm-opt -Oz`** from a pinned binaryen (`scripts/fetch-binaryen.sh`: version_133 from GitHub, SHA-256-checked, into `~/.cache/ocw/tools/`; Debian's binaryen is too old), the `preview` feature of `ocw-web`, no LiveKit SDK. `make web` keeps its profile and output; `WEB_WASM_OPT` chooses other passes (`off`: none).
- **Measured (marge, 2026-11-15, the WebGPU module; MiB, gzip -9 / brotli -q 11):**

| Build | raw | gzip | brotli | build (one module) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `web-release` (`make web`, thin LTO, "s") | 76.3 | 17.0 | 10.7 | ~6 min |
| `web-release` + `wasm-opt -Oz` | 56.8 | 17.2 | 11.0 | |
| fat LTO, one codegen unit, "s" | 59.9 | 14.3 | 9.2 | 15.7 min |
| … + `wasm-opt -Oz` / `-Os` / `-O3` | 48.0 / 53.9 / 54.8 | 15.1 / 15.3 / 15.4 | 9.8 / 9.8 / 9.9 | |
| **fat LTO, one codegen unit, "z"** | 51.0 | **12.6** | **8.5** | 12.6 min |
| **… + `wasm-opt -Oz` (the preview)** / `-Os` / `-O3` | **42.2** / 45.4 / 46.4 | **13.2** / 13.3 / 13.4 | **8.8** / 8.8 / 8.9 | + ~2 min |

  `wasm-opt` shrinks the raw module by 17–25 % but makes the compressed one 2–5 % larger (it removes the padded LEB128 numbers and the repetition that gzip and brotli thrive on). The preview keeps `-Oz`: the raw size is what the browser compiles and holds in memory, the extra download is 0.6 MiB. The frame rate (headless Chromium on marge's GPU, Hills with 30 bots, two runs each while other builds ran) did not separate "s" from "z" or `-Oz` from `-O3` (37–58 fps, all within the noise of a loaded machine); 10C's budget (≤ 30 MB compressed) holds with 13.2 MiB.
- **The preview's signing root:** a separate root and the signing key `web-preview-2026` (two years), made with `world-builder keys`, kept on marge in `~/.config/ocw/preview-keys/` (mode 700, outside every checkout; never in the repository, CI or a log). Its public key (key id `0e304f1125d98d87`) is `crates/ocw-worldstore/keys/preview-roots.json` (`ocw_worldstore::trust::preview_roots`). With the `preview` feature, `WorldOptions::trust_store` puts the preview roots **in place of** the production roots; the dev trust options (`trust=dev`, `trust-root`, `allow-unsigned`) stay localhost-only, so on the public page only packages signed under the preview root load, and no unsigned ones.
- **The worlds:** `scripts/publish-preview-worlds.sh [--upload] [PKG…]` (`make web-preview-worlds`, on marge) signs a staged copy of `liechtenstein.ocwpkg` (version 3, 87.6 MB) with the preview key, publishes it, verifies it against the preview root (`world-builder verify --no-dev-root`), writes flat release assets (`liechtenstein-3.ocwpkg`, `liechtenstein-3.manifest.json`, `liechtenstein.latest`, `preview-worlds.json` with layout, routes and SHA-256s, `SHA256SUMS`) and uploads them to the pre-release **`web-preview-worlds`**. The workflow downloads them (no secret in CI) and copies them into the site, so ranges and CORS of release downloads do not matter; GitHub Pages answers range requests (206) itself.
- **Page configuration** (`config.json` next to `index.html`, read before the module starts, `window.ocwConfig`; `ocw_web::page_config`): `worlds` (the worlds' base), `server`, `voice`, `signin` (a missing key changes nothing; an empty one means "none": on a public page `?server=` is ignored with a warning and voice says "voice chat is coming in the hosted version"), `channel` and `start` (the start page's rides) for the page. `make web` writes `channel: dev`. The preview's page shows the start page when no ride option is given (nothing big is fetched before a choice), a line in the ride (Rides · Credits · "Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors" for worlds) and loads LiveKit only where voice is on.
- **Credits and privacy (`credits.html`, written by `scripts/web-preview-site.py`):** each world's attribution from its manifest (OpenStreetMap ODbL; swissALTI3D and SRTM for Liechtenstein; the orthophotos; Copernicus Sentinel-2 and the HRL forest layers), the **road graph as an ODbL Derivative Database** with links to the package on the site and on the release and to its format (4.7), the generated models, Fira Mono (OFL, its text in `licenses/`), the desktop's CC0 textures (the browser draws flat colours), the Rust crates in the module with their licences (`cargo metadata`), and the privacy note (no tracking, no cookies, no other servers; settings in `localStorage`; worlds cached in the browser's storage; Bluetooth only through the browser's chooser; GitHub Pages' own logs). LiveKit is not included in the preview.
- **Site assembly (`make web-preview-site`):** the build, `worlds/` in the publish layout (SHA-256-checked against `preview-worlds.json`), `config.json`, `credits.html`, `.nojekyll`, `site.txt`; it fails over 1 GB. The site of 2026-11-15: 176.6 MB (the two modules 44.2 + 44.1 MB, Liechtenstein 87.6 MB, the rest a few hundred kB) of the 1 GB; `make web-preview` built both modules in 823 s on marge.
- **Download sizes on the start page (asked by the user 2026-11-15, v3.51):** every ride card has a line with what its first visit downloads and how long it takes at 50 Mbit/s (`size` in `config.json`, drawn below the text): the app (the larger gzipped wasm module plus its JS, as Pages serves it) for the test routes; app plus the world package for world rides, "up to", since the package is streamed while riding. Everything is cached for the next visit (OPFS). `scripts/test_web_scripts.py` (`PreviewRideSizes`).
- **Workflow `.github/workflows/web-preview.yml`:** on GitHub's runner: free disk, toolchain, `rust-cache`, `make deps-web`, `scripts/fetch-binaryen.sh`, `make web-preview`, `cargo metadata`, `gh release download web-preview-worlds`, the site, `actions/upload-pages-artifact` + `actions/deploy-pages`. Triggers: by hand (`workflow_dispatch`) and weekly (Monday 04:17 UTC), both on `main` – the `github-pages` environment deploys only from `main`. Pages is enabled for the repository with the build type "workflow".
- **Tests:** `page_config` (the preview's config, missing keys change nothing, bad configs refused, applied to the page options: no `?server=` and the voice note on a public page, everything on localhost), `the_preview_trusts_only_its_root_on_public_pages` (the built-in store is exactly the preview root; the dev options ignored on a public page; a stand-in preview root's packages accepted, another root's and unsigned ones refused; localhost keeps the dev options; the dev build does not trust the preview root), `a_page_without_voice_says_why`, the trust lists. **`make test-web-preview`** (`scripts/test-web-preview.py`): the assembled site served as a *public* page (host `ocw-preview.test` mapped to 127.0.0.1 and treated as a secure origin) or the live site (`PREVIEW_URL=…`) in the pinned Chromium: start page, Hills, Liechtenstein from the preview root, the dev trust options ignored, the WebGL 2 fallback, the credits page, and no response ≥ 400. Run on marge (2026-11-15, the assembled site as a public page; `test-output/web-preview/preview-20261115-100036*`): all six checks passed – the start page with 4 rides and no module fetched; Hills ticking and riding (1.6 km); Liechtenstein ready in 6.0 s, 15.4 MB from the network, "trust: signed by web-preview-2026 (d07b7723237a110b), root OCW web preview root … (0e304f1125d98d87)"; `trust=dev`, `allow-unsigned=1`, `trust-root=…` each "ignored"; WebGL 2 fallback riding; the credits page complete; no response ≥ 400. The local server sends the module uncompressed, so the live check of GitHub Pages' `content-encoding` comes with the first deployment.

### Phase 11 – VR mode (planning, 2026-11-13; X1 first step built, v4.67 – see 11F, 11G; the first headset run, the bike computer and the controllers, v4.68 – see 11H; the VR kiosk, v4.69 – 4.71 – see 11I; **X1 built and merged onto main, v6.48 – see 11J**)

**Goal:** ride Open Cycling World in a VR headset: Oculus / Meta Rift and Quest, Valve Index, HTC Vive, Pico, Varjo and other vendors. The rider sits on the trainer, sees the world in stereo with head tracking and the own bike and hands in front of them, and keeps every feature: multiplayer, voice (spatial), workouts, the time and weather machines.

#### 11A – Platform facts (as found 2026-11-13; re-check before starting)

- **OpenXR** (Khronos) is the one cross-vendor API. Every current PC-VR runtime implements it: Meta's Quest Link / Oculus PC app (Rift, Rift S, Quest via Link / Air Link), SteamVR (Index, Vive, Pico, Quest via Steam Link, many others), Varjo, Pimax. On Linux: **Monado** (open source), SteamVR, and **WiVRn / ALVR** for streaming to Quest / Pico. Coding against OpenXR alone covers all vendors. No vendor SDK (the old Oculus / LibOVR SDK is deprecated).
- **Oculus Rift / Rift S:** discontinued hardware, still usable on Windows through the Meta PC app's OpenXR runtime. Never on Linux or macOS natively, though some of these headsets run through community drivers on Linux with limited support.
- **Windows Mixed Reality** (HP Reverb, Samsung Odyssey…) was **removed in Windows 11 24H2** ([Road to VR](https://roadtovr.com/windows-11-drops-wmr-support-24h2/), [heise](https://heise.de/-9979921)). Only older Windows versions or community drivers on Linux / SteamVR can still use them; not a target.
- **macOS:** no mainstream OpenXR runtime for PC VR, so **no VR on macOS**. Apple Vision Pro uses visionOS (no OpenXR); a native visionOS app is out of scope (like iOS, 1.3).
- **Standalone headsets** (Quest, Pico): option 1 is **PC VR streaming** (Link / Air Link, Steam Link, Virtual Desktop, WiVRn, ALVR), so no extra build. Option 2 is a native **Android OpenXR** build (Quest / Pico store): planned in 14 Phase 14.
- **Browser:** **WebXR** (Quest Browser, Chrome with a PC headset) fits the browser app (Phase 10) later.
- **Bevy integration:** the community crates `bevy_mod_xr` / `bevy_mod_openxr` (successor of the unmaintained `bevy_oxr`). The latest found is 0.4 for **Bevy 0.17** ([docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/bevy_mod_openxr/latest)), while OCW is on Bevy 0.20, so we need to port / fork it or write our own thin integration (the `openxr` crate + wgpu Vulkan / D3D12 interop, a stereo camera pair rendering into the OpenXR swapchain). To be decided by a spike (11D, X1).

#### 11B – Design

- **One app, a VR mode:** `ocw-desktop --vr` (and a menu switch) starts an OpenXR session. Without a runtime or headset the app runs as today, with a clear message. The **monitor** keeps a **spectator / mirror view**: chase camera or the headset view, for streaming, for the kiosk, and for the art project's captures (with the ISO timestamp). Captures come from the mirror, never from inside the headset.
- **Engine independence:** XR lives behind a `ocw-render` plugin; the sim, server, protocol and devices don't change. Head pose and controllers are only view inputs. The server stays authoritative (6.1).
- **Camera:** first-person from the rider's head on the bike (rider height from the profile, 2.6). Head tracking is added on top of the seated riding pose: the head can look around and lean, but the bike's path stays physics-driven. Recentre with a button or after a long head offset.
- **Own body:** the own bike, handlebar, arms, hands on the bars and legs pedalling at the real cadence, seen from the first-person view (the Phase 4 rig with IK). Optional: hands from controller or hand tracking if they leave the bars.
- **HUD in VR:** world-space panels instead of a flat HUD (**decided 2026-11-17, v4.68: no floating central panel – all ride information is on the bike computer on the bar**, 11H; the user after the first headset run: "the HUD is pretty central, thats disturbing. put all the information in to a bike navi"):
  - a **bike computer** on the stem (power, speed, cadence, HR, gradient, distance);
  - a **head-locked minimum** (critical warnings only);
  - **panels** for menus, workouts, the event leaderboard and junction arrows at road level ahead;
  - the ISO timestamp on the mirror view.
- **Controllers in VR (v4.68):** the Touch controllers are one more gamepad (11H) until the world-space menus of X3 bring the controller ray.
- **Input in VR:** hands are on the handlebar, so the main inputs are the **trainer / sensors** (power, cadence) and **steering by leaning the head** (optional, mapped to the existing lean steering, 5.2.1), handlebar buttons (BLE remotes, later), gamepad, voice commands (later), and controller pointer for menus (gaze + click as a fallback); the controller ray is one more pointer of the input model (3.2.2), so menus and the workshop scene need no VR-specific pages.
- **Comfort** (motion sickness is the main risk; on a trainer pedalling helps, since the vection matches effort):
  - stable horizon (no camera roll with the bike's lean by default);
  - no head bob;
  - smooth, rate-limited acceleration of the view;
  - a **comfort vignette** in sharp turns, hard braking and steep descents (strength setting);
  - always-visible cockpit (bike and bars) as a static reference;
  - snap or smooth turning only in menus;
  - a "seated / standing" calibration;
  - fade to black on teleports, ride switches and U-turns.
- **Performance:** stereo at the headset's native rate (72–120 Hz) costs roughly 2–3× the monitor budget.
  - **Rendering:** single-pass stereo / multiview where wgpu supports it, fixed foveated rendering (and eye-tracked where the runtime offers it), MSAA instead of TAA (less smear in VR), and a **VR quality preset** (shorter view distance, fewer trees and shadows, lower LOD bias).
  - **Frame budget:** stay under budget; runtime reprojection (ASW / motion smoothing) is a safety net, not the plan.
  - **Targets:** 90 Hz on a GTX 1070 / RX 5700-class GPU with the VR preset, 72 Hz minimum.
- **Audio:** game audio and **voice spatialised** with the head pose (the spatial audio of 7 already works with positions); the headset's audio device as the default output in VR.
- **Multiplayer:** other riders see a VR rider normally; optionally their head turns follow the real head (cosmetic, sent as a small orientation in the protocol, only added fields).

A stereo view of the test route with head tracking on the **Oculus Quest (first generation) through Quest Link / Air Link** via the Meta runtime (Windows) first, then the Quest 1 through ALVR + SteamVR (Linux) and Monado (CI) as the second runtime check. Measure the frame time. Decide on the integration (spec entry). **First step (v3.31):** the Quest 1 over Oculus Link as a *viewing device* of the desktop app – stereo, head tracking, the desktop's inputs unchanged.
- **X2 – Riding in VR:** `--vr`, first-person camera on the bike, own body with IK, recentre, mirror view, VR quality preset, captures from the mirror.
- **X3 – VR HUD and menus:** bike computer on the stem, world-space menus with controller / gaze input, junction arrows in the world. The photo preview (3.2 *Photo preview*, v4.74) is to be off in VR (the VR branch sets `PhotoPreview::enabled` false); it belongs on the bike computer (the last photo on its screen for 3 s).
- **X4 – Comfort:** vignette, horizon lock, fades, calibration, settings page *VR comfort*.
- **X5 – Audio and voice in VR:** head-relative spatial audio, the headset's audio device, voice positions.

- **X8 – Native standalone build** (Android OpenXR for Quest / Pico) and **WebXR** in the browser app: planned in its own phase, 14 Phase 14 (milestones V1–V9).

**Unit tests** (no headset needed):

- head-pose composition (bike pose + seated head + tracking offset, recentre);
- the comfort vignette curve from turn rate / acceleration;
- horizon lock;
- world-space panel layout and hit testing;
- IK hand / handlebar placement;
- the head-lean → steering mapping;
- quality-preset selection.

**Integration tests:**

- the OpenXR loader against **Monado's headless / simulated device** on Linux in CI (session start, frame loop, swapchain), so VR code is exercised without hardware;
- screenshots of the mirror view with the scene harness.

#### 11F – X1 build note (v4.67, 2026-11-15)

**Built (the first step of v3.31: the headset as a viewing device of the desktop app):**

- **`ocw-desktop --vr`** (and the setting **`vr.enabled`**, *Settings → Display → Graphics → VR headset (next start)*; since v6.52 *Settings → Display → HUD → VR headset*) starts an OpenXR session before the renderer; the cargo feature **`vr`** of `ocw-desktop` (off by default, so the normal builds do not change) brings the OpenXR layer. Without the feature, an OpenXR loader, an active runtime or a headset the app runs as before and says why (a red note at the top for 20 s, stderr, the log, `vr status`). Riding stays on the trainer, keys and gamepad; no VR controllers, no VR menus (X3).
- **Stereo with head tracking:** two eye cameras (Bevy 0.20 has no multiview) with the runtime's asymmetric per-eye fields of view (infinite reverse-Z, Bevy's convention), at the runtime's recommended eye size; poses located for the frame's display time (one period later: Bevy's pipelined renderer); the app is paced by `xrWaitFrame` (the window's vsync is off in VR); the refresh rate is asked for within the 72–90 Hz budget (`XR_FB_display_refresh_rate`; the Quest 1: 72 Hz, 13.9 ms).
- **The camera rig:** the rider's first-person eye on the bike, from the posed rider (`ocw_assets::pose::eye_point` / `steady_eye`: the crank at rest and no rock, so no head bob), **horizon-locked** (only the bike's heading turns the view, no roll in corners, no pitch on climbs – the comfort default of 11B), plus the tracked head after a **yaw-only recentre** (`C` or `vr recentre`; at the session start; when the runtime's own recentre moved the `LOCAL` space; by itself after the head stayed 0.5 m away for 5 s – *proposal*). The rider's own head is hidden in the eyes (the eyes are inside it) – **since v4.71 only there**: the head and everything on it (helmet, glasses, hair, face, the status signs) are on their own render layer (`vr::OWN_HEAD_LAYER`) that the eye cameras do not draw and the follow camera (chase mirror) and the sun do, so the rider has a head on the monitor and in its shadow (the user, 2026-11-17: "the rider without the head looks weird, can show the head, but make sure that for the POV view it's faded away"; never drawn in the eyes rather than faded: no inside of the helmet). The follow camera stands at the head, so the distance-based detail (LODs, see-through trees, lamps, weather) is centred on the eyes.
- **HUD panel** (*replaced in v4.68 by the bike computer, 11H*): one fixed quad 0.95 m ahead and 0.36 m below the eyes (≈ 21° down, ≈ 29° wide, 1024 × 512 px), carried with the bike, showing power, speed, cadence, heart rate, gradient, distance and time. On the headset (2026-11-17) the user found it "pretty central, thats disturbing".
- **Mirror on the monitor (`vr.mirror`, `vr mirror eye|both|chase`):** the left eye (default), both eyes side by side, or the chase camera (for spectators; a third view). The eye images are shown as UI images – no extra rendering; the desktop HUD stays on top.
- **VR quality preset `vr`** (`quality vr`; `auto` picks it while VR runs): shadows 2048² × 2 cascades over 90 m, MSAA 4× (no TAA), view 12 km, trees 1.5 km, house LOD × 0.6, particles 35 %.
- **Console:** `vr status` (the session phase, runtime and headset, eye size and format, IPD, field of view, the head's offset, the frame statistics), `vr recentre`, `vr mirror …`, `vr reconnect` (restarts the app when only a new instance can help).
- **`--vr-sim`** (every build, no OpenXR): both eyes from a simulated head that glances around, side by side on the monitor, with the bike computer (v4.68; the HUD panel before) and the `vr` preset – for screenshots and tests without a headset.

**Code (pure parts reusable by the standalone Quest build, Phase 14, and WebXR):**

- **`ocw-xr`** (new, pure, Bevy-free, builds for wasm32 – in `make test-wasm` – and Android): `projection` (field of view → projection matrix and frustum corners, tested against hand-computed reference values and against `perspective_infinite_reverse_rh`), `view` (eye views, IPD, simulated eyes, a Quest 1-like field of view), `recentre`, `anchor` (horizon lock, the eye chain `world ∘ anchor ∘ recentre ∘ eye`), `hud` (the panel's place, angle and pixel density), `session` (the state machine idle → ready → visible → focused → stopping → idle; LOSS_PENDING / EXITING / errors → lost → a new session every 2 s on the same instance and device; INSTANCE_LOSS_PENDING → lost, restart needed), `frame` (the order of the frame calls `begin → acquire → wait → copy → release → end`, an empty frame when the runtime says not to render, a failed copy still releases and ends; frame-time / latency / missed-frame statistics), `swapchain` (the format choice: sRGB RGBA8 → sRGB BGRA8 → RGBA16F, linear UNORM refused, in Vulkan and DXGI numbers; the eye size from the recommendation, the render scale and the maximum), `headset` (profiles: the **Quest 1 – 1440 × 1600 per eye, 72 Hz**, render scale 1.0 on PC, 0.8 standalone; generic; the 72–90 Hz rate choice), `mock` (an in-memory runtime: scripted events, a call log). No platform assumptions: no Windows / desktop code, no clock reads, no threads.
- **`ocw-xr-openxr`** (new, native; Linux, Windows, Android): our own thin OpenXR layer – the `openxr` crate (0.21.1, MIT OR Apache-2.0, loader opened at run time), a Vulkan instance and device created through OpenXR (`XR_KHR_vulkan_enable2`) and wrapped for wgpu 30 with wgpu-hal (`ash` 0.38, MIT OR Apache-2.0), the `LOCAL` space, one swapchain with two array layers, the frame calls behind `ocw-xr`'s traits. **It is OCW's only crate with `unsafe`** (denied by its lints, allowed in `vulkan.rs` and three marked spots of `lib.rs` (loading the loader, `Send` / `Sync` for the handle holder); every block names the rule it keeps) – *proposal*: accept this one exception to the workspace's `unsafe_code = "forbid"`.
- **`ocw-render::vr`** (Bevy glue: eye cameras, the eye projection as a Bevy `CameraProjection`, the rig, the HUD panel, the mirror, the look of the follow camera – fog, exposure, MSAA, far plane, atmosphere – copied to the eyes); **`ocw-render::vr::openxr`** (feature `openxr`): `RenderCreation::Manual` with the device OpenXR made; the main world runs the session and `xrWaitFrame` / `xrLocateViews` in `First`; the render world, after the render graph, copies the two eye images into the swapchain layers (plus an empty pass, so the images go back as colour attachments) and ends the frame.
- **`apps/desktop/src/vr.rs`:** `--vr` / `--vr-sim`, the boot before the renderer, the message, the console command.

**Swapchain choice (*proposal*):** the eyes render into Bevy images and are **copied** into the swapchain each frame (2 × 1440 × 1600 × 4 B ≈ 18 MB a frame, ≈ 1.3 GB/s at 72 Hz – a fraction of a millisecond on a VR-capable GPU) instead of rendering into the runtime's images directly. It keeps the OpenXR frame calls in one place after the render graph (no acquire before Bevy prepares its views), makes the mirror free (the same images on the monitor) and is the same path for the simulated head.

**Checked (2026-11-15):** marge – `cargo fmt --check`, clippy `-D warnings` plain, with `--features ocw-desktop/vr` and with `voice`, `cargo test --workspace`, `make test-wasm` (with `ocw-xr`), `make test-web-build`, the vendored port with its examples; the Mac – the VR crates' tests and clippy, `ocw-render` with `openxr`, the desktop's VR tests with `vr`, the port; Win11Builder – `cargo build -p ocw-desktop --features vr --release` and the VR crates' tests. Screenshots of `--vr-sim` (both eyes, one eye, the chase mirror, the Black Forest) and of `--vr` in a build without VR (the message) in `test-output/vr/`.

#### 11G – The integration comparison (Q3; *proposal*, the user decides)

Both variants were built against Bevy 0.20.1 / wgpu 30.0.1 (2026-11-15). **No headset and no OpenXR runtime are reachable from the build machines**, so neither could start a session: the frame time, the latency and the stability on the Quest 1 are **not measured yet** – the instruments are built (`vr status`: the app's time per frame without the blocking wait – mean, p95, max against the display period –, the prediction horizon from the pose sample to the display time, missed frames; `ocw_xr::frame::FrameStats`), and the numbers go here once the Quest 1 runs over Link or Monado is installed (below).

| | **A – port of `bevy_mod_openxr`** | **B – our own thin layer** |
|---|---|---|
| What | `bevy_mod_xr` + `bevy_mod_openxr` **0.6.0** (the Bevy 0.19 / wgpu 29 release; 0.4 was Bevy 0.17, 0.5 Bevy 0.18 – upstream follows each Bevy release) vendored in `vendor/` (own workspace, excluded from the root's lints), ported to 0.20.1 / wgpu 30 | `ocw-xr-openxr` (the `openxr` crate 0.21.1 + `ash` + wgpu-hal, Bevy-free) + `ocw-render::vr::openxr` (the Bevy glue) on the pure `ocw-xr` |
| Port / build effort | small: **37 changed lines** in 9 files – 15 × `#[extract_app(RenderApp)]` on `ExtractResource` / `ExtractComponent` derives (Bevy 0.20 moved extraction into `bevy_extract`), 8 × the renderer's resources are now plain wrappers (`RenderQueue::new(queue)` instead of `RenderQueue(Arc::new(WgpuWrapper::new(…)))`), 1 × wgpu 30's `create_texture_from_hal` takes the image's initial state, 1 import, the manifests (`bevy_extract`, pinned versions). It compiles with its `3d_scene` example: see the check results below | written new: about 950 lines (OpenXR + Vulkan interop 620, Bevy glue 300), plus the shared pure crate (1,700 lines with tests) that A would need too for the rig, the HUD and the state machine |
| Code we carry | 6,430 lines of upstream Rust (95 `unsafe` sites); we follow every Bevy release ourselves or wait for upstream (0.7 for Bevy 0.20 was not out) | 950 lines, 25 `unsafe` sites in one file, every one with its rule |
| Features beyond X1 | hand tracking, controller actions and bindings, passthrough (FB), overlays, spaces, D3D12 on Windows, Android (JNI glue) – X3 (controllers, menus) would reuse them | stereo views, swapchain, session life cycle, refresh rate; actions / hands to be written for X3 (the `openxr` crate has them) |
| How it renders | XR cameras render **directly into the runtime's swapchain images** (re-pointed `ManualTextureView`s each frame), poses re-located in the render world (late latching); a mirror would need a third render or an extra blit it does not have | eye cameras render into Bevy images that are **copied** into the swapchain (≈ 1.3 GB/s at 72 Hz, under a millisecond); the mirror is free (the same images), the same path for `--vr-sim`; no late latching yet (poses located once per frame in `First`, for the display time one period on) |
| Without a runtime | its init falls back to a plain Vulkan device of its own – Vulkan only, also on Windows where Bevy would pick DX12 | the app starts exactly as without VR (Bevy's own device choice) and shows why |
| OpenXR loader | Windows: the `static` feature builds the Khronos loader from source (needs CMake on the build machine); Linux / Android: the system's | opened at run time everywhere (`loaded`): no CMake; `openxr_loader.dll` ships beside the exe on Windows |
| Fit with OCW | owns the session, cameras and tracking root (`XrTrackingRoot`), adds its plugins around `DefaultPlugins` (`add_xr_plugins`); OCW's rig would move the tracking root, the eye look (fog, exposure, MSAA, atmosphere) would be copied onto its cameras | OCW owns the cameras and the rig; the OpenXR calls sit behind `ocw-xr`'s traits, so the state machine and the frame order are unit-tested with a mock runtime |
| Standalone (Phase 14) | has the Android path (Quest store manifests, JNI) | the `openxr` crate and the Vulkan interop are the same on Android; the loader and the Android activity glue are still to do |

**Recommendation (*proposal*, the user decides): B – our own thin layer – for X2 onwards**, keeping the port in `vendor/` as the reference and as a parts store for X3 (actions, hand tracking) until our layer has them: it is small, OCW keeps control of the cameras and the mirror, the OpenXR logic is testable without a headset, there is one `unsafe` file to review, the plain build is unaffected, and no Bevy release waits for an upstream port. To be confirmed by the measurements on the Quest 1: if the copy into the swapchain or the missing late latching shows in the frame time or the latency, B renders into the swapchain directly (A's technique) before X2.

**Built (v4.68):**

- **The bike computer** (`ocw_xr::computer` pure: place, size, tilt, legibility; `ocw-render::vr::computer` the Bevy part; the model file `parts/computer/computer-head-unit-wedge.glb`, kind `part`, slot `computer`, from `ocw_assets::computer::build()` like the other exported models, Git LFS, manifest entry): a wedge-like body 52 × 20 × 78 mm at real size with rounded sides and a slightly lower nose, a 40 × 58 mm screen window with a raised bezel, seven LEDs behind the screen, two side buttons, a lap button on the nose, the twist-lock puck underneath (≈ 400 triangles, under the part budget of 1 500); new paint slots `computer_body`, `computer_screen`, `computer_led`. **Placement:** the unit's centre 28 mm above the bar's axis, ahead of the bar by its tilted half-length plus the bar's radius and 12 mm (at least 75 mm, like real out-front mounts), centred on the stem's line; the screen faces the rider's steady eye (`AvatarRig::steady_eye`) plus the rider's tilt; on the **TT bike** the bar's centre is taken by the extensions, so the unit sits 45 mm ahead of the extensions' tips (their bridge), at hand height. The mount's arm is drawn from the bar (or the extensions) to the puck. `BikeRig::bar_clamp` (the `handlebar` node) gives the bar on every bike. **Size:** a real unit's text is not readable on the Quest 1 (≈ 14 px per degree): the unit is drawn at **275 % by default** (`vr.computer_size`, 100–400 % in steps of 25; `vr.computer_tilt`, −30 … +30°; console `vr computer size | tilt`), so the smallest text (48 px of the 600 × 870 px screen texture) spans ≥ 0.6° – ≈ 9 Quest 1 pixels – from every bike's eye (tested per bike), while the texture has more than twice the display's pixels per degree. The screen stays ≥ 30° below the horizon. **Screen** (Bevy UI into the texture, unlit on a quad over the window): the clock of the place (`☼ 18:42`) and the weather summary; an LED bar in the gradient's colour (one lamp per 2 %); power large; speed, cadence, heart rate, gradient, distance and time in six fields; the next turn's arrow turned by the exit's angle with its distance and street (free ride), or the route's progress; the elevation profile ahead (the desktop's bars merged to 40) with the rider's mark; messages (dead end ahead, app messages, Strava) as a banner over the bottom. Only the eye cameras see it (the VR render layer).
- **Why the controllers did nothing:** X1 created no OpenXR action set (Q7: "no VR controllers yet"). Without `xrCreateActionSet` / `xrCreateAction`, `xrSuggestInteractionProfileBindings`, `xrAttachSessionActionSets` and `xrSyncActions` every frame, an OpenXR runtime routes no controller input to the app – Link's own system button still worked. **Now** (`ocw_xr::controllers` pure tables, `ocw_xr_openxr::controls`): one action set `ride` with an action per input (menu, A, B, X, Y, both triggers, both grips, both sticks and their clicks), suggested for `/interaction_profiles/oculus/touch_controller` and the Khronos simple controller (a fallback), attached to every session (also after a reconnect), synced after each `xrWaitFrame`; outside the input focus the actions are inactive and the pad rests. The binding table is tested against the profile's component paths (OpenXR 1.0 6.4). **What they do** – what the spec defines for VR input today (11B; Q4: no head-lean steering; X3 brings the pointer and world-space menus): **they are one more gamepad** (a Bevy gamepad "VR controllers" fed through Bevy's raw gamepad events): ☰ = Start (menu), A = South (confirm / autodrive), B = East (back / U-turn), X = West (wild), Y = North (back to the route), left stick = left stick (steering, junction exits, faster / stop) and its flicks the D-pad (menu), right stick = right stick, triggers = LT2 / RT2 (stop / faster), grips = LB / RB, stick clicks = L3 / R3 – and **both grips held 0.6 s recentre the view** (*proposal*). Every change is logged (`VR controllers: button_a down, trigger_right 0.75, …`); `vr status` names the profile the runtime bound per hand.
- **The crash on exit** (0xC0000005 after "rider left", in shutdown): two faults in the teardown. (1) The swapchain's `VkImage`s were wrapped for wgpu without a drop callback, so **wgpu-hal took them as its own and called `vkDestroyImage` on the runtime's images**, which `xrDestroySwapchain` then destroyed again. (2) The OpenXR session could be destroyed after the Vulkan device it was created on (Bevy drops the render world, with the device, in its own order). Now the images carry a no-op drop callback (the runtime owns them), and the app's last frame (`AppExit`, in `Last`) tears the session down itself (`SessionMachine::shutdown` → `XrRuntime::shutdown`): request the exit, wait for the GPU, drop the swapchain, the frame stream, the frame waiter, the space and the session – while the device lives; the render thread submits under a frame lock the teardown takes first, so it never copies into a swapchain being destroyed; the remaining handles drop in field order (session before action set, before the instance and the device). Regression tests: the mock's exit order (`the_exit_tears_the_session_down_once`), the Monado run's exit code.
- **The screenshot:** `--screenshot` in a headset session saves the **left eye** (the rule `autoshot::shot_from`; before, only a window without a surface did); `--vr-look-down DEG` / `vr look-down DEG` turn both eyes down about the head for the bike computer in the picture (screenshots only: in a worn headset it tilts the world).

**References looked at for the mount** (Wikimedia Commons, looked at only, nothing copied, no brand or logo used): *Bike computer support on Factor's handlebar (34384487583).jpg* (chelsom tsai, CC BY 2.0) – an out-front mount on an integrated bar and stem, the puck held centred a few centimetres ahead of the bar, a little above it; *Bike computer and sensors set 1.jpg* (JaredMcKenzie, CC0) – an out-front arm curving forward from the bar clamp to the puck and a portrait unit with rounded corners and its screen. The model follows those proportions (unit ≈ 8 cm ahead of the bar's centre at real size, the puck just above the bar), not their looks.
