Video: scene `god-plane-video` (a banked turn and a climb over Vaduz, then the wings from the side).
- **Built (v3.22): the guided camera path (G5) and the rider list page.**
  - **Guided camera paths for flyover videos** (`ocw_client::camera_path`, pure, wasm; `apps/desktop/src/camera_path.rs`): keyframes are camera poses (the eye in local metres, the look direction); `camera.path add` takes the camera's pose now (riding, flying or orbiting), `camera.path key X Y Z HEADING PITCH` gives one in numbers (scenes), `list`, `remove N`, `clear`, `save FILE` / `load FILE` (a text file: `key x y z look_x look_y look_z` lines, optional `seconds S` / `ease NAME`, `#` comments; a bare name lives in `<data dir>/ocw/camera-paths/NAME.campath`), `play [--seconds S] [--ease linear|smooth|in-out]` (default the file's, else 20 s smooth), `stop`. The eye moves on a **centripetal Catmull-Rom spline** through the keys (no loops or overshoot between unevenly spaced keys; the ends repeat their key), the look direction's yaw and pitch on a Catmull-Rom spline over the same parameter, unwrapped so the camera turns the short way; the timing is **by arc length** (an even speed, eased at the ends), a turn on the spot counting as 15 m per radian (*proposal*), so a pan between two keys at one place takes its time too. While a path plays the camera stands on it (`RideView::guided_camera`, before the flight and the chase camera; never less than 3 m above the ground or a solid object), the tiles stream around and ahead of it (`flight_world::stream_focus`, the ring growing with its height above the rider's road) and the neighbour packages load 10 s of its speed ahead. The pose is a function of the game time since `play`, so `ocw-desktop --capture` (a fixed game-time step per frame) renders a flyover smoothly and the same every run. Scene `g5-flyover-vaduz-video`.
  - **The rider list as a menu page** – **Navi → Riders in this ride** (*proposal*: the Ride page has its seven items; Navi had room) (`ocw_client::rider_list`, pure; `apps/desktop/src/riders_page.rs`): the own rider first ("(you)", km), then the others nearest first with the gap along the route ("120 m ahead", "1.5 km behind", "beside you") or, in free ride where everyone rides an own path, the straight-line distance ("350 m away"); "flying" / "down" before it; a **small unicorn** (the impostor's picture) before riders flying in unicorn mode and the **damage dot** after hurt riders or damaged bikes (▲ amber, ■ red, the icon and the colour – never colour alone; 12F); the status line counts them ("6 riders, 1 flying, 1 damaged"). Paged like the other lists (Up / Down, Left / Right pages, Enter, the gamepad, the mouse); everyone sees it, so the host sees who flies (13E). Scene `k13-rider-list`.
  - Tests: the spline through every key, an even and smooth motion without flips, the short way round, a pan, easing and playback, save / load and its errors, yaw / pitch; the console (add, key, list, save, load, play, the velocity, back to the chase camera, remove); the camera on the guided pose and the streaming around it; the rider list's rows, order, gaps, free ride, the summary; the menu's unicorn and dots (headless).
- **Built (v3.39): god mode in the browser app (G5).**
  - **One implementation:** the Bevy glue, the input mapping (`input`: `LayoutKeys`, `flight_input`, `look_delta`, `god_key`), the touch controls (`touch`) and the inspection (`inspect`: panel, crosshair, pins) moved from `apps/desktop/src/god/` into `ocw_ui::god` (`GodPlugin`), over the app's ride through `ocw_ui::RideAccess`: `gather_flight` reads keys, pads, mouse, wheel and touch into `FlightFrame`; the exclusive systems `god_keys`, `fly`, `inspect` and `update_view` reach the client (the ray's and the clearance's surfaces – `Ground`, `CameraObstacles`, `FlightObstacles` – are shared functions, cloned so the client can be borrowed mutably); `GodStatus` carries the phase to `grab_pointer`; `not_flying` is a `&World` run condition (the desktop's and the browser's riding keys). The systems run in `ViewExtrasSet`, after the app's `RideViewSet`. The desktop's `crate::god` re-exports it and keeps the end-to-end test on its local server; the shared menu frees a captured pointer before the app's own Esc hook (`free_pointer`).
  - **Browser** (`apps/web/src/god.rs`): `WebGodPlugin` adds it; the world page's World menu has the *Unicorn mode* row (`WorldHome.god`); the god-mode settings are no longer in `ocw_client::settings`' browser exclusions; the riding keys are gated by `not_flying` as on the desktop. **+ / −** by the typed character: Bevy's logical key is the `KeyboardEvent.key` on the web, so `LayoutKeys` works unchanged (the US `=` typing `+`, the German `+` at the US `]`). **Pointer Lock:** Bevy's `CursorGrabMode::Locked` on the canvas, asked for in the frame after the G key, the menu row or a click (within the browser's user activation); `PointerLockWatch` frees the captured pointer when `document.pointerLockElement` is gone (the browser's own Esc, which the page may not see) or never came within 1 s (refused) – then the left button held looks, the next Esc opens the menu, a click asks again. Touch: the desktop's mapping (left half steers, right half looks, the + / − buttons), the canvas with `touch-action: none` so the page does not scroll or zoom. Multiplayer over WebTransport: the server's `god_access` as for desktop riders (the host by default). `window.ocw.god()`: the flight as JSON (phase, pointer, position, height, panel, crosshair, pins).
  - Tests: `ocw-ui` – the shared plugin over a `RideAccess` ride on the in-memory `FrameServer` (G, + and − on US / German positions, the inspection, a pin, I, Esc frees the pointer before the menu opens, landing, `status`, `ride.riders`), the flight settings through `set` in the browser, `PointerLockWatch`, the moved input / touch / inspect tests; `ocw-web` – World → Unicorn mode flies on the page's local server, ↓ does not stop the trainer in flight, the flight view with the panel, the JSON, G lands; the desktop's end-to-end test unchanged. Headless Chromium (`make test-web`, `make test-web-unicorn` over Vaduz): G, + climbs, I hides and shows the inspection, P, Esc → World → Unicorn mode, G lands.
- **Built (v5.53): riding off the road after a unicorn landing (13A *Landing anywhere* and *Free 2D riding off the road*; Q7 (b), Q8 (a), Q9 (a)).**
  - **Where the unicorn lands** (`ocw_sim::offroad::landing`, the same rule on the server and for the ring): in a **free ride** (no route plan, no running event, a world with tiles) within the road's half width + 2 m on the road as before (the nearest edge), else **on the ground** below the unicorn – inside the world's tiles, **not on water, not inside a building's footprint, not on an obstacle** (the standing rider's footprint against the world's solids: trees near the roads, walls, fences, posts, lamp poles, a building's walls). The ring is **gold** on a road, **green** on the ground and **red** where landing is refused (`ocw_render::LandingKind`); G there says "cannot land here: not on water" (… a building, an obstacle, outside the world) and the unicorn flies on – the server refuses it too (`Session::leave_god` → error, still flying). **Fixed routes and route rides** land on the route as before (Q8 (a): "in events and on fixed routes on the route"; *as built*, "solo rides anywhere" is read as solo *free* rides – a route ride stays on its route, solo or not). Events never meet it: they need a fixed course, and unicorn mode is not available while one runs (13A *Who may use it*).
  - **Landing on the ground** stands the rider there, facing the unicorn's heading, in **wild mode** (autodrive off, upright lean steering; the client follows the snapshot); the distance goes on from where the flight began (the flight credits nothing, as before). Shift + G from the terrain flies back there.
  - **The ground** (`ocw_world::ground::GroundMap`, pure, wasm, in the road network like the obstacles): per tile the package's terrain heights (16-bit steps between the tile's lowest and highest point, at most 2 cm off; the grid triangulated like the drawn terrain mesh, so the wheels stand on what is drawn) and the **cover** at the land use's 5 m cells (run-length coded per row): grass (meadows, fields, parks, gardens), forest floor (woods, scrub), rock, soft ground (sand, scree, bare soil, wetland, glacier), water, building (footprints rasterised on top). Liechtenstein's 510 tiles take 12.9 MB (the server logs it); the browser adds its streamed tiles as they arrive (like the road feel), so its local server and prediction share the map.
  - **Riding on the terrain** (`ocw_sim::offroad::tick`): the rider's position (x, z) and direction of travel are an **`OffRoadTrack`** – a straight track along the heading through the rider, its heights and gradient from the ground (a central difference over ± 2 m along the heading), its surface from the cover – and each 50 Hz tick is one ordinary physics tick on it (`ride::tick_in`: power, gravity, rolling resistance, air, the weather, the brake, the damage's effects), after which the track is re-anchored where the rider got to, turned by the heading ridden. Lean steering as in wild mode (κ = g·tan(lean)/v², at most 1/5 m; the angle-to-the-road limits never bind, so the rider can ride circles); autodrive rides straight. Everything that reads a track works on it: the renderer (`RideView::off_road`, before the path), the chase camera, the HUD's gradient and surface ("manual | WILD | forest_floor"), the trainer in SIM (the terrain's gradient ahead), the GPS line, the FIT recording, the collisions in the world's plane.
  - **Every slope at its real gradient (Q7 (b)):** no "too steep" stop and no speed cap – 40 % up is ridden at the speed the power gives (300 W: ~1 m/s; without power the rider stops and never rolls back), 40 % down speeds up as gravity says (over 70 km/h on a long slope). **Numerically safe on cliffs:** the gradient is finite (the 10 m grid, bounded at 2,000 %), the rider always follows the terrain (never in the air), the horizontal step is the slope's length times its cosine, and the speed is bounded at 100 m/s (2 m a tick) – a bound for the numbers, never felt (air drag holds a rider below ~60 m/s even down a cliff). The physics and the virtual trainer (it holds the power) take the full gradient; a real trainer gets the terrain's gradient within the SIM settings' limits as on roads (up to 20 % by default – it caps what it can simulate).
  - **Rolling resistance by the cover** (new surfaces in `ocw_world::Surface`, factors on the asphalt Crr like 5.2.1's, scaled by the bike's off-road share): grass 6, forest floor 7.5, rock 3, soft ground (sand) 15 – *proposal* values; with their sounds (twigs and leaves, the rattle of rock, the hiss of sand) and colours.
  - **Water and the world's edge** stop the rider (the step is not taken, the speed is lost); leaning wheels the bike round on the spot (1 rad/s) so the rider can ride away. **Collisions** with buildings, trees, walls, fences, posts and lamp poles: the full K3 model in the world's plane (crashes with collisions on), as wild riders have it.
  - **Back on a road** (`ocw_sim::offroad::road_join`): on a road's carriageway (within half its width), at the road's height (± 1.5 m: not under a bridge, not over a tunnel) and at most ~57° to it, the rider **joins it**: a new path from there along the travel (the edge's direction by the heading; not against a one-way street), the lateral offset and the heading to the road where the rider is – continuous, no jump; wild mode stays on until the rider switches it off (13A *Back to the road*). Crossing a road more steeply rides over it in 2D. **J** puts the rider standing on the nearest road (as the landing does). In a **free ride** a wild rider who reaches the 60 m band's edge rides on into the terrain; on fixed routes and route rides the band holds as before.
  - **Server-authoritative and deterministic** (6.1): the session owns the 2D position (`Session::off_road`, `RiderSnapshot.off_road`; additive protocol fields `RiderUpdate.off_road` = `OffRoadPose` – x and z in mm, the yaw in 1e-5 rad – and `GodResult.off_road`); off the road the snapshot's distance is the odometer and the lateral offset and heading are 0 at the pose. The client **predicts** with the same tick (`Predictor::reconcile_off_road`: the server's state extrapolated by the snapshot's age, compared in the plane, errors above 5 m snapped, smaller ones blended in over 0.5 s, the direction halfway per snapshot); a join or J comes from the server (its path reset) and the client snaps to it. The others off the road are interpolated between snapshots (`offroad::PoseBuffer`) and drawn on their terrain tracks; their bodies for the predicted contacts stand at their places.
  - **Counts like any riding (Q9 (a)):** the distance goes on counting (the odometer: the FIT file's distance), the elevation and the GPS track follow the real off-road position (the track's heights, the local projection of x and z), the time as always; hearts by the accepted work and the terrain's real rise (at most 2 m a tick), never for virtual power (4E).
  - **Both apps:** all of it lives in the shared crates (`ocw-world`, `ocw-sim`, `ocw-protocol`, `ocw-server`, `ocw-client`, `ocw-render`, `ocw-ui`); the desktop, the browser (its local server and a remote one) and `ocw-server` build the ground from the home package.
  - **Tests:** the ground's heights against the drawn terrain, the gradient along a heading (40 % up, down, across, a cliff), the cover and the off-road track (`ocw-world`); 40 % up at its real gradient without rolling back, 40 % down without a cap, a 200 m cliff down and up staying finite and on the ground with a sane step, water and the world's edge stopping and turning on the spot, the covers' rolling, lean circles, landing allowed / refused (meadow, near the road, water, house, obstacle, outside the world), joining a road in the direction of travel (not across, not beside, not under), folding pushes into the track (`ocw-sim`); the session's landing in wild mode with hearts and no path changes, refused landings flying on, route rides on the route, joining by riding onto the road, leaving the band and J, the band holding on a route, flying back to the terrain; the client's ring kinds and the server's refusal, the prediction agreeing with the server off the road, the 40 % slope in the HUD's gradient and the trainer, the FIT file's distance, elevation and GPS track, riding onto the road, others seeing the rider on the terrain; the wire's `OffRoadPose`.
  - **Not yet (v5.53):** **drafting off the road** (13A: "with riders within reach") – riders on the terrain draft nobody and nobody drafts them; the client does not predict a join itself (it follows the server's path reset, one snapshot later). (The trees of the woods far from roads: built v5.60, below.)
- **Built (v5.60): off the road every drawn tree is an obstacle (Q10 (a)).**
  - **The trunks** (`ocw_world::woods`, pure, wasm): per **cell of 40 m** (5 × 5 candidates of the 8 m tree grid, 25 × 25 cells a tile) from the trees as the renderer draws them – the placement of `ocw_world::trees` windowed to the cell (`landuse_trees_in`: each candidate decided alone, the road margins and buildings checked within the window, the same trees as the whole tile's), the species and the drawn scale of `flora::GridTrees` (the region, the leaf mix of the package's place – by its origin, the same on every day for every viewer – and the side of Tenerife; moved out of the renderer, whose `tile_plants` draws with it) and the radius of the drawn trunk at its foot, `Species::trunk_radius_m` (conifers 1.6 % of the height, pines 2.2 %, broadleaves 2 % + 5 cm, the palms and the dragon tree their own; the generator draws with it) times the scale: 0.2 – 0.7 m. Shrubs, succulents and bananas stay soft. The orchards' rows and the mapped trees (`plantings::planted_points`, moved from the world builder; the trunk as `OBST` has it) come per tile. **No doubles:** the grid cells and planted trees `OBST` stores within 62 m of a road are left out (they stay the road-side trees of K3).
  - **Made on demand, dropped after** (`ocw_sim::collide::WorldCache`): only around riders **off the road** (their collisions and the landing check; wild riders in the 60 m band keep `OBST`), the cells a rider's footprint (+ 1 m) touches, kept 10 s after their last use (swept every 5 s), at most 2,048 cells (the oldest go); a tile not loaded yet (the browser) is asked again. One rider takes 1 – 4 cells (≈ 20 trunks each in a dense wood, ~1 KB); a whole square kilometre of wood, 625 cells, stays under 2 MB.
  - **The rules:** the full K3 model in the world's plane – a crash at a closing speed of 3.5 m/s or more (less on a wet ground), below it a stop at the trunk (the speed into it lost, pressed against it while pedalling, the bike turned away by leaning); group rides soft bumps only (12G); **collisions off: no trunks made** (the rider passes; the landing still refuses a spot inside a trunk, as inside a building). Unicorn landings are refused on a trunk (the red ring).
  - **Everywhere the same:** the server's session, the desktop's local server and its prediction (the renderer's package `Arc`, no copy), the browser's `FrameServer` and prediction (the resident tiles' package, set on each publish – no section added, `FRST` was in its base already; the phone budget of v5.46 unchanged: the cell cache is the only addition), `ocw-server` (the trees baked per tile at load, `woods::bake_tile`: each candidate's trunk radius in whole millimetres, deflated – 37 MB and ~1.3 s on 16 cores for the northern Black Forest's 2,200 tiles, where the trees' inputs – heights, roads, land use, buildings, `FRST`, `VEGE` – would be 310 MB) and a client of a remote server. Radii are whole millimetres on every path, so the server and the clients agree exactly. Only the home package's woods (as for `OBST`); packages without land use (the oldest's provisional patches) have none.
  - **Tick time** (leela, release, northern Black Forest; `services/server/tests/woods_bench.rs`, `OCW_BENCH_WORLD=… --ignored`): a rider over 200 m from any road in a wood of 25 trunks per cell, leaning about among the trunks for 60 s at 150 W: **2.7 µs per tick** with the trunks (2.9 µs without – noise), the slowest tick 50 µs (cells being made); a cell made in 30 µs from the server's baked tiles, 7 µs from a shared package.
  - **Phones:** a phone's browser draws every second tree (v5.46) but the server's trunks are all of them – there a rider deep in a wood can stop at a trunk not drawn (the trunks are the server's, the same for every rider).
  - **Tests:** a window places the tile's trees, the cells cover a tile once, the trunks are the drawn trees, `OBST`'s road-side trees left out, a tile not loaded gives nothing yet, a server's baked tiles give the same trunks (`ocw-world`); `ocw-render`: the trunks the server makes equal `tile_plants`' solid plants (foot and radius); `ocw-sim`: no doubles in the cache across the band's edge, cells made and dropped as a rider moves, the cap, a crash at speed and a stop at walking pace into a trunk deep in a wood, group rides bump, collisions off make none, the cells go 10 s after the rider rejoined the road, landing on a trunk refused, the prediction stops where the server does. Scenes `q10-woods-stop`, `q10-woods-crash-video` (a wood of the northern Black Forest over 200 m from any road).
- **Not yet:** G5's VR; the touch controls and the Pointer Lock on real phones, tablets and in Safari / Firefox.

### Phase 14 – Standalone VR: Quest, Pico and WebXR (planning, 2026-11-14; **14I W0 + W1 built v5.77** – WebXR in the browser app, proved in an emulated Quest 1, published at `/xr/` with `local-floor`, the sensor bridge and the beacon; **W2 + W3 built v5.79** – the bike computer on the bars, no flat HUD, the Touch controllers, the `quest1` level, the frame time on the unit, left-eye pictures over the bridge; W4, the first headset run, needs the user)

**Goal:** ride Open Cycling World **in a standalone headset without a PC**: a native Android OpenXR app, **first and for now only for the Oculus Quest (first generation)** (decided by the user 2026-11-14, v3.29; Quest 2 / 3 / 3S / Pro and Pico 4 / 4 Ultra are postponed), and **WebXR** in the browser app (Phase 10) for headsets with a WebXR browser. The rider sits on the trainer, the headset talks to the trainer, power meter and heart rate strap itself (or through a bridge), and every feature of Phases 10 / 11 is there: the same worlds, multiplayer, voice, workouts, the time and weather machines. **Decided (2026-11-14, Phase 11 Q5):** a standalone version and WebXR are wanted, as their own phase. Everything else below is a **proposal**.

It builds on Phase 11 (the VR mode of the desktop app: OpenXR, the first-person rig, the VR HUD, comfort, no head-lean steering, Phase 11 Q4) and Phase 10 (the browser app: full parity, WebGPU, WebTransport, Web Bluetooth, the sensor bridge, own hosting). Phase 14 adds the **Android target**, the **mobile-GPU performance tier** and the **standalone distribution**; it adds no new game rules.

#### 14A – Platform facts (as found 2026-11-14; re-check before starting)

**Headsets** (all Android-based, OpenXR, Vulkan on Qualcomm Adreno):

| Headset | SoC / RAM | Display rates | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Oculus Quest (1st gen, 2019) – the target (v3.29)** | Snapdragon 835, 4 GB | 72 Hz | 1440×1600 OLED per eye; grey passthrough; **far weaker than the Quest 2** – the budget has to be measured in V1, below the Quest 2's; Meta's SDKs dropped the Quest 1 after v50 (April 2023) and the Horizon Store takes **no new Quest 1 apps since 31 Jan 2024**, so a Quest 1 build is **sideloaded only** (developer mode, `adb install`); its OpenXR runtime stays on the device (last Horizon OS for the Quest 1) – to verify with the Khronos loader in V1; its Quest Browser is frozen at its last version (WebXR to check) |
| Meta Quest 2 (postponed) | XR2 Gen 1, 6 GB | 72 / 90 / 120 Hz | grey passthrough; the weakest target (Meta's guidance: < 100 draw calls, < 750k triangles per frame) |
| Meta Quest 3 (postponed) | XR2 Gen 2, 8 GB | 72 / 90 / 120 Hz | colour passthrough, depth sensor; GPU ≈ 2.5 × Quest 2 (< 200 draw calls, < 1.5M triangles) |
| Meta Quest 3S (postponed) | XR2 Gen 2, 8 GB | 72 / 90 / 120 Hz | Quest 3 performance with lower-resolution Fresnel lenses; the cheapest current Quest |
| Meta Quest Pro (postponed) | XR2+ Gen 1, 12 GB | 72 / 90 Hz | eye tracking (eye-tracked foveation); discontinued |
| Pico 4 (postponed) | XR2 Gen 1, 8 GB | 72 / 90 Hz | colour passthrough (low resolution) |
| Pico 4 Ultra (postponed) | XR2 Gen 2, 12 GB | 72 / 90 Hz | colour passthrough, depth; PICO OS 5.14 (OS 6 in developer early access) |

- **OpenXR is the only API on Quest:** Meta ended VrApi / the Oculus Mobile SDK on 31 Aug 2022; new Quest apps must use OpenXR ([Meta: OpenXR vs VrApi](https://developers.meta.com/vr/documentation/native/android/os-openxr-vrapi/), [Meta blog: all in on OpenXR](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/blog/oculus-all-in-on-openxr-deprecates-proprietary-apis/)). Quest uses the **standard Khronos OpenXR loader for Android** (`org.khronos.openxr:openxr_loader_for_android` ≥ 1.0.34, Horizon OS ≥ v62; no proprietary loader), launched by an activity with the intent category `org.khronos.openxr.intent.category.IMMERSIVE_HMD`, initialised via `XR_KHR_loader_init_android` / `XR_KHR_android_create_instance` ([Meta: Mobile OpenXR](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/documentation/native/android/mobile-openxr), updated 2025-01-23). **Pico** is OpenXR 1.1 compliant and takes the official Khronos SDK and loader since PICO OS 5.9 ([PICO developer news](https://developer.picoxr.com/news/oru5hv2u); [PICO 4 Ultra](https://developer.picoxr.com/pico4-ultra/)). So **one APK** with the Khronos loader can run on both, with vendor extensions (`XR_FB_*`, `XR_META_*`, `XR_BD_*` / `XR_PICO_*`) probed at runtime – the same approach as Godot's universal OpenXR APK ([UploadVR](https://www.uploadvr.com/godot-now-supports-more-xr-features-builds-a-universal-openxr-apk/)).
- **Rendering features:** all Quests support **multiview** on Vulkan (Vulkan 1.1 core; [Meta: multiview](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/documentation/unity/enable-multiview/)); fixed foveated rendering (`XR_FB_foveation`, Vulkan fragment density map; eye-tracked only on Quest Pro); refresh rate chosen per app (`XR_FB_display_refresh_rate`); the frame budget is 13.9 ms at 72 Hz, 11.1 ms at 90 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz, and **72 Hz is the store minimum** (VRC) ([Meta: device optimisation comparison](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/resources/device-optimization-comparison/)). CPU / GPU clock levels are set by the runtime with thermal throttling on long sessions – a cycling session of 60–90 min with the rider's body heat around the headset is the worst case; to measure (OVR Metrics Tool).
- **Rust / Bevy on Android:** Bevy runs on Android with `GameActivity` (feature `android-game-activity`) or `NativeActivity`; the native library is built with **`cargo-ndk`** (4.1.2) into a Gradle project; `cargo-apk` is deprecated and does not support `GameActivity`; `xbuild` (0.2.0, 2022) is barely maintained ([Bevy mobile example](https://github.com/bevyengine/bevy/tree/main/examples/mobile), [cargo-ndk](https://github.com/bbqsrc/cargo-ndk)). **`bevy_mod_openxr` 0.6.0 (2026-06-20) targets Bevy 0.19** with wgpu 29, openxr 0.21 and Android dependencies (`android-activity`, `ndk-context`) – newer than the 0.4 / Bevy 0.17 noted in 11A (crates.io, checked 2026-11-14); the starter template [`bevy_xr_app`](https://github.com/kcking/bevy_xr_app) builds for Quest with the Khronos loader. OCW is on Bevy 0.20.1 / wgpu 30, so the Phase 11 X1 choice (port of `bevy_mod_openxr` vs. our own layer) decides the Android path too. wgpu has no OpenXR or multiview-for-XR API of its own; the integrations create the Vulkan device through OpenXR (`XR_KHR_vulkan_enable2`) and wrap it with wgpu-hal.
- **APK and data size:** the store APK may be ≤ 1 GB, plus expansion / asset files of ≤ 4 GB each (≤ 2 GB recommended), uploaded with `ovr-platform-util` and delivered at install or as DLC ([Meta: publish APK](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/resources/publish-apk/), [asset files](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/documentation/unity/ps-assets/)). Our world packages (30–300 MB each, 4.7) are better **downloaded by the app itself** from our servers (Phase 10 Q4) into app-specific storage, verified and cached like on the desktop – no store asset files, no store update for a new world. Storage: Quest 3S from 128 GB, Quest 2 from 64 / 128 GB, shared with every other app.

**Bluetooth on the headset** (crucial for riding standalone):

- Horizon OS and PICO OS are Android, so the **Android BLE central APIs** (`BluetoothLeScanner`, `BluetoothGatt`) are there. **Direct BLE to FTMS trainers works on Quest in practice:** the fitness app HOLOFIT connects FTMS bikes, ellipticals and rowers and BLE cadence sensors directly to standalone Quest 2 / 3 / 3S / Pro, while its cadence sensor does *not* work with PC-tethered headsets ([HOLOFIT FAQ](https://www.holodia.com/?p=5719), [HOLOFIT compatibility](https://www.holodia.com/?p=4379)). Quest also pairs BLE heart rate straps at system level (Polar H10, Garmin HRM-Dual; Jan 2023, [Meta newsroom](https://about.fb.com/news/2023/01/track-fitness-stats-on-quest-heart-rate-monitoring-android-integration)) – that path feeds Meta's own overlay and Health Connect, not third-party apps.
- **Policy:** on the Horizon Store, `BLUETOOTH_SCAN`, `BLUETOOTH_CONNECT` and `BLUETOOTH_ADVERTISE` are "permissions review required": **permitted only for interoperability with a third-party Bluetooth device that can't be otherwise paired through the Meta Quest app Bluetooth interface** ([Meta: permissions review](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/resources/permissions-review-required/), updated 2025-11-26). Trainers and power meters are such devices, so a store app must justify the permissions in its submission; location permissions for scanning were rejected in 2021 ([Meta forum, 2021–22](https://communityforums.atmeta.com/discussions/dev-quest/bluetooth-scan-and-permissions-ble-and-the-companiondevicemanager/871648)). The user must allow "Nearby devices" (Settings → Privacy) for the app.
- **Known problems (forum reports, 2021–2023, unverified on current OS):** scans through `CompanionDeviceManager` failed silently until Horizon OS v37; auto-reconnect after a drop failing on Quest 2; Bluetooth access reset to off by an OS update. So the **reconnect logic and a visible device state** (already in `ble::runner`) matter more than on the desktop; the headset's BLE radio is shared with the controllers, so the link budget to a trainer 1 m away should be fine but is to measure.
- **Pico:** no source found on third-party BLE GATT access from PICO OS apps; it is Android 10/12-based, so the same APIs are expected, but **to verify on a device** before Pico is promised for riding with a trainer.
- **btleplug** has an Android backend (JNI to the Android BLE APIs, with its `droidplug` Java part), so the existing `BtleplugBackend` may work on Android with a JNI bootstrap; otherwise a thin `AndroidBleBackend` implements `GattLink` (3.4) over JNI. Either way the pure `ocw-devices` protocol state machine (`gatt`, `ble::protocol`) is unchanged.

**WebXR in headset browsers:**

- **Meta Quest Browser** (Chromium-based): WebXR `immersive-vr` and `immersive-ar` (passthrough, planes, anchors), hand tracking on by default since 15.1, **WebGPU** since 32.0 (March 2024), experimental foveation for WebGPU in WebXR in 150.1 ([Wikipedia: Meta Quest Browser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Quest_Browser), [Meta: browser 150.1](https://developers.meta.com/vr/downloads/package/browser/150.1)); `camera-access` refused in `immersive-ar` (Horizon OS v85, forum).
- **WebXR + WebGPU binding** (`XRGPUBinding`, WebGPU-backed projection layers): an **Immersive Web Editor's Draft (15 June 2026)**, "under development" ([W3C draft](https://immersive-web.github.io/WebXR-WebGPU-Binding/)); in Chrome behind flags ("WebXR/WebGPU Bindings", "WebXR Projection Layers"), no origin trial found; early-2026 reports that WebGPU-WebXR samples did not run on the Quest Browser ([Meta forum](https://communityforums.atmeta.com/discussions/WebXRDevelopment/webxr-webgpu-bindings-for-dynamic-gaussian-splatting/1255357), [X3D list, Feb 2026](https://web3d.org/pipermail/x3d-ecosystem_web3d.org/2026-February/000799.html)). **Consequence: WebXR today means WebGL2** (`XRWebGLLayer`, `OCULUS_multiview` / `OVR_multiview2`), i.e. the browser app's WebGL2 fallback (Phase 10) becomes the WebXR renderer until the binding ships; WebGPU in WebXR is a later switch.
- **Web Bluetooth in the Quest Browser: not available.** The API answers as if the headset had no Bluetooth (Meta forum, 20 Sep 2024, no answer from Meta; [thread](https://communityforums.atmeta.com/discussions/dev-quest/support-of-web-bluetooth-ble-in-quest-browser/1242380)); a sideloaded plain Chromium has working Web Bluetooth but poor WebXR (no Google services; [PiEEG tutorial](https://www.pieeg.com/tutorials/ble-quest-chromium-pieeg-xr), which also notes BLE is suspended when the window loses focus). No official Meta statement found. **So WebXR riding with a trainer needs the sensor bridge (Phase 10 Q2, 10D.2; **the local bridge is built, v5.76**: the desktop app shares the KICKR with the Quest browser over WebTransport, paired by a code)** – the trainer stays connected to a phone, PC or the native app, and the samples reach the session through the backend.
- **Pico Browser:** WebXR VR works (older reports of entering WebXR failing, 2023); Wolvic (Igalia, open source) runs on Pico 4 with passthrough. No Web Bluetooth found. **Desktop Chrome / Edge with a PC headset:** WebXR via the OpenXR runtime (and Web Bluetooth works there, Phase 10A) – but that case is better served by the native desktop VR mode (Phase 11).
- **WebTransport** in the Quest Browser: expected from its Chromium base (Phase 10A). On the **Quest 1** still not verified (2026-11-24): no source names its last browser version or Chromium base (Meta's browser specs give only example user agents; the release tables do not say which version was the last for the Quest 1) – WebTransport came in Chromium 97 and `serverCertificateHashes` in 100, so a 2023 build (≈ Chromium 110 – 116, W0) should have both. The XR page's pairing panel says "no WebTransport" when it is missing, and the beacon's report has the user agent (W4).

**WebXR on the Quest 1 (14I W0, checked 2026-11-18 from documentation – no headset yet; the open points are logged in the headset in W4):**

| Item | Finding | Source | Sure? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Browser version | The Quest 1 got no new features after OS **v50** (Feb 2023), bug and security fixes until about Aug 2024, no app updates (the browser included) since about May 2025. The **exact last Meta Quest Browser version and its Chromium base were not found**: Browser 31.4 already needs OS v62, so the Quest 1's frozen browser is older – probably a 2023 build (≈ 26 – 29, Chromium ≈ 110 – 116; inferred). Real Quest 1 user agents say `(Linux; Android …; Quest)`; the emulator's Quest 1 profile (`OculusBrowser/33.0`, 72 / 80 / 90 Hz, `immersive-ar`, planes, anchors) is a placeholder, not the device | [Meta help](https://www.meta.com/en-gb/help/quest/172903867975450/), [v50 notes](https://communityforums.atmeta.com/blog/AnnouncementsBlog/meta-quest-build-v50-release-notes/1031710), [UploadVR](https://www.uploadvr.com/quest-1-can-no-longer-get-new-app-updates/), [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta_Quest_Browser) | v50 high, end dates medium, version low |
| Sessions, spaces | `immersive-vr` with `local` and `local-floor` (long supported by the Oculus / Quest Browser); `bounded-floor` with a Guardian boundary; no `immersive-ar` (no colour passthrough). The app asks `local-floor` as optional and falls back to `local` | community reports ([three.js forum](https://discourse.threejs.org/t/none-of-the-vr-ar-webxr-examples-work-in-oculus-quest/26801)); no Quest-1 table from Meta | medium – high |
| WebGL 2, multiview | WebGL 2 yes; **`OCULUS_multiview` out of the box** (with MSAA: `framebufferTextureMultisampleMultiviewOVR`), `OVR_multiview2` behind a chrome://flags flag, both WebGL 2 only. Bevy / wgpu use neither (two eye cameras instead), so multiview is a later optimisation (raw WebGL) | [Meta: multiview](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/documentation/web/web-multiview/) | high (on the frozen build: medium) |
| `XRWebGLLayer` | `fixedFoveation` 0 … 1 (an attribute, the browser maps it to a level; [Meta: FFR](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/documentation/web/webxr-ffr/)); `framebufferScaleFactor` 1.0 = the recommended size, `getNativeFramebufferScaleFactor()` the factor for the panel's pixels ([MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/XRWebGLLayer/getNativeFramebufferScaleFactor)); `antialias`, `depth`, `alpha` default true (spec). W1 asks `antialias: false, depth: false, alpha: false` (the layer only receives a copy; a multisampled layer could not be the copy's target) | Meta, MDN, WebXR spec | high; the Quest 1's native factor (≈ 1.2 = 1440 / 1216, inferred) to log in W4 |
| Frame rate | 72 Hz on the Quest 1 (its panel has no other rate); `supportedFrameRates` / `updateTargetFrameRate` since Browser 16.4 – on the Quest 1 probably `[72]` or absent (not found); a known bug leaves `updateTargetFrameRate`'s promise pending. W1 does not set a rate | [Meta: frames](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/documentation/web/webxr-frames/), [webxr#1449](https://github.com/immersive-web/webxr/issues/1449) | 72 Hz high, the API medium |
| Render size | 1440 × 1600 px per eye panel; **1216 × 1344 per eye at render scale 1.0** (Meta's native-app figure; that the WebXR layer at 1.0 has this size is likely, to log in W4) | [Meta: render scale](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/essentials/render-scale) | high / medium |
| Touch controllers | WebXR gamepads with the `xr-standard` mapping, profile **`oculus-touch-v2`** (fallbacks `oculus-touch`, `generic-trigger-squeeze-thumbstick`): buttons 0 trigger, 1 squeeze, 2 – (none), 3 thumbstick press, 4 X / A, 5 Y / B, 6 thumbrest; axes 0 / 1 – (none), **2 / 3 thumbstick x / y**; the left menu button is reserved by the system. W2's stick mapping reads axes 2 / 3 | [webxr-input-profiles: oculus-touch-v2](https://github.com/immersive-web/webxr-input-profiles/blob/main/packages/registry/profiles/oculus/oculus-touch-v2.json) | high |
| Secure context, gesture | `navigator.xr` exists only in a secure context (HTTPS or localhost); `requestSession('immersive-vr')` needs a user gesture (the *Enter VR* click). The Quest Browser has chrome://flags with `unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure` (an `http://LAN-IP:port` can be listed – a way for Q6's local server without a certificate; on the old Quest 1 build: medium); a self-signed HTTPS certificate reportedly works after the warning is accepted | [WebXR spec](https://immersive-web.github.io/webxr/), [NVIDIA CloudXR setup](https://docs.nvidia.com/cloudxr-sdk/latest/usr_guide/cloudxr_js/client_setup.html) | high / medium |
| The page's frame loop | `window.requestAnimationFrame` may not run while an immersive session is active; on Quest it **stops** ([webxr#225](https://github.com/immersive-web/webxr/issues/225), [three.js forum](https://discourse.threejs.org/t/webxr-loader-spinning-forever-in-quest-w-oculus-browser/16132)) – so the app must be stepped from `XRSession.requestAnimationFrame`, which W1 does | spec + reports | medium – high |
| WebGPU | Browser 32.0 (March 2024) brought WebGPU, 156.0 (Nov 2026) WebGPU in WebXR – both after the Quest 1's last version: **no WebGPU on the Quest 1**, WebXR runs on WebGL 2 | Wikipedia, Meta release notes | high |
| Hardware | Snapdragon 835, Adreno 540 (tiled GPU: MSAA resolves cheaply, full-screen passes and overdraw are expensive) | general | high |

To log in the headset in W4 (the page can print them): `navigator.userAgent`, `XRWebGLLayer.getNativeFramebufferScaleFactor(session)`, the layer's framebuffer size, `session.supportedFrameRates` / `frameRate`, the WebGL extensions (`OCULUS_multiview`), whether `window.requestAnimationFrame` runs during the session.

**Distribution:**

- **Meta Horizon Store:** App Lab was merged into the store in August 2024 (complete 23 Aug 2024); former App Lab titles became regular or "Early Access" listings, still under the Virtual Reality Checks (VRC), content guidelines, data use and app policies ([UploadVR](https://www.uploadvr.com/quest-app-lab-merged-into-meta-horizon-store/), [Road to VR](https://roadtovr.com/meta-elevates-indie-app-lab-main-store/)). Free apps are allowed; Meta keeps 30 % of sales only. A developer account is free; publishing needs an organisation, developer verification and a review. Requirements relevant for us: a **live public privacy policy URL** explaining what is collected, how it is used and how to request deletion (VRC.Quest.Privacy.1–4; [Meta](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/resources/vrc-quest-privacy-1/)), a **Data Use Checkup** only if Platform SDK features are used (we use none: own accounts via OIDC, 9; [Meta](https://developers.meta.com/horizon/resources/publish-data-use/)), the Bluetooth permission justification (above), 72 Hz minimum, store assets (screenshots, trailer, ratings).
- **Sideloading:** developer mode on the headset (free developer account), `adb install` or SideQuest; no review. Suits the build machines, testers and early users.
- **Pico Store:** an agreement and a test before launch; PICO announced self-publishing and paid distribution for individual developers; "Pico Lab" (free apps only, lighter review) existed at the Pico 4 launch ([UploadVR: Pico Lab](https://www.uploadvr.com/pico-lab/), [PICO FAQ](https://sdk.picovr.com/docs/FAQ/chapter_twentyeight.html)); details to re-check in the PICO developer console.
- **Licences:** MIT / Apache-2.0 code is fine for both stores (13); the store terms bind only our listing. The OSM attribution and ODbL offer (13) appear in the app's credits and the store description. The Khronos loader is Apache-2.0. No commercial release is planned (Phase 8 Q2), so the app is **free**, with no in-app purchases (hearts are earned by riding only, Phase 4).

#### 14B – Architecture (proposal)

- **One codebase, a third target:** the same Bevy app and `ocw-render` as the desktop (Phase 11 VR mode) and the browser (Phase 10), built for `aarch64-linux-android` as **`apps/android`** – a thin crate (`cdylib` with the `android_main` entry, the Gradle project with the manifest, the Khronos loader AAR, icons) around the shared app library. The app library is split out of `apps/desktop` so both binaries (and `apps/web`) share it; desktop-only parts (the kiosk, ffmpeg captures, file dialogs, the window manager integration) are cfg-gated as for the web. The standalone app **always runs in VR** (no flat mode on the headset; a 2D panel app on Horizon OS is a possible later variant).
- **XR layer:** the Phase 11 integration chosen in X1 (Q3: both variants compared) gets an Android path: the loader init (`XR_KHR_loader_init_android`), Vulkan through `XR_KHR_vulkan_enable2`, multiview swapchains, `XR_FB_foveation`, `XR_FB_display_refresh_rate`, passthrough. X1's comparison should include a Quest build early, so the winner is not one that cannot run on Android.
- **Engine independence (3.5, 10):** unchanged – Android only touches the app and the render plugin; `ocw-core`, `ocw-sim`, `ocw-protocol`, `ocw-world`, `ocw-sky` stay platform-free (they already build for wasm, so Android is no harder). The **server stays authoritative** (6.1): single player runs the in-process `LocalServer` thread on the headset, as on the desktop.
- **WebXR:** the browser app (Phase 10, `apps/web`) gets an **XR mode** behind the same render plugin: `navigator.xr.requestSession('immersive-vr' | 'immersive-ar')` via `web-sys`, the WebGL2 path with `XRWebGLLayer` and multiview first, `XRGPUBinding` when it ships. Bevy has no WebXR backend; this is our own thin layer (to check whether `bevy_mod_xr`'s planned WebXR support has landed by then). The XR-specific logic (head pose composition, VR HUD layout, comfort) is the pure code of Phase 11, shared by OpenXR and WebXR.
- **World data on the device:** the app downloads world packages over HTTPS from our servers (Phase 10 Q4), verifies them (signatures, chunk hashes, 4.7) and keeps them in app storage (`Context.getExternalFilesDir` / `filesDir`), with a storage page in World (size per world, delete, "keep for offline"). Tile streaming from the file (3.5, 4.5) keeps memory bounded. **Mobile world builds:** the world builder can emit a **mobile LOD set** per package (coarser far meshes, fewer trees and house details, compressed textures in ASTC / ETC2 instead of BC) as an optional package section or a sibling package – only added sections, older readers skip them (4.7).
- **Multiplayer:** native **QUIC** (quinn, rustls with *ring*) runs on Android unchanged (6.2); WebXR uses the **WebTransport** endpoint of Phase 10 (B3). Same sessions as desktop and browser riders.
- **Voice:** LiveKit has an Android SDK and the Rust SDK builds for Android (`ocw-voice` with `livekit`, 7); the headset microphone and spatial audio from the head pose (Phase 11 X5). WebXR: `livekit-client` (JS) as in the browser app.
- **Devices:** a BLE backend for Android behind `DeviceBackend` (3.4) – btleplug's Android backend if it works with our runtime, else an `AndroidBleBackend` (`GattLink` over JNI) – with the existing pure protocol (FTMS, Cycling Power, CSC, Heart Rate, Wahoo control), ERG / SIM and wind (Phase 9 Q5). Runtime permissions (`BLUETOOTH_SCAN` with `neverForLocation`, `BLUETOOTH_CONNECT`), a device page usable in VR, and a robust reconnect (14A). **Fallback:** the **sensor bridge** (Phase 10 Q2) – the trainer is connected to the desktop app, the browser app on a phone or a future phone app, and the samples reach the headset's session through the backend. ANT+ stays deferred.
- **Accounts and settings:** OIDC sign-in (9) through a device-code flow or a code shown in VR and confirmed on the phone / web companion (no typing passwords in VR); settings sync as for the browser app. Anonymous riding follows Phase 10 Q5 (plain bike, no customisation) if the user wants that for standalone too.
- **Captures (art project):** screenshots and videos from the left eye or a spectator view rendered at a lower rate, with the ISO timestamp burnt in (art project 2.1); `adb` pulls them into `test-output/` on the build machines. Meta's system casting / recording also works for demos.

#### 14C – Rendering and performance budget (proposal)

- **Targets:** **72 Hz minimum on Quest 2 / Pico 4** with the *Standalone low* preset, **90 Hz on Quest 3 / 3S / Pico 4 Ultra** with *Standalone*, 120 Hz optional; never under budget for more than a frame (reprojection – Meta's Application SpaceWarp – as a safety net, not the plan). Per-frame budgets from Meta's guidance: ≤ 100 draw calls and ≤ 750k triangles on Quest 2, ≤ 200 / ≤ 1.5M on Quest 3 (14A); the tile and tree merging of 3.1.1 / 4.5 already works this way.
- **A standalone quality tier** (new presets beside *VR* of Phase 11): view distance 2–4 km near terrain and 20–40 km far terrain (instead of 120 km), trees as merged clusters and impostor cards beyond 150 m, houses as the mid / far LOD early (Phase 8 T4 levels), no real-time shadows on Quest 2 (one cascade on Quest 3), **baked lighting where sensible** (ambient occlusion and sky light baked into terrain and building vertex colours by the world builder's mobile LOD set; the sun direction from the world clock still lights them in a cheap forward pass), the sky and atmosphere (Phase 9) as a precomputed lookup, weather particles reduced, MSAA 4× (tile-based GPUs resolve it nearly free), no post-processing beyond tone mapping, ASTC textures.
- **Multiview** single-pass stereo and **fixed foveated rendering** (high level on Quest 2) from the start; dynamic resolution as a second lever; GPU-driven culling where it helps the CPU (draw calls are the Quest 2 bottleneck).
- **CPU:** the 50 Hz physics of the local server is cheap; the world streaming and mesh building run on worker threads with a lower priority so the render thread keeps its core; no shader compilation during a ride (pipelines warmed at load).
- **Thermals and battery:** measure a 60 min ride (OVR Metrics Tool: CPU / GPU level, temperature, battery); the target is a full 60 min ride on battery on Quest 3 with *Standalone*, and an "endurance" preset that drops to 72 Hz and lowers the resolution when the runtime reports throttling. A headset fan accessory or a charge cable is advised for longer rides (documentation, not code).
- **Memory:** ≤ 3 GB on Quest 2 (6 GB shared with the OS), ≤ 4 GB on Quest 3 / Pico.
- **App size:** APK ≤ 200 MB (the app, shaders, sounds, default bikes and characters); no world inside – the first start offers the test route (in the APK, a few MB) and downloads a world.

#### 14D – Devices and input (proposal)

- **Sensors** as in 14B: direct BLE on the headset (trainer, power meter, cadence, heart rate) as the main way, the sensor bridge as the fallback, virtual power for spectators and tests.
- **Controllers for menus:** the controller ray is a pointer of the input model (3.2.2) on the world-space panels (Phase 11 X3); the thumbsticks and buttons map to the gamepad actions (steering keys, U-turn, junction choice, menu), so riding needs no new bindings – steering stays on keys / gamepad / autodrive (Phase 11 Q4: no head-lean). A controller can rest in a handlebar mount; a BLE gamepad or handlebar remote works as on the desktop.
- **Hand tracking** for menus (pinch to select, `XR_EXT_hand_tracking`; WebXR hand input), useful because hands are on the bars and controllers get put down; never needed to ride.
- **Passthrough / mixed reality** (comfort and safety option): Quest 3 / 3S colour passthrough and Pico 4 / 4 Ultra passthrough through OpenXR (`XR_FB_passthrough` on Quest; the Pico equivalent to check) and WebXR `immersive-ar`. Modes: *off* (full VR), a **passthrough window around the handlebar and the floor** (see the trainer, the bottle, the towel and the real hands), **full passthrough while the menu is open or when stopped**, and a "look down to see the room" fade. On Quest 2 the grey passthrough is only a safety view. A guardian / boundary for a stationary seated user (Meta's stationary boundary) is enough; the app declares a seated, stationary experience.
- **Comfort** (the Phase 11 rules, which suit standalone riding): fixed horizon (no camera roll), no artificial rotation of the view outside the road's own turns, the comfort vignette on sharp turns and descents, fades on teleports / ride switches / U-turns, a visible cockpit; **seated** riding with a height calibration; recentre on a button.
- **Text input:** the system keyboard of Horizon OS / PICO OS for names and the console; the console's Dev commands stay limited to the local server as everywhere.

#### 14E – Distribution (proposal)

- **Stages:** (1) **sideloaded APKs** for our own tests and testers (developer mode, `adb`, a download page on our servers, release notes); (2) the **Meta Horizon Store** as a free app, first as an Early Access listing; (3) the **Pico Store** once Pico riding is verified (14A).
- **What the stores need from us:** an organisation and verified developer account, a privacy policy on our own website (what the server stores: account, rides, chat / voice routing, no sale of data; how to delete; 12), the Bluetooth permission justification, the content rating questionnaire, store art and a trailer (from the art project's videos), the OSM / data credits (13).
- **Updates:** store updates for the app; worlds come from our servers (14B), so new worlds need no store review.
- **WebXR** needs no store: the browser app's URL (Phase 10) works in the Quest and Pico browsers; a Horizon Store listing of the web app (a PWA wrapper) is possible later.

#### 14F – Tests (spec 11.4, proposal)

- **Unit tests (no headset):** the Android BLE `GattLink` against the protocol mocks (as for Web Bluetooth); reconnect and permission-denied state handling; the standalone preset selection per device (from the OpenXR system name and the GPU); the world storage manager (download, verify, quota, eviction, resume); the mobile LOD set writer and reader in the world builder (byte-identical rebuilds, old readers skip it); the passthrough mode state machine; the device-code sign-in flow; the WebXR session state machine (pure, wasm-tested).
- **Build checks:** `cargo ndk -t arm64-v8a build` for the app in CI (on marge; Linux only), the APK assembled by Gradle, `cargo check` for `aarch64-linux-android` of every crate the app uses; the wasm check (3.5) stays green.
- **Integration:** the OpenXR frame loop against Monado's simulated device (Phase 11 X1, native), the Android build on an emulator for start-up only (no XR); on a real headset over `adb` (when one is connected to a build machine): start, enter a world, a 60 s ride with the virtual trainer, a screenshot and the OVR Metrics frame-time log into `test-output/`.
- **Hardware in the loop:** the headset connected to the Wahoo KICKR next to marge (3.4) – scan, connect, ERG / SIM, reconnect after a trainer power cycle.
- **WebXR:** headless Chromium with the WebXR emulation (Immersive Web Emulator / `navigator.xr` mock) for session start and a frame; the Quest Browser by hand.
- **Performance gates:** frame time on Quest 2 and Quest 3 per release on the standard scenes (`scripts/scenes.toml`), with the 72 / 90 Hz budgets as pass / fail.

#### 14G – Milestones (proposal)

- **V1 – Android build:** the shared app library split out of `apps/desktop`; `apps/android` builds with `cargo-ndk` + Gradle; a flat Bevy scene starts on a Quest (sideloaded). CI builds the APK.
- **V2 – OpenXR on Quest:** the X1 integration (Phase 11) on Android with the Khronos loader: stereo test route with head tracking, multiview, foveation, refresh rate; frame time measured on Quest 2 / 3.
- **V3 – Standalone tier:** presets, the mobile LOD set from the world builder, ASTC textures, baked lighting, world download and storage on the device; Liechtenstein at 72 Hz on Quest 2 and 90 Hz on Quest 3.
- **V4 – Sensors on the headset:** the Android BLE backend with FTMS, Cycling Power, CSC, Heart Rate and Wahoo control, ERG / SIM, permissions, reconnect; hardware-in-the-loop with the KICKR; the sensor bridge as the fallback.
- **V5 – Riding parity:** VR HUD, menus with controllers and hands, comfort, passthrough modes, multiplayer over QUIC, voice (LiveKit), sign-in, captures.
- **V6 – Pico:** the same APK on Pico 4 / 4 Ultra with vendor extensions probed; BLE verified; Pico Store submission.
- **V7 – Store release:** privacy policy, permission justification, store assets; Meta Horizon Store Early Access, then a full listing.
- **V8 – WebXR:** the browser app's XR mode (WebGL2 + multiview first), controllers and hands, passthrough via `immersive-ar`, the sensor bridge for trainers; WebGPU via `XRGPUBinding` when browsers ship it.
- **V9 – Thermals and endurance:** the 60 min ride measurements, the endurance preset, battery and fan guidance.

#### 14H – Open questions (for the user)

- **Q1 – First headset: decided by the user (2026-11-14, v3.29): the Oculus Quest (first generation)** – the user's headset; focus on it, the other models are postponed. (The proposal was Quest 3 / 3S.) Consequences: the standalone quality tier targets the Snapdragon 835 at 72 Hz; distribution is sideloading (see Q3).
- **Q2 – Native or WebXR first: decided (2026-11-15, dashboard: "WebXR first … Native OpenXR later"):** **WebXR first** – the browser app (Phase 10) in the headset's browser: no store, no sideloading, the same build; it runs on **WebGL 2** (WebGPU in WebXR is not shipped yet) with the low preset and B7's workarounds, and trainers connect only **through the sensor bridge** (Phase 10, 10D.2; the headset browser has no Web Bluetooth). The **native Android OpenXR** app follows later. Was proposed: native first.
- **Q3 – Distribution: decided by the user (2026-11-14, v3.31): sideloading only for now** – the standalone app is installed by sideloading (developer mode, `adb install`); no store listing (Meta Horizon or Pico) for now. (The Horizon Store takes no new Quest 1 apps anyway.) *Earlier proposal:* sideloading for testers first, then a free Horizon Store listing.
- **Q4 – BLE fallback: postponed (2026-11-14, dashboard: "postpone")** – decided when standalone VR (Phase 14) starts; until then the question stays as written: if direct BLE on a headset turns out limited (Pico unverified; Quest reconnects reported flaky), is the **sensor bridge** through a PC or phone acceptable as the official way – and should that include a small **phone relay app** (Android first; iOS would be the first native iOS code, 1.3), or only the desktop and the browser app as bridges (Phase 10 Q2)?
- **Q5 – Priority: decided (2026-11-18, the user): start now with V8 WebXR basic, measure on the Quest 1, then decide** – the user: "start with V8 WebXR basic (about 1–2 days). After the first headset run, measure the frame rate on the Quest 1. Then decide whether V3 makes it smooth enough, or whether the native route is worth it." The plan is 14I. (Was: after Phase 11 X1 – X2, or after the browser app.)



#### 14I – Plan: WebXR first, measure, then decide (2026-11-18, Q5)

Decided by the user (Q5): build **V8 WebXR basic** first, measure the frame rate on the Quest 1 after the first headset run, and then decide between making WebXR smooth with **V3** (the standalone quality tier) or going **native** (V1 – V2). Steps:

- **W0 – Check the platform (a few hours, no headset; built v5.77):** the Quest 1's browser (Meta Quest Browser, frozen since Meta stopped updating the Quest 1) – its WebXR support for `immersive-vr`, WebGL 2, `OCULUS_multiview` / `OVR_multiview2`, `XRWebGLLayer` `fixedFoveation` and `framebufferScaleFactor`, the 72 Hz frame rate, the Touch controllers as WebXR gamepads – from Meta's and Immersive Web's documentation; written into 14A.
- **W1 – The XR session in the browser app (spike first; built v5.77 – the spike of 2026-11-18 merged onto main, see the result below):** an **Enter VR** button (WebXR needs a user gesture and a secure context: HTTPS or localhost), `navigator.xr.requestSession('immersive-vr', { requiredFeatures: ['local-floor'] })`, an `XRWebGLLayer` on the app's WebGL 2 context (made `xrCompatible`). The risky part, proved by a spike before anything else: Bevy's web loop runs on the window's `requestAnimationFrame`, but WebXR frames come from the session's own `requestAnimationFrame` with the eye poses – the app has to step Bevy from the XR frame callback and render each eye (or both with multiview) into the session's framebuffer. If wgpu's WebGL 2 backend cannot draw into that framebuffer directly, the eyes render to textures and a small blit copies them in. The spike shows one stereo frame with head tracking in the **Immersive Web Emulator** (headless Chromium) before W2 starts.
  - **W1 result (2026-11-18): the approach works – proved in the emulator, not yet in a headset.** Built behind the feature **`webxr`** of `ocw-web` as a third module (`ocw_web_webxr.js`: features `webgl2,webxr`; `make web-xr`, the page's `?xr=1`); the WebGPU and WebGL 2 builds are unchanged. How:
    - **Stepping Bevy from the XR frames** (the risky part): Bevy's winit loop runs its update inside the window's `requestAnimationFrame` callback (winit's `RedrawRequested` → `about_to_wait` → `app.update()`, synchronously). The page's shim `apps/web/web/ocw-xr.js` wraps `window.requestAnimationFrame` from the start; when the session starts, the callback winit waits for is taken over, and while the session runs every window frame callback is kept and **run inside the session's `requestAnimationFrame`**, after the frame's viewer and eye poses, viewports and projections were handed to the app (`window.ocw.xrFrame(Float32Array)`, layout in `apps/web/src/xr.rs`). So one XR frame = one Bevy update and render with that frame's poses; on session end the waiting callbacks go back to the window. (On the Quest the window's frames stop during the session, 14A – this does not depend on them.)
    - **The eyes:** two `Camera3d` eye cameras (`apps/web/src/webxr.rs`) with a custom projection (WebXR's OpenGL matrix → its frustum tangents → Bevy's infinite reverse-Z matrix, `xr::eye_clip_from_view`, unit-tested against Bevy's own perspective) and the eye poses composed onto the rider (the reference space's floor on the road under the local rider's eyes, turned only by the bike's heading: no pitch or roll from the road); each eye draws into its part of the canvas (Bevy viewports from the layer's viewports, the second eye `ClearColorConfig::None`, split-screen style); the chase camera rests during the session; fog, exposure, MSAA, far plane and atmosphere are copied from it each frame.
    - **Into the headset's framebuffer:** wgpu's WebGL 2 backend cannot draw into the layer's opaque `XRWebGLLayer.framebuffer` (it only knows its own textures and the canvas). It does not need to: after the update wgpu's surface present has left both eyes in the canvas's default framebuffer, and the shim **copies the whole canvas onto the whole layer framebuffer with one `blitFramebuffer`** on the same WebGL 2 context (the context is created `xrCompatible` by wrapping `getContext`; the layer is `antialias: false, depth: false` – a blit cannot target a multisampled framebuffer; scissor off during the copy). Since each eye's canvas part is its viewport's fraction, one scaled copy puts each eye in place. No texture handles from wgpu are needed.
    - **Session states** (pure, `xr::XrState`): unknown → offered (isSessionSupported) / unsupported → entering (the click) → running ⇄ visible-blurred / hidden → ended (→ offered again); a refused session goes back to offered. *Enter VR* is shown only when `isSessionSupported('immersive-vr')` says yes; otherwise a note says why (not a secure context, no WebXR, no headset). `local-floor` is optional with a fallback to `local` (the origin then at a seated eye height, 1.5 m). The session's facts W4 needs (user agent, native scale factor, framebuffer size, frame rates, multiview extensions) are logged when it starts (`ocw-xr: device …`).
    - **Proof – `make test-web-xr`** (`scripts/test-web-xr.py`, headless Chromium on marge, WebGL 2 on the AMD GPU): the emulator is the **Immersive Web Emulation Runtime** (`iwer` 2.7.0, MIT, Meta – the runtime of the Immersive Web Emulator extension 2.x) **injected into the page** with its Oculus Quest 1 profile in stereo (`scripts/fetch-iwer.sh`, pinned and hash-checked). The extension itself was not used: its controls are a DevTools panel, which headless Chromium has not; the runtime is driven from the test (the headset's position, orientation, visibility). Its device frames run on the display's clock (the emulator's own `requestAnimationFrame` calls are pointed at the real one, as a headset compositor never runs on the page's clock). The emulator's layer has no framebuffer of its own (the canvas is the layer), so the test also copies into a framebuffer of ours (`?xrcopy=fbo`) and reads it back – the copy path a headset takes. Checked: Enter VR by a click, two eyes side by side 63 mm apart, the eyes following a 40° head turn and a 25° tilt (the picture changing), visible-blurred and back, exit to the flat view with the window's frames running again, the note without a headset; screenshots of both eyes, the emulated view, the copied framebuffer and a head-sweep video in `test-output/web-xr/`.
    - **Frame time in the emulator (a sanity number only):** marge (AMD GPU, headless Chromium, WebGL 2 through ANGLE on Vulkan, the Low preset, a 1280 × 720 canvas: two eyes of 640 × 720, the copy into the test framebuffer every frame) – the emulator's frames came at the display's **60 Hz** (gap p50 16.7 ms, p95 17.0 ms; iwer's Quest 1 profile reports 72 Hz but runs on the display's clock), and **the page's work per XR frame** (the app's update, both eyes, the copy) was **p50 9.7 ms, p95 11.0 ms** over ~1 270 frames (2026-11-18; a few late frames from the test's screenshots). The Quest 1's number comes from W4.
    - **Merged onto main (v5.77):** the spike's branch had stayed apart while main moved on (the memory work of B7, the explicit Bevy feature list of v5.66, the sensor bridge of v5.76); merged, the WebXR module builds with that feature list unchanged (`make test-web-build` builds all three modules), the pairing of the bridge and the reference space of Q8 were added, and `make test-web-xr` ran again on marge (results in the W1 checks below).
    - **The reference space (Q8 (a), built v5.77):** the session asks `local-floor` (optional) and the app takes what it got (`xr::Space`). The rig (`xr::space_origin`, `webxr.rs`): the **space's floor is the road under the bike**, so the real floor is the game floor and the headset's height above it is the rider's real eye height – right for every rider, and higher when standing on the pedals, with no number to set. Across the ground, the head where the session started (the **anchor**, taken from the first frame) is put on the **rider's seated eye point** – `ocw_assets::pose::eye_point`: the rider posed on the bike whose saddle `BodyFit` set for the profile's body height (spec 4C), the eyes at `EYES` in the head – and its heading onto the bike's (`AvatarRig::eye_point`, `saddle_height`). So a rider whose real saddle is as high as the profile's sees the bars and the road where they are. **Fallback `local`** (no floor known): the anchor's height goes to the seated eye point instead. **Recentre:** the controller's squeeze, or the headset's own recentring (the reference space's `reset` event), takes a new anchor. Without a rider (unicorn flight) the chase camera is the eye point, the floor `SEATED_EYE_M` (1.45 m) below. `window.ocw.xr()` reports `space`, `saddle_m`, `eye_seated_m`, `eye_standing_m`, `head_m` (the real eye height), `eye_above_road_m`, `eye_from_point_m`. Tests: `local_floor_puts_the_real_floor_on_the_road`, `local_falls_back_to_the_seated_eye_point` (pure), `the_eye_point_follows_the_saddle_height` (every bike, three body heights: the eyes above the saddle, higher for a taller rider, higher again standing; 1.1 – 1.65 m for the 1.78 m rider, the time-trial bike lowest), and in the emulator the eyes 1.45 m above the road with the head 1.45 m above the floor, 1.70 m out of the saddle, at the eye point across the ground.

The workflow `web-preview.yml` builds it after the normal preview (`continue-on-error`: a failed XR build deploys the normal preview without `/xr/`; timeout 240 min for the third fat-LTO module). The normal preview is unchanged byte for byte (a test compares the site with and without `xr/`). **Pages limits:** a site ≤ 1 GB (the assembly's `--max-mb` check counts `xr/`), soft 100 GB / month of traffic and 10 deployments an hour; `xr/` adds one module (about the WebGL 2 one's size) and shares the worlds, so it fits. The headset opens **https://newkit.github.io/OCW/xr/** (HTTPS: WebXR's secure context).
    - **The sensor bridge in VR (Q7 (b), built v5.77):** the XR page shows a **pairing panel above *Enter VR*** (only where VR is offered): the code the desktop shows (Settings → Trainer → Devices → Share with a browser) typed with the headset's keyboard, *Pair* → `bridge.pair CODE`; its line shows the bridge's state and the power that drives the ride (or "no WebTransport" in a browser without it). A link with `?bridge=CODE` (or a code used on this origin before – the code is kept in `localStorage`, per origin, so pairing on the normal preview carries over to `/xr/`) connects by itself, and the start page keeps `bridge=` on its ride links. In the headset the bridge is the ride's trainer as on the flat page (its readings are device events, the ride's SIM / ERG control goes back); it runs on the page's timers, which go on during the session (only the window's frames stop). The Quest 1 has no camera for a QR code in the browser: the code is typed.
    - **The beacon (W3's, built v5.77 over the bridge):** GitHub Pages cannot receive anything, so the headset's numbers go **to the desktop over the sensor bridge**: the bridge protocol's new `report` message (browser → desktop, `{kind, data}`, ≤ 16 KB; `ToHost::Report` → `HostEvent::Report`), sent by the page every 10 s during the session and once at its end (`ocwXr.report`, `window.ocw.xrReport`): `window.ocw.xr()` (fps, gap and work p50 / p95, longest gap, late frames, framebuffer, eye poses, the reference space and the heights), the page's state (user agent, native scale factor, framebuffer size, frame rates, multiview extensions, foveation, copy path), the bridge's round trip and readings, power and distance. The desktop appends each as a JSON line to **`<data dir>/ocw/reports/xr.jsonl`** (Linux `~/.local/share/ocw/reports/xr.jsonl`) and prints `bridge: xr report – N fps, work p50 M ms → path` in its console. No pictures yet (`vr.shot` over the bridge is W3's remaining part).
    - **Known limits of the spike (for W2 / W3):** the own body is drawn (the own head – its node with the helmet and the face – is hidden during the session since v5.77, after the emulator showed the helmet straps and the lips from inside); the flat HUD lands in one eye (Bevy UI's default camera is the highest-order eye) and the egui console moves with it; the head sways with the avatar's pedalling animation (the head node is the rig's anchor); shadows are computed per eye (two cascade sets); no multiview; the layer's scale and foveation are page options only (`xrscale=`, `xrfoveation=`); no controllers yet.

Into `ocw-render` came the branch's **`vr::computer`** (the bike computer) and **`vr::controllers`** (the controllers as a Bevy gamepad), their branch-only `VrState` / `VrConfig` replaced by one resource, `ocw_render::vr::VrSession` (the headset shows the ride, the controls hint, the status row, the controllers, the recentre gesture), and its layer 7 (the workshop's on main) by `VR_LAYER` 12; into `ocw-assets` the unit's generator (`computer.rs`, its three paint slots), the model file `parts/computer/computer-head-unit-wedge.glb` and `BikeRig::bar_clamp` (the stem's clamp, where the mount sits). Its screen (a Bevy UI drawn into a 600 × 870 texture, its camera on only while the headset shows the ride) shows the clock, the gradient's LEDs, **power**, **speed**, **cadence**, heart rate, **grade**, **distance**, the ride's time, the next turn with its distance (free ride) or the route's progress, the profile ahead, the messages; in the top row beside the clock **the sensor bridge's state** instead of the weather (which is all around in VR: `Bridge off / wait / ok / err`, `No bridge` without WebTransport), and a status row with **the frame time** (W3: the page's work per frame, median, and the frame rate, e.g. `11.8 ms · 72 fps`, twice a second; the first emulator run showed both in one row wrapping into the next line at the 48 px font, so they were split). The controls are on it for 5 s when the headset starts showing the ride.

While the **in-game menu is open** the camera draws and the picture is a **panel in the world**, 1.2 m wide, 1.1 m ahead of the rider's eye point and 0.12 m below it, turned with the bike (`xr::menu_panel_pose`); closed, the camera rests (no cost). The egui console still goes to the highest eye camera (it is closed unless a keyboard opens it).

The map (Q10's, with two WebXR changes): **right stick** – forward faster, back stop, left / right steer (virtual mode); **left stick sideways flicks – the junction exits** (the D-pad's left / right = Delete / Page Down; `exits_on_left_stick`), its up / down the free stick; **left stick press – the menu** (the Quest's left menu button belongs to the system in WebXR and is no gamepad button), inside the menu it confirms (kept for the whole press, so the press that opens the menu does not also confirm); A confirm / autodrive, **B back** (closes the menu) / U-turn, X wild mode, Y back to the route, the triggers stop / faster, the grips the menu's tabs; **recentre**: a squeeze (the session's `squeeze` event, not while the menu is open) or both grips held 0.6 s. The controllers are drawn at their grips (a handle and a tracking ring on `VR_LAYER`).
    - **W3 – the `quest1` level:** `ocw_render::quality::QualityLevel::Quest1` (named, not on the flat screen's ladder; `display.quality` / `quality quest1` can pin it): Low's single cascade at 1024² over 40 m, no MSAA, the view 4 km (Low 8 km) with the trees to 800 m, the houses' details at 0.4, 12 % of the particles, less road damage and ground detail, and **at most 8 other riders drawn** (the nearest along the road: `QualityPreset::max_riders`, `riders::riders_drawn`). **Chosen automatically**: in a session whose user agent is a Quest 1, `auto` resolves to it (`ocw_client::quality::resolve_xr`, "auto: Quest 1 in VR"); after the session the flat view's level again; a level chosen by name wins. **Render scale and fixed foveation:** before it creates the layer the page asks `window.ocw.xrLayer(userAgent)` – `quest1`: `framebufferScaleFactor` **0.8** (`ocw_xr::headset::QUEST_1.render_scale_standalone`: ≈ 973 × 1075 per eye of the recommended 1216 × 1344) and `fixedFoveation` **1.0** where the layer has it; `?xrscale=` / `?xrfoveation=` still win. Because the eyes draw into the canvas, **the canvas takes the layer framebuffer's pixels during the session** (`XrCanvasScale`: the window's scale factor so that its drawing buffer is the framebuffer's size – the render scale is then the eyes', and the copy 1 : 1); in the emulator the canvas is the layer, so nothing changes there. Fixed foveation only lowers the layer's (the copy's and the compositor's) cost, not the app's rendering into the canvas.

- **Decision (D, with the numbers, by the user):** target 72 fps (13.9 ms).
  - **≥ 65 fps** with the `quest1` level: stay on WebXR and polish (comfort, menus, the sensor bridge).
  - **36 – 65 fps:** V3 (mobile level-of-detail set from the world builder, compressed textures, baked light, fewer draw calls), then measure again.
  - **< 36 fps even on the plain test route:** the browser's overhead is too large on a Snapdragon 835 – compare with the native route (V1 – V2: an Android OpenXR build, sideloaded) by a small native spike before deciding.
